q: Walk me through your career from 2021 to now — CWS → ESparks → Cynsure Design → ChirpTech. What changed at each step?
a:
At CWS I started as a Laravel Developer, learning core Laravel, APIs, and pairing Laravel backends with React/Bootstrap frontends — this is where I built my base in MVC, Eloquent (Laravel's database tool), and REST API design. At ESparks I became a Software Engineer and moved into e-commerce — Magento 2 and WordPress — which taught me to work inside bigger, more restrictive systems built by someone else, instead of writing code from a blank slate.

At Cynsure Design I became Senior Backend Developer, working more with Livewire and API-heavy systems, and started making architecture decisions instead of just doing assigned tasks. Now at ChirpTech as Senior Laravel Developer, I've moved into IoT (internet-connected devices) and real-time systems (HOLOIN) and AI (AI-BDM), which pushed me past standard Laravel work into systems using multiple languages — Python services, MQTT (a messaging protocol for devices), Redis, Docker.

Each move added more complexity and more ownership, not just a new employer name.

q: What's the most complex project you've worked on, and why is it your strongest?
a:
HOLOIN. It's a multi-tenant IoT SaaS platform (serves many customers, collects live data from many devices) that takes in real-time data from potentially thousands of devices over MQTT, stores high-volume sensor data in MongoDB alongside regular customer/billing data in MySQL/PostgreSQL, pushes live updates to dashboards using WebSockets, and adds an AI/natural-language layer in Python on top.

It's complex not because any single piece is exotic, but because I had to get the boundaries right between five or six moving parts — data intake, storage, real-time delivery, billing, and AI — while keeping it fast under heavy write traffic. That's a very different kind of problem than a typical Laravel app that just does create/read/update/delete.

a: I'm a backend/full-stack engineer who specializes in Laravel-based systems, especially strong in API/integration work and, most recently, real-time and AI-powered architecture — the e-commerce work (Magento/Shopify/WooCommerce) is real, valuable experience, but the harder layer on top of Laravel (IoT, AI, integrations) is where I'm growing and want to keep specializing.

I believe I'm ready for a Senior Backend Engineer / Full-Stack Engineer title (or a Team Lead track), because my recent project work goes beyond 'Laravel developer' — I'm making architecture decisions across multiple databases, designing how Laravel and Python talk to each other, and taking ownership of infrastructure (Docker, deployment), not just writing application code.

q: Tell me about a time you had to learn an entirely new technology under deadline pressure (like MQTT or the Python/AI integration).
a:
When HOLOIN needed real-time device data, I hadn't used MQTT (a lightweight messaging system for devices) in production before. I spent focused time learning its publish/subscribe model and message-delivery levels, built a small test connection before wiring it into the real system, and used Laravel's existing background-job system to safely handle and buffer incoming messages instead of trying to process everything live and all at once.

Lesson learned: test the unfamiliar piece on its own first, then connect it — don't learn a new system and build it into a live product in the same step.

q: How do you handle working with old code you didn't write (like Rentigo or the University Seekers migration)?
a:
First I map out the system before touching anything — how data flows, which models matter, and where the real business logic actually lives (often scattered across controllers, models, and views in older code). Then I add test coverage, or at least a manual checklist, around the part I'm about to change, since old code rarely has reliable automated tests.

I make small, easy-to-undo changes and release them gradually instead of one giant rewrite — the Laravel 5-to-8 migration on University Seekers, for example, was done step by step, not as a single cutover, specifically so multilingual and SEO-important pages could be checked one by one.

q: Draw the system architecture from a device to the dashboard, including every service involved.
a:
Device → MQTT broker → queue (buffers incoming data) → worker checks/writes to MongoDB (batched) → event fired for warning/alert conditions → live update sent over WebSocket → React dashboard updates live. In parallel: customer/user/billing data lives in MySQL/PostgreSQL, Redis powers caching + queues + Horizon, and a Python/FastAPI service provides plain-English analytics over the summarized data, called by Laravel when a user asks an analytics question.

Nginx + PHP-FPM run the Laravel app in front; the whole stack runs through Docker Compose.

q: How does multi-tenancy work — shared database with a tenant_id, one database per customer, or a separate schema per customer? Why, and what would you change?
a:
Fill inState your real model here. A shared database with a tenant_id column (the most common pattern for a mid-size multi-tenant SaaS) is usually the practical choice — it avoids the extra work of setting up a new database per customer, and Laravel's global scopes make it easy to automatically enforce customer separation at the query level.

The trade-off is a bigger risk if a query ever leaks across customers (a missing scope is a real risk), and one very heavy customer can slow things down for others sharing the same database. If starting over with hindsight, I'd only consider a separate database per customer for a specific large customer that needed dedicated performance/compliance guarantees, not as the default for everyone.

q: How does Stripe/Cashier subscription billing connect to customer setup — what happens when a subscription lapses?
a: A new customer signup creates the customer record and a Stripe subscription through Cashier (Laravel's billing package); webhook events from Stripe drive the customer's access state — a failed payment doesn't instantly cut access (I'd set up a grace period, matching Stripe's own retry behavior), but a subscription reaching a final failed/cancelled state switches the customer to a restricted mode (read-only or fully locked, depending on plan) through a check on customer status, rather than deleting any data.

q: What was the single hardest performance problem you solved on this project?
a: The dashboard summarizing bottleneck described earlier — calculating raw per-second device data live on dashboard load became unworkable as data piled up. Fixing it meant rethinking the whole way data gets read (pre-summarized rollups, targeted indexes, and only touching raw data for a short recent window), not just trying to speed up the original query further — sometimes the fix isn't a better query, it's a different way of reading the data.

q: Explain the full request path for a plain-English business question, from user input to the final answer.
a: User submits a question through the Laravel-backed screen → Laravel forwards it (in the background) to the Python/FastAPI AI service → the service figures out intent, finds the relevant records (searching against the business data), builds a grounded prompt for the AI model, and returns a structured result → Laravel receives the result via callback or checking, saves/caches it, and pushes it to the screen alongside the actual source records so the user can verify the answer.

q: How do you check whether the AI's answers are actually correct/useful, with no simple test for 'is this a good lead'?
a: I rely on grounding (always showing the actual retrieved source records next to the AI's summary, so correctness is easy to check at a glance) and periodically testing real questions against known-correct answers to catch drift or regressions after any change to the search/prompt logic. For genuinely subjective quality ('is this a good lead'), I'd track what happens after — did the user act on the recommendation — as a stand-in measure over time, instead of trying to score answer quality automatically upfront.

q: What was the worst part of the existing codebase, and how did you improve it without breaking production?
a: Fill inyour real specific pain point — commonly: inconsistent data from years of manual fixes, no test coverage, or business logic copy-pasted across controllers. q: How does document upload + digital signing work securely, and what happens if a signing session is interrupted?
a: Documents are stored in secure, access-controlled storage (not public), and the signing process tracks its state explicitly (draft → sent → in-progress → completed) so an interrupted session simply picks up from its last confirmed step instead of losing progress — no signature counts as final until the entire signing process (all required people, all fields) is recorded and the document is locked, so a partial or tampered signature is never treated as valid.

q: How did Redis/queues get used here specifically, versus in HOLOIN?
a: In Rentigo, queues are used more for document processing (generating signed PDF copies, sending emails when documents are signed) than for high-frequency data intake — a much lower-volume, more one-off use of the same infrastructure pattern HOLOIN uses for device data, which shows that queues/Redis are a general-purpose tool applied differently depending on the actual kind of work.

q: Walk through your migration strategy — one big cutover, or step by step?
a: Step by step, version by version (5→6→7→8), following the official upgrade guide at each step and running/expanding test coverage after each step, instead of trying to jump straight from 5 to 8. For the multilingual, SEO-sensitive pages, I did manual checks on a staging site for each language after each major step, since automated coverage for rendered SEO details was thin to begin with.

q: What specific Laravel 5→8 breaking changes tripped you up, and how did you find them?
a: Fill inyour real specific examples — commonly: changes to default model folder structure, login scaffolding changes, and Eloquent behavior changes across versions. I found most issues through a combination of the upgrade guide's explicit 'breaking changes' list, running the test suite after each version bump, and manually testing key user flows (search, application submission, language switching) that weren't well covered by automated tests.

q: What happens on uninstall — how do you clean up data and revoke tokens?
a: Shopify sends an 'app uninstalled' webhook, which I handle by marking the store's record as inactive (rather than instantly deleting everything, in case of an accidental uninstall/reinstall), revoking the stored access token so it can no longer be used, and stopping any scheduled sync jobs for that store. Actual data deletion follows a retention policy rather than happening instantly, balancing privacy expectations against the chance of recovering from an accidental uninstall.

q: How does WebRTC fit into this — are you building the signaling server yourself, or using a third-party service?
a: Fill inState your real answer. WebRTC itself handles the actual direct audio/video connection, but it needs a separate 'signaling' step to set up that connection (exchanging technical connection details) — that signaling typically runs over your own WebSocket/Laravel Echo channel rather than WebRTC itself, while the actual audio/video stream goes directly between the two people (or through a relay server when a direct connection isn't possible, like behind strict networks).

q: How do Firebase notifications integrate with a Laravel backend?
a: Laravel sends a push notification (like 'your appointment is starting') by calling Firebase's messaging service with the target device's registered notification token, usually sent as a background job so notification delivery doesn't hold up the request that triggered it. Delivery isn't 100% guaranteed (device offline, token expired) — I handle expired tokens by removing/refreshing them when Firebase reports one as no longer valid, instead of repeatedly trying to send to a dead token.

q: Walk through how dynamic, department-specific medical forms were built.
a: The form layout (fields, validation rules, which department it belongs to) is stored in the database and displayed dynamically, instead of hardcoding a separate form template per department — this means adding a new department's form is a data/setting change, not a code deployment. Each field's validation rules are enforced both on the screen (for a better user experience) and on the server (for actual security, since checks on the screen alone are never trusted).

q: How does digital signature capture work, and how is the signed document generated?
a: The signature is captured on-screen (usually through a drawing pad) and submitted as image data alongside the form, then the backend generates the final PDF (using a PDF tool) embedding both the form data and the captured signature image, storing the finished document securely instead of regenerating it every time it's viewed.

q: How do you approach code review, and how do you give feedback to a junior developer without discouraging them?
a: I focus review comments on things that matter — correctness, security, maintainability — instead of nitpicking style that a linter (an automated style-checking tool) should catch. For junior developers specifically, I frame feedback as questions where possible ('what happens if this list is empty?') rather than instructions, which builds their own debugging instinct instead of just teaching them to fix this one instance, and I always mention what's done well, not just what needs to change — code review should build confidence, not just catch mistakes.

q: What's your general approach to safely changing old code you didn't write and don't fully trust?
a: Understand before changing — trace the actual data flow and business logic instead of guessing from naming alone. Add test coverage, or at least a manual checklist, around the specific area before touching it. Make the smallest change that achieves the goal, release it gradually, and watch closely after each change instead of bundling many risky changes into one release — this is exactly the approach I used across Rentigo, the University Seekers migration, and other legacy-code projects.

q: How do you decide when to introduce a new technology (like MongoDB or Python) into an existing stack, versus forcing everything to fit?
a:
I look for a genuine mismatch between what the existing stack is good at and what the actual workload needs — not novelty for its own sake. MongoDB entered HOLOIN because storing high-volume, mostly uniform device data as relational tables was actively working against MySQL's strengths; Python entered AI-BDM because the AI/machine-learning world genuinely doesn't exist in PHP.

In both cases the bar was 'this workload is meaningfully worse to build in the existing stack,' not 'this technology is popular' — every new technology adds real ongoing cost (another thing to deploy, monitor, and staff for), so it needs to earn its place.

q: Describe how you estimate a task or project when the requirements are vague.
a: I break the vague request into smaller, more concrete pieces and estimate each piece separately, clearly flagging which pieces are well-understood versus genuinely uncertain — a single number for a vague scope is usually wrong in one direction or the other. Where real ambiguity remains (common in agency/freelance customization work), I build in a short discovery/clarification phase before committing to a hard estimate, and communicate estimates as ranges tied to stated assumptions, so if an assumption turns out wrong, the estimate visibly needs revisiting rather than silently being blown.

q: How do you handle a production incident at 2 AM — walk through your actual triage process.
a:
Assess how bad it is and who's affected first (is this hitting all customers or one, is data at risk, is it getting worse) before digging into the root cause — the first priority is stopping the damage (roll back a bad deploy, turn off a misbehaving feature, scale up an overwhelmed resource) even before fully understanding why it happened.

Once stable, I investigate the root cause with logs/monitoring, clearly communicate status to whoever needs to know, and write up what happened afterward — not to assign blame, but to identify what monitoring/safeguard would have caught it earlier next time.

q: If you were leading a small team building something like HOLOIN or AI-BDM from scratch, what would you insist on getting right early, even under deadline pressure?
a:
A working testing pipeline with at least core test coverage from day one — adding tests onto a codebase that grew without them is far more expensive later than the discipline of writing them alongside the code. Clear boundaries and agreed data formats between components (especially for a system using two languages, where Laravel and Python need to agree on what data looks like), written down explicitly rather than just understood informally.

And basic monitoring/logging from the start, since debugging a spread-out system in production without it is far harder than the up-front cost of setting it up properly.

a: Fill ina genuine, specific example — interviewers respond well to real self-reflection, not a humble-brag disguised as a weakness. q: How would you explain the trade-off between shipping fast (agency mindset) and building for long-term maintainability (enterprise mindset) to a non-technical stakeholder?
a: I'd frame it in terms of cost, not abstract quality: shipping fast without maintainability is like renting instead of buying — cheaper right now, but every future change costs more than it should, and eventually you're paying interest on that in the form of bugs and slow feature delivery. The right balance depends on the actual lifespan and stakes of the project — a short-term marketing site genuinely doesn't need the same rigor as a core billing system — so I make that trade-off clear and let the stakeholder choose with the real cost visible, instead of silently picking one extreme.

q: What do you check in code review at senior level?
a: Correctness and edge cases; architecture (right layer/service, boundaries, coupling); security (authz on objects, input validation, secrets, injection); performance (query count, indexes, complexity, memory, N+1, unbounded arrays in Mongo documents); concurrency (races, idempotency, transactions, lock ordering); resilience (timeouts, retries, error handling); operability (logs, metrics, feature flags, migrations safe to roll back); tests that prove behavior; readability. Automate style so humans review design.

q: How do you establish coding standards across a team?
a: Written guidelines (with examples and reasons), templates/skeletons for new services, automated enforcement (Pint, PHPStan, Pest arch tests, CI gates), PR template/checklist, ADRs, regular tech talks, pairing, lead by example; revisit standards when they stop helping.

q: How do you mentor mid-level developers toward senior?
a: Give ownership of a feature end-to-end including production support, involve them in design reviews, ask guiding questions instead of giving answers, teach debugging methods, encourage writing design docs, give specific feedback, share incident post-mortems as learning.

q: How do you handle technical debt?
a: Make it visible (register with impact: incidents, slow delivery, risk), prioritize by business impact, pay down continuously (a % of each sprint), refactor while touching code, big migrations with the strangler pattern, never let it block security fixes.

q: How do you estimate a complex project?
a: Break down into components and unknowns, spike risky parts, estimate in ranges with confidence levels, include testing/migration/deployment/monitoring effort, identify dependencies on other teams, re-plan at milestones, communicate early.

q: Tell me about a time you made a wrong architectural decision.
a: Senior interviewers love this. Show: the context, why the decision looked right, the signals it was wrong, how you corrected it with minimal disruption, and what you changed in your decision process.

q: How do you push back on product/management?
a: Translate technical risk into business terms (downtime, cost, data loss, delay), offer options (MVP vs full, phased rollout), make the trade-off explicit, agree, and document.

q: Difference between var, let, and const?1 follow-up
a:
var is function-scoped and hoisted with value undefined. let and const are block-scoped and hoisted but stay in the "temporal dead zone" until the line runs, so using them early throws an error. const means the variable can't be re-assigned — but an object or array inside it can still be changed.

Cross-questionSo is a const array immutable?

No. const arr = []; arr.push(1) works. Use Object.freeze() for shallow immutability.

q: What is a closure?code1 follow-up
a:
A function that remembers variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function finished.

function counter() { let c = 0; return () => ++c; }
const next = counter(); next(); // 1, next(); // 2

Real use: private state, debounce functions, React hooks internally.

Cross-questionWhat's a stale closure in React?

A useEffect or callback captures an old state value because it was created in an older render. Fix: add the value to the dependency array, use functional updates setCount(c => c + 1), or use a ref.

q: Explain the event loop.code1 follow-up
a:
JS runs on one thread. There's a call stack, a microtask queue (Promises, queueMicrotask) and a macrotask queue (setTimeout, I/O, events). After the stack is empty, all microtasks run first, then one macrotask, then microtasks again.

console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
// 1, 4, 3, 2

Cross-questionWhy does a heavy loop freeze the page?

It blocks the single thread so the browser can't paint or handle clicks. Fix: split work into chunks, use Web Workers, or move it to the backend.
=== checks value and type, == converts types first ('1' == 1 is true). Always use ===.

q: Promises vs async/await?2 follow-ups
a:
Same thing underneath; async/await is cleaner syntax. Use try/catch for errors.

Cross-questionHow do you run 3 API calls in parallel?

await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()]). If one failing shouldn't kill the others → Promise.allSettled. First to finish → Promise.race. First success → Promise.any.

DeepWhat's wrong with await inside forEach?

forEach doesn't wait for promises. Use for...of (sequential) or Promise.all(arr.map(...)) (parallel).

q: What is this?
a: It depends on how the function is called: method call → the object; plain call → undefined in strict mode; new → the new object; arrow functions don't have their own this, they take it from the outer scope.

q: Shallow vs deep copy?
a: Spread {...obj} copies one level only; nested objects are still shared. Deep copy: structuredClone(obj) (modern, handles Dates, Maps, etc.).

q: Debounce vs throttle?
a: Debounce: run only after the user stops doing something (search input). Throttle: run at most once every X ms (scroll, resize, drag in a canvas editor).

q: ES6+ features you use daily?1 follow-up
a:
Destructuring, spread/rest, arrow functions, template literals, modules (import/export), optional chaining a?.b, nullish coalescing a ?? 'default', Array.prototype.at(), Object.groupBy(), structuredClone, Array.prototype.toSorted()/toReversed() (non-mutating).

Cross-question|| vs ???

0 || 5 gives 5 but 0 ?? 5 gives 0. ?? only replaces null/undefined.

q: Memory leaks in JS — common causes?
a: Forgotten event listeners, intervals not cleared, closures holding big objects, detached DOM nodes, global variables, huge caches without limits. In React: not cleaning up in useEffect. Find them with Chrome DevTools → Memory → heap snapshots.

q: TypeScript — why use it and what's the difference between interface and type?
a: Catches bugs before runtime, better autocomplete, safer refactors. interface can be extended/merged, good for object shapes; type can do unions, intersections, mapped types. Know unknown vs any (unknown forces you to check the type first), generics, Partial, Pick, Omit, Record.

q: What is AJAX?
a: Asynchronous JavaScript And XML — sending requests to the server without reloading the page (today usually with JSON). Examples: live search, "add to cart" without reload, loading more products, form validation.

q: AJAX with jQuery vs fetch?code1 follow-up
a:
// jQuery
$.ajax({
  url: '/products', type: 'POST', data: { name: 'Shirt' }, dataType: 'json',
  headers: { 'X-CSRF-TOKEN': $('meta[name="csrf-token"]').attr('content') },
  beforeSend: () => $('#btn').prop('disabled', true),
  success: res => showToast(res.message),
  error: xhr => showErrors(xhr.responseJSON?.errors),
  complete: () => $('#btn').prop('disabled', false)
});

// fetch (modern, no library)
const res = await fetch('/products', {
  method: 'POST',
  headers: { 'Content-Type': 'application/json', 'X-CSRF-TOKEN': token },
  body: JSON.stringify({ name: 'Shirt' })
});
if (!res.ok) throw new Error('Request failed');
const data = await res.json();

Cross-questionDoes fetch reject on a 404 or 500?

No! It only rejects on network failure. You must check res.ok. (jQuery's error callback does run on 4xx/5xx.) Axios also rejects on errors.

q: How do you send CSRF token with AJAX in Laravel?1 follow-up
a:
Put <meta name="csrf-token" content="{{ csrf_token() }}"> in the layout, then $.ajaxSetup({ headers: { 'X-CSRF-TOKEN': $('meta[name="csrf-token"]').attr('content') } }) once globally. Axios in Laravel does it automatically via the XSRF-TOKEN cookie.

Cross-questionGetting 419 Page Expired in Laravel?

Missing/expired CSRF token or session expired.

q: How do you show Laravel validation errors from AJAX?
a: Laravel returns 422 with { errors: { field: ['message'] } }. Loop through xhr.responseJSON.errors and show each message under its input.

q: How do you upload a file with AJAX?code1 follow-up
a:
const fd = new FormData($('#form')[0]);
$.ajax({ url: '/upload', type: 'POST', data: fd, processData: false, contentType: false });

Cross-questionWhy processData: false and contentType: false?

So jQuery doesn't convert the data to a string and the browser sets the correct multipart/form-data boundary itself.

q: Event delegation — why does my click not work on elements added by AJAX?
a:
$('.delete').click(...) only attaches to elements that exist now. Use delegation on a parent:

$(document).on('click', '.delete', function () { ... });

Same idea in plain JS: listen on the parent and check e.target.closest('.delete').

q: $(document).ready() vs window.onload?
a: ready fires when the DOM is built; onload waits for images/CSS too.

q: Common jQuery methods?1 follow-up
a:
Selectors $('#id'), .find(), .closest(), .val(), .text(), .html(), .attr(), .prop(), .addClass(), .toggle(), .append(), .remove(), .each(), .serialize() (form to query string), .fadeIn().

Cross-question.attr() vs .prop()?

.prop() for current state like checked/disabled; .attr() for the original HTML attribute.

q: How do you avoid sending too many AJAX requests in live search?
a: Debounce (wait 300 ms after typing stops), cancel the previous request (xhr.abort() or AbortController with fetch), minimum 2–3 characters, cache results.

q: jQuery vs React — why still use jQuery?2 follow-ups
a:
jQuery is great for adding small interactions to server-rendered pages (Blade, CI views) and is everywhere in old projects. React is better for complex UIs with lots of state. Modern browsers can do most jQuery things in plain JS (querySelector, fetch, classList).

Cross-questionCan React and jQuery work on the same page?

Yes, but don't let jQuery change DOM that React controls — React won't know and things break. Keep them in separate areas, or mount React in one <div id="app">.

Latest

jQuery 4.0 was released in early 2026 — it drops very old browsers (IE) and removes some old deprecated functions.

q: Core JavaScript questions (quick answers)
a:
• let/const/var → block vs function scope; const can't be reassigned.
  • Closure → function remembers outer variables.
  • Event loop → sync code first, then microtasks (Promises), then macrotasks (setTimeout).
  • == vs === → always use ===.
  • Promise states → pending, fulfilled, rejected. Promise.all for parallel calls.
  • Event bubbling → events go from the clicked element up to parents; e.stopPropagation() stops it; e.preventDefault() stops default behavior (form submit, link).
  • JSON → JSON.stringify() object → string; JSON.parse() string → object.

q: What is CORS and why does my AJAX call to another domain fail?
a: The browser blocks cross-domain requests unless the server sends Access-Control-Allow-Origin. Fix on the server (Laravel config/cors.php, CI4 CORS filter), not in JavaScript.

q: What's the difference between let and var when redeclaring a variable?
a: Using var, you can redeclare the same variable name more than once in the same scope without an error. Using let, you cannot redeclare the same variable name twice in the same block scope — attempting to do so causes an error. let is generally preferred in modern JavaScript because this stricter behavior helps catch accidental bugs.

q: What is a callback function, and what does 'asynchronous' mean in JavaScript?
a: A callback is a function that runs after some amount of time or after some event happens — like code inside setTimeout(). JavaScript is asynchronous in the sense that it doesn't have to wait for a slow operation (like a network request or a timer) to finish before moving on to other code — it registers a callback to run later when that operation completes, instead of freezing everything until it's done.

q: What are Promises in JavaScript, in simple terms?
a: A Promise represents a value that will be available in the future, either successfully ('resolved') or unsuccessfully ('rejected'). Promises are a cleaner way to work with asynchronous code than deeply nested callbacks.

q: How does a Single Page Application (SPA) generally work?
a: On the first request, the server sends back the initial HTML/CSS/JS. After that first load, JavaScript takes over — later user actions trigger JavaScript to call APIs directly and update the page's content dynamically, instead of the browser loading a whole new page from the server for every action.

q: What is React, and why do teams choose it?1 follow-up
a:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces out of small, reusable components. You describe what the screen should look like for a given state, and React works out how to update the browser efficiently. Teams pick it because components are easy to reuse and test, the ecosystem is huge (routing, forms, data fetching, UI kits), and the same skills carry over to mobile with React Native.

Cross-questionIs React a framework?

No, it's a UI library. Frameworks such as Next.js or Remix add routing, data loading, server rendering and build tooling on top of it.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: What is JSX, and what does it turn into?code1 follow-up
a:
JSX is HTML-like syntax inside JavaScript. A build tool (Babel, SWC, esbuild) turns it into plain function calls that create React elements — small objects describing what to show.

const el = <h1 className="title">Hello {name}</h1>;
// becomes roughly: jsx('h1', { className: 'title', children: ['Hello ', name] })

Cross-questionWhy className and not class?

class is a reserved word in JavaScript, and JSX props follow DOM property names.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Function components vs class components — which do you write today?
a: Function components with hooks. They're shorter, easier to test, and share logic through custom hooks instead of HOCs and inheritance. Class components still work and you'll meet them in older code (and Error Boundaries still need a class, or a library like react-error-boundary).
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Props vs state vs context — explain with one example.
a: In a product page: the product object passed from the page to <ProductCard> is a prop (read-only input). Whether the size dropdown is open is state (owned by the component, changes over time). The logged-in user and theme used everywhere come from context (shared data without passing props through every level).
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: What happens when state changes? Describe a render.1 follow-up
a:
1. You call setState → React schedules an update.
  2. Render phase: React calls your component function again to get the new JSX (pure calculation, no DOM changes).
  3. Reconciliation: React compares the new element tree with the previous one.
  4. Commit phase: React applies only the needed DOM changes, then runs useLayoutEffect, the browser paints, then useEffect runs.

Cross-questionDoes a re-render always change the DOM?

No. Re-rendering means calling the function again; if the output is the same, React touches nothing in the DOM.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: When does a component re-render?
a:
When its own state changes, when its parent re-renders (even if props didn't change, unless it's memoized), or when a context it reads changes.

Common trap

"A component re-renders when its props change." Not quite — it re-renders because the parent re-rendered. Props changing is just the usual reason the parent re-rendered.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Why is state update "asynchronous", and what is batching?
a:
setCount(count + 1) doesn't change count right away inside the same function — you get the new value on the next render. Since React 18, multiple updates in the same event, timeout or promise are batched into one render.

setCount(count + 1); setCount(count + 1);   // count goes up by 1, not 2
setCount(c => c + 1); setCount(c => c + 1); // goes up by 2 — functional updates use the latest value
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Why must you never mutate state directly?
a: React compares old and new state by reference (Object.is). If you push into the same array, the reference doesn't change, so React may skip the update, and memoized children won't see it. Always create new objects/arrays: setItems(prev => [...prev, item]), setUser(u => ({ ...u, name })). For deep updates, Immer (built into Redux Toolkit) lets you write "mutating" code that produces new objects safely.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Conditional rendering — any pitfalls?
a: Use &&, ternaries or early returns. Pitfall: {items.length && <List />} renders a literal 0 when the array is empty. Use {items.length > 0 && <List />}.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: Composition vs inheritance — how do you share UI in React?
a:
Composition. Pass components as children or as props ("slots"):

function Card({ title, actions, children }) {
  return <section className="card"><header>{title}{actions}</header>{children}</section>;
}
<Card title="Orders" actions={<Button>Export</Button>}><OrdersTable /></Card>

React's docs have never recommended inheritance between components.
c: React Fundamentals (Asked in Almost Every Round)

q: What are the Rules of Hooks, and why do they exist?
a: Only call hooks at the top level of a component or custom hook — never inside conditions, loops or nested functions — and only from React functions. React tracks hooks by call order; if the order changes between renders, state gets attached to the wrong hook. The ESLint plugin eslint-plugin-react-hooks enforces this.

q: Walk me through useEffect properly: when does it run, and what is cleanup for?code1 follow-up
a:
It runs after the browser paints. The dependency array decides when: none → after every render; [] → after mount; [a, b] → when a or b changed. The returned function is cleanup: it runs before the effect runs again and when the component unmounts — remove listeners, clear timers, abort requests, close sockets.

useEffect(() => {
  const id = setInterval(tick, 1000);
  return () => clearInterval(id);
}, []);

Cross-questionWhy does my effect run twice in development?

StrictMode mounts, unmounts and remounts to expose missing cleanup. Production runs it once.

q: "You Might Not Need an Effect" — give examples of effects that should be removed.
a:
• Derived data: don't store fullName in state and sync it with an effect; compute it during render.
  • Resetting state when a prop changes: give the component a key instead (<Profile key={userId} />).
  • Handling user events: logic triggered by a click belongs in the click handler, not in an effect watching state.
  • Chains of effects that set state which triggers another effect — combine them into one event handler or reducer.

Effects are for syncing with things outside React: network, subscriptions, timers, the DOM, third-party widgets.

q: How do you fetch data correctly inside useEffect (race conditions)?code1 follow-up
a:
If the user switches from product 1 to product 2 quickly, the slower response for product 1 can arrive last and overwrite the screen. Abort or ignore stale responses:

useEffect(() => {
  const ctrl = new AbortController();
  setStatus('loading');
  fetch(`/api/products/${id}`, { signal: ctrl.signal })
    .then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(r.status); return r.json(); })
    .then(data => { setProduct(data); setStatus('done'); })
    .catch(e => { if (e.name !== 'AbortError') setStatus('error'); });
  return () => ctrl.abort();
}, [id]);

Cross-questionWould you write this by hand in a real app?

Usually not. TanStack Query or SWR handle caching, deduping, retries, refetching and race conditions for you; in Next.js, Server Components fetch on the server.

q: useState vs useReducer — when do you switch?
a:
useReducer when state has several related fields that change together, the next state depends on the previous in complex ways, or you want all transitions in one testable function (forms, wizards, carts).

function cartReducer(state, action) {
  switch (action.type) {
    case 'add': return { ...state, items: [...state.items, action.item] };
    case 'remove': return { ...state, items: state.items.filter(i => i.id !== action.id) };
    default: return state;
  }
}
const [cart, dispatch] = useReducer(cartReducer, { items: [] });

q: useRef — what can it do that state can't?
a:
It holds a mutable value that survives renders without causing a re-render: DOM nodes (focus an input, measure a chart container, a <canvas>), timer IDs, the previous value, an AbortController, or the latest callback for an event listener.

Common trap

Reading or writing ref.current during render for things that affect output — React won't know it changed, so the UI goes stale.

q: useMemo, useCallback, React.memo — when are they worth it?
a: Use them when (1) a calculation is genuinely expensive, (2) you pass objects/functions to a memo child and want it to skip re-rendering, or (3) a value is an effect dependency and must stay stable. Don't wrap everything — memoization has a cost and makes code harder to read. The React Compiler (stable since late 2025) now adds most of this memoization automatically at build time.

q: useLayoutEffect vs useEffect?
a: useLayoutEffect runs after DOM changes but before the browser paints — use it to measure layout (tooltip position) and adjust without a visible flicker. It blocks painting, so use it rarely. On the server it doesn't run.

q: What does useId solve?
a: Unique IDs that match between server and client rendering, for linking labels and inputs: const id = useId(); <label htmlFor={id}>…<input id={id} />. Never use Math.random() for this — it causes hydration mismatches.

q: Explain useTransition and useDeferredValue with a real example.
a:
Both mark work as non-urgent so typing stays responsive.

  • useTransition: wrap a state update — startTransition(() => setFilter(value)) — React keeps the input snappy and renders the heavy filtered list when it can; isPending lets you show a subtle spinner.
  • useDeferredValue: when you don't control the update, defer a value — const deferredQuery = useDeferredValue(query) and render the big list from deferredQuery.

Real use: searching 5,000 rows in an admin table, or switching dashboard tabs with heavy charts.

q: What is useSyncExternalStore for?
a: Safely subscribing to data that lives outside React (browser APIs like navigator.onLine, a WebSocket store, Redux/Zustand internals) without "tearing" — different parts of the UI showing different versions of the data during concurrent rendering. Libraries use it internally; you use it for custom stores.

q: Write a useDebounce hook and explain it.
a:
function useDebounce(value, delay = 300) {
  const [debounced, setDebounced] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => {
    const t = setTimeout(() => setDebounced(value), delay);
    return () => clearTimeout(t);   // restart the timer on every change
  }, [value, delay]);
  return debounced;
}
// usage: const q = useDebounce(search); useQuery({ queryKey: ['users', q], ... })

Each keystroke clears the previous timer, so the API is called only after the user stops typing.

q: How does reconciliation decide what to update? Why do keys matter?
a:
React compares trees level by level. Different element type at the same spot (a div becoming a section, or <A/> becoming <B/>) → the old subtree is destroyed with its state and a new one is created. Same type → React updates props and keeps state. In lists, keys tell React which item is which between renders.

Common trap

Using the array index as key in a list that can be reordered, filtered or have items removed — inputs keep the wrong values and state jumps between rows. Use a stable ID from the data.

q: What is React Fiber, and what did it make possible?
a: Fiber is React's internal engine (since React 16). Each component is a "fiber" unit of work, so React can pause, prioritize, resume or throw away rendering work instead of doing it all in one blocking pass. That's what enables concurrent features: transitions, Suspense, streaming server rendering, and keeping urgent updates (typing) ahead of slow ones (rendering a huge list).

q: A page feels slow. How do you find the cause in a React app?
a:
Measure first:

  1. React DevTools Profiler — which components render, how often, and why ("props changed", "parent rendered").
  2. Chrome Performance tab — long tasks blocking the main thread; check INP (interaction delay) in Lighthouse/Web Vitals.
  3. Network tab — maybe it's a slow API, not React at all.
  4. Bundle analyzer — too much JavaScript on first load.

Then fix the biggest cause only.

q: Common fixes for too many re-renders?
a: Move state down to the component that actually uses it; split big components; lift expensive children out and pass them as children (they won't re-render with the parent's state); split contexts or use a store with selectors; memoize callbacks passed to memoized children; avoid creating new objects/arrays in JSX props for memo children; debounce fast inputs.

q: How do you render a list of 10,000 rows smoothly?
a: Virtualization — only render the rows visible on screen (TanStack Virtual, react-window). Plus server-side pagination or infinite scroll, stable keys, memoized row components, and avoiding heavy work per row.

q: Code-splitting — how and where?
a: Load code only when it's needed: const Editor = lazy(() => import('./Editor')) wrapped in <Suspense fallback={<Spinner/>}>. Split by route first (biggest win), then heavy widgets (charts, rich-text editors, maps, PDF viewers). In Next.js use next/dynamic.

q: Context performance — why can Context slow an app down, and what do you do?
a: Every component that reads a context re-renders whenever its value changes — and if you create the value object inline, it changes on every provider render. Fixes: memoize the value, split contexts by how often they change (auth vs. theme vs. live notifications), keep fast-changing data in a store with selectors (Zustand, Redux Toolkit), or pass a stable dispatch through context instead of the whole state.

q: How do you choose a state management approach?
a:
Ask what kind of state it is:

  • UI state local to a component → useState/useReducer.
  • Shared UI state (sidebar open, selected tool) → lift up, context, or Zustand.
  • Complex app-wide client state with many actions and devtools needs → Redux Toolkit.
  • Server data (lists, records from the API) → TanStack Query / SWR / RTK Query — not Redux by hand.
  • URL state (filters, page, sort) → the query string, so links are shareable.
  • Form state → React Hook Form (+ Zod for validation).

q: What does TanStack Query give you over plain fetch + useEffect?
a:
Caching by key, automatic background refetching, request deduplication, retries, pagination/infinite queries, loading and error states, cache invalidation after mutations, optimistic updates, and devtools.

const { data, isPending, error } = useQuery({
  queryKey: ['orders', page],
  queryFn: () => api.get(`/orders?page=${page}`).then(r => r.data),
  staleTime: 30_000,
});
const qc = useQueryClient();
const create = useMutation({
  mutationFn: body => api.post('/orders', body),
  onSuccess: () => qc.invalidateQueries({ queryKey: ['orders'] }),
});

q: Controlled vs uncontrolled forms — which do you use for a big form?
a: Controlled (value in React state) is simple and good for small forms or live formatting. For big forms, React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs with refs, so typing doesn't re-render the whole form. Pair it with a schema library (Zod/Yup) and show server-side validation errors (Laravel's 422 response) under the matching fields.

q: What is an optimistic update, and when is it risky?
a: Update the UI immediately as if the server said yes, then roll back if it fails — likes, toggles, reordering, marking tasks done. React 19's useOptimistic and TanStack Query's onMutate support it. Risky for payments, stock-limited purchases, or anything where showing a false success would mislead the user.

q: Where do you keep filters, sorting and pagination for a table?
a: In the URL query string (?status=paid&sort=-date&page=3). Refresh keeps the view, users can share or bookmark it, and the back button works. Read it with your router's search-params hook and use it as part of the query key.

q: What changed in React 19 that you'd actually use?
a:
• Actions: pass an async function to a form's action; React handles pending state and errors.
  • useActionState (form result + pending), useFormStatus (pending state inside a child button), useOptimistic.
  • use() to read a promise or context during render (with Suspense).
  • ref as a normal prop — forwardRef is no longer needed.
  • <title>, <meta> and stylesheet tags can be rendered inside components.
  • Better hydration error messages.
  • Server Components and Server Actions are stable, and the React Compiler handles memoization.
c: Modern React: React 19, Server Components & Next.js

q: Server Components vs Client Components — how do you decide the boundary?1 follow-up
a:
Server Components (the default in the Next.js App Router) run only on the server: they can read the database or call internal APIs directly, keep secrets there, and send no JavaScript to the browser. Client Components ('use client') are needed for state, effects, event handlers and browser APIs. Rule of thumb: fetch and render data on the server; push 'use client' as far down the tree as possible — for example, a server-rendered product page with a small client-side "Add to cart" button.

Cross-questionCan a Client Component import a Server Component?

Not directly. Pass the Server Component as children or a prop from a server parent instead.
c: Modern React: React 19, Server Components & Next.js

q: What is Suspense, and how do loading states work with it?
a: <Suspense fallback={...}> shows a fallback while something inside is "not ready" — lazy-loaded code or data read with use()/a Suspense-enabled library. Nesting Suspense boundaries lets parts of the page appear independently; in Next.js a loading.js file creates a boundary, and server rendering streams the HTML as each part becomes ready.
c: Modern React: React 19, Server Components & Next.js

q: What is hydration, and how do you debug a hydration mismatch?
a: Hydration = React attaching event handlers to server-rendered HTML and taking over. A mismatch happens when the first client render differs from the server HTML. Common causes: Date.now()/random values, reading window/localStorage during render, locale/timezone formatting differences, invalid HTML nesting (<div> inside <p>), browser extensions. Fix: make the first render identical, move browser-only code into useEffect, or render that part client-only.
c: Modern React: React 19, Server Components & Next.js

q: Plain React (Vite SPA) vs Next.js — how do you choose?
a: Vite SPA: dashboards and admin panels behind a login where SEO doesn't matter and a separate API (like Laravel) already exists. Next.js: public pages that need SEO and fast first load, mixed static/dynamic content, or when you want server rendering and a BFF layer. Laravel + Inertia is a third option when the backend team wants Laravel routing and controllers with React pages and no separate API.
c: Modern React: React 19, Server Components & Next.js

q: How does authentication work between a React SPA and a Laravel API?1 follow-up
a:
Same top-level domain (e.g. app.site.com + api.site.com): Sanctum SPA (cookie) auth — call /sanctum/csrf-cookie first, then log in; the browser sends the session cookie and X-XSRF-TOKEN header automatically (withCredentials: true in Axios). Configure SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS, SESSION_DOMAIN and CORS supports_credentials. Different domains or mobile apps: Sanctum API tokens (Bearer token), stored carefully.

Cross-questionWhy not store a token in localStorage?

Any XSS script can read it. An HttpOnly cookie can't be read by JavaScript.

q: Laravel returns a 422. How do you show the errors in React?
a: Laravel sends { message, errors: { email: ['The email has already been taken.'] } }. Catch the error, and map errors onto the form fields — with React Hook Form, call setError(field, { message }) for each entry — and focus the first invalid field.

q: How do you structure API calls in a React app talking to Laravel?
a: One API client module (Axios instance with baseURL, credentials, interceptors for 401 → redirect to login and 419 → refresh CSRF), small typed service functions per resource (ordersApi.list(params)), TanStack Query hooks on top (useOrders(filters)), and components that only call hooks. Laravel API Resources keep response shapes stable, so the frontend doesn't break when a model changes.

q: Real-time updates from Laravel into React — how?
a: Laravel broadcasts events (ShouldBroadcast) through Reverb (or Pusher/Ably); React listens with Laravel Echo on private channels authorized by Laravel. On an event, either update the TanStack Query cache directly (setQueryData) or invalidate the query to refetch. Clean up listeners in useEffect cleanup. (This is the kind of live device-dashboard pattern used on IoT platforms.)

q: File upload with progress from React to Laravel?
a: Send FormData with Axios and use onUploadProgress for a progress bar; validate type/size on both sides; for large files upload directly to S3 with a pre-signed URL from Laravel, then tell Laravel the file key. Laravel validates with mimes/max rules and stores privately.

q: Paginated or infinite lists from Laravel in React?
a: Laravel paginate()/cursorPaginate() returns data plus links/meta (or next_cursor). In React, use useQuery with the page in the key for numbered pages, or useInfiniteQuery with getNextPageParam: last => last.meta.next_cursor and an IntersectionObserver sentinel at the bottom for infinite scroll.

q: Inertia.js vs a separate React SPA + API — trade-offs?
a: Inertia: Laravel controllers return React pages with props — no separate API, one auth system, server-side routing, fastest for a single team. Separate SPA + API: needed when mobile apps or third parties also use the API, or frontend and backend deploy independently — but you maintain API contracts, CORS and token/cookie auth.

q: How do you deploy a React frontend with a Laravel backend?
a: Option 1: Vite builds assets into Laravel's public/build (Blade/Inertia) — one deploy. Option 2: SPA built to static files served by Nginx/CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Netlify, Vercel) with the API on its own domain — set CORS and cookie domains correctly, and use environment variables at build time (VITE_API_URL) since static files can't read server env at runtime.

q: Why add TypeScript to a React project?
a: It catches wrong props, missing fields and null mistakes before the code runs, gives autocomplete across the codebase, and makes refactoring a large app much safer — especially when API response shapes change.

q: How do you type props, state and events?code1 follow-up
a:
type ButtonProps = { label: string; variant?: 'primary' | 'ghost'; onClick: () => void };
function Button({ label, variant = 'primary', onClick }: ButtonProps) { ... }

const [user, setUser] = useState<User | null>(null);
function onChange(e: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>) { setName(e.target.value); }
type CardProps = { title: string; children: React.ReactNode };

Cross-questioninterface or type for props?

Either works; many teams use type for props because it handles unions easily. Be consistent.

q: How do you keep TypeScript types in sync with a Laravel API?
a: Define response types once (hand-written, or generated from an OpenAPI spec), validate untrusted responses at runtime with Zod where it matters, and use generics in the API client (api.get<Order[]>('/orders')). Tools can also generate TypeScript types from Laravel models/resources.

q: How do you test React components?
a:
Vitest/Jest + React Testing Library: render the component, interact like a user (userEvent.type, click), and assert on what the user sees (getByRole('button', { name: /save/i })) — not on internal state. Mock the network with MSW so tests use realistic API responses. Playwright for end-to-end flows like login → create order → see it in the list.

test('shows validation error', async () => {
  render(<SignupForm />);
  await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole('button', { name: /sign up/i }));
  expect(await screen.findByText(/email is required/i)).toBeInTheDocument();
});

q: What makes a React test brittle, and how do you avoid it?
a: Testing implementation details (class names, internal state, number of renders, snapshot of huge trees). Prefer role/label queries, test behavior and outcomes, and keep one clear assertion focus per test.

q: Is React safe from XSS by default?
a: Mostly: React escapes text in JSX. Risk points: dangerouslySetInnerHTML (sanitize with DOMPurify), href={userInput} allowing javascript: URLs (validate protocols), injecting user data into inline scripts, and third-party scripts. Keep auth tokens out of JavaScript-readable storage.

q: Accessibility checklist for React components?
a: Use real elements (button, a, label, input), connect labels with htmlFor/useId, keep keyboard focus visible and logical, manage focus when modals open/close (and trap it inside), use ARIA only when native HTML can't express it, announce async results with aria-live, and check colour contrast. Test with keyboard only and a screen reader, plus eslint-plugin-jsx-a11y.

q: Error Boundaries — what do they catch and what don't they?
a: They catch errors thrown while rendering children and show a fallback UI instead of a blank screen. They don't catch errors in event handlers, async code (fetch), or the boundary itself — handle those with try/catch and error state. Report caught errors to Sentry.

q: What carries over from React to React Native, and what's different?
a: Same components, hooks, state management and data fetching. Different: no DOM — you use <View>, <Text>, <Pressable>, <FlatList>; styling is JavaScript objects with Flexbox (column by default); navigation via React Navigation or Expo Router; native features (camera, push notifications, secure storage) via libraries; builds go through the App Store/Play Store (Expo EAS makes this easier).
c: React Native Essentials (for Full Stack Roles)

q: Mobile app + Laravel backend — what changes on the API side?
a: Token auth (Sanctum personal access tokens stored in secure storage, not AsyncStorage), versioned APIs because old app versions stay installed for months, push notifications (Firebase/APNs) sent from Laravel jobs, careful pagination and payload size for slow networks, and graceful handling of offline/failed requests.
c: React Native Essentials (for Full Stack Roles)

q: Build a counter with increment, decrement and reset that never goes below zero.
a:
function Counter() {
  const [n, setN] = useState(0);
  return (
    <div>
      <button onClick={() => setN(c => Math.max(0, c - 1))} disabled={n === 0}>−</button>
      <output aria-live="polite">{n}</output>
      <button onClick={() => setN(c => c + 1)}>+</button>
      <button onClick={() => setN(0)}>Reset</button>
    </div>
  );
}

Talk through: functional updates, disabling the button, accessible output.

q: Build a searchable user list that calls an API as the user types.
a:
function UserSearch() {
  const [q, setQ] = useState('');
  const debounced = useDebounce(q, 300);
  const { data = [], isFetching } = useQuery({
    queryKey: ['users', debounced],
    queryFn: ({ signal }) => fetch(`/api/users?search=${encodeURIComponent(debounced)}`, { signal }).then(r => r.json()),
    enabled: debounced.length >= 2,
  });
  return (
    <>
      <label htmlFor="s">Search users</label>
      <input id="s" value={q} onChange={e => setQ(e.target.value)} />
      {isFetching && <p>Searching…</p>}
      <ul>{data.map(u => <li key={u.id}>{u.name}</li>)}</ul>
    </>
  );
}

Mention: debouncing, minimum length, abort via signal, stable keys, empty and error states.

q: Build a todo list with add, toggle, delete and a "remaining" count.
a:
function Todos() {
  const [todos, setTodos] = useState([]);
  const [text, setText] = useState('');
  const add = e => {
    e.preventDefault();
    if (!text.trim()) return;
    setTodos(t => [...t, { id: crypto.randomUUID(), text: text.trim(), done: false }]);
    setText('');
  };
  const toggle = id => setTodos(t => t.map(x => x.id === id ? { ...x, done: !x.done } : x));
  const remove = id => setTodos(t => t.filter(x => x.id !== id));
  const remaining = todos.filter(t => !t.done).length;   // derived, not stored
  return (
    <form onSubmit={add}>
      <input value={text} onChange={e => setText(e.target.value)} aria-label="New todo" />
      <button>Add</button>
      <p>{remaining} remaining</p>
      <ul>{todos.map(t => (
        <li key={t.id}>
          <label><input type="checkbox" checked={t.done} onChange={() => toggle(t.id)} /> {t.text}</label>
          <button type="button" onClick={() => remove(t.id)}>Delete</button>
        </li>))}
      </ul>
    </form>
  );
}

Points interviewers look for: immutable updates, derived count, stable IDs, form submit with Enter.

q: Build infinite scroll with IntersectionObserver.
a:
function InfiniteList({ fetchPage }) {
  const [items, setItems] = useState([]);
  const [cursor, setCursor] = useState(null);
  const [hasMore, setHasMore] = useState(true);
  const loading = useRef(false);
  const sentinel = useRef(null);

  useEffect(() => {
    const io = new IntersectionObserver(async ([entry]) => {
      if (!entry.isIntersecting || loading.current || !hasMore) return;
      loading.current = true;
      const res = await fetchPage(cursor);
      setItems(prev => [...prev, ...res.data]);
      setCursor(res.next_cursor);
      setHasMore(Boolean(res.next_cursor));
      loading.current = false;
    });
    if (sentinel.current) io.observe(sentinel.current);
    return () => io.disconnect();
  }, [cursor, hasMore, fetchPage]);

  return <>{items.map(i => <Row key={i.id} item={i} />)}{hasMore && <div ref={sentinel}>Loading…</div>}</>;
}

Mention the loading ref to stop double requests, cursor pagination from Laravel, and useInfiniteQuery as the production choice.

q: Write a useFetch hook with loading, error, abort and refetch.
a:
function useFetch(url, options) {
  const [state, setState] = useState({ data: null, error: null, loading: true });
  const [nonce, setNonce] = useState(0);
  useEffect(() => {
    const ctrl = new AbortController();
    setState(s => ({ ...s, loading: true, error: null }));
    fetch(url, { ...options, signal: ctrl.signal })
      .then(r => { if (!r.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${r.status}`); return r.json(); })
      .then(data => setState({ data, error: null, loading: false }))
      .catch(error => { if (error.name !== 'AbortError') setState({ data: null, error, loading: false }); });
    return () => ctrl.abort();
  }, [url, nonce]);   // options left out on purpose: callers pass new objects each render
  return { ...state, refetch: () => setNonce(n => n + 1) };
}

Explain why options is excluded from dependencies (or ask callers to memoize it), and why fetch doesn't reject on 404/500.

q: What is the Virtual DOM and reconciliation?1 follow-up
a:
React keeps a lightweight copy of the UI in memory. When state changes, it builds a new tree, compares ("diffs") it with the old one, and updates only the changed parts of the real DOM.

Cross-questionWhy do lists need key?

So React can match items between renders. Using the array index as key breaks things when items are reordered or deleted (wrong input values, wrong state). Use stable IDs.

q: State vs props?
a: Props come from the parent and are read-only. State is owned by the component and changes over time.

q: Explain useEffect and its dependency array.2 follow-ups
a:
Runs side effects after render (API calls, subscriptions, timers). No array → every render; [] → once on mount; [x] → when x changes. Return a cleanup function to remove listeners/timers.

Cross-questionWhy does my effect run twice in development?

React StrictMode mounts, unmounts, and mounts again to catch missing cleanups. It doesn't happen in production.

DeepShould you fetch data in useEffect?

It works, but in modern apps prefer TanStack Query / SWR (caching, retries, dedupe) or Server Components in Next.js. Many things people put in useEffect should just be computed during render.

q: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo?1 follow-up
a:
useMemo caches a computed value. useCallback caches a function. React.memo skips re-rendering a component if props didn't change. They work together: pass a useCallback function to a React.memo child.

Cross-questionShould you wrap everything in useMemo?

No, it has its own cost. Use it for expensive calculations or to keep references stable. Also, the React Compiler (stable since late 2025) can do much of this memoization automatically.

q: useRef — two uses?
a: 1) Access a DOM element (focus input, canvas element). 2) Store a mutable value that doesn't cause re-render (timer ID, previous value, drag position).

q: Controlled vs uncontrolled components?
a: Controlled: React state holds the input value. Uncontrolled: the DOM holds it, you read via ref. React Hook Form uses uncontrolled inputs for performance.

q: How do you share state between components?1 follow-up
a:
Lift state up → Context for low-frequency global data (theme, auth user) → a store like Zustand or Redux Toolkit for complex, frequently changing app state → TanStack Query for server data.

Cross-questionWhat's the problem with Context for everything?

Every consumer re-renders when the value changes. Split contexts or use a store with selectors.

q: Server state vs client state?
a: Server state = data from the API (can be stale, needs caching, refetching). Client state = UI stuff (modal open, selected tool). Mixing them in Redux causes a lot of manual code. Use TanStack Query for server state, Zustand/useState for client state.

q: How do you find and fix performance problems in React?
a: React DevTools Profiler to see which components re-render and why. Fixes: move state down closer to where it's used, split components, memoize, virtualize long lists (react-window, TanStack Virtual), lazy load routes (React.lazy + Suspense), avoid creating new objects/functions in props of memoized children, debounce inputs.

q: How do you design component architecture for a big app?
a: Feature-based folders (features/editor, features/billing), shared UI library (buttons, modals), container vs presentational separation where useful, custom hooks for logic (useCanvasHistory, useAuth), strict TypeScript types, and a clear data-fetching layer.

q: Error Boundaries?
a: Class components that catch render errors in children and show a fallback UI instead of a white screen. They don't catch errors in event handlers or async code — handle those with try/catch.

q: What's new in React 19?1 follow-up
a:
• Actions and useActionState for form submissions with pending/error states.
  • useOptimistic — show the result immediately, roll back if the server fails.
  • use() — read a promise or context inside render.
  • useFormStatus — know if the parent form is submitting.
  • ref can be passed as a normal prop (no more forwardRef needed).
  • Document metadata (<title>, <meta>) can be rendered inside components.
  • Server Components and Server Actions are stable.
  • React Compiler — auto-memoization at build time.

Cross-questionWhat is a Server Component?

A component that runs only on the server, can read the DB directly, and sends zero JavaScript to the browser. It can't use state, effects or browser APIs. Mark interactive parts with 'use client'.

q: Custom hook example you've written?
a: Have one ready. Example: useDebounce(value, delay), useUndoRedo(initialState) for an editor, or useInfiniteScroll. Explain why it was extracted (reused in 3 places, easier to test).

q: Basics of a Three.js scene?
a: Scene + Camera + Renderer + Meshes (Geometry + Material) + Lights, rendered in an animation loop. React Three Fiber (R3F) lets you write it as React components; drei gives helpers (OrbitControls, loaders).
c: Three.js / React Three Fiber (Nice to have)

q: 3D performance tips?
a: Reduce draw calls (instancing, merge geometries), compress models (glTF + Draco/Meshopt), texture compression, level of detail (LOD), dispose geometries/materials when removing them (memory leaks), render on demand (frameloop="demand" in R3F) instead of 60 fps always.
c: Three.js / React Three Fiber (Nice to have)

q: Use case with 2D editor?
a: 3D product preview — user designs a label/print in the 2D canvas, the canvas is used as a live texture on a 3D model (mug, box, t-shirt).
c: Three.js / React Three Fiber (Nice to have)

q: Why React?
a: Component-based, reusable UI, virtual DOM for efficient updates, huge ecosystem.

q: Props vs state?
a: Props come from parent (read-only); state is internal and changes.

q: useEffect with API call?
a:
useEffect(() => {
  const controller = new AbortController();
  fetch('/api/products', { signal: controller.signal })
    .then(r => r.json()).then(setProducts).catch(() => {});
  return () => controller.abort(); // cleanup
}, []);

q: Why key in lists?
a: Helps React identify items; use IDs, not indexes.

q: Controlled forms?
a: Input value comes from state, onChange updates state.

q: How do you connect React to a Laravel/CodeIgniter API?
a: Backend exposes JSON REST endpoints → React calls them with fetch/Axios → handle loading, errors, and 422 validation messages → auth via Sanctum cookie or Bearer token. For large apps use TanStack Query for caching.

q: How would you add React to an existing old PHP (jQuery) project?
a: Don't rewrite everything. Build React with Vite, mount it into one <div id="react-root"> on specific pages (e.g., a new dashboard), pass initial data via data-* attributes or an API. Slowly replace jQuery parts.

q: React 19 highlights?
a: Actions + useActionState, useOptimistic, use(), ref as a prop, Server Components, React Compiler (automatic memoization).

q: Explain the Virtual DOM — what problem does it actually solve, and what's the real mechanism, not just 'it's faster'?
a:
Directly changing the actual page (DOM) is expensive because the browser has to recalculate layout/style/drawing on every change. React's Virtual DOM is a lightweight, in-memory JavaScript copy of the actual page structure — when something changes, React builds a new virtual version, compares it against the previous one (called 'reconciliation' or 'diffing'), figures out the minimal set of actual page changes needed, and applies only those — grouped together — to the real page.

The performance win isn't 'the Virtual DOM is inherently faster than the real DOM' (it isn't, on its own) — it's that comparing in memory and grouping minimal real changes is faster than naively redoing/changing the page on every single individual update.

q: What's React Fiber, and why did React need to rewrite its comparison engine around it?
a:
Fiber (introduced in React 16) changed how React compares old and new versions — from a synchronous, all-at-once, uninterruptible process into one that can pause and resume. The old approach would walk the entire component tree in one uninterrupted pass, which could block the browser long enough to cause visible stutter on big updates.

Fiber treats each component as a unit of work in a structure React can pause, prioritize, resume, or throw away — this is the foundation that makes features like handling multiple updates smartly, breaking work into small chunks, and prioritizing urgent updates (like user typing) over less urgent ones (like a large list re-drawing) actually possible.

q: Walk through what actually happens when a state updater from useState is called — is it instant?
a:
Historically (and still, inside React's own event handlers), state updates are grouped together — several updates within the same event handler are collected and applied together in a single re-draw, not one re-draw per update, for performance. Since React 18, this grouping was extended to cover more situations (promises, timers, native event handlers) automatically, whereas before, updates outside React's own event handlers (like inside a timer) weren't grouped by default.

The state update itself doesn't change the current value right away — it schedules a re-draw, which is why reading the state variable immediately after calling its setter still shows the old value within that same piece of code.

q: Why does React need a stable key on list items — what actually breaks without one?
a: During comparison, React uses key to match items in the new version against items in the old one, so it can tell 'this is the same logical item, just possibly moved/updated' versus 'this is a brand new item.' Without a stable key (or using the array position as a key when the list can reorder/filter), React can misidentify which page element matches which logical item across an update — leading to component state (like a text box's current value, or internal component state) getting attached to the wrong item after a reorder, plus unnecessary re-draws/changes since React can't confidently tell what actually moved versus what's genuinely new.

q: Explain the Rules of Hooks (why hooks must be called every time, in the same order) — what's the actual mechanism that requires this?
a:
React tracks each hook's stored data internally by call order, not by name — each component instance has an associated list of hook data, and each useState/useEffect/etc. call is matched to its corresponding stored data purely by the position it's called in during that render. If a hook is called conditionally (skipped on some renders), this position-based matching breaks — a later hook's data could get matched to an earlier hook's slot, silently corrupting the component's state.

This is a direct result of how it's actually built, not an arbitrary style rule — understanding why is what makes the rule make sense instead of just feeling like a rule to memorize.

q: What's actually different between useEffect and useLayoutEffect — when does each one actually run relative to the browser drawing the page?
a: useEffect runs after the browser has already drawn the updated page to the screen — the user may briefly see the state before the effect ran. useLayoutEffect runs right after page changes but before the browser draws — blocking the drawing until it finishes. This matters for anything that needs to measure or instantly adjust the page before the user sees it (like measuring an element's size and repositioning something based on that, to avoid a visible flicker) — that specific kind of problem needs useLayoutEffect; nearly everything else (fetching data, subscriptions, most side effects) should use useEffect, since blocking the drawing unnecessarily hurts how fast the page feels.

q: Explain closures in the context of React hooks — what's the 'stale closure' bug, and why does it happen?
a:
Every render of a function component creates a fresh closure (a function that remembers its surroundings) using that render's specific props/state values — a function defined inside a component (including a callback passed to useEffect) captures the variables as they existed at the moment that render's code ran. A 'stale closure' bug happens when an effect or callback captures a value from an earlier render and keeps using that old value across later renders — usually because a useEffect's dependency list is missing a value it actually depends on, so the effect doesn't re-run (and re-capture the current values) when that value changes.

This is exactly why the ESLint 'exhaustive-deps' rule exists — it's catching a real correctness issue, not just a style preference.

q: What do React.memo/useMemo/useCallback actually do, and when does using them hurt rather than help?
a:
React.memo wraps a component and skips re-rendering it if its inputs are unchanged from the previous render. useMemo saves a calculated value between renders, only recalculating when its dependencies change. useCallback saves a function itself (important because a new inline function is created on every render by default, which would break React.memo's comparison on any child receiving that function as an input).

Memoization (saving/reusing results) hurts when the comparison/saving overhead costs more than just redoing the work — for cheap components or cheap calculations, useMemo/useCallback add real overhead (the comparison itself, plus memory for storing the result) without meaningful benefit, which is why memoizing everything by default is a common junior mistake, not a best practice.

q: Explain the Context API's re-render behavior — what's the actual mechanism, and why is it a common performance trap in a large app?
a: When a Context Provider's value changes, every component using that context re-renders, whether or not the specific piece of data that component actually uses changed — Context doesn't do fine-grained tracking of specific fields within the value by default. This becomes a real performance trap in a large app where many components use one large, frequently-changing context object — a more targeted state-management approach (splitting context into smaller, more specific providers, or using a tool with fine-grained tracking) is the actual fix, not just 'avoid Context,' since Context itself is fine for genuinely global, rarely-changing data (like a theme or the logged-in user).

q: In a React app talking to a WebSocket-based real-time backend (like your HOLOIN dashboard), what are the actual React-specific challenges of connecting an outside, non-React data source?
a:
React's rendering model expects updates to flow through its own state/props system — a WebSocket connection pushing data from outside React needs to be deliberately connected into that system (typically through useEffect to subscribe when the component mounts and clean up when it unmounts, saving incoming messages into component state so React re-renders properly) rather than changing the page directly from the WebSocket callback, which would bypass React's whole comparison system and lead to inconsistent state.

High-frequency updates (like live device readings) also need explicit slowing down/grouping on the frontend — pushing every single incoming message straight into state can cause excessive re-renders, so it's common to buffer/group incoming real-time data (like updating state at most every so many milliseconds) instead of triggering a re-render per message.

q: What is Vue, and how does it compare to React in one minute?
a: Vue is a progressive JavaScript framework for building UIs with components. Both use components, a virtual DOM (Vue can also skip it — see Vapor Mode) and one-way data flow. Differences: Vue uses HTML-based templates with directives (v-if, v-for, v-model) instead of JSX, has built-in reactivity (change a value and the UI updates — no setState), and ships official router (Vue Router) and state library (Pinia). Vue is popular in the Laravel world and easy to learn if you know React.

q: Show a Vue 3 component with <script setup>.
a:
<script setup>
import { ref, computed } from 'vue'
const props = defineProps({ start: { type: Number, default: 0 } })
const emit = defineEmits(['changed'])
const count = ref(props.start)
const double = computed(() => count.value * 2)
function inc() { count.value++; emit('changed', count.value) }
</script>

<template>
  <button @click="inc">{{ count }} (double: {{ double }})</button>
</template>

ref makes a reactive value (use .value in script, not in the template), computed is a cached derived value, props come in with defineProps, events go out with defineEmits.

q: Options API vs Composition API?
a: Options API groups code by type (data, methods, computed, watch) — easy for beginners, and common in Vue 2 code. Composition API (setup, ref, reactive) groups code by feature and makes logic reusable through composables — the standard for new Vue 3 apps, and closer to React hooks.

q: ref vs reactive?
a: ref wraps any value (including primitives) and is accessed with .value; it's the recommended default. reactive makes an object deeply reactive without .value, but you lose reactivity if you destructure it or replace the whole object — use toRefs() when destructuring.

q: Key directives?1 follow-up
a:
v-if / v-else (render or not), v-show (toggle CSS display), v-for="item in items" :key="item.id", v-bind / : (bind attributes and props), v-on / @ (events, with modifiers like @submit.prevent), v-model (two-way binding, with .trim, .number, .lazy), v-slot / # (slots).

Cross-questionv-if vs v-show?

v-if adds/removes elements (cheaper when rarely shown); v-show keeps them and toggles display (cheaper when toggled often).

q: computed vs watch vs watchEffect?
a: computed — derive a value from state (cached, no side effects). watch — run a side effect when a specific source changes, with old and new values (e.g. fetch results when search changes). watchEffect — runs immediately and re-runs when anything it uses changes. Prefer computed for data; use watchers only for side effects.

q: Vue component lifecycle hooks?
