a: onBeforeMount, onMounted (DOM ready — fetch data, init third-party libraries), onBeforeUpdate, onUpdated, onBeforeUnmount, onUnmounted (clean up timers, listeners, sockets). Similar to React's useEffect with cleanup.

q: How do components communicate in Vue?
a: Props down, events up (emit); v-model on components (defineModel() in Vue 3.4+); slots for passing markup; provide / inject for deep trees; Pinia stores for shared app state.

q: What is Pinia, and how does it compare to Vuex?
a:
Pinia is Vue's official state-management library (it replaced Vuex). A store has state, getters and actions, no mutations, full TypeScript support and devtools integration:

export const useCartStore = defineStore('cart', () => {
  const items = ref([])
  const total = computed(() => items.value.reduce((s, i) => s + i.price * i.qty, 0))
  function add(item) { items.value.push(item) }
  return { items, total, add }
})

q: What are composables?
a:
Functions that use Vue's Composition API to package reusable, stateful logic — Vue's version of custom React hooks:

export function useFetch(url) {
  const data = ref(null), error = ref(null), loading = ref(true)
  fetch(url).then(r => r.json()).then(d => data.value = d).catch(e => error.value = e).finally(() => loading.value = false)
  return { data, error, loading }
}

Naming convention: useSomething. VueUse is a popular library of ready-made composables.

q: What is Inertia.js, and why do Laravel teams use it?
a: Inertia lets you build a single-page app with Vue or React using normal Laravel routes and controllers — no separate API. A controller returns Inertia::render('Posts/Index', ['posts' => $posts]); Inertia loads the Posts/Index page component with those props. Navigation happens over XHR, so it feels like an SPA while auth, validation, routing and authorization stay in Laravel.

q: How do forms and validation work with Inertia?
a:
<script setup>
import { useForm } from '@inertiajs/vue3'
const form = useForm({ title: '', body: '' })
const submit = () => form.post('/posts', { onSuccess: () => form.reset() })
</script>
<template>
  <form @submit.prevent="submit">
    <input v-model="form.title" />
    <p v-if="form.errors.title">{{ form.errors.title }}</p>
    <button :disabled="form.processing">Save</button>
  </form>
</template>

Laravel validates as usual; on failure Inertia redirects back and the errors appear in form.errors automatically — no 422 JSON handling needed.

q: Inertia concepts you should know?
a: Shared data (HandleInertiaRequests middleware — current user, flash messages on every page), partial reloads (router.reload({ only: ['posts'] })), lazy/deferred props for slow data, persistent layouts (layout doesn't re-mount between pages), <Link> for SPA navigation, SSR support for SEO, and Ziggy for using Laravel route names in JavaScript. Inertia 2 added deferred props, polling, prefetching and infinite scrolling helpers.

q: Vue + Laravel as a separate SPA vs Inertia vs Livewire?
a: Separate SPA + API (Sanctum): needed for mobile apps or third-party API users. Inertia + Vue: one app, Laravel routing, rich Vue UI — the most common Laravel + Vue setup today. Livewire: no JavaScript framework at all, PHP components. Laravel's official starter kits offer Vue, React and Livewire versions.

q: Vue Router basics?
a: Define routes ({ path: '/posts/:id', component: PostShow }), use <RouterLink> and <RouterView>, read params with useRoute(), navigate with useRouter().push(), lazy-load routes with component: () => import('./Post.vue'), and protect pages with navigation guards (router.beforeEach checking auth). With Inertia you don't need Vue Router — Laravel handles routing.

q: Moving from Vue 2 to Vue 3 — what changed?
a: Composition API and <script setup>, multiple root nodes allowed, new reactivity based on Proxies (no more Vue.set), v-model changes on components, filters removed, event bus pattern removed, Vuex → Pinia, Vue CLI → Vite. Vue 2 reached end of life at the end of 2023, so older projects should be upgraded.

q: What's new in Vue?
a: Vue 3.5 is the stable line (smaller, faster reactivity, reactive props destructure, useTemplateRef, defineModel). Vue 3.6 introduces Vapor Mode, an opt-in compilation mode that skips the virtual DOM per component (<script setup vapor>), still labelled unstable in beta as of mid-2026. Nuxt is the Vue meta-framework (like Next.js for React).

q: I'm a React developer — how do I answer Vue questions honestly?
a: Map concepts: useState → ref, useMemo → computed, useEffect → watch/onMounted, custom hooks → composables, Context → provide/inject, Redux/Zustand → Pinia, Next.js → Nuxt, props/children → props/slots. Say what you've built with React, show you understand Vue's equivalents, and name a small Vue/Inertia project you've done to practise.

q: What is TypeScript, and what does it actually give a team?1 follow-up
a:
TypeScript is JavaScript plus a type system that's checked at build time and then removed — the browser still runs plain JavaScript. It catches mistakes before runtime (wrong property names, missing fields, undefined access), powers autocomplete and safe refactoring, and documents what functions expect.

Cross-questionDoes TypeScript protect you at runtime?

No. Data from an API, a form or JSON.parse can still be anything. Validate untrusted data at runtime (Zod, Valibot) and derive types from the schema.

q: Basic types you use daily?
a: string, number, boolean, arrays (string[] or Array<string>), tuples ([string, number]), object types, union types ('draft' | 'published'), null/undefined, unknown, any, never, void, function types ((id: number) => Promise<User>), optional properties (email?: string), readonly.

q: interface vs type?
a: Both describe object shapes. interface can be extended with extends and merged (declaration merging) — useful for public library types. type can also express unions, intersections, tuples, mapped and conditional types. Many teams use type by default and interface for objects that others extend. Be consistent.

q: any vs unknown vs never?
a:
any switches type checking off — avoid it. unknown means "could be anything, check first" — safe for API responses and catch errors:

function parse(input: unknown) {
  if (typeof input === 'string') return input.toUpperCase(); // narrowed to string
  throw new Error('Expected string');
}

never is a value that can't exist — used for exhaustive checks and functions that always throw.

q: What is type narrowing? Give examples.
a:
TypeScript refines a union type based on checks: typeof x === 'string', x instanceof Date, 'email' in user, truthiness checks, and discriminated unions:

type Result = { status: 'ok'; data: User[] } | { status: 'error'; message: string };
function show(r: Result) {
  if (r.status === 'ok') return r.data.length;   // r is the ok branch here
  return r.message;
}

Custom type guards: function isUser(x: unknown): x is User { ... }.

q: Explain generics with a practical example.
a:
Generics let a function or type work with many types while keeping them connected:

async function getJson<T>(url: string): Promise<T> {
  const res = await fetch(url);
  if (!res.ok) throw new Error(`HTTP ${res.status}`);
  return res.json() as Promise<T>;
}
const orders = await getJson<Order[]>('/api/orders');   // orders: Order[]

type Paginated<T> = { data: T[]; meta: { current_page: number; last_page: number } };

Constraints: function byId<T extends { id: number }>(items: T[], id: number) { ... }.

q: Utility types you actually use?
a:
Partial<T> (all optional — update forms), Required<T>, Readonly<T>, Pick<T, 'id' | 'name'>, Omit<T, 'password'>, Record<K, V> (dictionaries), ReturnType<typeof fn>, Parameters<typeof fn>, Awaited<T>, NonNullable<T>, Extract/Exclude for unions.

type UserForm = Omit<User, 'id' | 'created_at'>;
type UserUpdate = Partial<UserForm>;

q: as assertions vs satisfies?
a:
as tells the compiler "trust me" — it can hide real bugs. satisfies checks a value matches a type without widening it, so you keep the exact inferred types:

const routes = { home: '/', orders: '/orders' } satisfies Record<string, string>;
routes.orders; // still known exactly

q: Type a React component and hook.
a:
type Props = { user: User; onSave: (u: User) => Promise<void>; children?: React.ReactNode };
export function UserCard({ user, onSave, children }: Props) { ... }

function useLocalState<T>(key: string, initial: T) {
  const [value, setValue] = useState<T>(initial);
  return [value, setValue] as const;   // tuple, not (T | Dispatch)[]
}

Events: React.ChangeEvent<HTMLInputElement>, React.FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>; refs: useRef<HTMLInputElement>(null).

q: How do you share types between a Laravel API and a TypeScript frontend?
a: Options: write the types by hand next to the API client; generate them from an OpenAPI spec (e.g. openapi-typescript); generate from Laravel with packages like spatie/laravel-typescript-transformer (DTOs and enums → TS); or define Zod schemas on the frontend and infer types from them, which also validates responses at runtime.

q: Important tsconfig.json settings?
a: strict: true (turns on strictNullChecks, noImplicitAny and more — always use it), noUncheckedIndexedAccess (array/object index returns T | undefined), target/module/moduleResolution (bundler for Vite projects), paths for import aliases, skipLibCheck, isolatedModules, noEmit when a bundler does the compiling.

q: Enums vs union of string literals?
a:
String literal unions (type Status = 'draft' | 'paid') disappear at runtime and work well with JSON — most teams prefer them. TypeScript enums generate runtime code and don't work with Node's built-in type stripping; if you need a runtime list, use an as const object:

export const Status = { Draft: 'draft', Paid: 'paid' } as const;
export type Status = typeof Status[keyof typeof Status];

q: Typing an Express or Node API?
a: Type request bodies, params and responses (Request<Params, ResBody, ReqBody>), validate the body with Zod before trusting it, share DTO types between routes and services, and type environment variables at startup (parse process.env with Zod once). NestJS uses TypeScript classes and decorators throughout.

q: Migrating a JavaScript project to TypeScript — how?
a: Add tsconfig.json with allowJs, rename files gradually from .js to .ts/.tsx starting with shared utilities and API clients, add types for API responses first (biggest win), enable strict early for new files, avoid spreading any, and add tsc --noEmit to CI so type errors block merges.

q: What's new in TypeScript?
a: TypeScript 7.0 was released in 2026 with a native compiler written in Go ("Project Corsa") — typically about 8–12× faster builds and lower memory. It turns on strict by default and drops old options such as target: es5, baseUrl and moduleResolution: node10. TypeScript 6.0 was the bridge release that warns about those deprecations — fix its warnings first, then upgrade. Node.js can also run .ts files directly by stripping types (no enums or other TS-only runtime syntax).

q: How do I honestly describe limited TypeScript experience?
a: Say what's true: "My production React is mostly JavaScript. I use TypeScript for typing props, API responses and hooks, and I understand generics, unions and narrowing. I'd be productive on a TypeScript codebase quickly and I'd lean on strict mode and code review in the first weeks." Then show it — for example, a small typed API client you built for practice.

q: Why Next.js instead of plain React (Vite)?
a: Built-in routing, server-side rendering, static generation, SEO, image optimization, API routes, server components, and easy deployment. Plain React is fine for dashboards behind a login where SEO doesn't matter.

q: CSR vs SSR vs SSG vs ISR?1 follow-up
a:
• CSR — browser renders everything; slow first load, bad SEO.
  • SSR — HTML built on each request; fresh data, good SEO, more server cost.
  • SSG — HTML built at build time; fastest, but data can be old.
  • ISR — static page that regenerates in the background after X seconds or on demand.

Cross-questionProduct page for an eCommerce site with 50,000 products — which one?

SSG/ISR for the page with on-demand revalidation when a product changes; stock/price fetched fresh or streamed.

q: App Router vs Pages Router?
a: App Router (app/ folder) uses Server Components by default, nested layouts, loading.js, error.js, streaming, and Server Actions. Pages Router (pages/) is older with getServerSideProps/getStaticProps. New projects use App Router.

q: What are Server Actions?1 follow-up
a:
Functions marked 'use server' that you can call from a form or button; they run on the server (e.g., save to DB). No need to write a separate API route.

Cross-questionAre they secure by default?

No! They're public endpoints. You must check authentication and validate input inside every action.

q: How does caching work in Next.js?1 follow-up
a:
This changed a lot. In Next.js 15, fetch stopped being cached by default. In Next.js 16, the new model is Cache Components with the "use cache" directive — you opt in to caching explicitly, and use cacheLife / cacheTag and revalidateTag to control it. Partial Prerendering (static shell + streamed dynamic parts) is now the main model.

Tip

Say "caching is opt-in now, I mark what should be cached" — this shows you're up to date.

q: Middleware / proxy in Next.js?1 follow-up
a:
Code that runs before a request finishes — redirects, auth checks, locale detection. In Next.js 16 middleware.ts was renamed to proxy.ts to make its role clearer.

Cross-questionShould you do all auth checks in middleware?

No. Use it for quick redirects, but always verify auth again close to the data (in the server component, route handler, or action). A 2025 security issue showed middleware alone isn't a safe wall.

q: next/image benefits?
a: Automatic resizing, modern formats (WebP/AVIF), lazy loading, prevents layout shift with width/height.

q: How do you handle env variables?
a: .env.local for secrets. Only variables starting with NEXT_PUBLIC_ go to the browser — never put secrets there.

q: Hydration error — what is it and how do you fix it?
a: Server HTML doesn't match what React renders on the client. Common causes: Date.now(), Math.random(), window checks in render, invalid HTML nesting (<div> inside <p>), browser extensions. Fix: move browser-only code into useEffect, use dynamic import with ssr: false, or make server and client render the same thing.

q: Next.js with a Laravel backend — how would you structure it?
a: Next.js as frontend (SEO pages + app UI), Laravel as the API. Auth via Laravel Sanctum (cookie-based for same top-level domain, or tokens). Next server components call Laravel with the user's cookie/token. Keep business logic in Laravel; Next.js only for rendering and light BFF (backend-for-frontend) work.

q: Latest Next.js updates (2025–2026)?
a: Next.js 16 (late 2025): Turbopack as default bundler, Cache Components / "use cache", proxy.ts, React Compiler support, React 19.2 features. 16.2 (March 2026) added a stable Adapter API for deploying on different platforms. 16.3 (August 2026) focused on "instant navigations". Next.js also moved to a formal monthly security release process in mid-2026 — so keeping versions patched matters.

q: What is semantic HTML and why does it matter?1 follow-up
a:
Using the right tags — header, nav, main, article, section, button — instead of div everywhere. Helps SEO, screen readers (accessibility), and code readability.

Cross-questionWhy not a div with onClick as a button?

No keyboard focus, no Enter/Space support, screen readers don't announce it. Use <button>.

q: Flexbox vs Grid?
a: Flexbox = one direction (row or column), good for navbars and aligning items. Grid = two dimensions (rows and columns), good for page layouts and card galleries.

q: How do you make a site responsive?
a: Mobile-first CSS, media queries (Tailwind sm: md: lg:), relative units (rem, %, vw), flexible images (max-width: 100%), the viewport meta tag, and container queries for components.

q: CSS specificity?
a: Inline style > ID > class/attribute/pseudo-class > element. !important overrides all (avoid it).

q: Why Tailwind? What are the downsides?2 follow-ups
a:
Pros: fast building, consistent design system, no naming fights, unused CSS removed at build → tiny file. Cons: long class lists, HTML looks messy, learning curve.

Cross-questionHow do you avoid repeating the same 20 classes?

Make a React component (<Button>), use clsx/tailwind-merge for conditional classes, or @apply sparingly.

Cross-questionHow do you do dark mode in Tailwind?

dark: variant, with class-based or media-based strategy.

q: What's new in Tailwind v4?
a: Released early 2025. CSS-first configuration (you configure with @theme inside CSS instead of a big tailwind.config.js), a much faster engine, automatic content detection, native cascade layers, container queries built in, and a single @import "tailwindcss" to start.

q: Accessibility basics you follow?
a: Alt text on images, labels on inputs, good color contrast, keyboard navigation, focus states visible, ARIA only when native HTML isn't enough.

q: How do you avoid layout shift (CLS)?
a: Set width/height on images and videos, reserve space for ads/embeds, use font-display: swap with fallback fonts sized similarly, don't insert content above existing content.

q: Semantic HTML5 tags?
a: header, nav, main, section, article, aside, footer, figure. Better SEO and accessibility.

q: Bootstrap grid system?
a:
12-column grid inside .container → .row → .col-*. Breakpoints: sm ≥576, md ≥768, lg ≥992, xl ≥1200, xxl ≥1400.

<div class="container"><div class="row">
  <div class="col-12 col-md-6 col-lg-4">Card</div>
</div></div>

Means: full width on mobile, half on tablet, one-third on desktop.

q: Bootstrap 4 vs Bootstrap 5?1 follow-up
a:
Bootstrap 5 dropped jQuery (uses plain JS), dropped IE support, added xxl breakpoint, utilities API, RTL support (useful for Urdu/Arabic), data-bs-* attributes instead of data-*, form classes changed (form-group removed → use spacing utilities like mb-3). Current version is 5.3 with built-in dark mode (data-bs-theme="dark").

Cross-questionYou upgraded to BS5 and modals stopped opening — why?

Old data-toggle/data-target must become data-bs-toggle/data-bs-target, and jQuery plugin calls like $('#modal').modal('show') need the new JS API (bootstrap.Modal.getOrCreateInstance(el).show()).

q: How do you customize Bootstrap?
a: Override Sass variables ($primary) before importing Bootstrap and compile, or override CSS variables (--bs-primary). Don't edit Bootstrap's own files.

q: Bootstrap vs Tailwind?
a: Bootstrap: ready-made components (navbar, modal, cards), very fast to build admin panels, sites look similar. Tailwind: utility classes, fully custom designs, smaller final CSS.

q: In CSS layouts, when would you choose Flexbox over Grid, or the reverse?
a: Flexbox = one direction; Grid = rows and columns.

q: Position values?
a: static (default), relative (moves relative to itself, parent for absolute children), absolute (relative to nearest positioned parent), fixed (relative to screen), sticky (sticks when scrolling).

q: Make a site responsive?
a: Viewport meta tag, mobile-first, media queries/Bootstrap grid, responsive images (img-fluid), test on real devices and Chrome DevTools.

q: Canvas vs SVG — when which?
a: SVG: each shape is a DOM element, sharp at any zoom, easy events and CSS, great for fewer objects (up to a few thousand) and exporting vectors. Canvas: you draw pixels, super fast for many objects, animations, image filters — but you manage hit-testing yourself (libraries do this for you). WebGL (Three.js/PixiJS) for massive counts or 3D.

q: Fabric.js vs Konva vs Paper.js vs D3?
a:
• Fabric.js — object model on canvas, built-in selection, resize/rotate controls, text editing, JSON serialize/deserialize, SVG import/export. Great for Canva-like editors.
  • Konva (+ react-konva) — layers, very good performance, clean React integration, drag & drop, Transformer tool.
  • Paper.js — vector math, paths, boolean operations (great for illustration tools).
  • D3 — data-driven charts/visualizations, not an editor library.

q: How would you architect a layer-based editor in React?2 follow-ups
a:
• Single source of truth: a document model in a store (Zustand/Redux) — { layers: [{id, type, x, y, rotation, props, zIndex, locked, visible}], selection: [] }.
  • The canvas library renders from state; user actions dispatch commands that update state.
  • Keep high-frequency drag updates out of React re-renders (update the canvas node directly during drag, commit to state on dragend).
  • Layers panel = a list from the same state (drag-to-reorder changes zIndex).
  • Autosave with debounce to the Laravel API; versioning on the backend.

Cross-questionHow do you implement undo/redo?

Command pattern (each action has do and undo) or keep a history stack of state snapshots/patches (Immer patches are small). Limit history size. Group continuous actions (one drag = one undo step).

Cross-questionReal-time preview?

Render immediately on the client; for server-side previews (e.g., print output) debounce and generate low-res preview via a queue job, or render thumbnails with canvas.toDataURL() on the client.

q: Performance tips for canvas editors?
a: Multiple layers (static background layer vs. interactive layer), cache complex shapes as bitmaps, requestAnimationFrame for rendering, throttle mousemove, disable hit-detection on non-interactive objects, virtualize the layers panel, handle devicePixelRatio for sharp retina rendering, use OffscreenCanvas/Web Workers for heavy image processing.

q: Exporting — PNG, PDF, SVG for print?1 follow-up
a:
Client: toDataURL/toSVG for quick exports. For print-quality (high DPI, CMYK, bleed, exact fonts), generate on the server in a queue job — e.g., headless Chrome (Browsershot/Puppeteer) or a PDF library — then upload to S3 and notify the user.

Cross-questionFonts look different on server export?

Fonts must be installed/embedded on the server and loaded with the same files; wait for fonts to load before rendering on client (document.fonts.ready).

q: Coordinates, zoom, and pan?
a: Keep a transform (scale + offset). Convert between screen coordinates and canvas "world" coordinates. Zoom toward the mouse pointer by adjusting the offset. Store layer positions in world units, never screen pixels.

q: Collaboration (multiple users editing)?
a: WebSockets (Laravel Reverb / Pusher) to broadcast changes; conflict handling via last-write-wins per property, operational transform, or CRDTs (Yjs) for true real-time collaboration.

q: What's the difference between $this and self:: in a class?
a: $this points to the actual object you're working with right now, and it correctly follows the real (child) class if one exists. self:: points to the class where that code was written — even inside a class that gets extended, self:: still means the parent class, not the child. static:: is the version of self:: that does look at the real runtime class, like $this does.

q: Explain the 4 pillars of OOP with real examples.
a:
Encapsulation: hiding raw data behind Eloquent's accessors/mutators instead of exposing table columns directly. Inheritance: a base ApiController that handles the standard JSON response, which other controllers extend. Polymorphism: a shared interface (like NotificationChannel) implemented by email/SMS/push classes, all called the same way.

Abstraction: service classes (like the Shopify sync service) that hide complicated integration logic behind one simple method the controller calls.

q: Abstract class vs interface — what's the difference, and when do you use each?
a: An interface is just a list of method names with no actual code — a class can implement many interfaces. An abstract class can have real shared code plus some abstract (empty) methods — but a class can only extend one abstract class. I use an interface when different, unrelated classes need to follow the same rules (like Stripe and Square both following a Payment interface). I use an abstract class when there's real shared logic I don't want to repeat in every subclass.

q: What are traits in PHP, and what problem do they solve?
a: Traits let you reuse the same method code in different classes, without using inheritance — this matters because PHP only allows one parent class per class. If two unrelated classes both need the same feature (like a HasUuid trait that auto-generates an ID), a trait lets you share that code without forcing a fake parent-child relationship.

q: == vs === — why does it matter for security?
a: == compares values after converting types if needed (loose comparison); === compares both type and value exactly, with no conversion. This has caused real security bugs — for example, a password hash starting with '0e' could get wrongly read as scientific notation for zero, tricking a loose comparison into treating two different hashes as equal (this was a real bug before PHP 8). I always use === unless I specifically want type conversion.

q: What are PHP generators, and when would you use one instead of an array?
a: A generator (using the yield keyword) gives you values one at a time as needed, instead of building the whole list in memory first. I'd use this for very large datasets — like exporting millions of rows — where storing everything in an array at once would use too much memory. A generator keeps memory usage low no matter how big the data is.

q: What is autoloading in PHP, and what does composer dump-autoload do?
a: PHP calls a special function to load a class file automatically when that class is used but not yet loaded. Composer sets this up using the PSR-4 standard, which maps class names to file locations, and saves this mapping in files under vendor/composer for speed (instead of searching folders every time). Running composer dump-autoload rebuilds that map — needed after adding new classes in ways Composer didn't automatically detect, like after cloning a fresh copy of the project or moving files manually.

q: What is dependency injection, and why does it help with testing?
a: Instead of a class creating the things it needs by itself, those things are given to it from outside (through the constructor, a method, or a container). This helps testing because you can swap in a fake/mock version of a dependency without touching the class itself. It also means classes don't depend on one specific implementation — which is how I was able to swap Stripe for Square behind a shared interface without changing any code that calls it.

q: What is PHP and how does it run?
a: A server-side scripting language. The browser sends a request → web server (Apache/Nginx) passes it to PHP (via PHP-FPM or mod_php) → PHP runs the code, maybe talks to MySQL → sends back HTML/JSON. PHP runs fresh for every request (it's "stateless" — nothing stays in memory between requests, unless you use Octane/Swoole).

q: echo vs print vs print_r vs var_dump?
a: echo outputs strings (faster, multiple args). print returns 1, one arg. print_r shows arrays in readable form. var_dump shows type and length too — best for debugging.
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)

q: include vs require vs include_once vs require_once?1 follow-up
a:
require stops the script with a fatal error if the file is missing; include only gives a warning and continues. _once versions make sure the file loads only one time (avoids "function already declared").

Cross-questionWhich one for a config/database file?

require_once, because the app can't work without it.
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)

q: == vs === in PHP?
a: === checks value and type. == converts types first. In PHP 8, 0 == "abc" is false (in PHP 7 it was true — a famous change).
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)

q: Superglobals?1 follow-up
a:
$_GET, $_POST, $_REQUEST, $_SERVER, $_SESSION, $_COOKIE, $_FILES, $_ENV, $GLOBALS.

Cross-questionWhy avoid $_REQUEST?

It mixes GET, POST and cookies, so you don't know where data came from.
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)

q: GET vs POST?
a: GET: data in URL, visible, cached, bookmarkable, limited length — use for reading/search. POST: data in body, not in URL, for creating/changing data and file uploads. POST is not "secure" by itself — use HTTPS.
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)

q: Sessions vs cookies?1 follow-up
a:
Cookie: small data stored in the browser. Session: data stored on the server; the browser only keeps a session ID cookie (PHPSESSID). Sessions are safer for login data.

Cross-questionHow do you secure sessions?

session_regenerate_id(true) after login (stops session fixation), cookies with HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite, session timeout, destroy on logout.
c: Core PHP (Most Important for This Role)
