q: What actually happens when a PHP script runs — walk through it at the engine level, not the framework level.
a:
PHP source code first goes through the lexer, which breaks it into small pieces called tokens, then the parser, which builds a tree structure (an AST) from those pieces. The compiler then walks that tree and generates 'opcodes' — a low-level set of instructions, kind of like a simplified machine language. The Zend Virtual Machine then runs those opcodes one after another.

Without OPcache, this entire lex-parse-compile process runs on every single request — which is why OPcache (saving the compiled opcodes in shared memory, tied to the file and its last-modified time) is such a big performance win in production: it skips straight to running the code on future requests instead of redoing all that work.

q: Explain PHP's memory management — how does garbage collection actually work?
a:
PHP mainly uses reference counting — every internal value container keeps count of how many things point to it, and when that count hits zero, the memory is freed right away. The one thing reference counting alone can't solve is circular references (object A points to B, B points to A, and nothing outside points to either) — those would leak memory forever under pure reference counting.

PHP's cycle collector (added in PHP 5.3) periodically runs a separate check specifically to find and break these reference cycles, so PHP doesn't need a full generational garbage collector like some other languages — it's a mix: immediate counting for the normal case, and periodic cleanup for the tricky case.

q: What's the actual difference between passing by value and passing by reference in PHP, and what's a real performance/correctness effect?
a:
By default, PHP passes by value — but behind the scenes, PHP uses 'copy-on-write': passing a large array to a function doesn't actually copy the data right away, it copies a reference to the same underlying value and increases a counter; the actual copy only happens the moment either side changes the data. Passing by reference (&$var) skips this entirely — both sides share the exact same value, so a change inside the function is visible outside immediately.

The performance takeaway: for large read-only data, PHP is already efficient by default (copy-on-write avoids the copy); passing by reference is really about intentionally sharing changes, not mainly a speed trick — using it for speed when you don't actually need shared changes just makes the code harder to follow.

q: What's the difference between == and === at a deeper level than 'one checks type' — what actually happens when comparing mismatched types with ==?
a: PHP applies type-conversion rules to make the two things comparable — for example, comparing a string to a number makes PHP try to convert the string to a number (with well-known surprising results, especially before PHP 8, like a text string being treated as equal to zero because of how the conversion worked). PHP 8 tightened several of these comparison rules specifically because they were a common source of subtle bugs and security problems (like in login/password-hash checks). === skips conversion entirely — it only returns true if both the type and the value match, which is why senior PHP developers default to === unless conversion is specifically and deliberately wanted.

q: Explain how PHP closures (anonymous functions) actually capture variables — what's the difference between capturing by value and by reference, and why does it matter in a loop?
a: use ($var) captures by value — a snapshot of $var's value at the moment the closure is created, copied into the closure's own private scope. use (&$var) captures by reference — the closure shares the exact same variable, so later changes to $var outside the closure show up inside it too. This causes a classic bug specifically in loops: creating several closures inside a loop that each do use (&$var) on the loop variable means all the closures end up referencing the same final value of $var after the loop finishes, not the value at each individual step — fixed by capturing by value instead, or explicitly passing the current step's value in as a parameter.

q: What's a PHP generator, and how is it fundamentally different from returning an array?
a: A generator (using the yield keyword) doesn't calculate and hold the entire result in memory at once — it produces values one at a time, pausing its progress between each value and picking back up exactly where it left off when the next value is asked for. This matters a lot for memory: going through a huge dataset (like millions of database rows) with a generator keeps memory usage flat, since only one item is in memory at a time, while returning a full array means holding the entire result in memory all at once.

q: How does PHP's autoloading actually work — what happens when you reference a class that hasn't been loaded yet?
a: PHP calls the registered autoload function(s) whenever an undefined class is used, passing it the class name — the autoloader is then responsible for finding and loading the correct file. Composer's autoloader follows the PSR-4 standard, mapping namespace prefixes to folder paths, so it can figure out the exact file path from the class's full name without scanning the filesystem — that mapping is pre-calculated and saved in files under vendor/composer, which is why running composer dump-autoload is necessary after adding classes in a way Composer's map doesn't automatically pick up.

q: Explain PHP's type system — is PHP 'weakly typed,' and how does that actually show up at runtime versus what type hints do?
a:
PHP is dynamically and (by default) weakly typed — variables don't have a fixed type, and values are converted between types fairly freely in many operations. Type hints (declaring expected types for function parameters/return values) don't fundamentally change this, but they add a runtime check — if declare(strict_types=1) is set, a type mismatch throws an error instead of converting; without strict types, PHP still tries to convert where the types are compatible (like passing the text '5' to a parameter expecting a number).

This is a real architectural decision on any serious codebase — I default to declare(strict_types=1) in new files specifically to avoid the class of bugs where a silent conversion hides a real logic error.

q: What actually happens during a PHP request when using PHP-FPM — how does it differ from the older mod_php model?
a:
PHP-FPM runs as a separate, ongoing pool of worker processes, independent of the web server. Nginx (or Apache set up to forward requests) hands off any PHP request to PHP-FPM over a special protocol, PHP-FPM assigns it to an available worker, that worker runs the script and returns the response, then becomes free for the next request.

This fully separates the web server from PHP — Nginx can serve static files efficiently on its own, while PHP-FPM's worker pool can be tuned (process count, memory limits) independently based on actual PHP workload, which is why FPM is the standard choice over embedding PHP directly into the web server process (the old mod_php Apache model).

q: Explain the difference between self:: and static:: in PHP — what's actually happening with 'late static binding'?
a: self:: always points to the class where the method is written, no matter which subclass actually calls it. static:: uses 'late static binding' — it points to the class that was actually called at runtime, which matters when a base class method needs to create or reference the calling subclass instead of itself. A common real use: a base Model::create() method using new static() so that calling User::create() actually creates a User, not the base Model class, even though create() itself is only written once on the base class.

q: Walk me through what happens from a request hitting public/index.php to a response being returned, in a Laravel 11 app.
a:
index.php loads Composer's autoloader and starts the app from bootstrap/app.php, which creates the service container (Laravel's tool for managing class dependencies). The request goes to the HTTP kernel, which runs startup tasks (error handling, environment detection, config loading) and then passes the request through the global middleware stack — session handling, CSRF security checks, maintenance-mode checks.

The router matches the request to a route, resolves the controller's dependencies through the service container, runs the controller, and the result is turned into a Response object that flows back out through the middleware (for anything that needs to touch the outgoing response, like adding headers) and gets sent to the browser.

q: What's the difference between the Service Container and a Facade? When do you bind something as a singleton vs. a fresh instance?
a:
The Service Container is the actual engine that manages and builds class dependencies. A Facade is just a shortcut/static-style way to call something the container already manages (like Cache::get() instead of manually fetching the cache manager). I bind something as a singleton when it should be shared and remembered across one request or the whole app — like a config object, a connection pool, or a service wrapping an expensive-to-create client.

I use a fresh instance when the class doesn't need shared state, or when sharing one could cause bugs from leftover state — most everyday classes fall here.

q: You upgraded University Seekers from Laravel 5 to Laravel 8. What were the riskiest breaking changes, and how did you make sure nothing silently broke?
a:
The riskiest areas were changes to the default folder structure for models, the login/authentication scaffolding (moving away from Laravel's old built-in auth controllers), and changes in how Eloquent handled certain database behavior across versions. I went through the official upgrade guide version by version instead of jumping straight from 5 to 8, running the full test suite (and adding missing tests first where coverage was thin) after each step.

For the multilingual and SEO-important pages specifically, I manually checked each page on a staging site, since automated tests didn't cover the rendering/SEO details well.

q: Explain Eloquent's N+1 problem and how you'd find it in code you inherited, without blindly adding ->with() everywhere.
a:
N+1 happens when you load a list (1 query) and then access a related item for each row in a loop, causing one extra query per row (N queries) instead of a single combined query. To find it in old code, I'd turn on query logging or use Laravel Debugbar/Telescope on a staging site, click through the key pages, and look for repeated near-identical queries during one request.

I don't add ->with() everywhere blindly — I only eager-load relationships that are actually used on that page, since loading extra data you don't need wastes memory and can slow requests down.

q: When would you use the Query Builder instead of Eloquent, on a system handling large datasets (like Rentigo's old data or HOLOIN's device data)?
a: For big reporting/summary queries, or when turning tens of thousands of rows into full Eloquent model objects would waste memory and CPU on features I don't need. In HOLOIN specifically, raw summary queries against device readings (like time-bucketed averages) go through the Query Builder or raw SQL instead of Eloquent, because I only need summary numbers back, not full model objects.

q: Explain $fillable vs $guarded, and describe a real mass-assignment risk you've seen or protected against.
a:
$fillable is an allow-list — only those fields can be set in bulk (like Model::create($request->all())). $guarded is a deny-list — everything except those fields can be set in bulk. The classic risk is a form submitting an unexpected field like role or is_admin along with the normal fields, which — without $fillable/$guarded protection — could silently let a user give themselves extra permissions.

In an HR-style system with roles, I always explicitly list $fillable on user-facing models instead of relying on $guarded, so anything not clearly meant to be editable in bulk is blocked by default.

q: How do database transactions work in Laravel? Describe a real situation where you used one.
a: DB::beginTransaction() starts a group of changes; if every step inside succeeds, DB::commit() makes them permanent; if any step fails, I catch it and call DB::rollBack(), which undoes everything since the transaction started. In an order-processing flow (or Rentigo's contract/document workflow), I wrap creating a main record and its related child records in one transaction, so a failure partway through — like inserting order items — never leaves a half-finished order in the database.

q: What's the difference between a Job, an Event/Listener, and an Observer? Give a real example of each.
a:
A Job is a single piece of background work sent to a queue — like sending a batch of alert emails in HOLOIN when a device crosses a warning limit. An Event/Listener pair separates 'something happened' from 'here's what should happen because of it' — like firing a DeviceWentOffline event that several listeners react to independently (log it, notify the customer, update a dashboard flag) without the main code needing to know about all of them.

An Observer centralizes actions tied to a model's lifecycle — like automatically creating an audit log entry whenever a Tenant record is updated, instead of repeating that logic in every controller that touches tenants.

q: How does Laravel's queue system work end-to-end — from dispatch() to a worker picking it up? What if a job keeps failing?
a:
dispatch() packages the job and sends it to a queue system (Redis, database, SQS, etc.). A separate worker process checks that queue, pulls jobs off, and runs their handle() method. If a job throws an error, Laravel retries it based on its configured settings; once retries run out, it moves to the failed_jobs table (or similar), and I can inspect and retry it manually or discard it.

In production I always set up a failed() method on important jobs (like a billing charge) so a permanent failure triggers an alert instead of silently vanishing.

q: You've used Laravel Horizon — what does it solve that plain queue:work doesn't, and how do you watch for failed/stuck jobs in production?
a: Horizon gives a real-time dashboard over Redis-based queues — throughput, wait times, failed jobs, and the ability to set up multiple worker groups and priorities from config instead of managing raw processes by hand. In HOLOIN, I use Horizon's dashboard to watch queue size during busy periods of device data coming in, and I've set up alerts so if the failed-jobs count crosses a limit, or a queue's wait time grows too long, I get notified instead of finding out when a customer complains their dashboard looks outdated.

q: What's Laravel's Scheduler, and how did you use it in HOLOIN or AI-BDM? What's the actual server cron entry that runs it?
a:
The Scheduler lets you define recurring tasks (like ->daily() or ->everyMinute()) inside the app itself instead of managing many separate server cron entries. Only one line is needed on the server: * * * * * cd /path-to-project && php artisan schedule:run — this single line triggers Laravel's own scheduler every minute, which then decides what actually needs to run.

In AI-BDM I use it for regular tasks like refreshing cached summary data or updating the AI's search index on a schedule instead of doing it on every request.

q: Gate vs. Policy vs. Middleware for authorization — which did you use for permissions in HOLOIN?
a: Middleware is best for broad, route-level checks (like 'must be logged in'). Gates are simple checks for actions not tied to a specific record. Policies organize permission logic around a specific model/record and handle complex permission sets better. For HOLOIN's role-based permissions (several roles per customer — admin, operator, viewer — each with different device/dashboard access), I used Policies, since the permission logic needed to be specific to each resource (can this user view/edit this particular customer's devices), not just a handful of simple global rules.

q: What is JWT, and how does token-based login differ from Laravel's default session-based login? Why did HOLOIN need JWT specifically?
a:
A JWT (JSON Web Token) is a signed token that carries information (user ID, roles, expiry) and can be checked without looking up a session on the server, since its signature proves it wasn't tampered with. Session-based login relies on the server remembering the session and a cookie pointing to it, which works well for one web app but doesn't scale cleanly across many separate clients.

HOLOIN needed JWT because it has multiple things using its API — the web dashboard, possibly mobile apps, and device-side login — and a token that doesn't need a shared server memory is easier to check across separate services (including the Python AI layer).

q: How would you organize a Laravel app into 'modules'? What problem does that solve, and what are the trade-offs?
a:
Modularizing means organizing the app into self-contained sections (like Modules/Devices, Modules/Billing, Modules/Tenants), each with its own routes, controllers, models, and database changes, instead of one flat folder for everything. It solves the problem of a large Laravel app becoming hard to manage as it grows — each module can be built, tested, and understood somewhat on its own, and it's a natural stepping stone toward eventually pulling a module out into its own separate service if needed.

The trade-off is extra structure and setup work for genuinely small apps — I'd only add this once a codebase is big enough that a flat structure is actively causing problems, which is exactly where HOLOIN ended up.

q: What's your approach to API versioning in a Laravel app used by both a mobile app and a web frontend at the same time?
a: I version at the URL level (/api/v1/..., /api/v2/...) for clarity, and I avoid breaking an existing version once something depends on it — new fields get added without removing old ones, and truly breaking changes go into a new version while the old one stays alive until everyone has switched. I also use Laravel API Resources so the response shape is defined in one place per version, instead of scattered formatting code across controllers.

q: Describe a production bug you diagnosed involving storage/cache file permissions on a Laravel API server.
a:
The API started throwing occasional server errors on file writes — logs and Laravel's cache folder. The cause was that a deployment step had run as a different server user than the actual web server process, leaving the storage and cache folders owned by that other user with restrictive permissions, so the web server couldn't write new logs or compiled views.

I fixed the immediate issue by correcting file ownership/permissions to match the web server user, and prevented it happening again by making the deployment script reset those permissions as its final step, instead of assuming it would happen automatically.

q: How do accessors/mutators differ from casts in Eloquent, and when would you use a custom cast class instead of a simple mutator?
a: Accessors/mutators transform a single field when it's read or set. Casts (the $casts setting) handle type conversion automatically (like turning a database value into an array, a date, or encrypting it) and can be reused across models through a custom cast class. I'd use a custom cast class when the same non-trivial transformation (like converting a stored block of sensor calibration data into a usable object) is needed on more than one model or field, so the logic lives in one reusable place instead of being copied and pasted.

q: Livewire — what problem does it solve compared to plain Blade + AJAX, and where does it fall short compared to a full React app?
a: Livewire lets you build interactive pages using regular server-rendered Blade templates with automatic syncing, without writing a separate JavaScript/API layer just for simple interactivity — it solves the 'I don't want to build a full app just for this form' problem. It falls short compared to React for genuinely complex, highly interactive screens (like a real-time IoT dashboard with live-updating charts), where the back-and-forth cost of Livewire's server calls and its lack of real client-side state management become limiting — that's exactly why HOLOIN's dashboard uses React with WebSockets instead of Livewire.

q: What happens between a request hitting public/index.php and a response coming back?
a: index.php loads Composer's autoloader and starts the app using bootstrap/app.php, which builds the service container (the tool that manages class dependencies). The request goes to the HTTP kernel, which runs startup tasks (detecting environment, error handling, logging), then passes the request through global middleware, finds the matching route (with its own middleware), builds the controller (auto-filling its dependencies), and finally the response travels back out through the middleware before being sent to the browser.

q: What is the Service Container, and when do you bind something as a singleton vs. a fresh instance?
a: The Service Container is Laravel's tool for automatically building classes and their dependencies, and for connecting interfaces to real implementations. I use singleton() when a class is expensive to build or needs to keep shared state during one request (like a connection to an outside service). I use bind() (a fresh instance every time) when each use genuinely needs its own separate state.

q: What is Eloquent's N+1 problem, and how would you find it in code you didn't write?
a:
N+1 happens when looping through a list triggers a separate database query for each item, instead of one combined query — for example, looping through orders and calling $order->customer->name without eager loading fires one extra query per order. To find it in old code, I'd turn on query logging in a dev environment (or use Laravel Debugbar / Telescope) and look for many similar repeated queries during one request.

I'd fix it with ->with() or ->load(), rather than adding eager loading everywhere blindly, which can load data you don't actually need.

q: $fillable vs $guarded — what's a real mass-assignment risk?
a: $fillable is a list of fields that ARE allowed to be set in bulk. $guarded is a list of fields that are NOT allowed (and by default, nothing is guarded, meaning everything is open — which is risky). The real danger: if a model isn't locked down and code does Model::create($request->all()), an attacker could sneak in extra fields like is_admin=1 that should never be user-editable. I always set an explicit $fillable list on anything user-facing, instead of relying on $guarded.

q: What's the difference between a Job, an Event/Listener, and an Observer?
a: A Job is a task you deliberately send off, usually to run in the background on a queue (like sending a batch of notifications). An Event/Listener is for 'something happened, and several things might need to react' — it's flexible, and you can attach multiple listeners without the event knowing about them. An Observer is tied to a specific model's lifecycle (created, updated, deleted) — I've used Observers for audit logging, so every change is logged the same way without repeating that code in every controller.

q: What is Laravel Horizon, and how do you watch for failed jobs in production?
a: Horizon is a dashboard for managing Redis-based queues — it shows you real-time stats, job counts, and failed jobs, and lets you control worker scaling through config instead of managing raw queue processes blindly. To catch failed jobs, I check the failed_jobs table or Horizon's failed tab, and for anything important, I'd set up alerts so a job that keeps failing gets noticed right away instead of being discovered days later.

q: Gates vs. Policies vs. Middleware — when do you use each?
a: Middleware: broad checks at the route level (is the user logged in, does their role even have access to this section). Gates: simple yes/no checks not tied to a specific record (can this user open the admin panel). Policies: checks tied to a specific record (can THIS user edit THIS specific post) — most real permission logic should live here, since it stays close to the model it's about instead of being scattered across controllers.

q: How do database transactions work in Laravel? Give a real example.
a: DB::transaction() wraps a group of database changes so they either all succeed together or all get undone together. Real example: creating an order plus its line items — if adding the line items fails partway through, you don't want an order left behind with no items. So both actions are wrapped in one transaction, and a failure rolls back the whole thing.

q: API Resources vs. returning raw Eloquent models — what's the difference?
a: API Resources let you control exactly what JSON shape is sent to the client, instead of accidentally exposing every database column (including private or internal fields) just because they exist on the model. It also creates a stable contract — I can change the database structure later without breaking apps that use the API, as long as the Resource keeps returning the same shape.

q: Explain Laravel's queue system end-to-end. What happens if a job keeps failing?
a: dispatch() packages the job and sends it to the queue (Redis, database, or SQS). A worker process (queue:work, or Horizon) pulls jobs off the queue, unpacks them, and runs the handle() method. If a job throws an error, Laravel retries it a set number of times, and after all retries fail, it moves to the failed_jobs table (if that's set up) instead of just disappearing — from there it can be checked and retried manually.

q: What's new in modern PHP (8.x)?
a: Named arguments, match expression, nullsafe ?->, constructor property promotion, enums (8.1), readonly properties/classes, first-class callables, fibers, typed class constants (8.3), property hooks and asymmetric visibility (8.4), and the pipe operator |> (8.5, Nov 2025).

q: Interface vs abstract class vs trait?
a: Interface = contract only (what methods must exist). Abstract class = partial implementation + contract, single inheritance. Trait = reusable code pasted into classes (Laravel uses them a lot: HasFactory, SoftDeletes).

q: SOLID principles — one example each in Laravel?
a: S: a Controller shouldn't send emails and generate PDFs — move to Services/Jobs. O: add a new payment gateway by adding a class, not editing a switch. L: any PaymentGateway implementation should work where the interface is expected. I: small interfaces. D: depend on interfaces, bind them in the Service Container.

q: Laravel request lifecycle?
a: public/index.php → bootstrap app → HTTP Kernel → service providers boot → middleware → router → controller → response back through middleware → sent to browser.

q: What is the Service Container and Service Providers?1 follow-up
a:
Container = a tool that creates objects and injects their dependencies automatically (Dependency Injection). Providers = where you register/bind things at startup ($this->app->bind(PaymentGateway::class, StripeGateway::class)).

Cross-questionbind vs singleton vs scoped?

bind new instance every time, singleton one for the whole app lifetime, scoped one per request/job (important with Octane).

q: Facades — how do they work?
a: Static-looking shortcuts (Cache::get()) that actually resolve an object from the container. Still testable with Cache::shouldReceive() or fakes.

q: Middleware examples?
a: auth, throttle, verified, CORS, custom ones like checking subscription plan or tenant. In Laravel 11+ middleware is registered in bootstrap/app.php (no more Kernel.php).

q: Form Requests — why use them?
a: Move validation and authorization out of the controller. Clean, reusable, returns 422 automatically.

q: API Resources?
a: Transform models into JSON consistently, hide fields, add computed fields, include relationships conditionally with whenLoaded(). Laravel 13 also adds first-class JSON:API resources.

q: What is the N+1 problem? How do you fix it?2 follow-ups
a:
Loading 100 posts, then running 1 query per post to get its author = 101 queries. Fix: eager load Post::with('author')->get() → 2 queries.

Cross-questionHow do you detect it automatically?

Model::preventLazyLoading(!app()->isProduction()) throws an error on lazy loading in dev. Also Laravel Debugbar/Telescope.

Deepwith() vs load() vs withCount()?

with before the query, load after you already have models, withCount adds a posts_count column without loading them.

q: Relationships you know?
a: hasOne, hasMany, belongsTo, belongsToMany (pivot), hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough, polymorphic (morphOne, morphMany, morphToMany — e.g., comments on posts and videos).

q: How do you process 1 million rows without running out of memory?1 follow-up
a:
Don't use ->get(). Use chunkById(1000, fn...) (safe when updating rows), lazyById(), or cursor() (one row at a time via generator). For bulk inserts use insert() / upsert() in batches instead of create() in a loop.

Cross-questionWhy chunkById instead of chunk when updating?

chunk uses offset; if you change the rows you filter on, rows get skipped.

q: Scopes, accessors/mutators, casts?
a: Local scope: scopeActive($q) → User::active(). Global scope: applied automatically (e.g., tenant filtering). Accessors/mutators via Attribute::make(get:, set:). Casts: 'settings' => 'array', enum casts, custom cast classes (e.g., Money).

q: Model events and Observers — any danger?
a: creating, updated, deleted etc. Useful for audit logs and cache clearing. Danger: hidden logic, and they don't fire on mass updates like Model::where()->update(). Use saveQuietly() when you don't want them.

q: Transactions and locking?
a: DB::transaction(fn() => ...) — all or nothing. For race conditions (two users buying the last item): lockForUpdate() inside a transaction, or atomic updates ->decrement('stock') with a where stock > 0, or Cache::lock() for distributed locks.

q: Why use queues?
a: Move slow work (emails, PDFs, image processing, API calls) out of the request so the user gets a fast response. Drivers: Redis (most common), database, SQS.

q: How do you make jobs reliable?1 follow-up
a:
• $tries, $backoff (e.g., [10, 60, 300]), $timeout.
  • failed() method to alert/cleanup; failed jobs table + queue:retry.
  • Idempotent jobs — safe to run twice (check if already done).
  • ShouldBeUnique to avoid duplicates, WithoutOverlapping middleware.
  • RateLimited middleware for third-party APIs.
  • Pass IDs, not huge objects (SerializesModels re-fetches the model).
  • Separate queues by priority: high, default, exports.

Cross-questiontimeout vs retry_after?

retry_after (in queue config) must be longer than job timeout, otherwise a second worker picks up the same job while the first is still running → duplicates.

q: Job batching and chaining?
a: Chain = run in order, stop if one fails (Bus::chain([ParseFile, ValidateRows, Import])). Batch = many jobs in parallel with progress tracking and then/catch/finally callbacks (Bus::batch([...])->dispatch()) — perfect for "import 50,000 rows, show progress bar".

q: Horizon — what is it?
a: Dashboard and supervisor for Redis queues: see throughput, failed jobs, wait times, auto-balance workers across queues.

q: Events and Listeners?1 follow-up
a:
Decouple actions: OrderPlaced event → listeners send email, update stats, notify Slack. Listeners can be queued (ShouldQueue).

Cross-questionEvent fires inside a DB transaction but the job reads data that isn't committed yet — fix?

Use afterCommit / ShouldDispatchAfterCommit so it runs only after commit.

q: Sanctum vs Passport?
a: Sanctum: simple — SPA cookie auth and personal API tokens. Passport: full OAuth2 server (when third parties need to log in via your app). Most projects need Sanctum.

q: Gates vs Policies?
a: Both for authorization. Gates = simple closures for general actions. Policies = classes grouped per model (PostPolicy@update). Use $this->authorize() or can middleware.

q: Caching in Laravel?
a: Cache::remember('key', ttl, fn), cache tags (Redis), invalidate on model update. Config/route/view/event caching in production (php artisan optimize). Watch for stale data and cache stampede (use locks or Cache::flexible() stale-while-revalidate).

q: Laravel Octane?
a: Keeps the app in memory (Swoole/RoadRunner/FrankenPHP) → much faster. Careful with static variables and singletons leaking data between requests.

q: What's new in Laravel 12 & 13?
a:
• Laravel 12 (Feb 2025): mostly maintenance, new starter kits (React, Vue, Livewire) with Inertia and optional WorkOS auth.
  • Laravel 13 (released March 17, 2026): requires PHP 8.3+, PHP Attributes for config (e.g., #[Table], #[Hidden] on models instead of properties), first-party Laravel AI SDK (text, embeddings, agents, vector stores), passkey authentication, native vector search with PostgreSQL pgvector, first-class JSON:API resources, Cache::touch(), Reverb database driver, very few breaking changes.
  • Ecosystem: Laravel Cloud (managed hosting), Laravel Boost (AI coding assistant helper), Reverb (first-party WebSockets), Pint (code style), Pest (testing).

q: How does a Laravel HTTP request pass through the kernel, middleware, router and response pipeline?
a: public/index.php → bootstrap → HTTP kernel → service providers → middleware → router → controller → response.

q: N+1 problem?
a: 100 orders then 1 query per order for customer = 101 queries. Fix Order::with('customer')->get().

q: $fillable vs $guarded?
a: Allow-list vs block-list for mass assignment protection.

q: Relationships?
a: hasOne, hasMany, belongsTo, belongsToMany (pivot), hasManyThrough, polymorphic.

q: Why queues?
a: Send emails, generate invoices, call slow APIs in the background so the user doesn't wait. Redis/database driver, Supervisor keeps workers running, php artisan queue:restart after deploy.

q: Sanctum?
a: Token/SPA cookie auth for APIs and mobile apps.

q: Blade vs React in Laravel?
a: Blade = server-rendered pages (good for admin panels, simple sites). React = rich interactive UIs; connect via REST API or Inertia.js (use React pages without building a separate API).

q: Latest Laravel?
a: Laravel 13 (March 2026): PHP 8.3+, PHP Attributes for model config, first-party AI SDK, passkeys, few breaking changes. Laravel 12 still widely used.

q: What's the bootstrap/ folder for?
a: It holds the files needed to start up the framework — app.php creates the application, and autoload.php connects Composer's autoloader.

q: What happens from a request coming in to a response going out?
a:
Every request enters through public/index.php, the single entry point the web server sends all requests to. index.php loads Composer's autoloader and gets the app instance from bootstrap/app.php. Laravel creates the service container. The request goes to the HTTP kernel (or the console kernel, for command-line use). The HTTP kernel runs startup tasks (error handling, logging, detecting the environment) before actually handling the request.

The request passes through the kernel's global middleware (session handling, maintenance-mode checks, security checks). The kernel's handle() method takes a Request and returns a Response — think of the kernel as a black box: feed it a request, get back a response.

q: What is the Service Container (IoC Container)?
a: Laravel's Service Container automatically manages class dependencies and builds them for you — you don't have to manually create and wire up every dependency. It's what lets you just type-hint a Request or a User model directly in a controller method and have Laravel fill it in for you (this is also how route-model binding works).

q: What is dependency injection?
a: A general programming idea (not just Laravel's): give a class or function everything it needs up front, instead of having it create or look up its own dependencies internally. This avoids hidden connections between classes and makes testing easier. Three types: constructor injection (passed through the constructor), setter injection (passed through a setter method), and interface injection (the dependency defines how it should be injected).

q: What are Service Providers?
a: The central place where a Laravel app is set up. They connect services/classes into the container, register event listeners, middleware, routes, and do other setup work. Common uses: binding classes/interfaces (often as singletons), registering event listeners, registering custom validation rules, extending Laravel's core behavior, registering Blade directives/view composers. Providers are registered in config/app.php.

q: What are Facades?
a:
Facades give a static-style way to call classes that are actually managed by the service container — a shortcut so you can call methods on an underlying object without manually building/fetching it yourself. All core facades live under Illuminate\Support\Facades.

Examples: DB::table('users')->get(), Cache::put('key', 'value', $minutes), Log::info('message'), Mail::to('email')->send(new SomeMailable()). Under the hood a facade is just a wrapper around a non-static class instance pulled from the container — it just gives cleaner, more readable syntax than traditional static calls.

q: What are Contracts?
a: A set of interfaces that define the core services Laravel provides (like Queue, Mailer). Contracts separate an implementation from its interface, so implementations can be swapped without touching the code that depends on them. Examples of areas with contracts: Routing, Mail, Events, Queue, Http, Encryption, Notifications, Hashing, Cookie, Pipeline, Filesystem, Database.

q: What is Artisan?
a: Laravel's command-line tool for scaffolding and managing the app. Common commands: php artisan make:controller, make:model, make:migration, make:seeder, make:factory, make:policy, make:middleware, make:command, make:observer --model=User, make:event, make:listener, make:job, make:mail. Also: php artisan migrate, php artisan tinker (interactive shell), php artisan queue:work, php artisan down/up (maintenance mode off/on), php artisan config:cache, php artisan route:cache.

q: What is Tinker?
a: A REPL (a command-line tool that lets you type code and see results immediately) built on PsySH, letting you interact with your app — including the database — from the command line, via php artisan tinker.

q: What is Lumen?
a: A micro-framework built on Laravel's core pieces, made by Taylor Otwell for building lightweight APIs and microservices. It's faster than Laravel but strips out things like HTTP sessions, cookies, and full templating.

q: What is Homestead?
a: An official, ready-made Vagrant virtual machine that comes with everything needed to develop Laravel apps (PHP, web server, Ubuntu, and more) without installing them on your own computer.

q: What are route groups?
a: A way to group shared settings (middleware, prefixes, namespaces) across multiple routes instead of repeating them on each one — like wrapping several routes in Route::middleware(['throttleMiddleware'])->group(function () { ... }).

q: What's the point of named routes and reverse routing?
a: You give a route a name (like Route::get('/login', ...)->name('login')), and 'reverse routing' means generating a URL from that name instead of hardcoding the path. Benefit: if the URL changes later (like /login becoming /users/signin), you only update it in one place (routes/web.php) and every reference through the route's name updates automatically — no hunting down hardcoded links across the app.

q: What is route model binding?
a: Laravel automatically injects a model instance into a route/controller method based on a route parameter (like {id} turning into an actual Eloquent model), resolved by the service container.

q: What is throttling?
a: Rate-limiting requests per IP address, useful against brute-force attacks or overload. Applied through middleware, active on API routes by default — like Route::middleware('auth:api', 'throttle:60,1')->group(...).

q: What is middleware?
a: Middleware filters HTTP requests entering the app — like checking that someone is logged in before letting them access a route. Two types: global middleware (runs on every request) and route middleware (assigned to specific routes only). Registered in app/Http/Kernel.php. Pros: simple for route-level protection, good for broad access control. Cons: not suited to fine-grained, per-action permission checks.

q: What's the difference between API and web routes?
a: routes/api.php routes are for a stateless API (no sessions, no memory between requests) and are prefixed/middlewared with the api group by default. routes/web.php routes run through the web middleware group (sessions, security checks, etc.).

q: Eloquent vs. Query Builder vs. raw DB queries — why use Eloquent?
a:
Eloquent lets you query in an object-oriented style, is easier/more readable than raw queries or the query builder, isn't tightly tied to the table structure (change the table name once in the model, not in every query), expresses relationships between tables elegantly (no manual JOIN syntax needed for common cases), and supports scopes, accessors, mutators, and other model-level conveniences.

When to use which: for simple/small create-read-update-delete work, use Eloquent. For large volumes of records or heavier queries, the Query Builder (DB::table(...)) tends to be faster.

q: What are common Query Builder / Eloquent methods?
a: table(), select(), join(), get(), where(), update(), insertGetId() for building queries. max(), min(), sum(), avg(), count() for summary numbers. Common Eloquent operations: Product::create([...]) to insert, Students::all() to get everything, Students::find(1) to get by ID, Students::where('name', '=', 'John Doe')->first() to get the first match, updating by loading a record then calling ->save(), and deleting with ->delete() or Students::destroy(1) (or destroy(1, 2, 3) for several at once).

q: insert() vs. insertGetId(); delete() vs. soft deletes?
a: insert() just inserts a row; insertGetId() inserts and also returns the new auto-generated ID. delete() permanently removes the row; soft deletes flag the row as deleted (setting a deleted_at timestamp) without physically removing it, so it can be recovered or excluded from normal queries.

q: How do you check if a table exists, and what are query scopes?
a: Schema::hasTable('table_name') checks table existence. Query scopes are reusable, named query rules defined on a model so you don't repeat the same 'where' logic across the app.

q: How do relationships work in Eloquent?
a: One-to-One: a User hasOne a Car, and the Car belongsTo the User (owner_id lives on the cars table). One-to-Many: a User hasMany phoneNumbers, and each PhoneNumber belongsTo a User. Many-to-Many: a Post belongsToMany Tags, using a pivot table behind the scenes. Other relationship types available: Has-Many-Through and Polymorphic relationships. hasOne vs. belongsTo depends on which table actually holds the foreign key — if the users table has account_id, User belongsTo Account; if accounts has user_id, User hasOne/hasMany Accounts.

q: What's Eager Loading vs. Lazy Loading (the N+1 problem)?
a: Lazy loading (the default) fetches related data only when it's accessed, causing one query per related lookup — looping over 100 posts and accessing each post's comments becomes 101 queries total (1 for the posts, 1 per post for its comments). That's the classic N+1 query problem, a major performance trap. Eager loading fixes it by loading relationships up front, in one extra query: Post::with('comments')->get() (just 2 queries total), or Post::with(['comments', 'author'])->get() to eager-load several relationships at once.

q: What are accessors and mutators?
a: An accessor transforms data when it's retrieved — like a getFullNameAttribute() method letting you call $user->full_name. A mutator transforms data before it's saved — like a setFirstNameAttribute($value) method that automatically uppercases the value before storing it.

q: What is mass assignment, and what's $fillable vs. $guarded?
a:
Mass assignment lets you set many model fields in one call instead of one at a time, like new User(request()->all()). This is convenient but dangerous — a malicious request could sneak in an unexpected field (like user_type=admin) and silently give someone extra permissions. $fillable is an allow-list (only those fields can be set this way); $guarded is a deny-list (everything except those fields can be set this way).

Setting $guarded = ['*'] blocks all mass assignment entirely. To update a guarded field, you set it explicitly: $user->user_type = 'admin'; $user->save();

q: How do you use multiple database connections?
a: You define extra connections in config/database.php (like a second 'mysql2' connection), then either query it directly with DB::connection('mysql2')->table('users')->get(), or set protected $connection = 'mysql2'; on a specific model so it always uses that connection. You can also switch connections dynamically per query, and optionally configure read/write splitting (sending reads and writes to different database servers) under one connection.

q: How do database transactions work?
a: A transaction makes sure a group of operations either all succeed or all get undone — critical when writing to multiple related tables (like orders + order_items). DB::beginTransaction() starts it, DB::commit() saves all the changes permanently, and DB::rollBack() (called inside a catch block) undoes everything in the transaction if an error was caught.

q: What are migrations, seeders, and factories?
a:
Migrations are version control for your database structure — they let a team share and keep a consistent database structure across different environments; without them, keeping a database structure in sync across a team is painful. Seeders fill the database with data (php artisan db:seed). Factories automatically generate realistic fake data for a model, typically for testing — every new Laravel app comes with an example UserFactory.php.

Laravel supports MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, and SQLite.

q: What is a guard?
a: A guard defines how users are authenticated (logged in) for each request. Incoming requests are checked against the guard to validate credentials. Guards are defined in config/auth.php.

q: What's the difference between authentication and authorization?
a: Authentication confirms who the user is (their identity/credentials). Authorization determines what that logged-in user is allowed to do (their permissions).

q: Gate vs. Policy vs. Middleware — when do you use each?
a:
A Gate is a simple closure-based rule, defined in a service provider's boot() method, for checks not tied to a specific model — like Gate::define('update-article', function (User $user, Article $article) { return $user->id === $article->user_id; }); and then checked with Gate::allows('update', $post). A Policy is a dedicated class (made with php artisan make:policy PostPolicy) holding methods like update(User $user, Post $post), registered in a $policies array — it's better organized for structured, model-centric permission logic.

Rule of thumb: middleware for route-level checks, gates for single-action checks unrelated to a specific model, policies for structured, model-centric authorization logic.

q: What is Laravel Passport?
a: It provides a full OAuth2 login server for API authentication — it issues tokens to client applications and checks them on protected endpoints. Ideal for building a complete API authentication system, including access for outside third-party apps. Setup: install the package, run migrations, run passport:install, and set the 'api' guard's driver to 'passport' in config/auth.php.

q: How do you share a login session across multiple Laravel sites (Single Sign-On)?
a: 1. Use the same session driver (like database or redis) in both apps. 2. Use the same session name. 3. Set a shared cookie domain (like '.yourdomain.com'). 4. Keep the relevant .env session settings consistent across both apps. 5. For true SSO, share user data through a central authentication server using Laravel Passport/OAuth or SAML, so both apps check against the same source of truth.

q: What are Laravel's built-in auth controllers?
a: RegisterController, LoginController, ResetPasswordController, and ForgetPasswordController.

q: How does CSRF protection work?
a: CSRF protection detects and blocks unauthorized cross-site requests. A CSRF token is generated per session and checked on any request that changes data. Specific routes can be excluded by listing them in the $except array on VerifyCsrfToken.

q: What session drivers does Laravel support, and how do you use sessions?
a:
Laravel supports several session drivers: file, cookie, database, memcached, redis, array — set in config/session.php or via SESSION_DRIVER in .env. Storing: session(['key' => 'value']). Retrieving: session('key'), or session('key', 'default') with a fallback value, or session()->all() for everything. Deleting: session()->forget('key') or session()->flush() to clear everything.

Flash data (like session()->flash('status', 'Task was successful!')) is available only for the very next request and then automatically deleted — useful for one-time success/error messages.

q: How do you choose a session driver?
a:
File is fast and simple, fine for a single server not already using Redis/Memcached. Database is accessible from multiple servers (good behind a load balancer) but can become a bottleneck under very heavy load, though it's generally fine for low/medium traffic. Redis/Memcached are shareable across servers with very high read/write speed, ideal for medium/high-traffic, load-balanced setups.

Session handling is applied automatically to routes in the web middleware group. You can also build a custom session driver by implementing SessionHandlerInterface and registering it via Session::extend().

q: How does Laravel's caching work?
a:
Laravel gives you one unified caching API across different drivers (file, Redis, Memcached, etc.), set in config/cache.php. The 'remember' pattern caches the result of an expensive operation: Cache::remember('users', 60, function () { return DB::table('users')->get(); }); (caches for 60 minutes). You can also manage the cache manually with Cache::put(), Cache::get(), and Cache::forget().

Cache tags (Redis/Memcached only) let you group related cache entries and clear them all at once with ->flush().

q: When do you cache vs. use sessions?
a: Rule of thumb: cache data that's expensive to fetch/calculate and safe to discard/regenerate; use sessions for data tied to one specific user's current visit.

q: How do you cache paginated API results?
a: Cache the raw paginated query result, not the already-transformed API Resource — apply the transformation after pulling from the cache, so the cache stays simple and reusable across different response shapes.

q: What is Redis?
a: An in-memory data store used as a database, cache, and message broker. Common uses: caching layer, session storage, real-time analytics, message/job queues, leaderboards (using its 'sorted sets' feature), and rate limiting. Strengths: speed, rich data structures, pub/sub messaging, queue management, location-based (geospatial) indexing, and the ability to scale out across multiple servers with replication for read copies.

q: Queues vs. Scheduling vs. Cron jobs — how do they relate?
a:
The only crontab entry Laravel needs on the server is one line that triggers Laravel's own in-app schedule every minute: * * * * * cd /path-to-your-project && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1. Inside the app, you then define recurring tasks in App\Console\Kernel.php, like $schedule->call(function () { ... })->daily();.

Queues are for running background work asynchronously (not on a schedule, but dispatched when needed); the Scheduler is for running tasks on a recurring timetable, using the app's own code instead of many separate server-level cron entries.

q: How do you create and dispatch a job?
a: Run php artisan make:job SendEmailJob to generate a job class. It implements ShouldQueue, has a constructor that stores what it needs, and a handle() method with the actual work (like looping through emails and sending them). You dispatch it with SendBulkEmailsJob::dispatch($emails, $data);, and a worker (php artisan queue:work) picks it up and runs it. Queue drivers include database, redis, beanstalkd, sqs, and others, configured in config/queue.php.

q: What are Events & Listeners?
a: You generate them with php artisan make:event OrderShipped and php artisan make:listener SendShipmentNotification, then fire the event with event(new OrderShipped($order));. This is useful for decoupling side effects from the main flow of an action — multiple listeners can react to the same event without the code that fired it needing to know about all of them.

q: What are Observers?
a:
Observers centralize the logic for a model's lifecycle events (retrieved, creating, created, updating, updated, saving, saved, deleting, deleted, restoring, restored) instead of scattering that logic across controllers. You generate one with php artisan make:observer UserObserver --model=User, define methods like creating(), created(), updated(), deleted(), and register it in a service provider's boot() method with User::observe(UserObserver::class);.

Use cases: logging changes, sending notifications on create/delete, enforcing data integrity (like auto-generating an API token when a record is created).

q: How does broadcasting & WebSockets work?
a: Laravel Echo plus broadcasting pushes events to client-side JavaScript in real time (notifications, live updates). All broadcasting happens through queued jobs, so it doesn't block the main request/response cycle. Options: Pusher Channels, Ably, or the self-hosted laravel-websockets package (a pure-PHP, Pusher-compatible WebSocket server that avoids needing a paid provider).

q: How do you share data with all views, and how does layout inheritance work?
a:
You can share data with every view using View::share('key', 'value'); inside a service provider's boot() method. @yield defines a section in a master layout that gets filled in by a child view's @section. When Blade compiles a child view, it checks whether the view @extends a layout; if so, it renders the layout and inserts the child's @section content into the matching @yield.

Laravel 7+ also supports Blade component tags, a more expressive syntax for defining and using reusable Blade components.

q: What are API Resources, and what do they give you?
a: API Resources transform Eloquent models/collections into a consistent, controlled JSON structure for API responses. Benefits: consistency across endpoints, keeping JSON-shaping logic out of the controller, control over exactly which fields are included, and built-in pagination support. When combining related models in one resource, use null-coalescing (like $this->details->address ?? null) to avoid errors on a missing relationship, and eager-load the relation (User::with('details')) to avoid the N+1 problem when the resource accesses it.

q: REST vs. GraphQL vs. SOAP, briefly?
a: REST exposes multiple endpoints, each returning a fixed data shape. GraphQL exposes a single endpoint with a typed structure, letting the client ask for exactly the fields it needs. SOAP (for contrast, an older style) uses only the POST method for both retrieving and sending data, and only XML as the data format.

q: What common design patterns show up in Laravel?
a:
Facade pattern — a static-style shortcut to services managed by the container. Builder/Manager pattern — building complex objects/configurations step by step in a readable way. Factory pattern — centralizes how objects get created. Repository pattern — a middle layer between business logic and database access. Strategy pattern — swaps interchangeable behaviors at runtime.

Provider pattern — Service Providers (covered in section 1). Observer pattern — Observers (covered in section 7).

q: What is the Repository pattern in Laravel specifically?
a: It creates a bridge between models and controllers so a model isn't responsible for query/data-access logic — it should just represent a table/entity. Why use it: it follows an established, well-understood pattern (easier to maintain), improves clarity and reduces bugs, and avoids duplicated data-access code being written by different team members in different places.

q: My Laravel app is slow — what's the checklist?
a:
Use server-side processing (like DataTables) for large tables instead of rendering everything in the browser at once. Use pagination instead of loading a full result set. Use eager loading to avoid N+1 queries. Use Laravel Debugbar during development to spot slow queries. Serve static files through a CDN. Tune server configuration (PHP-FPM worker count, OPcache, etc.).

Cache expensive queries, config, and routes (config:cache, route:cache). Write efficient, properly indexed queries.

q: How do you make a Laravel app more asynchronous?
a: Laravel is synchronous by default (each request handled one step at a time), but several tools push work off the main thread: Queues (defer slow tasks), Events & Listeners (decouple side effects), Broadcasting (real-time updates via WebSockets), async HTTP requests (like Guzzle's requestAsync()), Laravel Octane (serves the app through high-performance servers like Swoole or RoadRunner, supporting real simultaneous handling), and WebSockets (Pusher or laravel-websockets for real-time, two-way communication).

q: What is Laravel Octane?
a: It supercharges performance by keeping the application loaded in memory and serving requests through Swoole or RoadRunner instead of the traditional PHP-FPM request cycle — this supports genuine simultaneous request handling instead of one request fully finishing before the next starts.

q: What's a custom helper function, and how do you register one?
a: A plain function you define (like in app/helpers.php) wrapped in if (!function_exists('my_custom_helper')) { ... } so it doesn't clash if defined elsewhere. You register the file in composer.json's autoload.files array, then run composer dump-autoload so Composer picks it up.

q: What's a trait, and what's an example?
a: A trait lets you share method code across classes without full inheritance. Example: a HasUUID trait that automatically generates a UUID whenever a model is created, using a static::creating() hook — any model that does 'use HasUUID;' gets that behavior for free.

q: Can a trait have 'nested' methods?
a: PHP doesn't support defining a function inside another function, but a trait method can call another (private) method defined in the same trait, which achieves a similar organizing effect — one public method calling a private helper method within the same trait.

q: What are Laravel Collections?
a: Collections wrap arrays with a rich, chainable set of methods for working with data. Eloquent query results are returned as collections automatically. Common operations: ->filter() to keep only items matching a condition, ->map() to transform every item, ->get(0) to retrieve a specific item, and ->contains('value') to check if something is in the collection.

q: What should I know about Laravel version differences (7 → 8 → 9 and beyond)?
a: Across versions, expect ongoing performance improvements, security patches, and documentation updates, along with occasional structural changes (like the newer, more streamlined app structure introduced in Laravel 11). It's worth knowing which version a specific job's codebase uses, and being ready to explain what's changed since the version you're most familiar with.

q: What are the basic HTTP status code categories, and what's PUT vs. PATCH?
a: Status codes fall into classes: 1xx Informational, 2xx Success, 3xx Redirection, 4xx Client Error, 5xx Server Error. PUT replaces the entire resource (send all fields); PATCH sends only the specific fields that need to change.

q: What does 'stateless vs. stateful' mean for HTTP?
a:
HTTP itself is stateless — each request is handled independently, with no memory of previous requests. This is true no matter which backend language you use. To simulate 'state' (like staying logged in), the developer has to save relevant data (usually through sessions and cookies) and read it back on each following request.

Stateless apps have no memory of past interactions — every transaction is self-contained (like a one-off web search) — and are simpler to scale, since any server can handle any request. Stateful apps keep context across requests (like online banking or email) and typically need to route a user back to the same server/session store, or use a shared session store (database/Redis) reachable from any server behind a load balancer.

Why this matters in a load-balanced setup: if Server 1 handles a login but Server 2 (behind the load balancer) gets the next request, and session data isn't shared, the user appears logged out. A shared/central session store (database or Redis) fixes this.

q: What's the difference between port 80 and port 443?
a: Port 80 is HTTP (plain text, not encrypted). Port 443 is HTTPS (encrypted with TLS) — the modern default for nearly all production traffic.

q: What testing support does Laravel have built in?
a: Laravel ships with built-in testing support (PHPUnit) to catch regressions, run through the Artisan command-line tool. The same TDD principle (writing a test before the code that makes it pass) applies to Laravel's feature/unit tests as it does to general PHP testing.

q: What are the key Composer commands and concepts?
a: composer install installs the packages listed in composer.json/composer.lock into the vendor/ folder. composer update updates packages to the latest versions allowed by the version rules in composer.json. composer dump-autoload regenerates the autoloader's class map without downloading anything new — needed after adding new classes that aren't being found, or after registering a new file in autoload.files. composer.json has a require section (production dependencies) and a require-dev section (development-only dependencies), each with version rules.

q: What is Docker, and why use it for a Laravel app?
a: Docker packages an application with everything it needs (PHP version, extensions, web server, etc.) into a portable, isolated container. This eliminates 'works on my machine' problems — every developer and every environment (dev, staging, production) runs the exact same setup.

q: What is a Dockerfile?
a: A text file with step-by-step instructions to build an image: which base image to start from (FROM), copying files (COPY), running setup commands (RUN), exposing ports (EXPOSE), and the default startup command (CMD/ENTRYPOINT). Example structure: start from a PHP-FPM base image, install needed system packages and PHP extensions, copy the app code in, install Composer and run composer install, expose port 9000, and run php-fpm as the startup command.

q: What is docker-compose, and why use it for Laravel?
a: docker-compose.yml defines and runs a multi-container setup (app, web server, database, cache, queue worker) as a single stack with one command (docker-compose up). Laravel typically needs several containers working together (PHP-FPM, Nginx, MySQL, Redis), so Compose is the standard way to run them all together locally — with each service (app, nginx, mysql, redis) defined in one file, connected on a shared network, with named volumes for data that needs to persist.

q: What is a multi-stage Docker build, and why use it for a Laravel app?
a: A Dockerfile with multiple FROM stages — one stage installs Composer dependencies and compiles frontend assets, and a final, slimmer stage copies only the built output into the production image. This keeps the final image small (no dev tools, no node_modules, no build cache).

q: How do you keep database data safe in Docker?
a: Mount a named volume (like dbdata:/var/lib/mysql) so MySQL's data folder lives outside the container's own writable layer. Without this, running docker-compose down (or removing the container) wipes all the data.

q: docker-compose up vs. docker-compose up -d?
a: Without -d, containers run in the foreground and stream their logs to your terminal. With -d (detached), they run in the background, freeing up your terminal.

q: What are common day-to-day Docker commands for Laravel work?
a: docker-compose up -d starts the stack in the background. docker-compose down stops and removes containers (volumes stay unless you add -v). docker-compose ps lists running services. docker-compose logs -f app tails the app service's logs. docker-compose exec app php artisan migrate runs an artisan command inside the app container. docker-compose exec app bash opens a shell inside the app container. docker-compose build --no-cache rebuilds an image completely from scratch.

q: How do you run MySQL for a Laravel app in Docker?
a: Use the official mysql image, set credentials through environment variables, mount a volume for saved data, and point Laravel's .env at the container's service name (not 127.0.0.1) when the app itself also runs in a container on the same Docker network. In .env: DB_CONNECTION=mysql, DB_HOST=mysql (the container's service name, not localhost), DB_PORT=3306, plus the database name/username/password.

q: Why does DB_HOST=127.0.0.1 fail inside a container but work from the host machine?
a: Inside Docker's internal network, 127.0.0.1 refers to the container itself, not the MySQL container. You have to use the MySQL service name (like mysql in the compose file) as the hostname — Docker's internal DNS resolves it to the right container. From your host machine's browser/command line (outside Docker), 127.0.0.1:3306 works because the port is explicitly published in the compose file.

q: How do you back up and restore MySQL from a container?
a: Back up by running mysqldump inside the container and redirecting the output to a file on your host (docker-compose exec mysql sh -c 'mysqldump...' > backup.sql). Restore by piping a saved SQL file back in (docker-compose exec -T mysql mysql -u root -p"root" laravel < backup.sql). To open a MySQL shell directly, run docker-compose exec mysql mysql -u root -p.

q: What happens to MySQL data if you run docker-compose down -v?
a: The -v flag also removes named volumes — this deletes all database data. Plain docker-compose down (without -v) stops and removes containers but keeps the volumes, so the data survives.

q: What is DDEV, and how does it compare to plain Docker Compose or Laravel Sail?
a:
DDEV is an open-source, Docker-based local development tool built specifically for PHP projects (Laravel, WordPress, Drupal, etc.). It wraps Docker Compose with sensible, project-aware defaults so you don't have to hand-write docker-compose.yml and Dockerfiles yourself. Compared to plain Docker Compose, it's much less manual setup.

Compared to Laravel Sail (Laravel's own Docker tool), DDEV is more general-purpose across different PHP frameworks and includes some extras — like automatic local HTTPS with trusted certificates, built-in database snapshotting/restoring, and easy switching between PHP/database versions per project without hand-editing YAML files.

q: What are common DDEV commands?
a: ddev config --project-type=laravel --docroot=public --create-docroot sets up a project. ddev start boots the project's containers, ddev stop stops them. ddev ssh opens a shell in the web container. ddev artisan migrate runs artisan commands. ddev composer install installs dependencies. ddev mysql opens a MySQL shell. ddev export-db / ddev import-db back up and restore the database. ddev describe shows project URLs, ports, and service status.

q: SQL (MySQL) vs. NoSQL (MongoDB) — key differences?
a: MySQL stores data in strict, related tables with a fixed structure, and is strong for related data, complex joins, and ACID transactions across multiple tables. MongoDB stores data as flexible documents that don't need a fixed structure, and is strong for data that varies a lot in shape, deeply nested data, or very high write volumes where scaling out matters more than strict relational guarantees.

q: When would you choose MongoDB over MySQL in a Laravel project?
a: When data doesn't fit a rigid relational structure well (like varied product attributes, activity logs, event streams), when you need to store deeply nested/hierarchical data without excessive joins, or when you have very high write volume where scaling out across servers matters more than strict relational integrity. MySQL remains the better default for anything needing strong relational integrity, complex joins, or ACID transactions across multiple tables.

q: How do you actually use MongoDB with Laravel?
a:
Laravel doesn't support MongoDB natively — you add a package (commonly mongodb/laravel-mongodb, maintained by MongoDB Inc.) that gives you an Eloquent-like model layer over MongoDB. You configure a 'mongodb' connection in config/database.php with the host/port/database, then build models extending MongoDB\Laravel\Eloquent\Model with protected $connection = 'mongodb'; and protected $collection = 'logs';.

You can then use normal-feeling Eloquent syntax like Log::create([...]) and Log::where('event', 'user_login')->get().

q: Can a single Laravel app use both MySQL and MongoDB?
a: Yes — Laravel supports multiple database connections at once. It's common to keep core relational data (users, orders) in MySQL and use MongoDB for logs, analytics events, or flexible/unstructured data, choosing the connection per model with protected $connection.

q: How do you run MongoDB in Docker?
a: Add a mongo service in docker-compose.yml using the official mongo image, set root username/password through environment variables, expose port 27017, and mount a named volume (like mongodata:/data/db) so the data survives container restarts.

q: What is Laravel Mix?
a: Laravel Mix is a friendly wrapper around webpack, giving Laravel projects a simple way to compile and bundle frontend assets — turning SCSS/Sass/Less into CSS, modern JS/JSX into browser-compatible JS, minifying files, and adding versioning/cache-busting — without hand-writing raw webpack configuration. A typical webpack.mix.js compiles JS and Sass files and calls .version() to add a content hash for cache-busting in production.

q: What are common Laravel Mix / npm commands?
a: npm install installs dependencies. npm run dev compiles assets for development (unminified, with source maps). npm run watch recompiles automatically whenever files change. npm run production minifies and optimizes for production, adding versioning if .version() is used.

q: How do you output the correct hashed asset filenames in Blade?
a: Using the mix() helper, like . mix() looks up the real, hashed filename from public/mix-manifest.json (generated by the .version() call), so browsers reliably fetch the newest asset after a deploy instead of serving a stale cached copy.

q: Laravel Mix vs. Vite — what changed?
a: Starting with Laravel 9 (and the default from Laravel 10 onward), new projects ship with Vite instead of Mix. Vite uses native ES modules and a dev server for near-instant hot reloading, making local development significantly faster than webpack-based Mix, especially on larger projects. Mix still works and is maintained for existing/older apps, but Vite is the modern default — the equivalent Blade syntax is @vite(['resources/css/app.css', 'resources/js/app.js']).

q: How does localization (translations) work?
a: Translation files live in resources/lang/{locale}, and you retrieve strings using a helper like __('auth.error'), based on the visitor's language preference.

q: How do environment variables work?
a: They're defined in .env (usually copied from a .env.example template). You access them via env('VARIABLE_NAME') in PHP, or a check like @if (env('APP_ENV') == 'local') in Blade. Best practice: read env values through config() in your application code, and reserve direct env() calls for the config files themselves, since config values can be cached (and a cached config wouldn't reflect a direct env() call elsewhere).

q: What's maintenance mode?
a: You turn it on with php artisan down and off with php artisan up. While it's on, incoming requests get a 'maintenance mode' error (HTTP 503); specific IP addresses can be allowed through to bypass it.

q: What file permissions should be used?
a: 755 is a commonly recommended default for directories (owner: read/write/execute; group and others: read/execute). 777 (full read/write/execute for everyone) should be avoided in production, since it's a real security risk.

q: What does compact() do?
a: It builds an associative array from variable names — compact('name', 'age') becomes ['name' => $name, 'age' => $age], handy for passing variables to a view without listing them twice.

q: What's a 'wrapper class' in general OOP terms?
a: A class that wraps/contains another class or component, giving a simpler interface to it (Laravel Facades are one form of this).

q: What are webhooks?
a: Webhooks let one system automatically push real-time data/notifications to another when something happens, instead of the receiving system having to repeatedly check for updates. Common examples: GitHub, Stripe, and Slack all use webhooks to notify other systems of events.

q: What is object caching?
a: Storing frequently accessed data (like expensive query results or rendered page output) in a fast temporary store (RAM, disk, or a distributed cache) to avoid repeating the work of calculating/fetching it. Key things to think about: where the cache is stored, how/when it gets cleared (invalidated), keeping the cache consistent with the real data (write-through/write-back/write-around strategies), and using a distributed cache (Memcached, Redis) when you need it shared across multiple servers.

q: What's the DB facade used for?
a: The DB facade is used to run SQL-style queries directly: create, select, update, insert, and delete. Common methods: table(), select(), join(), get(), where(), update(), insertGetId().

q: What is reverse routing, and why is it useful?
a:
Reverse routing generates a URL based on a route's name (or symbol) instead of a hardcoded path, creating a link between routes and the links/tags that point to them. The benefit: if you want to change a URL — say, from /login to /users/signin — without named routes you'd have to manually find and change every hardcoded link across the app.

With named routes, you just update the route definition once in routes/web.php, and every link generated through that route's name updates automatically.

q: What are 'bundles' in Laravel?
a: In Laravel, bundles are what's now called packages — they extend Laravel's functionality and can include their own views, configuration, migrations, routes, and scheduled tasks.

q: Where is robots.txt placed in a Laravel project?
a: In the public directory, alongside other publicly accessible files.

q: What are the basic building-block concepts of Laravel?
a: Routing, Eloquent ORM, Middleware, Security, Caching, and Blade Templating.

q: What's the difference in behavior between GET and POST requests?
a: GET requests can be cached, stay in the browser's history, can be bookmarked, should never be used for sensitive data, have length limits on the data sent, and are meant only for requesting data (not changing it). POST requests are never cached, don't stay in browser history, can't be bookmarked, and have no meaningful limit on how much data can be sent.

q: What is a namespace in Laravel/PHP?
a: A namespace lets you group related functions, classes, and constants under a specific name, avoiding naming clashes between similarly-named classes from different parts of an app or different packages.

q: What is Ajax, and how is it used in Laravel?
a: Ajax (Asynchronous JavaScript and XML) is a web development technique for building web pages that update without a full page reload. In Laravel, the response() and json() helper functions are commonly used on the backend to return data for these asynchronous requests.

q: What's a 'wrapper class' in general programming terms?
a:
A class that wraps or contains the functionality of another class or component. It's useful because it gives a layer of abstraction away from how the underlying class actually works — for example, a wrapper around a complex external component can manage the details of using it without exposing that complexity to the code calling it.

It can also make the underlying object simpler and safer to use by reducing how many different methods/points of contact the calling code needs to know about.
c: Extra Laravel Details Not Already Covered

q: Is PHP (or a PHP-based framework like Laravel) stateful or stateless by itself?
a:
PHP by itself has no memory between requests — each request is entirely separate, very close to how raw HTTP itself works. HTTP is a stateless protocol, and this isn't specific to PHP or any one language. To make an application feel 'stateful' (like staying logged in), the developer has to explicitly save relevant information (usually in a session and/or cookie) and read it back in on each following request.

Example of why this matters with multiple servers: if you have two web servers behind a load balancer, and someone logs in on Server 1, but their next request (like opening their inbox) gets routed to Server 2, and login info isn't shared between the two servers, they'll appear logged out — a bad experience. In a fully stateless design, every request carries everything needed to complete it, so it wouldn't matter which server handles it.

Most session management systems exist specifically to solve this shared-state problem across multiple servers.

q: What's the practical difference between $fillable and $guarded again, with a concrete example?
a:
$fillable lists which fields ARE allowed to be set through mass assignment; $guarded lists which fields are NOT allowed to be set that way.

Concrete example: if a users table has a user_type field that can be 'user' or 'admin', you don't want users to be able to set this themselves. If your code blindly does new User(request()->all()), someone could sneak in an extra user_type=admin field through the form and upgrade their own account. Setting protected $fillable = ['name', 'password', 'email']; on the model means only those three fields can ever be set through mass assignment — user_type is protected by not being on the list.

To actually update user_type, you'd have to do it explicitly and deliberately: $user->user_type = 'admin'; $user->save();

q: What are the common HTTP status code categories, in plain terms?
a: 1xx = informational (rarely seen directly). 2xx = success (200 OK is the classic one; 201 means something was created; 204 typically means success with no content to return). 3xx = redirection. 4xx = client error — the request itself was the problem: 400 Bad Request, 401 Unauthorized (not logged in), 403 Forbidden (logged in, but not allowed), 404 Not Found, 422 Unprocessable Entity (the request was well-formed but failed validation rules). 5xx = server error — the problem is on the server's side: 500 Internal Server Error, 502 Bad Gateway, 503 Service Unavailable (often means the server is overloaded or under maintenance — worth simply retrying later).
