Teams use it so every developer gets the same PHP/database versions without installing them on their laptop, and new developers are productive in minutes.

q: How do you start a Laravel project with DDEV?
a:
mkdir myapp && cd myapp
ddev config --project-type=laravel --docroot=public --php-version=8.4 --database=mysql:8.4
ddev start
ddev composer create-project laravel/laravel .
ddev launch            # opens https://myapp.ddev.site

For an existing project, clone it, run ddev config once (it writes .ddev/config.yaml, which you commit), then ddev start, ddev composer install, ddev artisan migrate.

q: Everyday DDEV commands?
a: ddev start / stop / restart · ddev describe (URLs, ports, services) · ddev ssh (shell in the web container) · ddev exec <cmd> · ddev composer ... · ddev artisan ... (Laravel) · ddev npm ... · ddev logs · ddev import-db --file=dump.sql.gz / ddev export-db · ddev snapshot / ddev snapshot restore · ddev xdebug on · ddev poweroff (stop all projects) · ddev delete (remove a project's containers and database).

q: What's inside .ddev/config.yaml, and what should be committed?
a: Project name, type, docroot, PHP version, web server type, database type/version, Node.js version, extra hostnames, ports and environment settings. Commit .ddev/config.yaml and any custom commands, add-ons and Docker overrides so the whole team shares the setup. Keep machine-specific or secret values out — use config.local.yaml or gitignored .local env files for those.

q: How is DDEV structured under the hood?
a: A shared router container (Traefik) receives requests for *.ddev.site and routes them to the right project. Each project has a web container (web server + PHP-FPM + Composer + Node) and a db container (MySQL, MariaDB or PostgreSQL). Extra services — Redis, Elasticsearch, Mailpit, phpMyAdmin — come from add-ons. Your project folder is mounted into the web container, with Mutagen file syncing available to speed things up on macOS.

q: How do you add Redis, a queue worker or other services?
a: Install an add-on: ddev add-on get ddev/ddev-redis, then ddev restart. For a Laravel queue worker or Vite dev server, use web_extra_daemons in config.yaml (DDEV keeps them running) and web_extra_exposed_ports for Vite's port. Anything unusual can be added with a docker-compose.<name>.yaml file inside .ddev/.

q: How do you debug PHP with Xdebug in DDEV?
a: ddev xdebug on, then start listening in VS Code or PhpStorm (port 9003), set a breakpoint and load the page. Turn it off (ddev xdebug off) when you're done, because Xdebug slows every request. DDEV also ships XHGui for profiling.

q: How do you share a local site with a client or test a webhook?
a: ddev share creates a public tunnel URL to your local project — handy for showing a client work in progress or receiving webhooks from Stripe, Shopify or GitHub during development. Stop it when done, since it exposes your local site to the internet.

q: How do you work with databases in DDEV?
a: Import a production dump with ddev import-db --file=backup.sql.gz (always anonymize real customer data), export with ddev export-db, and take quick snapshots before risky migrations so you can roll back in seconds. Connect a GUI client using the host port from ddev describe, or use the built-in commands for TablePlus, Sequel Ace or phpMyAdmin.

q: DDEV vs Laravel Sail vs Laravel Herd vs plain Docker Compose?
a:
• DDEV: framework-agnostic, many projects at once, HTTPS, snapshots and add-ons — ideal for agencies with Laravel, WordPress, Magento and Drupal clients.
  • Sail: Laravel's own Compose setup; simplest for Laravel-only teams.
  • Herd: native (non-Docker) PHP/Nginx for macOS and Windows — very fast, but less identical to production.
  • Plain Compose: full control, closest to your production images, but you maintain everything yourself.

q: What's new in DDEV lately?
a: The current line is v1.25.x (v1.25.4 released September 2026). Recent changes include database seeding and reset commands, MySQL 9.7 LTS support, global Dockerfiles and env files shared across projects, gitignored .local env files for credentials, performance tracking, and commands like ddev exec and ddev ssh auto-starting a stopped project. The old ddev nvm command was removed in v1.25.0 — set the Node.js version with nodejs_version in config.yaml instead.

q: Explain CI, Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment.
a: CI (Continuous Integration): every push and pull request is automatically built and checked — code style, static analysis, tests — so broken code is caught within minutes. Continuous Delivery: every change that passes is automatically packaged and ready to release; a person clicks "deploy". Continuous Deployment: it goes all the way to production automatically, with no manual step.

q: What are the building blocks of GitHub Actions?
a:
• Workflow: a YAML file in .github/workflows/.
  • Event (on:): what starts it — push, pull_request, schedule (cron), workflow_dispatch (manual button), release.
  • Jobs: run in parallel by default on a fresh runner VM (ubuntu-latest); needs: makes them run in order.
  • Steps: shell commands (run:) or reusable actions (uses: actions/checkout@v6).
  • Secrets and variables, artifacts (files passed between jobs) and environments (staging/production with protection rules).

q: Write a CI workflow for a Laravel + React app.
a:
name: CI
on:
  pull_request:
  push:
    branches: [main]
concurrency:
  group: ci-${{ github.ref }}
  cancel-in-progress: true
permissions:
  contents: read
jobs:
  backend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      mysql:
        image: mysql:8.4
        env: { MYSQL_DATABASE: testing, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: secret }
        ports: ["3306:3306"]
        options: --health-cmd="mysqladmin ping" --health-interval=10s --health-retries=5
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.4', coverage: none }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: vendor/bin/pint --test
      - run: vendor/bin/phpstan analyse --memory-limit=1G
      - run: php artisan test --parallel
        env: { DB_CONNECTION: mysql, DB_HOST: 127.0.0.1, DB_DATABASE: testing, DB_PASSWORD: secret }
  frontend:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - uses: actions/setup-node@v6
        with: { node-version: 24, cache: npm }
      - run: npm ci
      - run: npm run lint && npm run test -- --run && npm run build

Explain: two parallel jobs, a real MySQL service container, npm caching through setup-node (add actions/cache for Composer's cache directory), fail-fast checks (style → static analysis → tests), concurrency cancels outdated runs on the same branch, and minimal permissions.

q: Add a deployment job that runs only after CI passes on main.
a:
deploy:
    needs: [backend, frontend]
    if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main' && github.event_name == 'push'
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    environment:
      name: production
      url: https://app.example.com
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v6
      - name: Deploy over SSH
        uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
        with:
          host: ${{ secrets.PROD_HOST }}
          username: deploy
          key: ${{ secrets.PROD_SSH_KEY }}
          script: cd /var/www/app && ./deploy.sh

The production environment can require a reviewer's approval, restrict which branches may deploy, and hold its own secrets. The deploy script itself should do a zero-downtime release (see the Server Deployment chapter), or you can trigger Forge/Envoyer with a deploy hook URL.

q: How do you use a build matrix?
a:
Run the same job across combinations, e.g. PHP 8.3 and 8.4 × MySQL and PostgreSQL:

strategy:
  fail-fast: false
  matrix:
    php: ['8.3', '8.4']
    db: [mysql, pgsql]

Useful for packages and for proving an upgrade works before switching production. For an app that runs one PHP version in production, keep the matrix small so CI stays fast and cheap.

q: How do you make pipelines faster?
a: Cache dependencies (actions/cache, or the built-in cache: of setup actions), run independent jobs in parallel, run tests in parallel (php artisan test --parallel), use path filters so frontend-only changes don't run backend jobs, cancel superseded runs with concurrency, cache Docker layers (cache-from: type=gha), and split slow end-to-end tests into a separate job that runs on main or nightly.

q: Secrets in GitHub Actions — how do they work, and what are the rules?1 follow-up
a:
Store them under repository/environment/organization Secrets; reference them as ${{ secrets.NAME }}. They're masked in logs, not passed to workflows triggered from forks, and environment secrets are only available to jobs using that environment. Rules: least privilege, rotate regularly, never echo them, and prefer short-lived credentials.

Cross-questionHow do you deploy to AWS without storing access keys?

OIDC: give the job permissions: id-token: write, create an IAM role that trusts GitHub's OIDC provider for your repo/branch, and use aws-actions/configure-aws-credentials to get temporary credentials for each run.

q: How do you secure GitHub Actions workflows?
a:
• Set permissions: to the minimum (default contents: read) at the workflow or job level.
  • Pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA (tags can be moved), and let Dependabot update them.
  • Be very careful with pull_request_target and workflow_run: they run with secrets, so never check out and run untrusted fork code in them.
  • Don't interpolate untrusted input (PR titles, branch names) directly into run: scripts — pass it through env: to avoid script injection.
  • Protect main with required status checks and reviews; use environments with required reviewers for production.
  • Use OIDC instead of long-lived cloud keys; scan for secrets and dependency CVEs.

q: Reusable workflows vs composite actions?
a: A reusable workflow (on: workflow_call) is a whole workflow with jobs that other repos call with uses: org/repo/.github/workflows/ci.yml@main — great for a standard pipeline across many projects. A composite action bundles several steps into one step (uses: ./.github/actions/setup-laravel) — great for repeated setup like "install PHP, restore cache, composer install".

q: Build a Docker image in CI and push it to a registry.
a:
- uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3
      - uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with: { registry: ghcr.io, username: ${{ github.actor }}, password: ${{ secrets.GITHUB_TOKEN }} }
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with:
          push: true
          tags: ghcr.io/acme/app:${{ github.sha }}
          cache-from: type=gha
          cache-to: type=gha,mode=max

Tag images with the commit SHA (immutable, traceable) and deploy that exact tag. The job needs permissions: packages: write. Check each action's latest major version before using it — many actions have released new majors for the Node 24 runtime.

q: A pipeline fails but everything passes locally. How do you investigate?
a: Read the failing step's log from the top of the error; check environment differences — PHP/Node versions, missing extensions, env vars, timezone, file-name case sensitivity (Linux runner vs macOS/Windows laptop), service readiness (MySQL not up yet), missing built assets, and test order or shared state. Re-run with debug logging (ACTIONS_STEP_DEBUG secret), reproduce locally with act or in the same Docker image, and fix flaky tests instead of just re-running them.

q: What is branch protection, and how does it connect to CI?
a: Rules on main such as: pull request required, at least one approving review, required status checks (the CI jobs must pass), up-to-date branch before merge, no force pushes, signed commits if needed. CI becomes the gate — nothing reaches main (and therefore production) without passing it.

q: Other CI/CD tools you should be able to compare?
a: GitLab CI (.gitlab-ci.yml, stages and runners, built-in registry and environments), Bitbucket Pipelines (bitbucket-pipelines.yml, popular with Jira teams), Jenkins (self-hosted, very flexible, more maintenance), CircleCI, and deploy-focused tools like Laravel Forge/Envoyer/Cloud, Deployer and Ploi. The concepts carry over: triggers, jobs/stages, caching, secrets, artifacts, environments and approvals.

q: What's changed in GitHub Actions recently?
a:
• JavaScript actions moved to Node.js 24: runners began defaulting to Node 24 on 2 June 2026, and Node 20 was removed from runners on 16 September 2026.
  • Upgrade to the Node 24 majors: actions/checkout@v6, actions/setup-node@v6, actions/upload-artifact@v6, actions/setup-python@v6. Self-hosted runners need a recent runner version (v2.327.1 or later).
  • actions/checkout@v6 stores persisted credentials in a separate file instead of the repo's git config, and GitHub tightened pull_request_target defaults in June 2026.
  • Old workflows that still use @v4 versions of these actions will fail or warn — a quick, visible fix to mention in an interview.

q: Design a complete delivery pipeline for a Laravel + React product.
a:
1. Pull request: lint (Pint, ESLint), static analysis (PHPStan), unit and feature tests, frontend tests and build, dependency and secret scanning. Required to merge.
  2. Merge to main: build a versioned artifact or Docker image tagged with the commit SHA.
  3. Deploy to staging automatically; run smoke tests and a small Playwright suite.
  4. Production behind an environment approval; zero-downtime deploy; run backward-compatible migrations; restart queue workers.
  5. After deploy: health check, error-rate watch in Sentry, automatic rollback to the previous release if checks fail, Slack notification.
  6. Database changes follow expand → migrate → contract, so rollback stays safe.

q: Walk me through deploying a Laravel app to a fresh Ubuntu VPS.
a:
1. Create a non-root deploy user with SSH-key login; disable password and root login; enable the firewall (UFW: 22, 80, 443).
  2. Install Nginx, PHP-FPM with the needed extensions (mbstring, xml, curl, zip, bcmath, intl, pdo_mysql, redis), Composer, Node (to build assets), MySQL/PostgreSQL (or use a managed database), Redis, Supervisor.
  3. Clone the repo, composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader, npm ci && npm run build.
  4. Create .env with production values (APP_ENV=production, APP_DEBUG=false), php artisan key:generate (first time only).
  5. Point the Nginx root to public/, fix ownership of storage/ and bootstrap/cache/.
  6. php artisan migrate --force, php artisan optimize, php artisan storage:link.
  7. HTTPS with Certbot; Supervisor for queue workers; cron for the scheduler.
  8. Set up log rotation, backups and uptime monitoring.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Show a production Nginx config for Laravel and explain it.
a:
server {
    listen 443 ssl http2;
    server_name app.example.com;
    root /var/www/app/current/public;
    index index.php;

    add_header X-Frame-Options "SAMEORIGIN";
    add_header X-Content-Type-Options "nosniff";
    client_max_body_size 20M;

    location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string; }

    location ~ \.php$ {
        fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.4-fpm.sock;
        fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $realpath_root$fastcgi_script_name;
        include fastcgi_params;
    }
    location ~ /\.(?!well-known).* { deny all; }
    location ~* \.(css|js|png|jpg|svg|woff2)$ { expires 30d; access_log off; }
}

root points to public/ so .env and app code are never web-accessible; try_files sends every non-file request to Laravel's front controller; PHP goes to PHP-FPM over a Unix socket; $realpath_root makes symlinked zero-downtime releases work correctly; hidden files are blocked; static assets get long cache headers.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: What does a zero-downtime deployment look like on disk, and why does it work?
a:
/var/www/app/
├── releases/
│   ├── 20260920-101500/
│   └── 20260925-093000/      ← newest release
├── shared/
│   ├── .env
│   └── storage/
└── current → releases/20260925-093000   (symlink)

Each deploy goes into a new release folder: clone, composer install, build assets, link the shared .env and storage/, run migrations, cache config and routes. Only when everything succeeds does the current symlink switch to the new folder — an atomic, instant change. Nginx serves current/public, so users never see a half-deployed app. Rollback = point current back to the previous release. Keep the last 3–5 releases. Tools that do this: Laravel Forge (zero-downtime is on by default for new sites), Envoyer (multiple servers), Deployer (PHP, open source), Laravel Cloud, or your own script.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Write a simple deploy script with safe ordering.
a:
#!/usr/bin/env bash
set -euo pipefail
APP=/var/www/app; REL=$APP/releases/$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M%S)
git clone --depth 1 --branch main git@github.com:acme/app.git "$REL"
cd "$REL"
ln -s $APP/shared/.env .env
rm -rf storage && ln -s $APP/shared/storage storage
composer install --no-dev --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader --no-interaction
npm ci && npm run build
php artisan migrate --force
php artisan optimize
ln -sfn "$REL" $APP/current          # atomic switch
sudo systemctl reload php8.4-fpm     # clears OPcache for the new code
php artisan queue:restart            # workers pick up new code after their current job
ls -1dt $APP/releases/* | tail -n +6 | xargs -r rm -rf   # keep 5 releases

set -euo pipefail stops the script at the first error, so a failed build never becomes the live release.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Why must you restart queue workers and reload PHP-FPM on every deploy?
a: Queue workers (queue:work, Horizon) are long-running processes that loaded the old code into memory; without php artisan queue:restart (or horizon:terminate), they keep running old code — a classic "I deployed but the job still behaves the old way" bug. PHP-FPM with OPcache (and validate_timestamps=0) also caches compiled files, so reload it (or reset OPcache) so the new release is actually used.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: How do you keep queue workers and the scheduler running on a server?
a:
Supervisor keeps workers alive and restarts them if they crash:

[program:app-worker]
command=php /var/www/app/current/artisan queue:work redis --sleep=3 --tries=3 --max-time=3600
user=deploy
numprocs=2
autostart=true
autorestart=true
stopwaitsecs=3600
stdout_logfile=/var/www/app/shared/storage/logs/worker.log

The scheduler needs one cron entry: * * * * * cd /var/www/app/current && php artisan schedule:run >> /dev/null 2>&1. With several servers, use ->onOneServer() so tasks don't run twice.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: How do you run database migrations safely in production?
a: Take a backup (or snapshot) first, run php artisan migrate --force as part of the deploy, and keep migrations backward compatible with the code that's still running: add columns as nullable, backfill in a job, switch the code, and only drop old columns in a later release (expand → migrate → contract). Avoid long table locks on large tables during business hours, and never rely on migrate:rollback in production — fix forward with a new migration.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Laravel Forge vs Envoyer vs Laravel Cloud vs Vapor vs a manual VPS — how do you choose?
a:
• Manual VPS: cheapest and full control, but you own security patches, setup and on-call.
  • Forge: provisions and manages your own servers (DigitalOcean, AWS, Hetzner, or its built-in Laravel VPS), SSL, queues, cron and deployments. Since the October 2025 relaunch, zero-downtime deployment is on by default for new sites (on one server).
  • Envoyer: zero-downtime deployments to multiple servers, health checks, rollbacks.
  • Laravel Cloud: fully managed platform — push code, it handles servers, autoscaling, databases, queues; now offers scale-to-zero compute and a low-cost starter plan.
  • Vapor: serverless on AWS Lambda; great for spiky traffic, with Lambda's limits. Choose based on team size, budget, traffic pattern and how much server work the team wants to own.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: How do you deploy the React side of a full-stack app?
a: If React is part of Laravel (Vite + Blade/Inertia), npm run build during deploy and the files in public/build go out with the release. A separate SPA is built to static files and served from Nginx, a CDN (S3 + CloudFront, Cloudflare Pages, Netlify) or Vercel, with VITE_API_URL set at build time and CORS/cookie domains configured on the API. A Next.js app runs as a Node server (Vercel, or output: 'standalone' behind Nginx with PM2 or Docker).
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: How do you deploy a Node.js service next to Laravel on the same server?
a: Run it with PM2 (pm2 start dist/server.js -i max, pm2 save, pm2 startup) or systemd, listen on localhost only, and proxy through Nginx on a subdomain or path (with Upgrade/Connection headers for WebSockets). Deploy with the same release/symlink pattern and pm2 reload for zero-downtime restarts.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: What is php artisan down, and when do you use it?
a: Maintenance mode returns a 503 page while you do something risky (a big migration that can't be backward compatible). php artisan down --secret="bypass-token" lets your team keep using the site, --render="errors::503" pre-renders the page, and php artisan up brings it back. With zero-downtime deploys you rarely need it.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: After a deploy the site shows a 500 error. What do you check, in order?
a:
1. storage/logs/laravel.log and the Nginx/PHP-FPM error logs.
  2. .env present and correct in the new release (symlink to shared/.env)?
  3. Cached config built with the wrong env → php artisan optimize:clear, then optimize again.
  4. Permissions on storage/ and bootstrap/cache/.
  5. Missing PHP extension or a changed PHP version.
  6. A failed migration or missing table/column.
  7. Composer autoload out of date.

If it isn't obvious within minutes, roll back first, then investigate.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: 502 vs 504 errors from Nginx — what's the difference?
a: 502 Bad Gateway: Nginx couldn't talk to PHP-FPM/Node at all — the service is down, crashed, or the socket path/permissions are wrong. 504 Gateway Timeout: the backend answered too slowly — a slow query or external API, or all PHP-FPM workers busy. Check systemctl status php8.4-fpm, the FPM log ("max_children reached") and slow logs.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Production performance settings you always apply?
a: OPcache on (with enough memory and validate_timestamps=0, reset on deploy), composer install --optimize-autoloader --no-dev, php artisan optimize (config, routes, views, events), Redis for cache/sessions/queues, PHP-FPM pm.max_children sized to available RAM, gzip/Brotli and long cache headers for static assets, a CDN for assets and uploads, HTTP/2, and queues for anything slow.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: How do you handle environment variables and secrets on servers?
a: One .env per environment stored only on the server (in shared/), readable by the deploy user and web server only, never committed. Keep .env.example updated in Git. For teams, use a secret manager or Laravel's encrypted env files (php artisan env:encrypt / env:decrypt with the key stored in CI). Rotate keys when staff leave.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Backups and disaster recovery for a production app?
a: Automated daily database backups (plus binary logs or provider point-in-time recovery), backups of uploaded files (or versioned object storage like S3/R2), copies stored off-server and encrypted, and a tested restore at least monthly. Know your RPO (how much data you can lose) and RTO (how fast you must be back). Tools: spatie/laravel-backup, provider snapshots, managed database backups.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: What do you monitor after going live?
a: Uptime checks, error tracking (Sentry, Flare, Bugsnag), application performance (Laravel Pulse, Nightwatch or an APM), queue health (Horizon: failed jobs, wait times), server metrics (CPU, RAM, disk — alert at 80%), SSL expiry, scheduled-task heartbeats, and centralized logs. Alerts should go to a channel someone actually watches.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Shared hosting (cPanel) deployment — what's different?
a: Often no SSH root access, no Supervisor and limited cron. Point the domain's document root to public/ (or move public contents into public_html and fix paths in index.php), upload with Git or SFTP, run Composer through the terminal if allowed, use the database or sync queue driver, and set a cron job for schedule:run. Fine for small sites; move to a VPS or managed platform once you need workers, Redis or zero-downtime deploys.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Production deployment checklist you'd give a junior developer.
a: APP_DEBUG=false, correct APP_URL, HTTPS + HSTS, .env secured, optimize run, OPcache on, queues supervised and restarted, scheduler cron set, migrations backward compatible and backed up, storage permissions right, log rotation, backups verified, error tracking and uptime monitors on, rate limits on login and API, security headers, firewall and SSH hardening, and a written rollback plan.
c: Server Deployment: VPS, Forge, Cloud & Zero Downtime

q: Which AWS services matter most for a web developer?
a: EC2 (virtual servers), S3 (file/object storage), RDS (managed MySQL/PostgreSQL), ElastiCache (managed Redis/Valkey), CloudFront (CDN), Route 53 (DNS), IAM (users, roles, permissions), SES (email), SQS (queues), Lambda (serverless functions), ALB (load balancer), CloudWatch (logs, metrics, alarms), ACM (free TLS certificates for AWS services), Secrets Manager / Parameter Store (config and secrets), VPC (private network).
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Regions and Availability Zones?
a: A region is a geographic area (e.g. me-central-1 UAE, ap-south-1 Mumbai, eu-west-1 Ireland); each region has several isolated Availability Zones (separate data centres). Pick a region close to your users and allowed by the client's data rules; spread important resources across two or more AZs for high availability.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: What is IAM, and what are the golden rules?
a:
IAM controls who can do what in the AWS account. Users (people), groups, roles (temporary permissions assumed by services, EC2 instances, Lambda or CI pipelines) and policies (JSON documents allowing actions on resources). Rules: never use the root account day to day (enable MFA on it), least privilege, give EC2 and Lambda roles instead of access keys on disk, use OIDC for GitHub Actions instead of long-lived keys, and rotate or delete unused keys.

{ "Effect": "Allow", "Action": ["s3:PutObject", "s3:GetObject"], "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::acme-uploads/*" }
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: How do you use S3 with Laravel correctly?
a: composer require league/flysystem-aws-s3-v3, set FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3 and the bucket/region in .env, then Storage::disk('s3')->put(...). Keep buckets private (Block Public Access on); serve private files with temporary signed URLs (Storage::temporaryUrl($path, now()->addMinutes(10))) and public assets through CloudFront. For big uploads, let the browser upload straight to S3 with a pre-signed URL from Laravel. Enable versioning and lifecycle rules (e.g. move old files to cheaper storage).
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Deploy a Laravel app on AWS — a simple, solid architecture.
a: Route 53 (DNS) → CloudFront (optional, for assets) → ALB with an ACM certificate → EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group across two AZs (Nginx + PHP-FPM, or containers on ECS Fargate) → RDS MySQL (Multi-AZ for production) and ElastiCache Redis in private subnets → S3 for uploads → SES for email → SQS or Redis for queues → CloudWatch for logs and alarms. Secrets from Parameter Store/Secrets Manager. For smaller projects: one EC2 (or Lightsail) server with RDS, managed through Laravel Forge.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Security groups vs NACLs, public vs private subnets?
a: A security group is a stateful firewall attached to an instance/database (e.g. RDS allows port 3306 only from the web servers' security group). NACLs are stateless subnet-level rules (rarely customised). Public subnets have a route to the internet (load balancers, bastion); private subnets don't (databases, cache, app servers behind an ALB). Never expose RDS or Redis to 0.0.0.0/0.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: RDS — why use it instead of MySQL on EC2?
a: AWS handles installation, patching, automated backups with point-in-time recovery, Multi-AZ failover, read replicas and monitoring. You still own query performance and indexes. Costs more than self-hosting, but saves a lot of operational risk.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Scaling a Laravel app horizontally on AWS — what must change?
a: Make the app stateless: sessions and cache in Redis (ElastiCache), uploads in S3 (not local disk), queues in Redis/SQS, scheduled tasks with onOneServer(), logs to CloudWatch or stdout, and the same .env/secrets on every instance. Then an Auto Scaling group behind an ALB can add and remove servers safely.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: What is Lambda, and when would you use it with Laravel?
a: Lambda runs code on demand without servers, billed per request and duration. Use it for event-driven jobs (resize images when a file lands in S3, process webhooks, scheduled scripts) or run a whole Laravel app serverless with Laravel Vapor or Bref. Limits: cold starts, execution time limits, no local disk persistence.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: SQS vs Redis for Laravel queues?
a: SQS: fully managed, scales automatically, very durable; delays up to 15 minutes, no Horizon dashboard. Redis: faster, works with Horizon (metrics, balancing), but you manage it (or pay for ElastiCache) and must avoid evicting queue data.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: How do you control AWS costs?
a: Set billing alerts and budgets on day one, right-size instances (start small, watch CloudWatch), use Savings Plans/Reserved Instances for steady workloads, stop dev/staging at night, S3 lifecycle rules, watch data-transfer and NAT Gateway charges (often a surprise), delete unused EBS volumes, snapshots and Elastic IPs, and tag resources per project/client.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Monitoring and logging on AWS?
a: CloudWatch metrics (CPU, memory with the agent, RDS connections, ALB 5xx) with alarms to email/Slack, CloudWatch Logs for app and Nginx logs, CloudTrail for who changed what in the account, and application-level tools (Sentry, Pulse/Nightwatch) on top.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: AWS vs DigitalOcean/Hetzner vs Laravel Cloud for a Pakistani startup or agency client?
a: AWS: most services and enterprise trust, but complex and easy to overspend. DigitalOcean/Hetzner (+ Forge): simple, predictable monthly pricing — ideal for most small and medium projects. Laravel Cloud / Vercel-style platforms: least ops work, pay for convenience. Recommend based on budget, required compliance, team skills and expected traffic.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: How do I answer if my AWS experience is limited?
a: Be precise about what you've actually done ("deployed and managed apps on EC2 with S3 for storage", "configured RDS", "used SES") versus what you understand in theory (Auto Scaling, VPC design). Mention you'd follow least-privilege IAM and billing alerts from day one. The AWS Certified Cloud Practitioner or Developer Associate is a good way to close the gap if many target jobs ask for AWS.
c: AWS Basics for Laravel & Full Stack Developers

q: Unit vs feature (integration) vs end-to-end tests?
a: Unit: one class or function in isolation, no database or HTTP — fast (a price calculator, a value object). Feature: a full request through Laravel with the database — the most valuable tests in a Laravel app (POST /orders creates an order and returns 201). End-to-end: a real browser clicking through the app (Laravel Dusk, Playwright) — slow, so keep a few for critical journeys like login and checkout.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Write a feature test for creating a post (PHPUnit style).
a:
class CreatePostTest extends TestCase
{
    use RefreshDatabase;

    public function test_logged_in_user_can_create_a_post(): void
    {
        $user = User::factory()->create();

        $response = $this->actingAs($user)->postJson('/api/posts', [
            'title' => 'Hello Lahore',
            'body'  => 'First post',
        ]);

        $response->assertCreated()->assertJsonPath('data.title', 'Hello Lahore');
        $this->assertDatabaseHas('posts', ['title' => 'Hello Lahore', 'user_id' => $user->id]);
    }

    public function test_title_is_required(): void
    {
        $this->actingAs(User::factory()->create())
             ->postJson('/api/posts', ['body' => 'x'])
             ->assertUnprocessable()
             ->assertJsonValidationErrors('title');
    }

    public function test_guest_cannot_create_a_post(): void
    {
        $this->postJson('/api/posts', ['title' => 'x', 'body' => 'y'])->assertUnauthorized();
    }
}

Pattern: Arrange (factory data, logged-in user) → Act (request) → Assert (status, JSON, database).
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: The same test in Pest?
a:
use function Pest\Laravel\actingAs;

uses(RefreshDatabase::class);

it('lets a logged-in user create a post', function () {
    $user = User::factory()->create();

    actingAs($user)->postJson('/api/posts', ['title' => 'Hello', 'body' => 'x'])
        ->assertCreated();

    expect(Post::where('title', 'Hello')->exists())->toBeTrue();
});

it('requires a title', function () {
    actingAs(User::factory()->create())
        ->postJson('/api/posts', ['body' => 'x'])
        ->assertJsonValidationErrors('title');
});

Pest is a testing framework built on PHPUnit with a shorter, readable syntax, datasets, architecture tests (arch()->expect('App\Models')->toExtend(Model::class)) and parallel runs. New Laravel apps offer Pest by default.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: What are factories and states?
a: Factories generate realistic test data: User::factory()->count(5)->create(). States describe variations: Order::factory()->paid()->create(). Relationships: User::factory()->has(Order::factory()->count(3))->create() or Order::factory()->for($user)->create(). Sequences vary values across many models. Seeders reuse the same factories for local demo data.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: How do you test code that calls an external API?
a:
Never call the real API in tests. Use Laravel's HTTP fake:

Http::fake([
    'api.payfast.pk/*' => Http::response(['status' => 'SUCCESS', 'txn' => 'T123'], 200),
    '*' => Http::response('Not found', 404),
]);
$this->postJson('/api/checkout', [...])->assertOk();
Http::assertSent(fn ($req) => $req->url() === 'https://api.payfast.pk/v1/pay' && $req['amount'] === 5000);

Also test the failure path: Http::response([], 500) and Http::failedConnection().
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Fakes for queues, mail, events, notifications and storage?
a:
Queue::fake();      // then Queue::assertPushed(SendInvoice::class);
Mail::fake();       // Mail::assertSent(OrderShipped::class, fn ($m) => $m->hasTo('ali@example.com'));
Event::fake();      // Event::assertDispatched(OrderPlaced::class);
Notification::fake(); // Notification::assertSentTo($user, InvoicePaid::class);
Storage::fake('s3');  // UploadedFile::fake()->image('cnic.jpg'); Storage::disk('s3')->assertExists(...)

Fakes let you check that something was dispatched without actually sending emails or running jobs.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Mocking vs faking vs stubbing — what's the difference?
a: A stub returns canned answers. A fake is a working lightweight implementation (Laravel's Mail::fake(), an in-memory repository). A mock also verifies it was called in a specific way ($this->mock(PaymentGateway::class, fn ($m) => $m->shouldReceive('charge')->once()->andReturn(true))). Prefer fakes; use mocks at boundaries (payment gateway, SMS provider). Over-mocking makes tests pass while the real code fails.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: How do you test authorization and policies?
a: Feature tests for each role: owner can update (200), another user gets 403, guest gets 401. Unit-test complex policy rules directly: $this->assertTrue((new PostPolicy)->update($owner, $post));. Also test that list endpoints and exports don't leak other users' or tenants' records.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Testing jobs, commands and scheduled tasks?
a: Call the job's handle() directly with fakes around it, or dispatch synchronously in tests (QUEUE_CONNECTION=sync in phpunit.xml). Test Artisan commands with $this->artisan('invoices:send')->expectsOutput('Sent 3 invoices')->assertExitCode(0);. Use $this->travel(2)->days() or Carbon::setTestNow() to test time-based logic.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Which database should tests use?
a: SQLite in memory is fastest for simple apps, but MySQL/PostgreSQL-specific features (JSON columns, full-text search, some migrations) can behave differently — so many teams run tests against the same database engine as production (a Docker service locally, a service container in CI). RefreshDatabase wraps each test in a transaction so tests stay isolated.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: What is TDD, and do you use it?
a: Test-Driven Development: write a failing test, write the minimum code to pass, refactor (red → green → refactor). Useful for business rules, bug fixes (write a test that reproduces the bug first) and APIs. Be honest about your real practice — e.g. "I write feature tests for critical flows and a regression test for every bug I fix" is a strong, believable answer.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: How much coverage is enough?
a: Coverage percentage is a hint, not a goal. Aim for strong coverage of money, permissions, data integrity and integrations; don't chase 100% on trivial getters. Run coverage in CI (php artisan test --coverage --min=70) to stop it silently dropping.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Frontend testing in a React or Vue project?
a: Vitest + Testing Library for components (test what the user sees and does), MSW to mock the API, and Playwright for end-to-end flows. Test forms with validation errors, loading and empty states, and permission-based UI.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: "Have you written tests?" — how to answer if your experience is limited.
a: Be honest and specific: which kinds you've written (feature tests for APIs, a few unit tests), on which project, and what you'd like to do more of. Then prove it by writing a quick feature test in the interview using the pattern above — many interviewers care more about seeing you do it than about your history.
c: Practical Testing: PHPUnit, Pest & Frontend Tests

q: Describe the full Docker Compose setup for HOLOIN or AI-BDM.
a: Roughly: an app service (PHP-FPM running Laravel), an Nginx service in front of it, a mysql/postgres service, a redis service, a python-ai service (FastAPI), and in HOLOIN's case a mongo service for device data — each with its own named storage area for keeping data safe, connected on a shared Docker network so services can reach each other by name instead of by IP address.

q: Why does DB_HOST=127.0.0.1 fail inside a container but work fine directly on the host machine?
a:
Inside a container, 127.0.0.1/localhost refers to that container itself, not any other container — so pointing at 127.0.0.1 for the database only works if the database is running inside the exact same container as the app, which it isn't in a multi-container setup. Instead, Docker's built-in naming system turns the database container's service name (like mysql) into its real internal address, so a .env file inside a container should set DB_HOST=mysql, not 127.0.0.1.

From the host machine itself (outside any container), 127.0.0.1 works because the port is explicitly opened up in the compose file.

q: What's the difference between a bind mount and a named volume, and which did you use for what?
a:
A bind mount connects a specific folder on your computer into the container (useful for live-editing code during development, since changes on your computer show up instantly inside the container). A named volume is managed by Docker itself, not tied to a specific folder on your computer, and is the right choice for data that needs to survive independent of your computer's file layout — database data folders, for example.

I use bind mounts for app code during local development and named volumes for MySQL/Postgres/MongoDB data folders.

q: Explain your Nginx + PHP-FPM setup — what does Nginx hand off to PHP-FPM, and what's different for a high-traffic API?
a: Nginx serves static files directly and passes any request for a .php file to PHP-FPM (using a protocol called FastCGI), which runs the actual Laravel app and returns the response for Nginx to send back to the client. For a high-traffic API, I tune PHP-FPM's worker settings (how many processes, when to start more) based on expected traffic and available memory, keep responses lean, and make sure anything slow (like calling the AI service) happens in the background instead of holding a PHP worker busy the whole time.

q: What is Cloudflare R2, and why did you choose it over AWS S3 or local disk?
a:
R2 is Cloudflare's file-storage service that works the same way as AWS S3, notable for having no fee for downloading data out of it, which matters for a system serving a meaningful amount of file downloads (device firmware, exported reports, uploaded documents). It works with the same 'S3-style' rules, so it plugs into Laravel's existing S3-style storage setup with minimal code change, while avoiding the download costs that can add up with S3 at scale.

Local disk wasn't an option for a containerized, possibly multi-server setup, since local storage isn't shared or safe across multiple servers or container restarts.

q: Walk through how you'd debug a container that keeps restarting/crashing in production.
a: First, check the crashing service's logs to see the actual error right before the crash. If the logs don't explain it, check the container's exit code (an out-of-memory crash shows a distinct code, for example) and its resource limits/usage. I'd also check that the health check setup isn't itself the cause (a too-strict health check can restart a container that's just slow to start, not actually broken), and check whether a recent deployment changed an environment variable or dependency the container now can't find at startup.

q: What's a multi-stage Docker build, and did you use one to keep the production image lean?
a: A Dockerfile with multiple stages, where an early stage installs build-time tools (dev packages, or frontend build tools) and a later, final stage copies only the finished, necessary files into a clean, minimal base image. Yes — production images leave out development dependencies, extra build files, and build caches, which keeps the image smaller, reduces ways to break in, and speeds up deployments.

q: How do you handle secrets in a Dockerized Laravel app?
a: For local development, .env files (kept out of version control/Git) are fine. In production, I avoid baking secrets into the image itself or committing them anywhere — they're set as environment variables at deploy time through the hosting platform's secrets system, so the image itself stays identical and shareable across environments, and rotating a secret doesn't require rebuilding the image.

q: Describe your deployment process — what happens if a deploy fails halfway through a database migration?
a:
Fill inDescribe your actual pipeline — e.g., automated tests run, an image is built and pushed, then a deploy runs migrations before switching traffic to the new containers. If a migration fails partway, Laravel wraps most migration steps in a transaction where the database allows it (Postgres does for structure changes; MySQL's support is more limited), so I write migrations to be as all-or-nothing and reversible as possible, and I always have a rollback method ready.

For anything genuinely risky, I test the migration against a production-sized copy first, so a partial failure in production is rare, not routine.

q: Walk through your Git branching workflow.
a: I create feature branches off main/develop, open a pull request for review before merging, and keep commits reasonably small and clearly described — this makes it easier to trace history later or undo a change. At Cynsure Design and ChirpTech, I also reviewed other people's pull requests as part of a team-lead role, not just submitted my own.

q: git rebase vs. git merge — when do you use each?
a: Merge keeps the full history, including a merge commit that shows exactly how branches came together. Rebase moves your branch's commits on top of the latest target branch, giving a clean, straight-line history with no merge commit. I use rebase to tidy up my own branch before opening a PR, but I avoid rebasing anything already pushed and shared with others, since it rewrites history they may already be building on.

q: What's your real CI/CD experience — what have you personally built vs. just used?
a: Fill inhonestly — if you've mostly deployed into an existing pipeline rather than built one from scratch, say that plainly. If you have set up GitHub Actions (or similar) to run tests/builds on push, name it specifically — that's a strong answer here.

q: How would you set up a basic CI pipeline for a Laravel app?
a: On every push/PR: install dependencies (composer install), run static analysis if set up (PHPStan/Larastan), run the automated test suite (PHPUnit/Pest) against a test database, and block the merge if anything fails. For deployment: a successful merge to main triggers a deploy — pull the latest code, run migrations, restart queue workers, rebuild caches (config:cache, route:cache) — ideally with a way to roll back if the deploy fails a health check.

q: How do you handle a merge conflict on a shared branch?
a: I read and understand both changes before resolving — I never blindly pick 'theirs' or 'ours' without knowing what each side was actually trying to do, because a careless fix can silently delete someone's work. For anything important, I'd talk to whoever wrote the conflicting code instead of guessing from the diff alone.

q: What's your testing experience?
a: Fill inhonestly — if your testing has mostly been manual rather than automated test suites, say that clearly instead of claiming experience you don't have. JD3 directly asks about PHPUnit/Pest, and JD1/JD6 hint at it with 'testable code' language, so have a real, rehearsed answer instead of dodging the question.
c: Testing (PHPUnit / Pest) — Be Honest About This One

q: Unit test vs. feature test vs. integration test — what's the difference in Laravel?
a: A unit test checks a single class or method alone, usually with its dependencies faked/mocked. A feature test (Laravel's term) tests the app through its normal HTTP layer — like checking that a POST to an endpoint returns the right status and correctly updates the database. An integration test sits between the two — checking that multiple real pieces (like a service plus the actual database) work together correctly, without faking anything.
c: Testing (PHPUnit / Pest) — Be Honest About This One

q: How would you test a class that calls an external API?
a: I'd fake the HTTP client instead of making a real network call (Laravel's Http::fake() is built exactly for this) — then check that the request was built correctly, and that my code handles both the mocked success response and a failure response properly. This is how I'd cover something like the Shopify sync tool's webhook handling, if I built its test suite from scratch.
c: Testing (PHPUnit / Pest) — Be Honest About This One

q: PHPUnit vs. Pest — which would you pick for a new project?
a: Pest is built on top of PHPUnit (same assertions and mocking underneath), but uses simpler, function-style syntax instead of class-based test methods, plus some nice extras (readable expectations, architecture tests). For a brand new project, I'd lean toward Pest for its cleaner syntax — but on an existing PHPUnit codebase, I wouldn't rewrite it just for style, since matching what's already there usually matters more.
c: Testing (PHPUnit / Pest) — Be Honest About This One

q: merge vs rebase?1 follow-up
a:
Merge keeps full history with a merge commit. Rebase rewrites your commits on top of the latest main → clean straight history. Never rebase shared/public branches.

Cross-questionHow do you resolve a merge conflict?

Pull latest, open conflicted files, choose/combine changes, run tests, commit. Talk to the other developer if the logic conflicts.

q: Useful commands?
a: git stash, cherry-pick, revert (safe undo on shared branches) vs reset (rewrite local history), reflog (recover "lost" commits), bisect (find the commit that introduced a bug), commit --amend, interactive rebase to squash.

q: Branching strategy?
a: GitHub Flow / trunk-based: short-lived feature branches → PR → review → merge to main → deploy. GitFlow (develop/release/hotfix branches) for scheduled releases. Use Conventional Commits (feat:, fix:, chore:).

q: What do you check in a code review?
a: Does it work and match requirements? Readability, naming, small functions, no duplicated logic, security (validation, auth checks), performance (N+1, re-renders), tests included, error handling, no secrets in code. Be kind: comment on the code, not the person; explain why.

q: How do you enforce coding standards in a team?
a: Automate it: ESLint + Prettier, Laravel Pint, PHPStan/Larastan (static analysis), TypeScript strict mode, Husky pre-commit hooks, CI blocks merge if checks fail, PR template, branch protection (at least 1 approval). Write short team guidelines doc.

q: Types of tests?
a: Unit (one function/class), Feature/Integration (an API endpoint with DB), End-to-End (real browser clicking through the app). The testing pyramid: many unit, fewer integration, few E2E.

q: Tools?
a: Frontend: Vitest/Jest + React Testing Library (test behavior, not internals), Playwright or Cypress for E2E, MSW to mock APIs. Backend: Pest or PHPUnit, RefreshDatabase, factories, fakes (Queue::fake(), Mail::fake(), Http::fake(), Storage::fake()).

q: How do you test a queued job that calls a third-party API?
a: Http::fake() with success, failure and timeout responses; assert retries and final state; assert job is dispatched with Queue::fake() in the controller test; test the job itself separately by calling handle().

q: Explain CI/CD simply.
a: CI (Continuous Integration): every push/PR automatically installs dependencies, runs linting, tests, and builds. CD (Continuous Delivery/Deployment): after CI passes, automatically deploy to staging and then production (with or without manual approval).

q: What does a typical pipeline look like for a React + Laravel app?
a:
Push/PR →
  1. Checkout code
  2. Install deps (composer install, npm ci) — with caching
  3. Lint & static analysis (ESLint, Pint, PHPStan)
  4. Tests (Pest with MySQL/Redis service containers, Vitest)
  5. Build frontend (npm run build)
  6. Build Docker image / artifact, tag with commit SHA
  7. Security scan (npm audit, composer audit)
Merge to main →
  8. Deploy to staging → smoke tests / E2E
  9. Manual approval → deploy to production
 10. Run migrations, cache config/routes, restart queue workers
 11. Health check → auto rollback if failing
 12. Notify Slack

q: Example GitHub Actions workflow (Laravel)?
a:
name: CI
on: [push, pull_request]
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    services:
      mysql:
        image: mysql:8
        env: { MYSQL_DATABASE: testing, MYSQL_ROOT_PASSWORD: secret }
        ports: ['3306:3306']
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: shivammathur/setup-php@v2
        with: { php-version: '8.4' }
      - run: composer install --no-interaction --prefer-dist
      - run: cp .env.example .env && php artisan key:generate
      - run: vendor/bin/pint --test
      - run: php artisan test
        env: { DB_HOST: 127.0.0.1, DB_DATABASE: testing, DB_PASSWORD: secret }

q: Laravel production deployment steps?1 follow-up
a:
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader → php artisan migrate --force → php artisan optimize (config/route/view/event cache) → npm run build → php artisan queue:restart (workers pick up new code!) → restart PHP-FPM/Octane → storage:link. Set APP_ENV=production, APP_DEBUG=false. Keep workers alive with Supervisor (or Horizon). Cron runs schedule:run every minute.

Cross-questionYou deployed but jobs still behave like old code — why?

Queue workers are long-running processes holding old code in memory. You forgot queue:restart / horizon:terminate.

q: Zero-downtime deployment?
a: Atomic releases (Envoyer / Deployer / Laravel Forge): each deploy in a new folder releases/2026..., shared storage and .env symlinked, switch the current symlink at the end → instant switch, instant rollback. In containers: rolling updates or blue-green (two identical environments, switch traffic) or canary (send 5% of traffic first). Migrations must be backward compatible (expand/contract).

q: Docker basics?1 follow-up
a:
Image = packaged app + dependencies. Container = running image. Dockerfile builds the image; docker-compose runs multiple services locally (app, nginx, mysql, redis). Laravel Sail is a ready docker-compose setup.

Cross-questionHow do you make images smaller/faster?

Multi-stage builds (build assets in a Node stage, copy only output), Alpine/slim base images, .dockerignore, order layers so dependencies are cached (copy composer.json before app code).

q: How is a Next.js app deployed?
a: Vercel (easiest), or output: 'standalone' in a Docker container on AWS/GCP/any VPS behind Nginx, or static export for fully static sites. Next.js 16.2's Adapter API makes other platforms (Netlify, Cloudflare, AWS) better supported.

q: AWS services you'd use for a Laravel + React app?
a: EC2 or ECS/Fargate (containers) for app & workers, RDS (MySQL/Postgres), ElastiCache (Redis), S3 (files) + CloudFront (CDN), SQS (queue option), SES (email), Route 53 (DNS), ALB (load balancer), CloudWatch (logs/alarms), Secrets Manager, IAM roles. Alternatives: Laravel Forge + DigitalOcean/Hetzner, Laravel Vapor (serverless), Laravel Cloud. GCP/Azure have equivalents (Cloud Run, Cloud SQL, Blob Storage…).

q: How do you scale horizontally?
a: Put multiple app servers behind a load balancer. For that, the app must be stateless: sessions in Redis/DB (not files), uploads in S3 (not local disk), cache in Redis, scheduled tasks run on one server only (->onOneServer()).

q: Infrastructure as Code?
a: Terraform / AWS CDK / Pulumi — infra defined in code, reviewed in PRs, reproducible environments.

q: Monitoring and observability?
a: Logs (centralized — CloudWatch, ELK, Better Stack), errors (Sentry, Flare), metrics/APM (New Relic, Datadog), uptime checks, queue monitoring (Horizon), alerts on error rate/latency/failed jobs. Laravel Pulse for app health dashboard.

q: Environments?
a: local → dev → staging (copy of production) → production. Different .env per environment, seeded fake data outside production, never test with real customer data.

q: What is SDLC?
a: Software Development Life Cycle: Requirement gathering → Analysis/Planning → Design → Development → Testing → Deployment → Maintenance.

q: Waterfall vs Agile?
a: Waterfall: step by step, fixed requirements, hard to change. Agile (Scrum): short sprints (1–2 weeks), deliver small working pieces, get feedback, adapt. Scrum events: sprint planning, daily standup, sprint review, retrospective.

q: Bug life cycle?
a: New → Assigned → Open → Fixed → Retest → Verified → Closed (or Reopened / Rejected / Deferred / Duplicate).

q: QA reports a bug you can't reproduce. What do you do?
a: Ask for exact steps, environment, browser, user role, data, screenshots/video, and logs. Try on the same environment (staging). Check logs for errors at that time. Politely work together — don't say "works on my machine" and close it.

q: Types of testing?
a: Unit, integration, functional, regression (old features still work), smoke (quick basic check after deploy), UAT (client tests), performance/load, security testing. Developers write unit/feature tests (PHPUnit/Pest); QA does manual and automated (Selenium, Cypress, Playwright).

q: Severity vs priority?
a: Severity = how bad the bug is technically. Priority = how quickly it must be fixed for the business. A typo on the homepage logo: low severity, high priority.

q: How do you convert business requirements into a technical solution?
a: Understand the goal (ask "why"), list user roles and flows, identify data (tables), define APIs/screens, note edge cases, estimate tasks, confirm with PM/client before coding, deliver in small parts.

q: How do you debug a PHP application?
a: Enable error reporting in local (error_reporting(E_ALL)), read logs (storage/logs, writable/logs in CI4, Apache/Nginx error logs, PHP-FPM log), var_dump/dd(), Xdebug with breakpoints in VS Code/PhpStorm, Laravel Telescope/Debugbar, browser Network tab for AJAX responses.

q: White screen / 500 error in production — steps?
a: Check server error log and app log → recent deploy or file change? → permissions on storage/writable folders → PHP version mismatch / missing extension → .env/config problem → memory limit → roll back if critical.

q: You got an old project with no documentation. How do you start?
a: Get it running locally (Docker with matching PHP version), check composer.json and framework version, read routes → controllers → models for main flows, look at the DB schema, put it in Git if it isn't, make small safe changes, write down what you learn.

q: Upgrading PHP 7.x → 8.x on an old project — what breaks?
a: Removed functions (each(), create_function), stricter type errors, 0 == "abc" behavior change, deprecated dynamic properties (8.2), null passed to internal functions deprecated (8.1), old libraries not compatible. Use Rector (automatic upgrades) and PHPStan (find errors), test on staging.

q: How do you add a feature without breaking existing things?
a: Understand the affected code, create a Git branch, write/run tests if possible, test related modules (regression), code review, deploy to staging, QA tests, then production with a rollback plan.

q: How do you deploy a PHP project to shared hosting (cPanel)?1 follow-up
a:
Upload via Git (cPanel Git Version Control) or FTP/File Manager, point domain to the public folder (Laravel/CI4), create DB and import SQL in phpMyAdmin, set .env, set folder permissions, run composer install via terminal/SSH if available, set cron for scheduler.

Cross-questionCan't point the domain to public/?

Move public contents to public_html and fix paths in index.php, or use .htaccess rewrite — but ensure .env and app files aren't web-accessible.

q: Deploy on a VPS (Ubuntu) — stack?
a: Nginx + PHP-FPM + MySQL (LEMP) or Apache (LAMP), Composer, Node (for building assets), Git, Supervisor for queue workers, cron for scheduler, Certbot/Let's Encrypt for SSL, firewall (UFW). Tools that automate this: Laravel Forge, Ploi, RunCloud, Envoyer.

q: Laravel production deploy commands?
a:
git pull origin main
composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader
php artisan migrate --force
npm ci && npm run build
php artisan optimize        # caches config, routes, views
php artisan queue:restart

CodeIgniter 4: composer install --no-dev, php spark migrate, set CI_ENVIRONMENT = production, make writable/ writable.

q: Apache .htaccess purpose?
a: URL rewriting (remove index.php from URLs — needed in CodeIgniter and Laravel), redirects (HTTP → HTTPS), security rules. Nginx doesn't use .htaccess; rules go in the server config (try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;).

q: What is CI/CD? Simple pipeline?
a: On every push: install dependencies → code style check → run tests → build assets. On merge to main: deploy to staging → test → deploy to production (via SSH/Forge/Envoyer) → run migrations → restart workers. Tools: GitHub Actions, GitLab CI, Bitbucket Pipelines, Jenkins.

q: Docker for PHP projects?
a: Great for running old projects with old PHP versions without messing your machine: containers for PHP-FPM (specific version), Nginx, MySQL, Redis using docker-compose.yml. Laravel Sail is a ready setup.

q: How should local, staging and production environments be separated and configured safely?
a: Local → Staging (client/QA testing) → Production. Different .env files; never test on the live database.

q: Daily Git commands?
a: clone, status, add, commit, pull, push, branch, checkout/switch, merge, log, diff, stash.

q: How do you handle a merge conflict?
a: Pull latest, open conflicted files, keep correct code (talk to teammate if needed), test, commit.

q: merge vs rebase?
a: Merge keeps history with merge commit; rebase makes history linear. Don't rebase shared branches.

q: revert vs reset?
a: revert creates a new commit that undoes a change (safe on shared branches). reset moves the branch back (rewrites history — local only).

q: You committed .env with passwords by mistake. What now?
a: Remove it and add to .gitignore — but it's still in history, so change all the passwords/keys immediately. Clean history with git filter-repo/BFG only if needed, and inform the lead.

q: Branching?
a: main (production), develop, feature/xyz, hotfix/xyz. Pull Requests with review before merging.

q: What does a real testing strategy look like on an enterprise project, not just 'we have some tests'?
a:
A deliberate mix of test types, each catching a different kind of mistake. Unit tests check a single class or method in isolation, with dependencies faked/mocked, and should be fast enough to run constantly during development. Feature tests (Laravel's term) go through the actual HTTP layer — hitting a real route and checking the real response and database state — catching integration mistakes unit tests can't see.

A smaller number of end-to-end/browser tests (using something like Laravel Dusk or a JS tool like Playwright/Cypress) verify that critical user flows genuinely work through the real UI, since these are slow and brittle and shouldn't be the bulk of the suite. The right ratio is usually described as a pyramid: lots of fast unit tests, a solid layer of feature tests, and just a few slow end-to-end tests covering the most critical paths (signup, checkout, login).

q: What should actually be tested, if you can't test everything?
a:
Prioritize by risk and blast radius, not by what's easiest to test. Business-critical logic (billing calculations, permission checks, anything involving money or access control) deserves thorough coverage, since a bug there is expensive or dangerous. Code that's changed often is worth covering well, since tests are what let you change it confidently without fear of silently breaking something.

And code that's genuinely simple and unlikely to break (a basic getter, a trivial pass-through) is a reasonable place to accept lighter coverage, rather than chasing 100% coverage as a vanity metric — a high coverage number with weak assertions is worse than an honest, lower number with meaningful tests.

q: How do tests fit into the actual development workflow, not just exist as an afterthought?
a:
Tests run automatically on every pull request through CI, and a PR that fails tests simply can't merge — this is a hard gate, not a suggestion. For genuinely critical logic, writing the test before (or alongside) the code, rather than only after, helps clarify what 'correct' actually means before you've committed to one implementation.

And test data should be built with factories (Laravel's model factories) rather than hand-written fixtures, so tests stay fast, realistic, and easy to extend as the schema evolves.

q: What testing considerations are specific to APIs and integrations?
a:
For any code that calls an outside service (a payment gateway, a third-party API), fake the HTTP layer in tests (Laravel's Http::fake()) rather than making real network calls — this makes tests fast, reliable, and independent of whether the third party is actually up. Test both the success path and realistic failure paths (a timeout, a 500 error, a malformed response), since production incidents are far more often caused by an unhandled failure case than by the happy path breaking.

And for webhook-receiving endpoints specifically, test signature verification and idempotency (safe-to-repeat processing) explicitly, since those are exactly the areas where a subtle bug becomes a real security or data-integrity incident.

q: What should an automated CI pipeline actually do, end to end?
a:
On every push or pull request: install dependencies from the locked versions, run static analysis (Larastan/PHPStan) to catch type and logic errors, run the code style checker (Pint) to enforce formatting automatically instead of relying on manual review for it, and run the full automated test suite against a real test database.

If any step fails, the merge is blocked — this needs to be a hard rule, not a courtesy. On a successful merge to the main/production branch, the pipeline should then build the deployable artifact (or container image), and trigger the actual deployment.

q: What does a safe, modern deployment process actually involve?
a:
Zero-downtime deployment — the new version is prepared and warmed up before traffic is switched to it, rather than taking the app offline mid-deploy. Database migrations run as part of the deploy, written to be safe even if a migration only partially completes (per the schema-design point earlier). Configuration and route caches are rebuilt (php artisan config:cache, route:cache) as part of the deploy, not left stale.

And a genuine rollback plan exists and has actually been tested — 'we can roll back' is only true if you've verified it works, not just assumed it would.

q: What's changed recently in how Laravel apps are actually served in production?
a:
Traditional PHP-FPM plus Nginx is still common and perfectly valid, but Laravel Octane (running the app through FrankenPHP, Swoole, or RoadRunner) has become a mainstream production option — it keeps the application booted in memory between requests instead of bootstrapping Laravel fresh on every single request, giving meaningfully better throughput and lower latency, especially under heavy API traffic.

FrankenPHP specifically has gained traction because it bundles the Caddy web server and the PHP runtime into a single process, simplifying the deployment story compared to running Nginx and PHP-FPM as two separate pieces. The trade-off: Octane-style servers require your code to be genuinely stateless between requests — static properties, singletons holding request-specific data, and other assumptions that were harmless under traditional PHP-FPM (where each request got a completely fresh process) can cause subtle bugs or memory leaks under Octane, since the application instance is reused across requests.

This is a real, non-trivial thing to audit for before switching.

q: What's the role of infrastructure-as-code and containerization in an enterprise deployment?
a:
Defining infrastructure in version-controlled code (Terraform, or platform-specific config) rather than manually clicking through a cloud provider's dashboard, so infrastructure changes go through the same review process as application code, and the exact setup can be recreated or audited later. Docker (or an equivalent) packages the application with its exact dependencies so 'works in staging' reliably means 'works in production' too.

For teams without dedicated DevOps capacity, managed platforms (Laravel Forge, Laravel Cloud, or similar) have matured enough that a small team can run production-grade infrastructure — automated SSL, zero-downtime deploys, managed backups — without needing to build all of that tooling themselves from scratch.

q: What's the difference between 'we have logs' and genuine observability?
a: Logs alone tell you what happened in one specific request, if you already know where to look. Real observability means you can answer questions you didn't anticipate in advance — structured logging (consistent, machine-parseable log entries, not free-form text) sent to a centralized log system rather than scattered across individual servers; metrics tracking trends over time (response times, error rates, queue depth, memory usage) so you can see a problem building before it becomes an outage; and distributed tracing for systems with multiple services, so you can follow one request's full path across every component it touched, not just see each service's logs in isolation.

q: What should actually be monitored on a production Laravel app?
a:
Application health: error rates and exception tracking (a tool like Sentry or Bugsnag, catching and grouping errors instead of relying on someone noticing a log line), request response times and slow-query logs to catch regressions before users report them. Queue health specifically: Horizon's dashboard for throughput, wait times, and failed jobs, with alerting if the failed-jobs count crosses a threshold, since a silently stuck queue can go unnoticed for a long time otherwise.

Infrastructure health: server resource usage (CPU, memory, disk), database connection pool usage, and uptime/availability checks hitting the app from outside, so you find out about downtime the same way a user would, immediately, rather than from a support ticket.

q: What's the point of alerting, and how do you avoid the common failure mode of alert fatigue?
a: The point is catching a problem while it's still small and before a human notices it the hard way. The common failure mode is setting up so many low-value alerts that the team starts ignoring all of them, including the important ones — so alerts should be tuned to genuinely actionable thresholds (not every single error, but an error rate crossing a meaningful level), routed to the right person/channel, and periodically reviewed and pruned, the same way code itself needs maintenance.

q: Linux commands you use for troubleshooting?
a:
• Files/logs: ls -la, cd, tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log, less, grep -i "error" file, grep -r "text" dir, journalctl -u nginx -f, zcat for rotated logs.
  • Processes: ps aux | grep php, top/htop, kill, systemctl status|restart php8.3-fpm nginx supervisor.
  • Disk/memory: df -h, du -sh * | sort -h, free -m.
  • Network: curl -I https://site, ss -tulpn (ports), ping, dig domain, nslookup, traceroute.
  • Permissions: chmod, chown -R www-data:www-data storage bootstrap/cache.
  • Misc: crontab -e, scp/rsync, ssh, tar, history.

q: File permissions for Laravel?1 follow-up
a:
Code owned by the deploy user, web server group (www-data) needs write access only to storage/ and bootstrap/cache/ (775 dirs / 664 files). Never chmod 777.

Cross-questionLog file permission denied after running a command as root.

laravel.log was created by root; web user can't write. Run artisan as the web/deploy user (sudo -u www-data php artisan ...) and fix ownership.

q: Nginx + PHP-FPM — how do they work together?
a:
Nginx serves static files and passes .php requests to PHP-FPM through a Unix socket or port (FastCGI). PHP-FPM keeps a pool of worker processes.

server {
  listen 443 ssl http2;
  server_name crm.example.com;
  root /var/www/crm/current/public;
  index index.php;
  location / { try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string; }
  location ~ \.php$ {
    include fastcgi_params;
    fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php8.3-fpm.sock;
    fastcgi_param SCRIPT_FILENAME $realpath_root$fastcgi_script_name;
  }
  location ~ /\.(?!well-known) { deny all; }
  client_max_body_size 50M;
}

q: 502 Bad Gateway vs 504 Gateway Timeout?
a: 502: Nginx can't talk to PHP-FPM/Node — service down, crashed, wrong socket path, socket permissions. 504: backend too slow — long query/API call exceeding fastcgi_read_timeout/proxy_read_timeout, or all PHP-FPM workers busy. Check Nginx error log + PHP-FPM log ("server reached pm.max_children").

q: PHP-FPM tuning?
a: pm = dynamic|static|ondemand, pm.max_children ≈ (RAM available for PHP) ÷ (average memory per PHP process). Too high → server swaps/OOM; too low → requests queue → 504s. Also pm.max_requests (recycle workers to avoid leaks), request_terminate_timeout, OPcache on with enough memory, realpath_cache. Enable the slow log (request_slowlog_timeout = 5s) to find slow scripts.

q: Apache vs Nginx?
a: Apache: .htaccess per-directory configs, mod_php or PHP-FPM, common on shared hosting. Nginx: event-driven, lower memory, great reverse proxy and static file server, config only in server files.

q: SSL/TLS setup and renewal?1 follow-up
a:
Let's Encrypt with Certbot (certbot --nginx -d crm.example.com), auto-renew via systemd timer/cron (certs last 90 days — and lifetimes are getting shorter industry-wide, so automation is essential). Redirect HTTP → HTTPS, HSTS header. Check expiry: openssl s_client -connect host:443 | openssl x509 -noout -dates.

Cross-questionWebhooks suddenly failing, site works in browser.

Certificate chain incomplete (browsers fix it, API clients don't) or cert expired on a subdomain used only for webhooks.

q: DNS records you should know?1 follow-up
a:
A (domain → IPv4), AAAA (IPv6), CNAME (alias to another name), MX (mail servers), TXT (SPF, DKIM, DMARC, domain verification), NS (nameservers), CAA (which CAs may issue certificates), TTL (cache time — lower it before a migration).

Cross-questionMoved the CRM to a new server, some users still hit the old one.

DNS propagation/cached old record due to TTL. Lower TTL a day before, keep the old server running (or proxying) during the switch.

q: Supervisor config for Laravel workers?
a:
[program:crm-worker]
command=php /var/www/crm/current/artisan queue:work redis --queue=high,default --sleep=3 --tries=3 --max-time=3600
user=www-data
numprocs=4
autostart=true
autorestart=true
stopwaitsecs=3600
redirect_stderr=true
stdout_logfile=/var/www/crm/shared/storage/logs/worker.log

Commands: supervisorctl reread, update, status, restart crm-worker:*. With Horizon, supervise php artisan horizon instead.

q: Server hardening basics?
a: SSH keys only (disable password + root login), firewall (UFW: allow 22/80/443 only), fail2ban, automatic security updates, DB not exposed publicly (bind to localhost/private network), separate users per app, regular patching, monitoring disk/CPU/RAM.

q: Server disk is 100% full and the CRM is down. What do you do?
a: df -h → du -sh /var/* | sort -h to find the culprit → usual suspects: huge laravel.log (set up logrotate / daily log channel), MySQL binlogs (set binlog_expire_logs_seconds), old releases, backups stored locally, Docker images (docker system prune), temp export files. Free space safely (truncate logs, don't delete open files blindly), restart services, then add monitoring alerts at 80%.

q: Cloud/VPS options?
a: VPS (DigitalOcean, Hetzner, Linode, AWS Lightsail), managed Laravel hosting (Forge, Ploi, Laravel Cloud, Vapor), AWS (EC2, RDS, ElastiCache, S3, SES, SQS). Managed DB services give automatic backups and failover.

q: How would you dockerize a Laravel + Node CRM?
a: Services in docker-compose.yml: app (PHP-FPM with extensions), nginx, mysql, redis, queue (same PHP image running queue:work/Horizon), scheduler (runs schedule:work), node (Socket.io/integration service), mailpit (catch emails locally). Volumes for DB data; .env per environment.

q: Dockerfile best practices?
a: Multi-stage (build assets and composer install --no-dev in build stages, copy results to a slim runtime image), pin versions, non-root user, .dockerignore, copy composer.json/lock before app code for layer caching, one process per container, health checks, logs to stdout.

q: Docker cross-questions?
a:
• Image vs container? → Template vs running instance.
  • Volume vs bind mount? → Docker-managed storage (DB data) vs host folder (local code).
  • Container can't reach MySQL at localhost? → Inside Docker, localhost is the container itself; use the service name (DB_HOST=mysql).
  • Data lost after docker compose down -v? → -v deletes volumes.

q: Your Git workflow?
a: main = production, develop/staging branch, feature/CRM-123-lead-scoring branches, Pull Requests with review + passing CI, squash/merge, tags for releases (v2.4.0), hotfix/* from main. Conventional commit messages with ticket IDs.

q: Git rescue questions?
a: Undo a pushed commit → git revert <sha>. Lost commit → git reflog. Find which commit broke something → git bisect. Move one fix to another branch → git cherry-pick. Clean up local commits before PR → git rebase -i. Pushed secrets → rotate the secret immediately, then purge history if needed.

q: Describe a safe deployment workflow for the CRM.2 follow-ups
a:
PR → CI (Pint/PHPStan/ESLint, tests with MySQL + Redis services, build) → merge to staging → auto deploy to staging → QA tests → tag release → deploy to production (atomic: new release folder, composer install --no-dev -o, build assets, symlink .env and storage, migrate --force, optimize, switch current symlink, reload PHP-FPM, horizon:terminate/queue:restart, restart Node via PM2 reload) → smoke test + health check → monitor errors for 30 min → rollback = switch symlink back. Tools: GitHub Actions/GitLab CI + Deployer/Envoyer/Forge, or Docker images deployed to the server.

Cross-questionMigration drops a column the old code still uses — rollback breaks.

Expand/contract: never make destructive schema changes in the same release as the code change.

Cross-questionDeploying during working hours with 200 agents using the CRM?

Zero-downtime atomic deploy, backward-compatible migrations, maintenance window only for risky changes, php artisan down --secret=... if needed, communicate beforehand.

q: Example GitHub Actions deploy step (SSH)?
a:
deploy:
  needs: test
  if: github.ref == 'refs/heads/main'
  runs-on: ubuntu-latest
  steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4
    - name: Deploy
      uses: appleboy/ssh-action@v1
      with:
        host: ${{ secrets.HOST }}
        username: deploy
        key: ${{ secrets.SSH_KEY }}
        script: cd /var/www/crm && ./deploy.sh

q: Backup policy (the 3-2-1 rule)?
a: 3 copies, 2 different storage types, 1 off-site. Daily DB backups + binlogs, file storage backups (or versioned S3), keep 7 daily/4 weekly/12 monthly, encrypt, restore test monthly, backup before every risky migration. Tools: spatie/laravel-backup, XtraBackup, provider snapshots.
