a: Check Horizon/failed jobs: a chunk failing repeatedly (bad row causing exception → catch per row, log, continue), worker killed by memory/timeout (smaller chunks), DB deadlocks with live traffic (smaller transactions, retry), rate limit on an enrichment API. Batches let you resume failed chunks only.

q: "Node real-time notifications work locally but not in production."
a: Nginx missing WebSocket Upgrade/Connection headers, SSL/WSS mixed content, load balancer without sticky sessions or Socket.io Redis adapter, CORS origin settings, firewall/port, PM2 cluster instances not sharing state.

q: "MySQL CPU is at 100%."
a: SHOW FULL PROCESSLIST → find long-running queries → EXPLAIN them → missing index, report query with no date filter, N+1 storm from a new feature, runaway import. Kill the query if needed, fix index/query, add query timeouts (max_execution_time), move reports to replica.

q: Design a CRM for a company with 300 sales agents, leads from website/Facebook/WhatsApp/calls, automations, and reports.
a:
Answer in this order:

  1. Requirements: users/roles, lead sources, volume (e.g., 5k leads/day, 100k activities/day), integrations, reports, SLA.
  2. Architecture: Laravel modular monolith (core CRM, API, workflows) + Node service for real-time (Socket.io) and high-volume webhooks + MySQL (primary + read replica) + Redis (cache, queues, locks, pub/sub) + S3 (files, recordings) + search engine (Meilisearch/OpenSearch).
  3. Data model: leads, contacts, accounts, deals, pipelines/stages + history, activities (polymorphic), custom fields (JSON + generated columns), audit logs, integration tables.
  4. Ingestion: all lead sources → one LeadIngestion pipeline (normalize → dedupe → score → assign → notify → start workflows).
  5. Integrations: provider service classes, webhook receiver with signatures + idempotency, OAuth token store, rate limiting, retries, sync logs, replay UI.
  6. Automation engine: trigger/condition/action with queued delayed steps and run history.
  7. Security: RBAC + record/field permissions, audit, encryption, 2FA/SSO.
  8. Performance: indexes, cursor pagination, pre-aggregated dashboards, caching, replica for reports, queues for heavy work.
  9. Ops: Docker/VPS or cloud, CI/CD, zero-downtime deploys, Horizon/PM2 supervision, monitoring + alerts, backups + PITR.
  10. Future: multi-tenancy, AI features (call summaries, lead scoring, email drafting) via queued AI API calls.
c: System Design — "Design a Custom CRM" (Full Answer Structure)

q: Monolith or microservices for this CRM?
a: Modular monolith in Laravel first (one codebase, clear domain modules, one DB) — faster to build and debug with a small team. Extract a service only for a clear reason: different runtime needs (Node real-time), independent scaling (webhook ingestion), or a separate team.
c: System Design — "Design a Custom CRM" (Full Answer Structure)

q: SOLID with CRM examples?
a:
• S: LeadController doesn't send WhatsApp — WhatsAppService does.
  • O: add a new SMS provider by adding a class implementing SmsProvider, not editing a switch.
  • L: any SmsProvider implementation works wherever the interface is used.
  • I: separate CanSendSms and CanMakeCalls instead of one huge TelephonyProvider.
  • D: controllers depend on SmsProvider interface; container binds the real one (easy to fake in tests).

q: Patterns you use?
a:
• Strategy — different providers/assignment rules/lead scoring strategies.
  • Adapter — wrap each third-party API into your common interface.
  • Factory — create the right provider from config (SmsManager::driver('twilio'), Laravel Manager pattern).
  • Observer/Events — side effects of CRM changes.
  • Pipeline/Chain of responsibility — lead ingestion steps.
  • Command — jobs, workflow actions.
  • Repository — optional; useful when querying multiple data sources.
  • State — deal/lead status transitions.
  • DTOs — typed data objects between layers (e.g., spatie/laravel-data).

q: Clean code rules you follow?
a: Meaningful names, small single-purpose functions, early returns, no magic numbers (use enums/config), no duplicated business rules, typed properties/returns, comments explain why not what, consistent style (Pint), tests for important logic.

q: MVC — where does business logic go?
a: Not in views, not bloated controllers. Models for data rules/relations/scopes; services/actions for business processes. "Fat model, thin controller" is okay for small apps; services for larger ones.

q: SOLID — senior-level explanation with Laravel?
a:
• SRP: one reason to change. PlaceOrderAction doesn't format emails.
  • OCP: extend without editing — new payment provider = new class via Strategy/Manager.
  • LSP: subclasses/implementations must honor the contract (a ReadOnlyRepository that throws on save() breaks LSP).
  • ISP: small focused interfaces (PaymentCharger, PaymentRefunder).
  • DIP: high-level policy depends on abstractions; infrastructure implements them; the container wires them.

q: DRY, KISS, YAGNI — when do they conflict?
a: Aggressive DRY creates wrong abstractions coupling unrelated features ("two things look similar today but change for different reasons"). Rule: duplication is cheaper than the wrong abstraction — wait for the third occurrence. KISS/YAGNI: don't build a plugin system for one provider.

q: How do you structure a large Laravel codebase (clean architecture)?1 follow-up
a:
Layers (dependencies point inward):

  • Domain — entities/value objects, domain rules, domain events, repository interfaces. No framework code ideally.
  • Application — use cases/actions (PlaceOrder), DTOs, orchestration, transactions.
  • Infrastructure — Eloquent/MongoDB repositories, HTTP clients, queues, mail.
  • Interface/Delivery — controllers, console commands, API resources, listeners. Pragmatic middle ground: domain modules (app/Modules/Orders/{Actions,Models,Http,Events,Data}) + actions + DTOs, without fighting Eloquent.

Cross-questionIsn't full hexagonal overkill with Eloquent?

Often yes. Active Record mixes persistence and domain. Apply strict layering to complex core domains (billing, pricing), keep CRUD modules simple. Say "it depends on domain complexity" and explain the cost.

q: Repository pattern with Eloquent — for or against?
a: Against (as default): Eloquent already is an abstraction; generic repositories (find, all) add boilerplate without value. For: when switching storage is realistic (MySQL ↔ MongoDB across services), when queries are complex and should be named (findOverdueInvoicesForTenant), or for testing domain logic without DB. Senior answer = specific repositories for specific needs, not generic CRUD wrappers.

q: DTOs and Value Objects?
a: DTO: typed data carrier between layers (readonly class / spatie/laravel-data) instead of arrays. Value Object: immutable, validated, compared by value (Money(amount, currency), Email, PhoneNumber) — puts rules in one place.

q: Patterns with real examples.
a: Strategy (pricing/shipping calculators), Factory/Manager (Laravel Manager for drivers), Adapter (third-party SDKs), Decorator (caching repository wrapping a DB repository; logging HTTP client), Pipeline/Chain of Responsibility (validation steps), Observer (events), Command (jobs), State (order status machine), Specification (reusable business rules), Template Method, Builder (complex queries/requests), Outbox (reliable events — Section 4), Saga (distributed workflows).

q: Separation of concerns — how do you spot violations in code review?
a: Controllers with business rules or SQL, models calling external APIs, Blade/Resources running queries, jobs containing all logic instead of delegating to actions, validation spread in many places, domain code reading request() or config() directly.

q: How do you make code testable?
a: Constructor injection, interfaces at boundaries (HTTP clients, clock, random/UUID generators), pure functions for business rules, no static calls to infrastructure in domain code, small classes, Carbon::setTestNow()/$this->travel() for time.

q: When would you choose microservices over a monolith?
a:
When you have: independent teams, parts with very different scaling/reliability needs, different tech needs, independent deploy cadence. Costs: network failures, distributed data consistency, harder debugging, more DevOps, versioning contracts. Senior default: modular monolith first, extract services along proven boundaries.

Common trap

"Microservices are always more scalable." A well-built monolith scales horizontally too; microservices mainly scale teams and isolate failures.

q: How do you define service boundaries?
a: Around business capabilities / bounded contexts (DDD): Orders, Payments, Inventory, Catalog, Notifications, Identity. Each service owns its data (no shared database), exposes a contract, and changes for one business reason. Signs of bad boundaries: services always deployed together, chatty synchronous calls, distributed transactions everywhere ("distributed monolith").

q: Database per service — how do you query data across services?1 follow-up
a:
Options: (1) API composition (call services and join in memory — watch latency and failures); (2) data replication via events — service keeps a local read-only copy of the data it needs (e.g., Orders stores customer name/email snapshot); (3) CQRS read models built from events for reporting; (4) a separate reporting/analytics store.

Cross-questionCopying customer name into orders — isn't that duplication?

Yes, intentional. Often it's even correct (order must keep the address at time of purchase). Keep it updated via CustomerUpdated events where freshness matters, accept eventual consistency.

q: Sync (REST/gRPC) vs async (messaging) communication?
a: Sync: simple, immediate response, but creates temporal coupling — if Payments is down, Orders fails; latency adds up in chains. Async (RabbitMQ, Kafka, SQS/SNS, Redis Streams): decoupled, resilient, absorbs spikes, but eventual consistency, harder debugging, ordering and duplicates to handle. Rule: queries often sync; state changes/notifications async via events.

q: Commands vs events?
a: Command = "please do X" to one receiver (ChargePayment). Event = "X happened" broadcast to anyone interested (OrderPlaced), past tense, producer doesn't know consumers.

q: Kafka vs RabbitMQ vs SQS?
a:
• RabbitMQ: message broker with routing (exchanges/queues), per-message acks, good for task distribution and commands.
  • Kafka: distributed append-only log, high throughput, retention and replay, ordering per partition, consumer groups — good for event streaming, event sourcing, analytics.
  • SQS/SNS: managed, simple, at-least-once, FIFO option; SNS fan-out + SQS queues per consumer. Laravel: native queue drivers for Redis/SQS/database; RabbitMQ/Kafka via packages or dedicated consumer commands.

q: How do you guarantee an event is published when the DB transaction commits? (Dual-write problem)
a: Writing to the DB and publishing to the broker are two systems — one can fail. Solution: Transactional Outbox: in the same DB transaction, save the business change and an outbox record; a relay process reads unsent outbox rows and publishes them, marking them sent (or use change streams/CDC like Debezium). Consumers must be idempotent because the relay can publish twice. With MongoDB: write the document + outbox document in one multi-document transaction, or embed the pending event in the same document (single-document atomicity), then relay via change streams.

q: Idempotent consumers — how?
a: Every message has a unique ID; consumer stores processed IDs (unique index) in the same transaction as its state change → duplicates are skipped. Or make the operation naturally idempotent (SET status='paid' vs balance += 100).

q: Distributed transactions — Saga pattern?2 follow-ups
a:
A business process across services as a sequence of local transactions; if a step fails, run compensating actions to undo previous steps. Example "Place order": Orders creates PENDING → Inventory reserves stock → Payments charges → Orders CONFIRMED. If payment fails → Inventory releases reservation → Order CANCELLED.

  • Choreography: services react to each other's events (simple, but flow is hidden, risk of cycles).
  • Orchestration: a central orchestrator (state machine) sends commands and tracks state (clear, easier to monitor/retry). Tools: Temporal, AWS Step Functions, or a Laravel state machine + queued jobs.

Cross-questionWhy not 2-phase commit?

Blocking, poor availability, not supported across heterogeneous stores/brokers, coordinator is a single point of failure.

Cross-questionCompensation can also fail.

Retry with backoff, make compensations idempotent, alert + manual resolution queue, design semantic locks (PENDING states visible to users).

q: API contracts between services — how do you keep them stable?
a: OpenAPI/JSON Schema/Protobuf definitions in a shared repo, backward-compatible changes only (add optional fields; never remove/rename without versioning), tolerant readers (ignore unknown fields), versioned endpoints/event schemas (order.placed.v2), consumer-driven contract tests (Pact) in CI, deprecation timelines.

q: API Gateway / BFF?
a: Single entry point: routing, auth (validate JWT once), rate limiting, TLS termination, request aggregation, CORS. BFF = gateway per client type (web, mobile). Tools: Kong, NGINX, AWS API Gateway, Traefik, Envoy. Risk: becoming a bottleneck or holding business logic.

q: Authentication across microservices?
a: Identity service issues JWTs (RS256/ES256 — services verify with the public key via JWKS, no call per request). Gateway validates, forwards identity claims. Service-to-service: OAuth2 client credentials tokens or mTLS (service mesh). Authorization still enforced inside each service (don't trust only the gateway). Short token expiry + refresh; propagate user context and correlation IDs.

q: Service discovery, config, deployment?
a: Kubernetes Services/DNS (or Consul), config via env/ConfigMaps/Secrets (Vault, AWS Secrets Manager), each service with its own CI/CD pipeline, container images, health checks (liveness vs readiness), independent scaling (HPA).

q: How do you debug a request crossing 5 services?
a: Distributed tracing (OpenTelemetry → Jaeger/Tempo/Datadog/Honeycomb) with trace context propagated in HTTP headers (traceparent) and message metadata; correlation ID in every log line; centralized structured logs; per-service RED metrics.

q: Microservices anti-patterns?
a: Shared database, distributed monolith (lockstep deploys), chatty sync chains, nano-services, no idempotency, no timeouts, shared domain library that couples everyone, synchronous call inside a DB transaction, missing observability.

q: Explain timeouts, retries, backoff and jitter.
a:
• Timeout: never wait forever — set connect and total timeouts on every HTTP/DB/queue call (Laravel Http::timeout()->connectTimeout()).
  • Retry: only for transient errors (network, 429, 502/503/504) and only for idempotent operations (or with idempotency keys).
  • Exponential backoff: 100 ms, 200, 400, 800…
  • Jitter: randomize delays so thousands of clients don't retry at the same moment (thundering herd).
  • Retry budget: limit total retries across layers — retries at 3 layers × 3 attempts = 27x load (retry storm).

q: Circuit breaker?
a: Tracks failures to a dependency. Closed (normal) → too many failures → Open (fail fast, don't call, return fallback) → after cooldown Half-open (let a few test calls through) → success closes, failure re-opens. Protects your threads/workers and gives the failing service time to recover. Laravel: implement with cache counters/locks, or ThrottlesExceptions job middleware; libraries exist (e.g., ackintosh/ganesha).

q: Bulkhead pattern?
a: Isolate resources so one failing dependency can't consume everything: separate queues and worker pools per dependency/priority, separate connection pools, separate PHP-FPM pools for admin vs public traffic, per-tenant rate limits.

q: Graceful degradation — examples?
a: Recommendations service down → show bestsellers from cache. Search down → basic DB search. Payment provider slow → accept order as PENDING_PAYMENT and confirm async. Feature flags to turn off expensive features under load. Serve stale cache when the source fails.

q: Idempotency keys in APIs (e.g., payment/order creation)?
a: Client sends Idempotency-Key header. Server stores key + request hash + response (unique index, with TTL). Same key again → return the stored response without re-executing. Same key + different body → 422. Use a lock while the first request is in progress (return 409 for concurrent duplicates).

q: Backpressure and load shedding?
a: When input is faster than you can process: bounded queues, rate limit producers, reject early with 429/503 + Retry-After, autoscale workers based on queue depth, drop or defer low-priority work.

q: Dead Letter Queues?
a: Messages that fail after max retries go to a DLQ instead of blocking the queue or being lost. Alert on DLQ size, inspect, fix, replay. Laravel equivalent: failed_jobs table + queue:retry.

q: Poison messages?
a: A message that always crashes the consumer (bad data). Without limits it's retried forever and blocks partition ordering (Kafka). Fix: max attempts → DLQ, validate schema on consume, catch and log per-message errors.

q: High availability — what does it take?
a: No single points of failure: multiple app instances across availability zones behind a load balancer, stateless apps (sessions/cache in Redis, files in S3), DB replicas with automatic failover (MongoDB replica sets, RDS Multi-AZ), Redis Sentinel/Cluster or managed Redis, health checks, graceful shutdown, zero-downtime deploys, backups + tested restores, defined RTO/RPO.

q: SLI, SLO, SLA, error budget?
a: SLI = measured indicator (p99 latency, success rate). SLO = target (99.9% of requests succeed monthly). SLA = contractual promise with penalties. Error budget = allowed failure (0.1% ≈ 43 min/month); if exhausted, prioritize reliability over features.

q: CAP and PACELC in simple words?
a: During a network Partition, a distributed system must choose Consistency (reject some requests) or Availability (answer with possibly stale data). PACELC adds: Else (no partition) choose between Latency and Consistency. MongoDB lets you tune this per operation with read/write concerns and read preference.

q: Design an order processing system with Orders, Inventory, Payments, Notifications services.
a:
• Orders service (MongoDB): POST /orders with idempotency key → order PENDING + outbox event OrderPlaced in one transaction.
  • Orchestrated saga: reserve inventory (atomic findOneAndUpdate with stock check + reservation doc with TTL/expiry) → create payment intent → on PaymentSucceeded webhook confirm order → OrderConfirmed event → Notifications sends email/SMS.
  • Failure paths: payment failed/timeout → release reservation (compensation) → order CANCELLED; reservation expires if saga stalls.
  • Messaging: RabbitMQ/Kafka/SQS; consumers idempotent; DLQs; outbox relay via change streams.
  • Resilience: timeouts, retries with jitter, circuit breaker on payment provider, bulkheaded queues.
  • Read models: order history view in Orders; admin reporting via CQRS projection.
  • Observability: trace ID from API to every event; saga state dashboard; alerts on stuck sagas.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: Design a notification service (email/SMS/push/WhatsApp) sending 5M messages/day.
a: API accepts notification requests (idempotency key, template, channel preferences) → store in MongoDB (notifications with status history, TTL for old records) → queue per channel and priority (OTP high, marketing low) → workers call providers through adapters with rate limiting per provider, circuit breakers and failover to a secondary provider → delivery webhooks update status → user preferences/opt-outs/quiet hours → templates with versioning → metrics: sent, delivered, failed per provider. ~58 msgs/sec average, peaks 10x → scale workers horizontally.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: Design a rate limiter for a public API (multi-instance).
a: Token bucket per API key in Redis with atomic Lua script (read tokens, refill based on elapsed time, decrement), keys with TTL, response headers (X-RateLimit-Remaining, Retry-After), tiers per plan, local in-memory pre-check to reduce Redis calls, fail-open vs fail-closed decision if Redis is down (usually fail-open with a stricter local limit).
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: Design a URL shortener / unique ID generator (classic warm-up).
a: Base62 encoding of a unique ID (DB sequence, Snowflake-style IDs, or pre-generated ranges per instance to avoid coordination), MongoDB/MySQL store code → url with unique index, heavy read cache (Redis/CDN), 301 vs 302 (analytics), analytics events async, abuse protection.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: Design a multi-tenant SaaS on Laravel + MongoDB for 5,000 tenants.
a: Tenant resolution (subdomain/header/JWT claim) → scoped tenant context (Octane-safe) → shared collections with tenantId as the first field of every compound index and part of the shard key ({tenantId: 1, _id: 1}) → isolation tests → large "noisy" tenants moved to dedicated collections/clusters (outlier pattern) → per-tenant rate limits and queues → per-tenant encryption keys if required → tenant-aware cache keys and logs.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: Design an activity feed / audit log with billions of events.
a: Append-only writes → MongoDB time-series collection or bucket pattern (per entity per day), or Kafka → storage; TTL/archival to cheap storage (S3 + Athena/Online Archive); index {tenantId, entityId, ts:-1}; shard by {tenantId, entityId} hashed; async writes via queue with batching (insertMany, ordered:false); reads with keyset pagination.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: "Traffic will grow 10x next quarter." What do you do?
a: Load test to find the first bottleneck; review slow queries and indexes; cache hot reads; make services stateless and autoscale; move sync side effects to queues; check DB capacity (connections, working set, IOPS) → read replicas / sharding plan; CDN for static; capacity dashboards and alerts; runbooks; cost estimate.
c: System Design Questions (Practice These Out Loud)

q: "Orders service latency went from 200 ms to 8 s. Nothing was deployed."
a: Check traces: which span is slow? Likely a downstream dependency (Payments/Inventory) degraded → without timeouts, PHP workers wait → worker pool exhausted → whole service slow (cascading failure). Immediate: enable circuit breaker/fallback, lower timeouts, scale. Also check MongoDB (slow ops, replication lag, working set exceeded, index dropped?), connection pool saturation, a noisy tenant, traffic spike. Long-term: timeouts everywhere, bulkheads, alerts on dependency latency.

q: "Customers are charged twice."
a: Retry of a payment call without idempotency key; duplicate webhook processed twice; queue job ran twice (retry_after < job duration, or worker crash after charging but before ack); double-click without frontend guard. Fix: provider idempotency keys, unique constraint on payment_intent_id, idempotent consumers, refund affected customers, add reconciliation job comparing provider records and orders.

q: "Events are processed out of order: OrderShipped arrives before OrderPaid."
a: Parallel consumers / multiple partitions / retries reorder messages. Fixes: partition by aggregate ID (Kafka key = orderId), sequence numbers/versions per aggregate — ignore or buffer older versions, design consumers to handle any order (state machine rejects invalid transitions and retries later), avoid depending on global ordering.

q: "Two services disagree about an order's status."
a: Missed event (published without outbox), consumer failure in DLQ, non-idempotent consumer ignored a retry, manual DB edit. Investigate with event logs/traces; replay events from outbox/Kafka; add reconciliation jobs; make the owner service the source of truth.

q: "MongoDB primary stepped down; errors for 15 seconds; some writes missing."
a: Election window is expected — drivers need retryWrites=true, app should retry transient errors. Missing writes → were they w:1? Rolled back on the old primary (check rollback directory). Fix: w:"majority" for important writes, retry logic, alert on elections, check why the step-down happened (maintenance, resource exhaustion, network).

q: "Queue workers keep restarting with 'Allowed memory size exhausted'."
a: Job loads too much data (use cursors/chunks), memory leak across jobs (static caches, query log, Telescope), a huge payload serialized in the job (pass IDs), image processing of huge files. Set --memory, --max-jobs, split jobs, profile one job locally.

q: "Race condition: two users booked the same slot."
a: Check-then-insert without guarantee. Fix: unique index on (resourceId, slotStart) (MySQL or MongoDB) and handle duplicate key error as "slot taken"; or atomic findOneAndUpdate on a slot document {status:'free'} → 'booked'. Application-level checks alone are never enough.

q: "After deploying v2, the old consumers crash on new events."
a: Breaking event schema change. Fix: roll back or publish both versions, tolerant readers, schema registry/versioned event names, contract tests in CI, deploy consumers first, then producers.

q: What are these six job descriptions about?
a: All six jobs want almost the same thing: 3.5–5+ years of PHP and Laravel experience, MySQL, REST APIs, Git, and clean code that's easy to test. So instead of six separate prep sheets, this is one big sheet that covers the common questions, then the extra questions specific to each job, then harder follow-up questions, then a few bonus topics a senior-level interview often asks about.

q: What's the strategy for each JD?
a: For JD1, JD5, and JD6 — you're a strong match. Focus on telling real stories about your projects (HOLOIN, AI-BDM, the Shopify sync tool, University Seekers, Rentigo) instead of textbook answers. For JD3 — be honest about the gaps in AWS, Angular, and PHPUnit. For JD2 and JD4 — find out exactly which role and tech stack they mean before the interview, so you don't prepare for the wrong thing.

q: What's new in Laravel 11 compared to older versions you've used?
a:
Laravel 11 made the default app structure much simpler — one AppServiceProvider by default, a streamlined bootstrap/app.php for setting up middleware and error handling in one place (instead of separate Kernel classes). I've worked across Laravel 5 through recent versions (including a University Seekers upgrade from 5 to 8), so I keep up with version changes as a normal part of the job.

q: How does WordPress load a page?
a: index.php → wp-blog-header.php → wp-load.php loads wp-config.php (database, keys) → WordPress core loads → must-use plugins, then active plugins → the active theme's functions.php → init and other hooks fire → WordPress parses the URL into a query (WP_Query) → the template hierarchy picks the template file (e.g. single-product.php → single.php → index.php) → the page renders.

q: What are hooks? Actions vs filters?
a:
Hooks let you change WordPress without editing core files.

  • Actions run your code at a moment: add_action('init', 'register_my_cpt'); — you do something (send an email, register a post type, enqueue scripts).
  • Filters receive a value, change it and return it: add_filter('the_title', fn($t) => strtoupper($t));. You create your own with do_action('myplugin_after_save', $id) and apply_filters('myplugin_price', $price). The optional priority (default 10) controls order; the last argument is how many parameters your callback accepts.

Common trap

Forgetting to return in a filter callback — the value becomes null and content disappears.

q: Theme vs plugin — where should code go?
a: Presentation (templates, styles) goes in the theme — ideally a child theme so parent-theme updates don't wipe your changes. Functionality that should survive a theme change (custom post types, integrations, shortcodes, APIs) goes in a plugin. A classic mistake is putting business logic in functions.php, which disappears when the client changes theme.

q: Show the basic structure of a custom plugin.
a:
<?php
/**
 * Plugin Name: Clinic Appointments
 * Version: 1.0.0
 */
if (!defined('ABSPATH')) exit;                        // block direct access

register_activation_hook(__FILE__, ['Clinic\\Installer', 'activate']);   // create tables, default options
add_action('init', ['Clinic\\PostTypes', 'register']);
add_action('admin_menu', ['Clinic\\Admin', 'menu']);
add_action('wp_enqueue_scripts', function () {
    wp_enqueue_script('clinic', plugins_url('assets/app.js', __FILE__), [], '1.0.0', true);
});

Use a namespace or prefix for everything, autoload classes with Composer, and clean up on uninstall (uninstall.php).

q: How do you register a custom post type and taxonomy?
a:
add_action('init', function () {
    register_post_type('doctor', [
        'label' => 'Doctors', 'public' => true, 'has_archive' => true,
        'supports' => ['title', 'editor', 'thumbnail'], 'show_in_rest' => true,
        'rewrite' => ['slug' => 'doctors'],
    ]);
    register_taxonomy('specialty', 'doctor', ['label' => 'Specialties', 'hierarchical' => true, 'show_in_rest' => true]);
});

show_in_rest enables the block editor and REST API. Flush permalinks once after registering (visit Settings → Permalinks, or flush_rewrite_rules() on activation only).

q: Custom fields — post meta, ACF and custom tables?
a: Post meta (get_post_meta, update_post_meta) stores key/value data per post — fine for a few fields. ACF (Advanced Custom Fields) gives a UI for building field groups and is common in agency work. For large or heavily queried data (appointments, logs, orders), use custom tables created with dbDelta() — meta queries on big sites are slow because wp_postmeta isn't designed for filtering millions of rows.

q: How do you query posts correctly?
a:
$q = new WP_Query([
    'post_type' => 'doctor', 'posts_per_page' => 12, 'paged' => get_query_var('paged') ?: 1,
    'tax_query' => [['taxonomy' => 'specialty', 'field' => 'slug', 'terms' => 'cardiology']],
    'no_found_rows' => true,   // skip counting when you don't need pagination
]);
while ($q->have_posts()) { $q->the_post(); the_title(); }
wp_reset_postdata();

To change the main query (e.g. archive page size), use the pre_get_posts action instead of running a second query. Avoid query_posts().

q: Security in WordPress development?
a:
• Nonces for forms and AJAX (wp_nonce_field / check_admin_referer / check_ajax_referer) against CSRF.
  • Capability checks (current_user_can('edit_posts')) for every privileged action.
  • Sanitize input (sanitize_text_field, absint, sanitize_email) and escape output (esc_html, esc_attr, esc_url, wp_kses_post).
  • $wpdb->prepare() for every custom SQL query.
  • Validate file uploads, keep core/plugins/themes updated, and remove unused plugins (most WordPress hacks come through outdated plugins).

q: AJAX and the REST API in WordPress?
a:
Classic AJAX: admin-ajax.php with wp_ajax_{action} (logged-in) and wp_ajax_nopriv_{action} hooks. Modern approach: register REST routes:

add_action('rest_api_init', function () {
    register_rest_route('clinic/v1', '/slots', [
        'methods' => 'GET', 'callback' => 'clinic_slots',
        'permission_callback' => fn() => current_user_can('read'),
        'args' => ['doctor' => ['required' => true, 'sanitize_callback' => 'absint']],
    ]);
});

Always set a permission_callback (use __return_true only for genuinely public data).

q: How do you make a slow WordPress site fast?
a: Measure first (Query Monitor plugin, PageSpeed). Then: page caching (server-level or a caching plugin), object caching with Redis, image optimisation and WebP/AVIF, lazy loading, a CDN, fewer and lighter plugins, avoid heavy page builders where possible, fix slow meta queries, use transients for expensive API calls, keep autoload options small, and use a current PHP version (8.3/8.4).

q: What are transients and WP-Cron?
a: Transients cache data with an expiry (set_transient('rates', $data, HOUR_IN_SECONDS)) — stored in the database or in Redis if an object cache is installed. WP-Cron runs scheduled events when someone visits the site, so timing isn't guaranteed on low-traffic sites; for reliable jobs, disable it (DISABLE_WP_CRON) and trigger wp-cron.php from a real server cron. Action Scheduler (used by WooCommerce) handles large background job queues.

q: WooCommerce hooks you've used?
a: Add or change checkout fields (woocommerce_checkout_fields filter), react to orders (woocommerce_order_status_completed, woocommerce_payment_complete), change cart prices (woocommerce_before_calculate_totals), add product tabs (woocommerce_product_tabs), and override templates by copying them into yourtheme/woocommerce/. Build custom payment gateways by extending WC_Payment_Gateway — common in Pakistan for JazzCash/Easypaisa integrations.

q: What is WooCommerce HPOS, and why does it matter?
a: High-Performance Order Storage moves orders from wp_posts/wp_postmeta into dedicated order tables — much faster for stores with many orders, and the default for new stores. Custom code must use the CRUD API (wc_get_order($id)->get_meta(), $order->update_meta_data(), $order->save()) instead of get_post_meta() on orders, and plugins should declare HPOS compatibility.

q: Recurring payments and subscriptions in WooCommerce?
a: Use WooCommerce Subscriptions (or a similar plugin) with a gateway that supports tokenization (Stripe, some local gateways). Many local wallets and bank gateways don't support saved-card recurring charges, so the workaround is manual renewal invoices with payment links and reminders — worth explaining honestly to clients.

q: How do you develop and deploy WordPress professionally?
a: Local environment with DDEV or LocalWP, code (theme/plugins) in Git — not uploads or core — Composer for dependencies (Bedrock is a popular structure), WP-CLI for everything (wp plugin update --all, wp search-replace old.com new.com, wp db export), staging site before production, and database migration tools for pushing content changes. Never edit files directly on production.

q: What's new in WordPress?
a: WordPress 7.0 was released on 20 May 2026: a refreshed admin with DataViews, visual revisions, new blocks (Icon, Breadcrumbs) and block-level CSS controls, and AI foundations in core (AI Client, Abilities API, Connectors screen). Real-time collaboration was pulled before release. For developers, block themes, theme.json and the Interactivity API are the direction of travel; classic themes still work.

q: Tell me about WordPress work you've done. (Personal)
a: Use your real project: a custom WordPress plugin for a healthcare client (Garrick Solutions) with its own data model, forms and admin screens, plus WordPress/CMS client sites and fixing upload-size and server configuration issues. Explain one decision — for example, custom tables vs post meta, or how you secured forms with nonces and capability checks.

q: What can a developer customise on Shopify?
a: Shopify is hosted SaaS, so you don't touch servers or the database. You extend it through themes (Liquid, JSON templates, sections and blocks), apps (public or custom, using the Admin and Storefront APIs, webhooks and app extensions), Shopify Functions (custom discount, shipping, payment and validation logic at checkout), checkout UI extensions, metafields/metaobjects for custom data, and headless storefronts (Hydrogen or any frontend using the Storefront API).

q: What is Liquid? Explain objects, tags and filters.
a: Liquid is Shopify's template language. Objects output data: {{ product.title }}. Tags add logic: {% if product.available %}…{% endif %}, {% for item in cart.items %}, {% render 'price', product: product %}. Filters transform output: {{ product.price | money }}, {{ image | image_url: width: 600 | image_tag }}.

q: Online Store 2.0: JSON templates, sections and blocks?
a: Templates are JSON files listing which sections appear on a page, so merchants can add, remove and reorder sections in the theme editor on every page. Sections are reusable Liquid files with a {% schema %} that defines settings (text, image, colour pickers) and blocks (repeatable pieces inside a section). Good theme work means giving merchants flexible settings without letting them break the design.

q: Metafields and metaobjects?
a: Metafields add custom fields to products, collections, customers and orders (e.g. "fabric care", "size guide"). Metaobjects are custom content types (e.g. "Designer" with name, bio and photo) that can be linked from products. Both are available in Liquid and the APIs, so merchants can edit data without a developer.

q: How do you build a custom Shopify app with a Laravel backend?1 follow-up
a:
OAuth install flow (or the newer managed install for embedded apps) to get an access token, store tokens encrypted per shop, call the GraphQL Admin API (REST is legacy and new public apps must use GraphQL), register webhooks (orders/create, products/update, app/uninstalled) and verify each webhook's HMAC signature, process them in queues idempotently, respect API rate limits (GraphQL uses a cost-based bucket), and handle the mandatory privacy webhooks. Embedded apps use App Bridge and session tokens.

Cross-questionHow do you verify a Shopify webhook?

Compute an HMAC-SHA256 of the raw request body with the app's secret, base64-encode it and compare it with the X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256 header using a timing-safe comparison. Reject if it doesn't match.

q: What are Shopify Functions, and what replaced Shopify Scripts?
a: Functions are small pieces of custom logic (compiled to WebAssembly, often written in Rust or JavaScript) that run inside Shopify's checkout for discounts, delivery and payment customisation, cart validation and more. Shopify Scripts (Ruby, Plus-only) stopped running on 30 June 2026, so stores that used them for discounts or shipping rules had to migrate to Functions. checkout.liquid was replaced by checkout extensibility (checkout UI extensions and Functions).

q: How do you automate products, menus and imports through the API?
a: Use GraphQL mutations (productSet/productCreate, menuUpdate etc.) from a queued job, map CSV columns to product fields and variants, handle variants and images carefully, use bulk operations for large jobs, respect rate limits with backoff, and log every row's result so failed rows can be fixed and re-run. (You've done CSV → Shopify product/menu imports — mention it.)

q: How do you keep a Shopify store fast?
a: Limit apps (each can inject scripts), use image_url with sizes and loading="lazy", avoid heavy JavaScript and large sliders, render only what's needed in Liquid (avoid deep loops over all products), preload key assets, and check Core Web Vitals in Shopify's web performance report and PageSpeed.

q: Explain Magento 2's architecture in one minute.
a: Magento 2 is a modular PHP e-commerce platform built on Composer, with modules (features), themes, dependency injection configured in di.xml, an EAV database model for flexible product attributes, a service layer with service contracts (interfaces), and areas (frontend, adminhtml, webapi). Adobe Commerce is the paid edition; Magento Open Source is free (and Mage-OS is a community distribution).

q: Minimal files for a custom module?
a: app/code/Vendor/Module/registration.php (registers the module) and etc/module.xml (name and load order). Then add what you need: etc/di.xml (preferences, plugins, virtual types), etc/frontend/routes.xml + a Controller, etc/events.xml + an Observer, Setup/Patch/Data and etc/db_schema.xml (declarative schema), view/frontend/layout and templates. Enable with bin/magento module:enable Vendor_Module && bin/magento setup:upgrade.

q: Plugins (interceptors) vs observers vs preferences?
a: Plugins change the behaviour of a public method — before (change arguments), after (change the result), around (wrap the call; use sparingly because it's slower and harder to combine). Observers react to events dispatched by Magento (e.g. sales_order_place_after). Preferences replace a whole class through DI — the most invasive option; use only when plugins can't do the job, because two modules overriding the same class conflict.

q: What is EAV, and what's the performance impact?
a: Entity-Attribute-Value stores product attributes as rows across typed tables (catalog_product_entity_varchar, _int, _decimal…) so merchants can add attributes without schema changes. Loading a product means many joins, so Magento relies on indexers (flat tables, price and stock indexes) and caching. Run indexers "on schedule" via cron in production.

q: Common Magento CLI commands and deployment steps?
a: bin/magento setup:upgrade (after module changes), setup:di:compile (generate DI code), setup:static-content:deploy -f (build frontend assets), indexer:reindex, cache:flush, deploy:mode:set production, and maintenance:enable/disable. A production deploy runs these in a build step, then switches releases — Magento deploys are slow, so zero-downtime pipelines matter.

q: Upgrading Magento and PHP — what goes wrong?
a: Third-party extensions not compatible with the new PHP or Magento version, deprecated functions, changed class signatures that break plugins and preferences, Composer dependency conflicts, and PDF or payment extensions that need new versions. Approach: upgrade on a staging copy, update extensions first, run setup:di:compile to catch errors, and test checkout end to end. (You handled Magento 2 + PHP 8.1 compatibility and PDF-customizer issues — use them as examples.)

q: How do you speed up a Magento store?
a: Production mode, full-page cache with Varnish, Redis for cache and sessions, Elasticsearch/OpenSearch for catalog search, indexers on schedule, JS/CSS bundling and minification, image optimisation, a CDN, disable unused modules, and profile slow pages (built-in profiler, New Relic, Blackfire).

q: Laravel/custom build vs Shopify vs WooCommerce vs Magento — how do you advise a client?
a:
• Shopify: fastest to launch, hosted and secure, great apps; less control, monthly fees and transaction rules.
  • WooCommerce: flexible and cheap to start on WordPress; needs good hosting and plugin discipline as it grows.
  • Magento: powerful for large catalogs, B2B and multi-store; expensive to build, host and maintain.
  • Custom Laravel: when the business rules are unusual (marketplaces, complex pricing, deep integrations) and the client can fund ongoing development. Decide by budget, catalogue size, customisation needs, team skills and total cost of ownership.

q: Native vs cross-platform — what are the options?
a: Native: Swift/SwiftUI (iOS) and Kotlin/Jetpack Compose (Android) — best performance and platform feel, two codebases. Cross-platform: React Native (JavaScript/TypeScript, real native UI components, huge overlap with React web skills) and Flutter (Dart, draws its own UI with its rendering engine, very consistent look across platforms). Both are widely used by Pakistani software houses.

q: React Native essentials for a React developer?
a: Components: View, Text, Image, Pressable, ScrollView, FlatList (virtualised lists — use it for long lists). Styling with StyleSheet and Flexbox (column by default). Navigation with React Navigation or Expo Router. Expo is the recommended way to start (managed builds with EAS, over-the-air updates, many native modules). Storage: SecureStore/Keychain for tokens, AsyncStorage for non-sensitive data. The New Architecture (Fabric renderer, TurboModules, JSI) is now the standard for new apps.

q: Flutter essentials?
a: Everything is a widget: StatelessWidget vs StatefulWidget, layout with Row, Column, Stack, ListView.builder. State management: setState for local state, then Provider, Riverpod or BLoC for app state. Networking with http or dio, JSON models (often generated with json_serializable), navigation with go_router. Dart 3 adds null safety, records and pattern matching. Hot reload makes UI work fast.

q: React Native vs Flutter — how do you compare them in an interview?
a: React Native: reuse JavaScript/TypeScript and React knowledge, share logic with a React web app, native look per platform, large npm ecosystem. Flutter: excellent performance and pixel-consistent UI, strong tooling, one language (Dart) the team must learn. Choose by team skills, need to share code with the web, design requirements and available libraries.

q: What does a mobile app need from the Laravel backend?
a: Token auth (Sanctum personal access tokens) stored in secure storage, versioned APIs (old app versions stay installed for months — never break them), consistent JSON errors, pagination and small payloads for slow networks, image resizing/thumbnails, push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging/APNs sent from queued jobs, deep links, a "minimum supported version" endpoint to force updates, and rate limiting for OTP endpoints.

q: Publishing and updating mobile apps — what should a full stack developer know?
a: App Store and Play Store accounts, signing keys/certificates (keep them safe), build pipelines (Expo EAS, Codemagic, Fastlane), review times and store policies (privacy labels, account deletion requirement), staged rollouts, crash reporting (Crashlytics, Sentry), and over-the-air JavaScript updates for React Native (Expo Updates) for small fixes without a new store release.

q: Talk about your mobile-related experience. (Personal)
a: Use what's real: Laravel backends for React Native apps at ESparks — the Doctoring App (patient and doctor apps with Firebase, Stripe and WebRTC video) and MetaBuddy. Focus on the backend side you owned (APIs, auth, push notifications, payments) and what you learned about mobile clients (versioning, offline and slow-network behaviour).

In an interview, one specific example beats a long list: "We upgraded our GitHub Actions to the Node 24 versions before the September cutoff."

q: What does this print, and why?
a:
console.log(a); var a = 5;
console.log(b); let b = 5;

First line prints undefined — var is hoisted and initialised to undefined. Second line throws ReferenceError — let is hoisted but stays in the "temporal dead zone" until its line runs.

q: What is printed by the `var` and `let` loop callbacks, and why?
a:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i), 0);
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log(j), 0);

3 3 3 then 0 1 2. var has one shared i (already 3 when the timers run); let creates a new j for every loop iteration.

q: Output order?
a:
console.log('A');
setTimeout(() => console.log('B'), 0);
Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log('C'));
queueMicrotask(() => console.log('D'));
console.log('E');

A E C D B. Synchronous code first, then microtasks (promise callbacks, queueMicrotask) in order, then macrotasks (setTimeout).

q: Type coercion — what are these?
a:
1 + '2'      // '12'  (string concatenation)
'5' - 2      // 3     (minus converts to number)
[] + []      // ''    (both become empty strings)
[] + {}      // '[object Object]'
true + true  // 2
null == undefined   // true
null === undefined  // false
NaN === NaN         // false  (use Number.isNaN)
typeof null         // 'object' (a historic bug)
0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3   // false  (floating point)

q: What is this here?
a:
const obj = {
  name: 'Ali',
  regular() { return this.name; },
  arrow: () => this?.name,
  later() { setTimeout(function () { console.log(this?.name); }, 0); },
};
obj.regular(); // 'Ali'
obj.arrow();   // not 'Ali' — arrow functions take `this` from the outer scope (undefined in a module)
obj.later();   // not 'Ali' — a plain function called by setTimeout loses `this`
const f = obj.regular; f(); // undefined in strict mode (or error when reading .name)

q: Closures — output?
a:
function counter() { let n = 0; return { inc: () => ++n, get: () => n }; }
const c1 = counter(), c2 = counter();
c1.inc(); c1.inc(); c2.inc();
console.log(c1.get(), c2.get());   // 2 1 — each call creates its own n

q: Objects and references — output?
a:
const a = { x: 1 };
const b = a;
b.x = 2;
console.log(a.x);                  // 2 — same object
console.log({ x: 1 } === { x: 1 }); // false — different objects
const c = { ...a }; c.x = 9;
console.log(a.x);                  // 2 — shallow copy is a new object

q: Array method traps — output?
a:
[1, 2, 3].map(parseInt);           // [1, NaN, NaN] — map passes (value, index)
[10, 1, 3].sort();                 // [1, 10, 3] — default sort compares strings
[10, 1, 3].sort((a, b) => a - b);  // [1, 3, 10]
const arr = [1, 2, 3]; arr.length = 0; // arr is now []

q: async/await — output order?
a:
async function run() {
  console.log(1);
  await null;
  console.log(2);
}
run();
console.log(3);

1 3 2. Everything after await runs later as a microtask, after the current synchronous code finishes.

q: Destructuring and defaults — output?
a:
const { a = 10, b = 20 } = { a: undefined, b: null };
console.log(a, b);   // 10 null — defaults apply only for undefined
const [x, , y = 5] = [1, 2];
console.log(x, y);   // 1 5

q: PHP 8 comparisons — true or false?
a:
var_dump(0 == "a");      // false in PHP 8 (true in PHP 7!)
var_dump("1" == "01");   // true  — numeric strings compared as numbers
var_dump("10" == "1e1"); // true
var_dump(100 == "1e2");  // true
var_dump(null == false); // true
var_dump([] == false);   // true
var_dump("abc" === "abc"); // true

Rule for tests: use === unless you really want type juggling.

q: What values do PHP numeric conversion, concatenation, spaceship comparison and division produce?
a:
$a = "5"; $b = 5;
echo $a + $b;      // 10
echo $a . $b;      // 55
echo 7 <=> 3;      // 1  (spaceship: -1, 0 or 1)
echo intdiv(7, 2); // 3
echo 7 % 3;        // 1
echo 10 / 4;       // 2.5

q: References — output?
a:
$arr = [1, 2, 3];
foreach ($arr as &$v) { $v *= 2; }
foreach ($arr as $v) {}
print_r($arr);   // [2, 4, 4]

After the first loop, $v is still a reference to the last element. The second loop keeps writing into it, so the last element ends up equal to the previous one. Fix: unset($v); after a by-reference loop.

q: Static and late static binding — output?
a:
class A { public static function create() { return new static(); } public function name() { return static::class; } }
class B extends A {}
echo (B::create())->name();   // B  — `new self()` would return A

q: String functions trap — what's wrong?
a:
if (strpos("hello", "h")) { echo "found"; }   // prints nothing!

strpos returns 0 (the position), which is falsy. Use strpos(...) !== false or PHP 8's str_contains("hello", "h").

q: How do PHP default parameters, variadic arguments and named arguments affect this function's output?
a:
function add(int $a, int $b = 5, ...$rest) { return $a + $b + array_sum($rest); }
echo add(1);            // 6
echo add(1, 2, 3, 4);   // 10
echo add(b: 1, a: 2);   // 3 — named arguments

q: isset, empty, null coalescing — output?
a:
$x = 0; $y = null;
var_dump(isset($x));   // true
var_dump(empty($x));   // true — 0 is "empty"
var_dump(isset($y));   // false
echo $y ?? 'default';  // default
echo $x ?: 'fallback'; // fallback — ?: checks truthiness, ?? checks null

q: Write the query: departments with more than 5 employees, highest average salary first.
a:
SELECT department_id, COUNT(*) AS staff, AVG(salary) AS avg_salary
FROM employees
GROUP BY department_id
HAVING COUNT(*) > 5
ORDER BY avg_salary DESC;

q: Nth highest salary (N = 3), handling ties correctly.
a:
SELECT DISTINCT salary FROM employees ORDER BY salary DESC LIMIT 1 OFFSET 2;
-- or with a window function (MySQL 8+):
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) AS rnk FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 3 LIMIT 1;

DENSE_RANK gives tied salaries the same rank without gaps, which is usually what "third highest" means.

q: Customers who ordered in January but not in February.
a:
SELECT DISTINCT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id AND o.created_at >= '2026-01-01' AND o.created_at < '2026-02-01'
WHERE NOT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM orders o2
  WHERE o2.customer_id = c.id AND o2.created_at >= '2026-02-01' AND o2.created_at < '2026-03-01'
);

q: MCQ-style: what does each JOIN return for tables A (1,2,3) and B (2,3,4) joined on the id?
a: INNER JOIN → 2, 3. LEFT JOIN → 1 (with NULLs), 2, 3. RIGHT JOIN → 2, 3, 4 (with NULLs). FULL OUTER JOIN (not native in MySQL; use UNION of LEFT and RIGHT) → 1, 2, 3, 4. CROSS JOIN → 9 rows.

q: Running total of daily sales.
a:
SELECT DATE(created_at) AS day, SUM(total) AS sales,
       SUM(SUM(total)) OVER (ORDER BY DATE(created_at)) AS running_total
FROM orders GROUP BY DATE(created_at) ORDER BY day;

q: Reverse the words in a sentence without built-in reverse functions.
a:
function reverseWords(s) {
  const words = s.trim().split(/\s+/);
  let out = [];
  for (let i = words.length - 1; i >= 0; i--) out.push(words[i]);
  return out.join(' ');
}

Complexity O(n). Mention edge cases: extra spaces, empty string.

q: First non-repeating character.
a:
function firstUnique(s) {
  const count = {};
  for (const ch of s) count[ch] = (count[ch] || 0) + 1;
  for (const ch of s) if (count[ch] === 1) return ch;
  return null;
}

Two passes, O(n) time, O(k) space for k distinct characters.

q: Group an array of objects by a key (no library).
a:
function groupBy(items, key) {
  return items.reduce((acc, item) => {
    (acc[item[key]] ||= []).push(item);
    return acc;
  }, {});
}
// Modern JS also has Object.groupBy(items, i => i.status)

function groupBy(array $items, string $key): array {
    $out = [];
    foreach ($items as $item) { $out[$item[$key]][] = $item; }
    return $out;
}

q: Check balanced brackets ()[]{}.
a:
function isBalanced(s) {
  const pairs = { ')': '(', ']': '[', '}': '{' }, stack = [];
  for (const ch of s) {
    if ('([{'.includes(ch)) stack.push(ch);
    else if (pairs[ch] && stack.pop() !== pairs[ch]) return false;
  }
  return stack.length === 0;
}

q: Flatten a nested array to any depth without flat().
a:
function flatten(arr) {
  const out = [];
  for (const x of arr) Array.isArray(x) ? out.push(...flatten(x)) : out.push(x);
  return out;
}

q: Implement debounce.
a:
function debounce(fn, wait = 300) {
  let t;
  return function (...args) {
    clearTimeout(t);
    t = setTimeout(() => fn.apply(this, args), wait);
  };
}

q: How do you approach a timed online test?
a: Read every question first and do the quick ones; for coding, write a working simple solution before optimising; test edge cases (empty input, one item, duplicates, negatives); don't leave MCQs blank unless there's negative marking; keep an eye on the timer; and write clean variable names — some companies read the code afterwards. Practice on HackerRank or LeetCode (easy/medium), and read PHP and JavaScript output questions out loud to train your eye for traps.

q: What HTTP status code do you return for a validation failure?
a: 422 Unprocessable Entity.

q: What's the difference between PUT and PATCH?
a: PUT replaces the entire resource (send all fields); PATCH sends only the fields that need to change.

q: What does php artisan queue:work do, and what's different about php artisan horizon?
a: queue:work starts one worker process pulling and processing jobs from a queue. Horizon is a dashboard and manager specifically for Redis-backed queues — it manages multiple workers/queues/priorities from config and gives real-time visibility (throughput, failures, wait times) that plain queue:work doesn't.

q: Name the four pillars of OOP and give one PHP-specific example of each.
a: Encapsulation — private fields with public getter/setter methods on a model. Inheritance — a base Model class extended by specific Eloquent models. Polymorphism — an interface (like a payment gateway interface) implemented differently by different payment providers. Abstraction — an abstract class or interface (like a NotificationChannel interface) exposing one simple method without callers needing to know the implementation details.

q: What's the N+1 query problem, and how do you fix it in one line of Eloquent?
a: Loading a list and then triggering one additional query per item when accessing a relationship in a loop. Fix: Model::with('relationship')->get(); — loading the relationship ahead of time in the initial query.

q: What's the difference between hasOne and belongsTo?
a: They're opposites of each other — it depends on which table holds the foreign key (the link to the other table). If Model A's table has the foreign key, A belongsTo B; if Model B's table has the foreign key pointing back, B hasOne A (or hasMany).

q: What does ON DELETE CASCADE do?
a: It automatically deletes related child-table rows when the parent row they point to is deleted, through a foreign key rule.

q: What's the difference between MQTT and HTTP for IoT communication?
a: MQTT keeps a connection open and pushes messages instantly, built for lightweight, low-delay, low-bandwidth communication from limited devices; HTTP is request/response and needs repeated checking to get 'new' data, which is less efficient for frequent, event-driven device communication.

q: What's a Docker named volume for?
a: Storage for data (like a database's data folder) that needs to survive container restarts/removal, managed by Docker rather than tied to a specific folder on your computer.

q: What does idempotent mean in the context of an API?
a: Making the same request multiple times produces the same result as making it once — critical for safely handling retries (webhooks, payments) without side effects like duplicate records or double charges.

q: In a role-based application, how do authentication and authorization differ?
a: Authentication confirms who a user is; authorization determines what that logged-in user is allowed to do.

q: Name one thing Redis is used for besides caching.
a: Queue backend (job dispatching), session storage, pub/sub messaging, or rate limiting — any of these count.

q: What status code do you return for a validation error?
For a REST resource update endpoint, when should you use PUT rather than PATCH?
a: PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH updates only part of it.

q: What does composer dump-autoload do?
a: It rebuilds the map that connects class names to file locations.

q: hasOne vs. belongsTo in Eloquent — what's the difference?
a: hasOne is the side that does NOT hold the foreign key; belongsTo is the side that DOES hold the foreign key.

q: When a parent row is deleted, how does a foreign key with ON DELETE CASCADE affect its child rows?
a: It automatically deletes related (child) rows when the main (parent) row is deleted.

q: Authentication vs. authorization — what's the difference?
a: Authentication checks who you are; authorization checks what you're allowed to do.

q: What does 'idempotent' mean for an API?
a: Doing the same request more than once has the same result as doing it just once.

q: Name one use for Redis besides caching.
a: As a queue driver (or session storage, or pub/sub messaging).

q: How does an HTML form 'fake' a PUT or PATCH request?
a: The form actually sends POST, with a hidden _method field, because plain HTML forms only support GET and POST.

q: What is a foreign key constraint for?
a: It makes sure related data stays consistent at the database level, not just in the application code.

q: What does declare(strict_types=1) do?
a: If a value's type doesn't match what a function expects, PHP throws an error instead of quietly converting the type.

q: Big O basics — explain with PHP.
a:
Operation Complexity
Array access by key/index ($arr['x']) O(1) average (PHP arrays are ordered hash tables)
isset($map[$k]) / array_key_exists O(1)
in_array($v, $arr) / array_search O(n)
sort() / usort() O(n log n)
Nested loops over two lists O(n·m)
Binary search on sorted data O(log n)
B-tree index lookup (MySQL/MongoDB) O(log n)

Common trap

in_array inside a loop = O(n²). Flip the array once (array_flip → O(n)) and use isset → O(n) total.

q: Real example — optimizing O(n²) to O(n).
a:
// Slow: for 50k orders × 50k customers = 2.5 billion comparisons
foreach ($orders as $o) foreach ($customers as $c) if ($c['id'] === $o['customer_id']) $o['customer'] = $c;

// Fast: build a hash map once
$byId = array_column($customers, null, 'id');          // O(n)
foreach ($orders as &$o) $o['customer'] = $byId[$o['customer_id']] ?? null;   // O(m)

Eloquent's eager loading does exactly this internally.

q: Space complexity trade-offs?
a: Hash map uses O(n) extra memory to make lookups O(1). Generators/cursor() use O(1) memory instead of O(n). For 10M records choose streaming over loading.

q: Data structures and where they appear in backends?
a:
• Hash map → caches, dedupe, grouping, Redis hashes.
  • Queue (FIFO) → job queues, BFS. PHP: SplQueue.
  • Stack (LIFO) → undo, parsing, DFS. SplStack.
  • Heap / priority queue → top-K, scheduling, Dijkstra. SplPriorityQueue, SplMinHeap.
  • Set → unique IDs, Redis sets.
  • Sorted set → leaderboards, rate limiting windows, delayed jobs (Redis ZSET — skip list, O(log n)).
  • B-tree/B+tree → database indexes.
  • Trie → autocomplete.
  • Graph → dependencies, permissions hierarchies, recommendations.
  • Linked list → LRU cache (with hash map).
  • Bloom filter → "definitely not present" checks (username availability, cache penetration protection).

q: Implement an LRU cache — O(1) get/put.code1 follow-up
a:
Hash map + doubly linked list (most recent at head). In PHP, ordered arrays make a simple version possible:

class LRUCache {
    private array $data = [];
    public function __construct(private int $capacity) {}
    public function get(string $key): mixed {
        if (!array_key_exists($key, $this->data)) return null;
        $v = $this->data[$key]; unset($this->data[$key]); $this->data[$key] = $v; // move to end (most recent)
        return $v;
    }
    public function put(string $key, mixed $value): void {
        unset($this->data[$key]);
        $this->data[$key] = $value;
        if (count($this->data) > $this->capacity) unset($this->data[array_key_first($this->data)]); // evict oldest
    }
}

Cross-questionIs unset + re-add O(1)?

Amortized yes in PHP's hash table; array_key_first is O(1). Mention the classic hash map + doubly linked list design too.

q: Top K most frequent items from a huge list?
a: Count with a hash map O(n), then a min-heap of size K → O(n log K) instead of full sort O(n log n). For a stream too large for memory: Count-Min Sketch (approximate) or Redis sorted sets. In DB: GROUP BY ... ORDER BY count DESC LIMIT K with an index or aggregation $group + $sort + $limit.

q: Classic coding problems to practice (with the pattern):code
a:
• Two Sum → hash map O(n).
  • Valid parentheses → stack.
  • Merge intervals (booking overlaps) → sort + sweep O(n log n).
  • Longest substring without repeating chars → sliding window.
  • Detect cycle in dependencies (jobs/modules) → DFS / topological sort (Kahn's algorithm).
  • Find duplicates in large file → hashing / external sort.
  • Group anagrams → hash map with sorted key.
  • Binary search on sorted IDs/timestamps.
  • Kth largest → heap.
  • Rate limiter → sliding window / token bucket.
// Two Sum — O(n) time, O(n) space
function twoSum(array $nums, int $target): ?array {
    $seen = [];
    foreach ($nums as $i => $n) {
        if (isset($seen[$target - $n])) return [$seen[$target - $n], $i];
        $seen[$n] = $i;
    }
    return null;
}
// Merge overlapping time ranges
function merge(array $ranges): array {
    usort($ranges, fn($a, $b) => $a[0] <=> $b[0]);
    $out = [];
    foreach ($ranges as $r) {
        if ($out && $r[0] <= $out[count($out)-1][1]) $out[count($out)-1][1] = max($out[count($out)-1][1], $r[1]);
        else $out[] = $r;
    }
    return $out;
}
// Topological sort (job dependencies) — Kahn's algorithm, O(V+E)
function topo(array $deps): array { // ['b' => ['a'], 'c' => ['b']]
    $in = []; $adj = [];
    foreach ($deps as $n => $ds) { $in[$n] ??= 0; foreach ($ds as $d) { $adj[$d][] = $n; $in[$n]++; $in[$d] ??= 0; } }
    $q = array_keys(array_filter($in, fn($x) => $x === 0)); $order = [];
    while ($q) { $n = array_shift($q); $order[] = $n; foreach ($adj[$n] ?? [] as $m) if (--$in[$m] === 0) $q[] = $m; }
    if (count($order) !== count($in)) throw new RuntimeException('Cycle detected');
    return $order;
}

q: Rate limiting algorithms?
a:
• Fixed window: counter per minute — simple, bursty at window edges.
  • Sliding window log: store timestamps (Redis ZSET) — accurate, more memory.
  • Sliding window counter: weighted previous + current window — good balance.
  • Token bucket: tokens refill at a rate, allows bursts up to bucket size — most common for APIs.
  • Leaky bucket: smooth constant outflow. Laravel RateLimiter uses cache counters (window-based); distributed limits need a shared Redis, ideally with atomic Lua scripts.

q: Consistent hashing?
a: Maps keys and servers onto a ring so adding/removing a server moves only ~1/n of keys (instead of rehashing everything). Used in distributed caches, sharding, load balancing.

q: How do you evaluate an implementation choice by workload?
a: Estimate: data size, request rate, read/write ratio, growth. Example: dedupe 20M emails → in-memory PHP array ≈ several GB (too much) → use DB unique index, sort + stream, or Redis set/Bloom filter. Always say the numbers.

q: Walk me through how you approach a system design interview question.
a:
Use a fixed 6-step structure so you never freeze:

  • Clarify requirements (5 min): functional (what it does) and non-functional (users, reads vs writes, latency, availability, consistency).
  • Estimate scale: daily users → requests/sec, storage per year, bandwidth. Round numbers are fine.
  • API + data model: 3–5 endpoints and the main tables/collections.
  • High-level design: client → CDN → load balancer → app servers → cache → DB → queue/workers.
  • Deep dive into the 1–2 hardest parts (e.g. feed fan-out, hot keys, payment idempotency).
  • Bottlenecks & trade-offs: single points of failure, scaling, monitoring, what you'd do next.

Say trade-offs out loud — the interviewer grades your reasoning, not a perfect diagram.

Cross-questionWhat if the interviewer keeps changing requirements?

That's intended. Restate the new requirement, say which part of the design it affects, and adjust only that part.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: How do you do back-of-the-envelope estimation? Estimate QPS for 10M daily active users.
a:
Assume each user makes ~20 requests/day → 200M requests/day. A day has ~86,400 s ≈ 10^5, so average ≈ 2,000 QPS. Peak is usually 2–5× average → plan for ~10,000 QPS.

Storage: if each user writes 2 records/day of 1 KB → 20 GB/day → ~7 TB/year (before replication ×3).

Useful numbers: 1 day ≈ 10^5 s; 1 month ≈ 2.5×10^6 s; RAM read ~100 ns; SSD read ~100 µs; same-region round trip ~0.5 ms; cross-continent ~150 ms.

Common trap

Don't spend 10 minutes on maths. The goal is the order of magnitude, which decides whether one DB is enough or you need sharding.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Vertical vs horizontal scaling — what's the difference and when do you use each?
a:
Vertical = bigger machine (more CPU/RAM). Simple, no code changes, but has a hard ceiling and a single point of failure.

Horizontal = more machines behind a load balancer. Near-unlimited and fault tolerant, but the app must be stateless: sessions in Redis/DB, files in S3, not on local disk.

In practice: scale the DB vertically first (and add read replicas), scale app servers horizontally from day one.

Cross-questionWhat makes a Laravel app stateless?

SESSION_DRIVER=redis or database, CACHE_STORE=redis, uploads on S3 (FILESYSTEM_DISK=s3), queues on Redis/SQS, and no files written to local storage that other servers need.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: What is a load balancer and which algorithms does it use?
a:
A load balancer spreads incoming requests across several servers and removes unhealthy ones using health checks.

  • Round robin: each server in turn.
  • Least connections: to the least busy server — good for long requests.
  • IP hash: same client → same server (sticky), useful when state is local (better to avoid).
  • Weighted: bigger servers get more traffic.

L4 balancers route by IP/port (fast). L7 balancers read HTTP (path, headers, cookies) and can do TLS termination and path routing — e.g. Nginx, AWS ALB.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Explain the CAP theorem in simple words.
a:
In a distributed system, when a network partition happens (nodes can't talk), you must choose between:

  • Consistency — every read gets the latest write (or an error), or
  • Availability — every request gets a response, possibly stale.

Partitions are unavoidable, so the real choice is CP vs AP during a failure. Banking/inventory → CP. Social feeds, likes counters → AP (eventual consistency is fine).

Cross-questionWhat is PACELC?

Extends CAP: even when there is no partition (Else), you trade Latency vs Consistency. E.g. synchronous replication = consistent but slower.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: What is database sharding, and how do you pick a shard key?
a:
Sharding splits one big table across several databases, each holding a subset of rows (e.g. users 1–1M on shard A).

A good shard key: has high cardinality, spreads load evenly, and matches your main query so most queries hit one shard. tenant_id or user_id is common. Avoid time-based keys — all new writes hit the newest shard (hotspot).

Costs: cross-shard joins and transactions become hard, rebalancing is painful. So first try indexes → caching → read replicas → partitioning → then sharding.

Cross-questionWhat is consistent hashing?

Keys and servers are placed on a hash ring; a key goes to the next server clockwise. Adding a server only moves ~1/N of keys instead of reshuffling everything.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Explain caching strategies: cache-aside, write-through, write-behind.
a:
• Cache-aside (lazy loading): app reads cache; on miss reads DB and writes to cache. Most common — Laravel's Cache::remember().
  • Write-through: write to cache and DB together; cache always fresh, writes slower.
  • Write-behind: write to cache, flush to DB later asynchronously; fast but can lose data.

Plus invalidation: TTL, or delete the key when the model changes (model observer / event).

Common trap

Cache stampede — a hot key expires and 1,000 requests hit the DB at once. Fix with locks (Cache::lock), Cache::flexible() (stale-while-revalidate, Laravel 11+), or jittered TTLs.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.
a:
Requirements: create short link, redirect fast, optional expiry and click stats. Read-heavy (~100:1).

ID generation: auto-increment ID encoded in base62 (7 chars = 3.5 trillion codes), or a pre-generated key pool. Avoid hashing the URL (collisions).

Data: links(id, code UNIQUE, long_url, user_id, expires_at).

Redirect path: GET /{code} → Redis cache → DB on miss → 301 (cacheable, less stats) or 302 (every hit reaches you, better analytics).

Analytics: don't write to DB on each click — push to a queue/stream and aggregate in batches.

Scale: CDN/edge for hot links, read replicas, rate-limit creation to stop abuse.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a rate limiter.
a:
Algorithms:

  • Fixed window: counter per minute — simple, but allows bursts at window edges.
  • Sliding window log/counter: smoother, a bit more memory.
  • Token bucket: tokens refill at a steady rate; allows short bursts. Most common in APIs.
  • Leaky bucket: processes at a constant rate.

Where: API gateway / Nginx (limit_req) for global, app-level for per-user rules.

Storage: Redis with atomic INCR + EXPIRE (or a Lua script) so all app servers share counts.

Return 429 Too Many Requests with Retry-After and X-RateLimit-Remaining headers. In Laravel: RateLimiter::for('api', fn($r) => Limit::perMinute(60)->by($r->user()?->id ?: $r->ip())).
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a notification system (email, SMS, push).
a:
Flow: event (OrderShipped) → notification service checks user preferences & templates → pushes one job per channel to queues → channel workers call providers (SES, Twilio, FCM) → store delivery status.

Key points:

  • Separate queues per channel so slow SMS doesn't block push.
  • Retries with exponential backoff, and a dead-letter queue after N failures.
  • Idempotency key per notification so retries don't double-send.
  • Rate limits per provider and per user (no 50 pushes a minute).
  • Scheduling / quiet hours, and batching digests.

In Laravel: Notifications with ShouldQueue, via() returning channels, Horizon for monitoring.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a chat application like WhatsApp.
a:
Connections: clients keep a WebSocket to a chat gateway (Laravel Reverb / Soketi / Node). Gateways are stateful, so track user → gateway in Redis.

Send: client → gateway → persist message (DB, ordered by conversation + sequence id) → publish via Redis Pub/Sub or Kafka → recipient's gateway pushes it.

Offline users: store and deliver on reconnect; send push notification.

Receipts: sent / delivered / read as small events.

Storage: write-heavy, append-only → Cassandra/ScyllaDB at huge scale; MySQL partitioned by conversation is fine for most companies.

Group chat: fan-out on write for small groups, fan-out on read for huge channels.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a news feed (Twitter/Facebook timeline).
a:
Two approaches:

  • Fan-out on write (push): when a user posts, insert post ID into each follower's feed list (Redis). Reading is instant. Bad for celebrities with 10M followers.
  • Fan-out on read (pull): build the feed at read time by merging recent posts of people you follow. Cheap writes, slow reads.

Hybrid (what real systems do): push for normal users, pull for celebrities, merge at read time.

Store only IDs in feed lists, hydrate posts from cache. Paginate with cursors, not offsets. Ranking can run as a separate service.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design an e-commerce checkout that never oversells stock.
a:
Stock is the hard part. Options:

  • Atomic conditional update: UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1 WHERE id=? AND stock >= 1 — check affected rows. Simple and safe.
  • Pessimistic lock: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE inside a transaction (Laravel lockForUpdate()).
  • Reservation: reserve stock for 10–15 min when checkout starts; a scheduled job releases expired reservations.

Payment flow: create order as pending → payment gateway → webhook confirms → mark paid (idempotently). Never trust the redirect URL alone.

For flash sales: queue the purchase requests, pre-load stock into Redis and decrement atomically, then persist.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a payment system. How do you make it idempotent?
a:
Money must never be charged twice or lost.

  • Client sends an Idempotency-Key header; server stores key → result. A retry with the same key returns the stored result instead of charging again.
  • Use a state machine: created → pending → succeeded/failed → refunded, with only valid transitions.
  • Record every movement in a double-entry ledger (debit + credit rows that sum to zero). Never update balances without a ledger row.
  • Handle webhooks idempotently (store provider event IDs) and run a daily reconciliation job against the provider's report.
  • Store amounts as integers in minor units (paisa/cents), never floats.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a job/task scheduling system (like cron at scale).
a:
Store jobs (id, run_at, payload, status, attempts). A scheduler polls WHERE run_at <= now AND status='pending' using SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED so multiple schedulers don't grab the same job, then pushes to a queue.

Workers execute, update status, and retry with backoff. Make jobs idempotent because at-least-once delivery means duplicates happen.

In Laravel: schedule:run via one cron entry, plus ->onOneServer() (needs a shared cache lock) and ->withoutOverlapping() when you have multiple servers.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design autocomplete / type-ahead search.
a:
Requirements: suggestions under ~100 ms as the user types.

  • Build a trie or prefix index of popular queries, ranked by frequency. Precompute top-K per prefix.
  • Store in memory/Redis (sorted sets) or use Elasticsearch/Meilisearch/Typesense with edge n-grams.
  • Client: debounce 200–300 ms, cancel old requests, cache recent results in the browser.
  • Update rankings offline (hourly job from search logs), not on every keystroke.

In Laravel: Laravel Scout with Meilisearch/Typesense driver.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a file upload and image processing service.
a:
• Client asks the API for a pre-signed S3 URL and uploads directly to S3 (your servers don't carry the bytes).
  • S3 event or client callback → queue job → generate thumbnails / scan for malware / extract metadata.
  • Serve through a CDN (CloudFront) with long cache headers and versioned file names.
  • Validate type by content, not extension; set size limits in the signed URL policy.
  • Large files: multipart upload with resume.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Design a multi-tenant SaaS. Which tenancy model would you choose?
a:
Three models:

  • Shared DB, shared tables with tenant_id column — cheapest, easiest to operate; risk: a missing WHERE tenant_id leaks data. Use a global scope and tests.
  • Shared DB, schema per tenant — middle ground (common with PostgreSQL).
  • Database per tenant — strongest isolation, per-tenant backup/restore; harder migrations and more connections.

Most SaaS start with shared tables and move big/enterprise customers to dedicated DBs. Also plan: tenant resolution (subdomain/header), per-tenant cache prefixes, queue jobs that carry tenant context, and per-tenant rate limits. Packages: stancl/tenancy, spatie/laravel-multitenancy.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: How do you design for high availability? What are SPOFs?
a:
A single point of failure is any component whose failure takes everything down: one DB, one server, one load balancer, one region.

Remove them with redundancy: multiple app servers across availability zones, DB primary + replicas with automatic failover, managed/redundant load balancers, backups tested with restores, health checks + auto-healing.

Measure with SLOs (e.g. 99.9% = ~43 min downtime/month). Also: graceful degradation (serve cached data if a service is down), circuit breakers, and timeouts everywhere.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Message queue vs event streaming (RabbitMQ/SQS vs Kafka)?
a:
• Queue (SQS, RabbitMQ, Redis queue): a message is consumed by one worker and then deleted. Good for background jobs.
  • Stream (Kafka, Kinesis): an append-only log; messages stay for a retention period; many consumer groups each read at their own offset and can replay. Good for event sourcing, analytics, many independent consumers.

Kafka keeps ordering within a partition; choose the partition key (e.g. order_id) so related events stay ordered.
c: Framework: how to run any system design round
