q: What does 'eventual consistency' mean, and where is it acceptable?
a:
After a write, different replicas may briefly return different values, but they all converge to the same value if no new writes happen.

Acceptable: likes counts, view counters, search indexes, feeds, analytics, read replicas for listings. Not acceptable: account balances, stock at checkout, permissions changes.

Common fix for "I just saved but I don't see it": read-your-own-writes — route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds (Laravel's 'sticky' => true DB option does this).
c: Framework: how to run any system design round

q: Monolith vs microservices — which would you choose and why?
a:
Default: a well-structured (modular) monolith. One deploy, simple transactions, easy debugging, fast for small teams.

Microservices make sense when: several teams need to deploy independently, parts have very different scaling needs, or domains are clearly separated. Their costs: network failures, distributed transactions (sagas), observability, DevOps overhead, data duplication.

Good answer: "Start as a modular monolith with clear module boundaries; extract a service only when a real pain (team or scaling) justifies it."

Cross-questionWhat is a distributed monolith?

Services that must be deployed together or call each other synchronously in long chains — all the pain of microservices, none of the benefits.

q: What is a modular monolith and how would you structure one in Laravel?
a:
One deployable app split into modules by business domain (Billing, Catalog, Orders), each with its own models, services, routes, events and tests.

Rules: modules talk through public interfaces or events, never by reaching into each other's tables. Structure like app/Modules/Billing/{Http,Models,Actions,Events,Providers} or src/Domain/... with a service provider per module. Tools like deptrac / Pest arch tests enforce boundaries.

Benefit: you can later extract a module into a service with little rework.

q: Explain Clean Architecture / Hexagonal (Ports & Adapters) in simple terms.
a:
Business logic sits in the centre and knows nothing about frameworks, databases or HTTP. Outer layers depend inward, never the reverse.

  • Ports = interfaces the core defines (PaymentGateway, OrderRepository).
  • Adapters = implementations (StripeGateway, EloquentOrderRepository, HTTP controller, CLI command).

Benefit: swap a payment provider or test business rules without a DB. Cost: more files and indirection — use it for complex domains, not a CRUD admin panel.

q: What is Domain-Driven Design? Explain bounded context, aggregate, value object.
a:
DDD = model software around the business language (ubiquitous language).

  • Bounded context: a boundary where a word has one meaning ("Customer" in Billing ≠ "Customer" in Support).
  • Entity: has identity (Order #123).
  • Value object: defined by its values, immutable (Money, Address, Email).
  • Aggregate: a cluster with one root (Order + OrderLines); all changes go through the root to keep rules valid.
  • Domain event: something that happened (OrderPlaced).

q: What is CQRS and when is it worth it?
a:
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: separate the model that writes (commands, validation, business rules) from the model that reads (queries optimised for screens, maybe denormalised tables or a search index).

Worth it when reads and writes have very different shapes or loads (dashboards, reporting, event sourcing). Overkill for normal CRUD. A light version in Laravel: Action classes for writes, dedicated query classes / read models for complex listings.

q: What is Event Sourcing?
a:
Instead of storing current state, you store every event that happened (ItemAdded, ItemRemoved, OrderPaid) and rebuild state by replaying them. Projections build read tables from events.

Pros: full audit trail, time travel, easy new projections. Cons: complexity, event versioning, eventual consistency. Good for ledgers, audits, workflows. In Laravel: spatie/laravel-event-sourcing.

q: What is the Saga pattern?
a:
A way to do a "transaction" across several services without a distributed lock. Each step is a local transaction; if one fails, run compensating actions for the steps already done (refund payment, release stock).

  • Choreography: services react to each other's events (simple, harder to follow).
  • Orchestration: a coordinator tells each service what to do (clearer, central logic).

q: What is an API Gateway and a BFF (Backend for Frontend)?
a:
API Gateway: single entry point in front of services — routing, auth, rate limiting, TLS, request logging (Kong, AWS API Gateway, Nginx).

BFF: a small backend per client type (web, mobile) that shapes and aggregates data exactly for that client, so the mobile app doesn't make 6 calls or download fields it doesn't need.

q: Circuit breaker, retry, timeout, bulkhead — explain the resilience patterns.
a:
• Timeout: never wait forever on a remote call (Laravel Http::timeout(5)).
  • Retry with exponential backoff + jitter: for transient errors only, and only for idempotent operations.
  • Circuit breaker: after N failures, stop calling the service for a while and fail fast / use a fallback; then test with a few calls (half-open).
  • Bulkhead: isolate resources (separate queues / connection pools) so one failing dependency can't exhaust everything.

q: What is the outbox pattern?
a:
Problem: you save an order in the DB and publish an OrderPlaced message — if the app crashes between the two, they disagree.

Solution: in the same DB transaction, insert the order and a row into an outbox table. A separate relay process reads the outbox and publishes messages, marking them sent. Consumers must be idempotent because a message may be sent twice.

In Laravel, DB::afterCommit / ShouldDispatchAfterCommit helps with the simpler version: only dispatch the job after the transaction commits.

q: How do you document and communicate an architecture decision?
a:
Use ADRs (Architecture Decision Records): a short markdown file per decision — context, options considered, decision, consequences. Store in the repo (docs/adr/0007-use-redis-queues.md).

Plus a C4 diagram (Context → Containers → Components) for onboarding. Seniors are judged on explaining *why* and the trade-offs, not only *what*.

q: A page is slow in production. Walk through how you'd find the cause.
a: 1. Measure, don't guess: APM / Telescope / Pulse / Sentry performance / slow query log. 2. Split time: DB? external API? PHP CPU? frontend assets? 3. DB: N+1 queries (preventLazyLoading()), missing indexes (EXPLAIN), too many rows loaded. 4. External calls: add timeouts, cache, move to queue. 5. App: heavy loops, serialization, no OPcache, huge collections in memory. 6. Frontend: bundle size, images, no CDN. 7. Fix the biggest item, measure again, add a regression check.

q: How would you add an AI feature (LLM) to an existing Laravel product safely?
a:
• Wrap the provider behind an interface (or Laravel 13's AI SDK / Prism) so you can switch models.
  • Run calls in queued jobs with timeouts, retries and cost tracking per tenant.
  • Use RAG: embed your documents (pgvector/Qdrant), retrieve top chunks, send only those in the prompt.
  • Validate structured output (JSON schema) and never let the model run actions without permission checks.
  • Protect against prompt injection from user content, strip PII, log prompts/responses for evaluation.
  • Cache repeated answers and set per-user rate limits.

q: Explain SOLID with one real example each.
a:
• S — Single Responsibility: a class has one reason to change. InvoicePdfGenerator shouldn't also send emails.
  • O — Open/Closed: add new behaviour by adding code, not editing old code — new PaymentGateway class instead of another if in a switch.
  • L — Liskov Substitution: a subclass must work wherever the parent works. A ReadOnlyFile that throws on write() breaks LSP.
  • I — Interface Segregation: small interfaces; don't force a class to implement methods it doesn't use.
  • D — Dependency Inversion: depend on interfaces, not concrete classes; inject them (Laravel's container binds PaymentGateway → StripeGateway).

q: DRY, KISS, YAGNI — what do they mean and when do they conflict?
a:
• DRY: don't duplicate *knowledge* (business rules), not just lines.
  • KISS: keep it simple.
  • YAGNI: don't build features/abstractions until needed.

They conflict when making code "DRY" creates a complicated abstraction used by two things that only *look* similar. Rule of thumb: duplicate twice, abstract on the third time ("rule of three").

q: Composition vs inheritance — which do you prefer?
a:
Prefer composition ("has-a"): build behaviour by combining small objects injected into a class. Inheritance ("is-a") creates tight coupling and deep hierarchies that are hard to change.

Use inheritance for true is-a relationships and framework base classes (Model, Controller). PHP traits are a middle option for sharing small behaviour, but overusing them hides dependencies.

q: Which design patterns does Laravel itself use?
a:
• Service Container → Dependency Injection / IoC.
  • Facades → static proxy to container services (a Proxy/Facade pattern).
  • Middleware → Chain of Responsibility / Pipeline.
  • Eloquent → Active Record.
  • Events & Observers → Observer pattern.
  • Managers/Drivers (Cache, Queue, Mail, Filesystem) → Strategy + Factory.
  • Query Builder → Builder, fluent interface.
  • Service Providers → bootstrapping / registry.
  • Model factories → Factory pattern.

q: What is the Repository pattern? Is it useful with Eloquent?
a:
A repository hides data access behind an interface: OrderRepository::findPaidBetween($from,$to).

Pros: swap storage, centralise complex queries, mock in unit tests. Cons with Eloquent: Eloquent is already an abstraction, so a thin repository that just wraps find() adds boilerplate and hides useful features.

Balanced answer: use repositories or query classes for complex/reused queries or when the domain must be storage-agnostic; don't wrap every simple CRUD call.

q: Explain the Strategy pattern with a real example.
a:
Define a family of interchangeable algorithms behind one interface and choose one at runtime.

interface ShippingCalculator { public function cost(Order $o): int; }
class TcsShipping implements ShippingCalculator { /* ... */ }
class LeopardsShipping implements ShippingCalculator { /* ... */ }

$calc = match($order->courier) { 'tcs' => new TcsShipping, 'leopards' => new LeopardsShipping };
$calc->cost($order);

Replaces long if/else chains; adding a courier = adding a class (Open/Closed).

q: Factory vs Abstract Factory vs Builder?
a:
• Factory (method): one place decides which class to create (NotifierFactory::make('sms')).
  • Abstract Factory: creates *families* of related objects (a UI kit that makes matching Button + Input for a theme).
  • Builder: builds a complex object step by step with a fluent API (Query Builder, Mail::to()->cc()->send()).

q: What is the Singleton pattern and why is it often called an anti-pattern?
a:
Singleton ensures only one instance exists, with global access (Logger::getInstance()).

Problems: hidden global state, hard to test/mock, tight coupling. Better: let the DI container manage a single shared instance — $this->app->singleton(Client::class, ...) — so classes still receive it via injection.

Common trap

In PHP-FPM each request is a fresh process state, so a "singleton" only lives per request. With Octane it lives across requests — watch for leaked state.

q: Explain the Observer pattern and how Laravel uses it.
a:
Subjects notify subscribed observers when something happens, without knowing who they are.

Laravel: Events + Listeners (OrderPlaced → SendReceipt, UpdateStock) and Model Observers (created, updated, deleted hooks). Listeners can be queued.

Common trap

Too many hidden observers make the flow hard to follow and cause surprise side-effects in tests or seeders. Keep important business steps explicit.

q: Adapter vs Decorator vs Proxy vs Facade?
a:
• Adapter: converts one interface into another (wrap an old SMS SDK to fit your SmsSender interface).
  • Decorator: wraps an object to add behaviour without changing it (CachedProductRepository wraps ProductRepository).
  • Proxy: same interface, controls access (lazy loading, permission checks, remote calls).
  • Facade (GoF): a simple interface over a complex subsystem. Laravel Facades are really static proxies to container services.

q: What is the Pipeline / Chain of Responsibility pattern?
a:
A request passes through a series of handlers; each can act on it and pass it on, or stop it. Laravel middleware is exactly this, and you can use Illuminate\Pipeline\Pipeline yourself:

app(Pipeline::class)->send($query)
  ->through([FilterByStatus::class, FilterByDate::class, Sort::class])
  ->thenReturn();

Good for filters, checkout steps, import processing.

q: Command pattern, and how does it relate to Laravel jobs?
a: Wrap a request as an object with all the data needed to run it later. Laravel Jobs are commands: serialised, queued, retried, executed by a worker. Action classes (CreateOrderAction) are a simple synchronous version.

q: State pattern — when would you use it?
a:
When an object behaves differently depending on its state and has many if ($status === ...) checks. Each state becomes a class with allowed transitions (Pending → Paid → Shipped). Invalid transitions throw.

Laravel: spatie/laravel-model-states, or PHP enums with a canTransitionTo() method.

q: What is Dependency Injection vs Service Locator?
a:
DI: dependencies are passed in (constructor/method). Easy to see and test.

Service Locator: the class pulls dependencies itself (app(Mailer::class) inside a method). Hidden dependencies, harder to test.

Laravel supports both; prefer constructor injection in your own classes. Facades are convenient but act like a locator — fine in controllers, avoid deep in domain code.

q: What are anti-patterns you often see in legacy PHP projects?
a: God classes / fat controllers, business logic in Blade views, N+1 queries, copy-pasted code, magic strings for statuses, global helpers with side-effects, catching and ignoring exceptions, no tests, config values hard-coded, huge switch statements that should be Strategy/State, and anemic "Service" classes that are just 3,000-line procedure dumps.

q: How do you keep controllers thin? Service vs Action classes.
a:
Controller only: validate (FormRequest), authorise (Policy), call one unit of business logic, return a response/Resource.

  • Service class: groups related operations (OrderService with several methods). Risk: grows into a god class.
  • Action class: one class per use case with a single handle()/execute() (PlaceOrder, RefundOrder). Easy to reuse from controllers, jobs, Livewire and Artisan commands.

q: Value Objects and DTOs — what's the difference?
a:
• DTO: a plain data carrier between layers, no behaviour (CreateOrderData from a request). PHP 8 readonly classes with constructor promotion are perfect. spatie/laravel-data helps.
  • Value Object: represents a domain concept, immutable, validates itself and has behaviour (Money::add(), Email that rejects invalid addresses). Compared by value.

q: What happens when you type a URL into the browser and press Enter?
a:
• DNS: browser cache → OS → resolver → root → TLD → authoritative server returns the IP.
  • TCP handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK), then TLS handshake for HTTPS (certificate check, key exchange).
  • Browser sends the HTTP request (method, path, headers, cookies).
  • Server side: CDN/load balancer → Nginx → PHP-FPM → Laravel boots, routes, runs middleware, controller, returns a response.
  • Browser parses HTML → builds DOM, fetches CSS/JS/images, builds CSSOM, runs JS, layout, paint.

Mention caching at each layer (DNS TTL, CDN, HTTP cache headers) to show depth.

q: How does a request flow through Nginx, PHP-FPM and Laravel?
a:
• Nginx receives the request. Static files are served directly; .php requests go to PHP-FPM over FastCGI (fastcgi_pass).
  • PHP-FPM gives the request to a free worker process from its pool (pm.max_children).
  • The worker runs public/index.php → Composer autoload → bootstrap/app.php creates the Application (service container).
  • The HTTP Kernel runs global middleware, the router matches the route, route middleware runs, then the controller.
  • The response travels back through middleware, is sent, then terminable middleware runs.
  • The worker is reset for the next request (unless you use Octane, where the app stays in memory).

q: How does PHP execute code? What are OPcache and JIT?
a:
PHP source → lexer (tokens) → parser (AST) → compiler (opcodes) → Zend VM executes opcodes.

OPcache stores compiled opcodes in shared memory so files aren't recompiled every request — the single biggest free performance win. In production set opcache.validate_timestamps=0 and reset on deploy.

JIT (PHP 8.0+) compiles hot opcodes to machine code. Big gains for CPU-heavy maths, small gains for typical web apps, which are I/O-bound.

Preloading (opcache.preload) loads framework classes into memory once at server start.

q: How does PHP manage memory? What is garbage collection?
a:
Every value (zval) has a reference count. When it drops to 0, memory is freed immediately.

Problem: circular references (object A refers to B and B to A) never reach 0. The cycle collector runs periodically to find and free these.

Arrays and strings use copy-on-write: assigning $b = $a doesn't copy until one of them changes.

In long-running scripts (queue workers, Octane) memory can leak — use --memory / --max-jobs limits so workers restart.

q: How does Laravel's service container resolve dependencies automatically?
a:
When you type-hint a class (e.g. in a controller constructor), the container uses PHP Reflection to read the constructor's parameter types, recursively resolves each one, and builds the object (autowiring).

If a parameter is an interface, it needs a binding ($this->app->bind(PaymentGateway::class, StripeGateway::class)). singleton() caches the instance; scoped() caches per request/job (Octane-safe). Contextual binding gives different implementations to different classes.

q: How do Laravel Facades work under the hood?
a:
Cache::get('x') — the Cache facade class has no get method. PHP calls the magic static method __callStatic, which asks getFacadeAccessor() for a key ('cache'), resolves that object from the service container, and forwards the call to it.

So facades are a static-looking proxy to real, swappable objects. That's why Cache::fake() / Mail::fake() / Http::fake() work in tests.

Real-time facades: prefix a namespace with Facades\ to use any class as a facade.

q: How does Eloquent eager loading actually work? Why does it fix N+1?
a:
Without eager loading: 1 query for 100 posts + 1 query per post for its author = 101 queries.

Post::with('author')->get() runs 2 queries: select * from posts, then select * from users where id in (1, 5, 9, ...) using the collected foreign keys. Eloquent then matches users to posts in PHP by key and sets the relation.

Detect N+1 in dev with Model::preventLazyLoading(!app()->isProduction()). Laravel 12.8+ also offers automatic eager loading (Model::automaticallyEagerLoadRelationships()).

q: How do Laravel queues work internally?
a:
• dispatch(new SendInvoice($order)) serializes the job (models are stored as class + ID via SerializesModels) and pushes a JSON payload to the driver (Redis list, DB table, SQS).
  • php artisan queue:work is a long-running process that loops: pop a job, reserve it, unserialize (re-fetch models from DB), run handle().
  • Success → delete. Exception → release back with a delay until tries is reached → then failed() and the failed_jobs table.
  • retry_after must be longer than the job's max runtime or the job will be run twice.
  • Workers keep the app in memory, so restart them on deploy (queue:restart).

q: Explain the JavaScript event loop.
a:
JS runs on one thread with a call stack. Slow work (timers, network, I/O) is handed to the browser/Node APIs. When done, callbacks wait in queues:

  • Microtask queue: Promise .then, await continuations, queueMicrotask.
  • Macrotask (task) queue: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O, UI events.

The loop: run the current stack to empty → run all microtasks → render (browser) → take one macrotask → repeat.

console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4);
// 1 4 3 2

q: How does React rendering and reconciliation work?
a:
When state changes, React calls your component function again to get a new virtual DOM tree (the render phase). It diffs it against the previous tree:

  • Different element type → throw away and rebuild that subtree.
  • Same type → keep the DOM node and update changed props.
  • Lists → matched by key; stable keys let React move items instead of recreating them.

Then in the commit phase it applies the minimal DOM changes and runs effects. Fiber lets React split rendering into chunks and prioritise urgent updates (typing) over less urgent ones (useTransition).

q: How does Livewire work under the hood?
a:
• First load: the component renders to normal HTML on the server, plus a snapshot (its public properties + checksum) embedded in the page.
  • An interaction (wire:click, wire:model update) sends an AJAX request with the snapshot and the "updates/calls".
  • The server rehydrates the component from the snapshot, verifies the checksum (so users can't tamper), runs the method, re-renders Blade, and returns new HTML + new snapshot.
  • In the browser, Alpine's morph algorithm patches only the changed DOM.

So all state lives in public properties, sent on every request — keep them small, and never trust them for authorisation. Livewire 4 adds islands so only a region re-renders.

q: How does Docker work? Container vs virtual machine.
a:
A VM virtualises hardware and runs a full guest OS kernel — heavy (GBs, slow boot).

A container is just a normal Linux process isolated by kernel features: namespaces (own view of processes, network, filesystem, users) and cgroups (CPU/memory limits). It shares the host kernel — light (MBs, starts in ms).

An image is a stack of read-only layers (one per Dockerfile instruction) using a union filesystem; a container adds a thin writable layer on top. On Mac/Windows Docker runs a small Linux VM underneath.

q: How does HTTPS / TLS work?
a:
• Client says hello with supported ciphers; server replies with its certificate (public key signed by a Certificate Authority).
  • Browser verifies the certificate chain against trusted CAs and checks the domain name and expiry.
  • They agree a shared session key using key exchange (ECDHE), which gives forward secrecy.
  • All data is then encrypted with fast symmetric encryption (AES/ChaCha20).

TLS 1.3 needs only one round trip. HSTS tells browsers to always use HTTPS.

q: How does JWT authentication work? How is it different from session auth?
a:
Session: server stores session data (Redis/DB), browser keeps only a session ID cookie. Easy to revoke.

JWT: a token header.payload.signature (base64). Server signs it with a secret/private key; later it verifies the signature without a DB lookup. Stateless and good for APIs/microservices — but hard to revoke before expiry, so keep access tokens short-lived with refresh tokens.

The payload is only encoded, not encrypted — never put secrets in it. Laravel Sanctum uses DB-stored tokens (revocable) or cookie sessions for SPAs; Passport provides full OAuth2.

q: How does Git store data internally?
a:
Git is a content-addressed store. Everything is an object named by its hash: blob (file content), tree (a directory listing), commit (tree + parent(s) + author + message). Branches are just files pointing to a commit hash; HEAD points to the current branch.

So a branch is cheap (41 bytes), and rebase creates new commits with new hashes — which is why you shouldn't rebase shared branches.

q: How does a database index work (B-Tree)?
a:
An index is a separate sorted data structure — usually a B+Tree — mapping column values to row locations. Lookups go root → branch → leaf in a few steps (O(log n)) instead of scanning every row. Leaves are linked, so range queries (BETWEEN, ORDER BY) are fast too.

In InnoDB the table itself is stored in primary key order (clustered index); secondary indexes store the PK, so a lookup may need a second step unless the index covers all columns in the query.

Cost: every INSERT/UPDATE must also update each index, and indexes use disk and RAM.

q: Why is Redis so fast, and how does it persist data?
a:
Data lives in RAM, operations are simple data-structure ops, and the main command execution is single-threaded (no locks), with efficient I/O multiplexing (epoll). Network I/O threads were added in Redis 6.

Persistence: RDB snapshots at intervals (compact, may lose recent writes) and AOF append-only log of writes (safer, bigger; appendfsync everysec is common). Use both for safety. Single-threaded also means one slow command (KEYS *) blocks everyone — use SCAN.

q: How does CORS work?
a:
Browsers block JS from reading responses from a different origin (scheme + host + port) unless the server allows it.

For "non-simple" requests (JSON body, custom headers, PUT/DELETE) the browser first sends a preflight OPTIONS request. The server must answer with Access-Control-Allow-Origin, -Methods, -Headers (and -Credentials: true for cookies — then origin can't be *).

CORS is a browser protection — Postman/curl ignore it. In Laravel configure config/cors.php.

q: How does Node.js handle thousands of connections with one thread?
a:
Node uses non-blocking I/O with an event loop (libuv). A request that waits on the DB or network doesn't block the thread — Node registers a callback and serves other requests. File system and some crypto work run on a small thread pool.

Great for I/O-heavy, real-time apps (chat, websockets). Bad for CPU-heavy work, which blocks the loop — use worker threads or a separate service.

q: How does browser caching work (Cache-Control, ETag)?
a:
• Cache-Control: max-age=31536000, immutable → browser reuses the file without asking (use with hashed file names like app.3f9a.js).
  • Cache-Control: no-cache → must revalidate each time.
  • ETag / Last-Modified: browser sends If-None-Match; server returns 304 Not Modified with no body if unchanged.
  • private vs public decides if CDNs can store it. Never cache personalised pages publicly.

q: How does Laravel Octane differ from PHP-FPM?
a:
PHP-FPM boots the whole framework on every request and throws it away. Octane (Swoole, RoadRunner or FrankenPHP) boots the app once and keeps it in memory, serving many requests — often 2–5× faster.

Risks: state leaks between requests — static properties, singletons holding request data, growing arrays. Use scoped() bindings, avoid storing request/user in singletons, and restart workers after N requests.

q: How do WebSockets work?
a:
It starts as an HTTP request with Upgrade: websocket. The server replies 101 Switching Protocols, and the same TCP connection becomes a persistent, two-way channel with small frames.

Compared to polling it saves overhead and gives instant updates. You need sticky or shared state across servers (Redis pub/sub). Laravel: Reverb (first-party WebSocket server) + Laravel Echo on the frontend, broadcasting events on public/private/presence channels.

q: Explain the types of JOIN with examples.
a:
• INNER JOIN: only rows with a match in both tables.
  • LEFT JOIN: all rows from the left table; NULLs where the right has no match. "Customers and their orders, including customers with none."
  • RIGHT JOIN: the mirror.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: all rows from both (not in MySQL — emulate with UNION).
  • CROSS JOIN: every combination.
  • SELF JOIN: a table joined to itself (employee → manager).

Find customers with no orders: LEFT JOIN orders o ON ... WHERE o.id IS NULL.

q: WHERE vs HAVING? And the logical order of a SELECT.
a:
WHERE filters rows before grouping; HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY (can use aggregates).

Logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. That's why you can't use a SELECT alias in WHERE (in standard SQL).

SELECT customer_id, SUM(total) AS spent
FROM orders WHERE status='paid'
GROUP BY customer_id HAVING SUM(total) > 10000;

q: Find the second highest salary (and the Nth highest).
a:
-- 2nd highest, handles duplicates
SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees WHERE salary < (SELECT MAX(salary) FROM employees);

-- Nth with window function (MySQL 8+)
SELECT salary FROM (
  SELECT salary, DENSE_RANK() OVER (ORDER BY salary DESC) rnk FROM employees
) t WHERE rnk = 3 LIMIT 1;

DENSE_RANK keeps ties at the same rank without gaps; RANK leaves gaps; ROW_NUMBER is always unique.

q: How do you find and delete duplicate rows?
a:
-- find
SELECT email, COUNT(*) c FROM users GROUP BY email HAVING c > 1;

-- delete, keep the lowest id (MySQL)
DELETE u1 FROM users u1
JOIN users u2 ON u1.email = u2.email AND u1.id > u2.id;

Then add a UNIQUE index so it can't happen again.

q: What are window functions? Give practical examples.
a:
They compute over a set of rows without collapsing them like GROUP BY.

SELECT order_id, customer_id, total,
  SUM(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at) AS running_total,
  ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at DESC) AS rn,
  LAG(total) OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY created_at) AS prev_order
FROM orders;

Uses: running totals, latest row per group (rn = 1), rankings, comparing to previous row, moving averages.

q: What is a CTE? What is a recursive CTE?
a:
A CTE (WITH name AS (...)) is a named temporary result that makes complex queries readable.

A recursive CTE references itself — perfect for trees (categories, org charts, comment threads):

WITH RECURSIVE tree AS (
  SELECT id, parent_id, name, 0 AS depth FROM categories WHERE parent_id IS NULL
  UNION ALL
  SELECT c.id, c.parent_id, c.name, t.depth+1 FROM categories c JOIN tree t ON c.parent_id = t.id
) SELECT * FROM tree;

q: Explain ACID.
a:
• Atomicity: all statements in a transaction succeed or none do.
  • Consistency: the DB moves from one valid state to another (constraints hold).
  • Isolation: concurrent transactions don't see each other's half-done work.
  • Durability: once committed, data survives a crash (written to the redo log/WAL).

Laravel: DB::transaction(function () { ... }) commits, or rolls back on exception; add a second argument to retry on deadlock.

q: Explain transaction isolation levels and the problems they prevent.
a:
Problems: dirty read (see uncommitted data), non-repeatable read (same row changes between reads), phantom read (new rows appear in a range).

  • READ UNCOMMITTED: allows all three.
  • READ COMMITTED: no dirty reads (PostgreSQL default).
  • REPEATABLE READ: same rows stay the same (MySQL InnoDB default; InnoDB also prevents most phantoms using gap/next-key locks).
  • SERIALIZABLE: as if one at a time; slowest.

Implemented with MVCC: readers see a snapshot, so reads don't block writes.

q: Optimistic vs pessimistic locking?
a:
• Pessimistic: lock the row while you work — SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (Laravel lockForUpdate()). Safe for high contention (stock, balances); others wait.
  • Optimistic: no lock; keep a version column and update WHERE id=? AND version=?. If 0 rows changed, someone else won — retry or show a conflict. Great when conflicts are rare (editing a profile).

q: How do you optimise a slow query? What do you look for in EXPLAIN?
a:
Run EXPLAIN (or EXPLAIN ANALYZE in MySQL 8 / PostgreSQL). Look at:

  • type: ALL = full table scan (bad); ref/range/const are good.
  • key: which index was used (NULL = none).
  • rows: estimated rows scanned.
  • Extra: Using filesort, Using temporary are warning signs; Using index = covering index (great).

Fixes: add the right (composite) index, select only needed columns, avoid functions on indexed columns (WHERE DATE(created_at)=... → use a range), avoid leading wildcard LIKE '%x', paginate with keyset, and rewrite OR or correlated subqueries.

q: How do composite indexes work? What is the leftmost prefix rule?
a:
An index on (status, created_at) is sorted by status first, then by date within each status.

It can serve WHERE status=?, and WHERE status=? AND created_at > ?, and WHERE status=? ORDER BY created_at — but not WHERE created_at > ? alone (skips the leftmost column).

Rule of thumb: equality columns first, then the range/sort column. A range condition stops the use of later columns.

q: What is normalization? Explain 1NF, 2NF, 3NF. When do you denormalize?
a:
• 1NF: atomic values, no repeating groups (no "tags" comma lists).
  • 2NF: 1NF + no column depends on only part of a composite key.
  • 3NF: 2NF + no column depends on another non-key column (store city_id, not city name + postal code duplicated per user).

Denormalize for read performance: store orders_count on users, copy product name/price into order lines (you *want* a historical snapshot), reporting tables. Keep it in sync with events/jobs.

q: OFFSET pagination vs cursor/keyset pagination?
a:
LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000 makes the DB read and throw away 100,000 rows — slow on deep pages, and rows shift if new data arrives.

Keyset: WHERE id < :last_id ORDER BY id DESC LIMIT 20 uses the index directly — constant speed, stable. Can't jump to page 57.

Laravel: paginate() (offset + count), simplePaginate() (no count query), cursorPaginate() (keyset).

q: UNION vs UNION ALL? DELETE vs TRUNCATE vs DROP?
a:
UNION removes duplicates (extra sort/dedupe cost); UNION ALL keeps all rows — faster, use when duplicates are impossible or wanted.

  • DELETE: removes rows (can use WHERE), logged, fires triggers, can roll back.
  • TRUNCATE: removes all rows fast, resets auto-increment, DDL (implicit commit in MySQL).
  • DROP: removes the whole table structure.

q: What is a deadlock and how do you handle it?
a:
Two transactions each hold a lock the other needs, so both wait forever. The DB detects it and kills one (MySQL error 1213).

Prevent: always lock rows in the same order, keep transactions short, index the columns in WHERE so fewer rows are locked, avoid user interaction inside a transaction. Handle: retry — DB::transaction(fn() => ..., 3). Debug with SHOW ENGINE INNODB STATUS.

q: MySQL vs PostgreSQL — how would you choose?
a:
Both are excellent. MySQL: very common in PHP/Laravel hosting, simple replication, fast simple reads. PostgreSQL: richer SQL (CTEs, window functions, partial and expression indexes, strong JSONB with GIN indexes, arrays, pgvector for AI embeddings), stricter correctness, good for complex queries and analytics.

Choose by team skills, hosting, and features needed. Laravel 13 adds native vector search on PostgreSQL + pgvector.

q: CHAR vs VARCHAR vs TEXT; and why use DECIMAL for money?
a:
CHAR(n) fixed length (country codes), VARCHAR(n) variable up to n (can be indexed fully), TEXT for long content (limited indexing).

Money: never FLOAT/DOUBLE — binary floats can't represent 0.1 exactly. Use DECIMAL(12,2) or store integer minor units (paisa/cents) in BIGINT.

q: What is table partitioning?
a:
Splitting one big table into physical pieces by a key (range by month, list by region, hash) while still querying it as one table. Queries with the key in WHERE only scan relevant partitions (partition pruning), and dropping old data is instant (drop a partition).

Great for logs, events, IoT sensor data. Different from sharding, which spreads data across servers.

q: SQL vs NoSQL — when would you use MongoDB or Redis?
a:
SQL: structured data, relations, transactions, reporting — most business apps.

Document DB (MongoDB): flexible schema, nested documents read together, high write volume (logs, IoT readings, catalogs with varied attributes).

Key-value (Redis): caching, sessions, counters, queues, leaderboards.

Search (Elasticsearch/Meilisearch): full-text and faceted search. Time-series (Timescale, InfluxDB): metrics. Many systems use several ("polyglot persistence").

q: Write a query: top 3 products by revenue in each category.
a:
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT p.category_id, p.id, p.name, SUM(oi.qty * oi.price) AS revenue,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY p.category_id ORDER BY SUM(oi.qty*oi.price) DESC) AS rn
  FROM products p JOIN order_items oi ON oi.product_id = p.id
  GROUP BY p.category_id, p.id, p.name
) t WHERE rn <= 3;

q: What are read replicas and replication lag?
a:
The primary handles writes; replicas copy its changes (binlog in MySQL) and serve reads. Lag = replicas are a few ms–seconds behind, so a user may not see what they just saved.

Laravel: 'read' => [...hosts], 'write' => [...], 'sticky' => true — after a write in a request, reads in that request go to the primary.

q: How do you prevent SQL injection?
a:
Use prepared statements with bound parameters — the query and data are sent separately, so input can't change the SQL. Eloquent and the query builder do this.

Danger zones in Laravel: DB::raw(), whereRaw(), orderByRaw() with user input, and dynamic column names — whitelist column/sort values. Also use least-privilege DB users.

q: What's new in PHP 8.x that you actually use?
a:
• 8.0: named arguments, union types, match, nullsafe ?->, constructor property promotion, attributes, JIT.
  • 8.1: enums, readonly properties, first-class callables strlen(...), never type, fibers.
  • 8.2: readonly classes, DNF types, deprecated dynamic properties.
  • 8.3: typed class constants, #[\Override], json_validate().
  • 8.4: property hooks (get/set on properties), asymmetric visibility (public private(set)), new without parentheses in chains, array_find().
  • 8.5 (Nov 2025): the pipe operator |>.

Laravel 13 requires PHP 8.3+.

q: == vs === in PHP? And what changed in PHP 8 comparisons?
a:
== compares after type juggling; === compares value and type. Always prefer ===.

PHP 8 made string-number comparison saner: 0 == "foo" is now false (it was true in PHP 7), because a non-numeric string is compared as a string.

Common trap

in_array('1abc', [1]) is loose by default — pass true as the third argument for strict checks.

q: In PHP, how do interfaces, abstract classes and traits differ in purpose and reuse?
a:
• Interface: a contract — method signatures only (plus constants). A class can implement many.
  • Abstract class: partial implementation + abstract methods; can hold state; a class extends only one.
  • Trait: reusable methods copied into classes (horizontal reuse); no "is-a" relationship.

Use interfaces for dependencies (DI), abstract classes for shared base behaviour, traits for small cross-cutting helpers (HasUuids, SoftDeletes).

q: self vs static vs \$this? What is late static binding?
a:
$this = the current object. self:: = the class where the code is written. static:: = the class that was called at runtime (late static binding).

class Model { public static function create() { return new static(); } }
class User extends Model {}
User::create(); // returns User, not Model

Eloquent relies on this heavily.

q: What are PHP magic methods? Which does Laravel use?
a: __construct, __destruct, __get/__set (Eloquent attributes), __call/__callStatic (Facades, query scopes, macros), __toString, __invoke (invokable controllers/actions), __serialize/__unserialize (queued jobs), __clone, __isset/__unset.

q: How do PHP enums work and where do you use them?
a:
enum OrderStatus: string {
  case Pending = 'pending'; case Paid = 'paid';
  public function label(): string { return ucfirst($this->value); }
}

Backed enums map to DB values; OrderStatus::from('paid') / tryFrom(). In Laravel cast them: protected function casts(): array { return ['status' => OrderStatus::class]; } and validate with Rule::enum(OrderStatus::class). They remove magic strings.

q: What are generators and why are they memory-efficient?
a:
A function with yield returns values one at a time instead of building a whole array, so memory stays flat.

function readRows($file) { $h = fopen($file,'r'); while (($r = fgetcsv($h)) !== false) yield $r; }

Laravel's LazyCollection, cursor() and lazy() use generators to process millions of rows.

q: What are PSR standards? Name the important ones.
a: PHP-FIG recommendations so libraries interoperate: PSR-1/12 (coding style, now PER-CS), PSR-4 (autoloading: namespace → folder), PSR-3 (logger), PSR-7 (HTTP messages), PSR-11 (container), PSR-15 (middleware), PSR-18 (HTTP client).

q: How does Composer autoloading work?
a:
composer.json maps namespaces to folders (PSR-4). Composer generates vendor/autoload.php, which registers spl_autoload_register: when an unknown class is used, it converts the namespace to a file path and requires it.

Production: composer install --no-dev --optimize-autoloader builds a classmap (no file-system lookups). composer.lock pins exact versions — always commit it for apps.

q: How do you handle errors and exceptions in modern PHP?
a: PHP 7+ throws Error (engine problems like TypeError) and Exception; both implement Throwable. Use custom exceptions for domain errors (InsufficientStockException), catch where you can recover, let the framework handler log and render the rest. Don't swallow exceptions silently. Laravel 11+: configure reporting/rendering in bootstrap/app.php with ->withExceptions().

q: How do you hash passwords in PHP?
a: password_hash($pwd, PASSWORD_DEFAULT) (bcrypt, or Argon2id with PASSWORD_ARGON2ID) and password_verify(). Salt is automatic. password_needs_rehash() upgrades old hashes on login. Never use md5/sha1. Laravel: Hash::make() and the hashed cast.

q: What are closures, arrow functions and first-class callables?
a: Closures are anonymous functions; they capture outer variables with use ($x). Arrow functions fn($x) => $x * $rate capture automatically by value and are one expression. First-class callable syntax (8.1): $fn = strtoupper(...); array_map($this->format(...), $items).

q: Explain the Laravel request lifecycle.
a:
public/index.php → autoload → bootstrap/app.php builds the Application → service providers register() then boot() → HTTP Kernel → global middleware → router matches route → route middleware (auth, throttle) → controller/closure (with DI) → response → back through middleware → sent → terminate callbacks.

In Laravel 11+ middleware, routing and exceptions are configured in bootstrap/app.php (no Kernel.php).

q: What are service providers? register() vs boot()?
a:
Service providers are where the app is bootstrapped: bindings, event listeners, routes, macros, gates.

register(): only bind things into the container — other services may not be loaded yet. boot(): runs after all providers are registered, so you can use any service (define gates, Model::preventLazyLoading(), view composers). Deferred providers load only when their service is needed.

q: What's new in Laravel 11, 12 and 13?
a:
• Laravel 11 (2024): slim skeleton — no Kernel files, config in bootstrap/app.php, fewer config files, casts() method, per-second rate limiting, Reverb, health route /up, SQLite default.
  • Laravel 12 (Feb 2025): mostly maintenance; new React/Vue/Livewire starter kits (shadcn, Flux, WorkOS option).
  • Laravel 13 (March 2026): requires PHP 8.3, PHP attributes for config (#[Table], #[Fillable], #[Hidden] on models, also jobs/commands), first-party AI SDK, JSON:API resources, vector search with pgvector. Focus on minimal breaking changes.

q: How do you solve the N+1 problem in Laravel?
a:
Eager load: Post::with(['author','comments.user'])->get(); load() after the fact; withCount('comments') for counts; loadMissing().

Detect: Model::preventLazyLoading(!app()->isProduction()) in AppServiceProvider::boot(), Laravel Debugbar/Telescope query counts. Limit columns: with('author:id,name').

q: Explain Eloquent relationships, including polymorphic.
a:
hasOne, belongsTo, hasMany, belongsToMany (pivot table, withPivot, withTimestamps), hasOneThrough, hasManyThrough.

Polymorphic: one model belongs to several types — comments with commentable_id + commentable_type attached to Post or Video (morphTo / morphMany). Many-to-many polymorphic: tags for posts and videos (morphToMany). Use Relation::enforceMorphMap() to store short aliases instead of class names.

q: How does Laravel handle authentication and authorisation?
a:
Authentication (who are you): guards (session, token) + providers. Starter kits / Fortify / Breeze for UI, Sanctum for SPA cookies and API tokens, Passport for full OAuth2, Socialite for social login.

Authorisation (can you do this): Gates (closures for simple checks) and Policies (per model: view, update, delete). Use $this->authorize('update', $post), @can in Blade, can: middleware, Gate::before for super-admins.

q: What is middleware? Give real examples you've written.
a:
Filters that wrap the request/response. Examples: auth, throttle, set locale from header, force JSON for API, tenant resolution from subdomain, log request timing, check subscription is active, add security headers.

Laravel 11+ register in bootstrap/app.php: ->withMiddleware(fn($m) => $m->alias([...])->append(...)).

q: How does validation work? FormRequest vs inline?
a: $request->validate([...]) for small cases. FormRequest classes for real apps: rules(), authorize(), messages(), prepareForValidation(), after() hooks — keeps controllers thin and reusable. Custom rules via Rule objects or closures; Rule::unique('users')->ignore($id), Rule::enum(), sometimes, required_if, exists. On failure: redirect back with errors, or JSON 422 for API requests.

q: How do you build a well-designed REST API in Laravel?
a:
• Route::apiResource(), versioning (/api/v1).
  • API Resources to shape JSON (hide internals, consistent format); Laravel 13 adds JSON:API resources.
  • FormRequests for validation, Policies for authorization, Sanctum for auth.
  • Correct status codes (201 created, 204 no content, 422 validation, 404, 429).
  • Pagination, filtering, sorting (spatie/laravel-query-builder).
  • Rate limiting, idempotency for POST payments, consistent error format.
  • Docs with Scribe / OpenAPI; feature tests for each endpoint.

q: When do you use queues? How do you handle failures?
a:
Anything slow or unreliable: emails, PDFs, image processing, external APIs, webhooks, imports. Keeps responses fast.

Failures: $tries, $backoff = [10, 60, 300], retryUntil(), failed() method for cleanup/alerts, failed_jobs table + queue:retry. Make jobs idempotent. Use ShouldBeUnique, WithoutOverlapping middleware, rate-limited job middleware. Monitor with Horizon (Redis). Use batches (Bus::batch) and chains for multi-step work.

q: How do you use caching in Laravel?
a:
Cache::remember('key', $ttl, fn() => ...), rememberForever, tags (Redis/Memcached) for group invalidation, Cache::lock() for atomic locks, Cache::flexible() for stale-while-revalidate. Invalidate in observers/events when data changes.

Also framework caches for deploy: config:cache, route:cache, view:cache, event:cache (or php artisan optimize).

q: Accessors, mutators and casts in modern Laravel?
a:
protected function fullName(): Attribute {
  return Attribute::make(get: fn() => "{$this->first} {$this->last}");
}
protected function casts(): array {
  return ['meta' => 'array', 'paid_at' => 'datetime', 'status' => OrderStatus::class, 'password' => 'hashed'];
}

Custom cast classes (CastsAttributes) for value objects like Money/Address. Laravel 13 lets you configure more with attributes.

q: How do you handle large datasets in Laravel without running out of memory?
a: chunk(1000) / chunkById(1000) (use chunkById when updating rows you iterate), lazy() / lazyById() / cursor() (generators), queue each chunk as a job, insert() in batches instead of create() in a loop, upsert() for sync jobs, select only needed columns, and LazyCollection for files.

q: Explain Laravel events, listeners and when to use them.
a: Events decouple "something happened" from "what to do": OrderPlaced → listeners SendConfirmation, NotifyWarehouse, AwardPoints. Listeners can be queued (ShouldQueue). Use ShouldDispatchAfterCommit so listeners don't run if the transaction rolls back. Laravel auto-discovers listeners by type-hint.

q: How do you test Laravel applications?
a: Pest or PHPUnit. Mostly feature tests hitting routes: $this->actingAs($user)->postJson('/api/orders', $data)->assertCreated(). RefreshDatabase, factories with states, assertDatabaseHas. Fakes: Queue::fake(), Mail::fake(), Event::fake(), Http::fake(), Storage::fake(), Notification::fake(). Unit tests for pure domain logic. Pest arch tests (arch()->expect('App\Models')->toExtend(Model::class)). Run in CI with parallel testing.

q: What are Laravel Pulse, Telescope, Horizon and Pint?
a:
• Telescope: local debugging — requests, queries, jobs, exceptions.
  • Pulse: lightweight production dashboard — slow queries, slow jobs, busy users, server stats.
  • Horizon: dashboard + config for Redis queues (workers, balancing, failed jobs, metrics).
  • Pint: code style fixer (PSR-12/Laravel preset).

Also: Sail (Docker dev), Herd (local dev), Forge/Vapor/Cloud (deploy), Nightwatch (monitoring).

q: What security features does Laravel give you, and what must you still do?
a:
Built-in: CSRF tokens, Blade {{ }} escaping (XSS), Eloquent bindings (SQL injection), bcrypt/argon hashing, encrypted & signed cookies, signed URLs, rate limiting, mass-assignment protection.

You must: authorise every action (Policies), validate input, never use {!! !!} with user content, avoid raw queries with input, keep APP_DEBUG=false in production, protect .env, rotate APP_KEY carefully, validate file uploads, set security headers, keep dependencies updated (composer audit).

q: Explain soft deletes, model events and global scopes.
a:
SoftDeletes sets deleted_at instead of deleting; queries exclude them automatically; withTrashed(), restore(), forceDelete().

Model events: creating/created/updating/updated/deleting/... via observers or booted().

Global scopes add constraints to every query (e.g. tenant or is_active) — remove with withoutGlobalScope(). Local scopes: scopeActive() or the #[Scope] attribute → Post::active().

q: What is Inertia.js and when would you pick it over an API + SPA?
a:
Inertia lets you build a React/Vue/Svelte SPA using normal Laravel routes and controllers — the controller returns Inertia::render('Orders/Index', $props) instead of a Blade view. No separate API, auth stays session-based, routing stays in Laravel.

Pick it when one team owns backend + frontend of a web app. Choose a separate API when you have mobile apps or third-party consumers. Inertia 2 adds deferred props, prefetching, polling and infinite scroll.

q: How do you deploy Laravel with zero downtime?
a: Release-folder strategy (Envoyer/Deployer/CI): build in a new folder → composer install --no-dev -o → build assets → php artisan migrate --force (backward-compatible migrations!) → optimize → switch the current symlink atomically → reload PHP-FPM → queue:restart / horizon:terminate. Keep storage and .env shared. For breaking schema changes use expand → migrate → contract across releases.

q: What is Livewire and when would you choose it over React/Vue?
a:
Livewire builds reactive UIs with PHP classes + Blade — no separate API or JS framework. Each interaction is an AJAX round-trip to the server, which re-renders and morphs the DOM.

Choose it for admin panels, dashboards, CRUD, forms, internal tools — especially when the team is PHP-strong (Filament is built on it). Choose React/Vue when you need heavy client-side interactivity (editors, drag-heavy canvases), offline behaviour, or a shared API with mobile apps.

q: What's new in Livewire 4 (released January 2026)?
a:
• Single-file components are the default (⚡counter.blade.php holds PHP + Blade + scoped <style>/<script>); multi-file (--mfc) and class-based (--class) still work.
  • Islands (@island / wire:island): regions that update independently without re-rendering the whole component.
  • @placeholder for lazy/deferred loading states.
  • Built-in drag-and-drop sorting (wire:sort), optimistic UI directives, wire:transition.
  • Parallel requests, the Blaze compiler for faster Blade, and a JS interceptor system.
  • v3 components keep working.

q: Explain the Livewire component lifecycle hooks.
a: mount() (once, on first render — like a constructor, receives parameters) → hydrate() (every subsequent request, after state restored) → updating($prop, $value) / updated($prop) (and updatedEmail() per property) → action method → rendering() / render() / rendered() → dehydrate() (before state sent back). boot() runs on every request, before mount/hydrate.

q: wire:model vs wire:model.live vs .blur vs .lazy?
a: In Livewire 3+ wire:model is deferred: the value syncs with the next action (e.g. submit) — fewer requests. wire:model.live sends on every input (add .debounce.300ms). .blur syncs when the field loses focus. .change on change. .lazy was the v2 name for blur-style behaviour.

q: What are the security pitfalls in Livewire?
a:
Public properties are visible and modifiable by the user (they travel in the snapshot). So:

  • Authorise inside every action ($this->authorize('update', $this->post)) — a hidden button isn't protection.
  • Lock IDs with #[Locked] so they can't be tampered with.
  • Validate input with #[Validate] or $this->validate().
  • Don't store secrets or large models' sensitive fields in public properties.
  • Model properties are safe-ish (only class + ID stored) but still re-check ownership.

q: How do Livewire components communicate?
a:
• Events: $this->dispatch('post-created', id: $id) and listen with #[On('post-created')]; ->to(Component::class) to target one; dispatch from Alpine/JS too.
  • Props: pass data down <livewire:item :post="$post" />; #[Reactive] to update the child when the parent changes.
  • wire:model on child with #[Modelable] for two-way binding.
  • $parent in the child view to call parent methods.

q: How do you optimise Livewire performance?
a: Keep public state small (IDs, not big collections); use #[Computed] properties (cached per request, persist: true across requests); wire:model deferred instead of .live; .debounce; lazy load heavy components (lazy + @placeholder); wire:key in loops; islands in v4 to avoid full re-renders; paginate; eager load relations in queries; use Alpine ($wire, x-data) for pure UI toggles that don't need the server; wire:poll sparingly.

q: In a Livewire 3 component, which UI interactions belong in Alpine.js and which belong in Livewire?
a: Alpine handles instant client-side behaviour (dropdowns, tabs, modals); Livewire handles server state. Inside a component, $wire is a JS proxy to the Livewire component: x-on:click="$wire.save()", x-model="$wire.title" or $wire.entangle('title') to share state. Livewire 3+ ships with Alpine bundled.

q: How do you handle file uploads in Livewire?
a: use WithFileUploads; and wire:model="photo". Files are uploaded to a temporary directory immediately (with progress events), validated ('photo' => 'image|max:2048'), previewed with temporaryUrl(), then stored with $this->photo->store('photos', 's3'). Supports direct-to-S3 temporary uploads. Temp files are cleaned up automatically after 24h.

q: What are form objects in Livewire 3+?
a:
A Livewire\Form class holds fields, validation rules and save logic so big components stay clean:

class PostForm extends Form {
  #[Validate('required|min:5')] public $title = '';
  public function store() { $this->validate(); Post::create($this->all()); }
}
// component: public PostForm $form;  view: wire:model="form.title"

q: What is Filament and how does it relate to Livewire?
a: Filament is an admin-panel / app framework built on Livewire + Alpine + Tailwind. It gives resources (CRUD) with forms, tables, filters, actions, relation managers, widgets, multi-tenancy and auth out of the box. Very common in Laravel job descriptions for back-office tools. Filament v4 (2025) improved performance and added nested resources and schema-based layouts.

q: How would you write a Livewire component test that validates input, calls an action and checks emitted events?
a:
Livewire::test(CreatePost::class)
  ->set('title', 'Hello')
  ->call('save')
  ->assertHasNoErrors()
  ->assertDispatched('post-created');

Also assertSee, assertSet, assertRedirect, actingAs(). Pest works the same way.

q: What are props vs state?
a: Props are inputs passed from the parent — read-only for the child. State is data the component owns and can change with a setter; changing state re-renders the component. If two siblings need the same data, lift state up to their common parent.

q: Explain useEffect — dependencies, cleanup, and common mistakes.
a:
useEffect(fn, deps) runs after render to sync with outside systems (subscriptions, timers, DOM APIs, fetching).

  • [] → after first mount only. [a, b] → when a or b change. No array → after every render.
  • Return a cleanup function to unsubscribe / clear timers / abort fetches.

Mistakes: missing deps (stale values), objects/functions in deps recreated every render (infinite loops), using effects to compute derived data (just compute during render), fetching without handling race conditions (use AbortController or a library like TanStack Query).

q: useMemo vs useCallback vs React.memo?
a:
• useMemo(() => compute(a), [a]) caches a value.
  • useCallback(fn, [deps]) caches a function reference.
  • React.memo(Component) skips re-rendering a component if props are shallow-equal.

They work together: memo on the child is useless if the parent passes a new function each render, so wrap it in useCallback. Don't add them everywhere — measure first. The React Compiler (stable in 2025) auto-memoizes, reducing the need for manual memo.

q: Why do lists need keys? Why not use the index?
a: Keys let React match items between renders. With the index as key, inserting/removing/reordering items makes React reuse the wrong DOM nodes and state (e.g. an input's typed text jumps to another row). Use a stable unique ID from data. Index is OK only for static lists that never change order.

q: What's new in React 19?
a: Actions (async functions in transitions, <form action={fn}>), useActionState, useFormStatus, useOptimistic, the use() hook to read promises/context, Server Components and Server Actions (via frameworks like Next.js), ref as a normal prop (no forwardRef), <title>/<meta> rendered anywhere, better hydration errors. React 19.2 added <Activity> and useEffectEvent. The React Compiler is a separate opt-in tool.

q: Server Components vs Client Components?
a:
Server Components render on the server only: can read the DB / secrets directly, send zero JS to the browser, but can't use state, effects or event handlers. Client Components ('use client') run in the browser and handle interactivity.

Pattern: server components fetch data and render layout; small client components for buttons, forms, charts. Default in Next.js App Router is server.

q: How do you manage state in a React app? Context vs Redux vs Zustand vs TanStack Query.
a:
Split by type of state:

  • Local UI state: useState / useReducer.
  • Server state (API data): TanStack Query or SWR — caching, refetching, loading/error states. This removes most "global state".
  • Shared client state: Context for rarely-changing values (theme, auth user); Zustand or Redux Toolkit for frequently updated, complex state (Context re-renders all consumers).
  • URL state: filters/pagination in query params.

q: In React forms, how do controlled and uncontrolled inputs differ, and when is each useful?
a: Controlled: input value comes from React state (value + onChange) — easy validation, more re-renders. Uncontrolled: DOM keeps the value, read with a ref or FormData. Libraries like React Hook Form use uncontrolled inputs for performance; React 19 form actions also work with FormData.

q: What are custom hooks? Give an example.
a:
Functions starting with use that reuse stateful logic between components.

function useDebounce(value, ms = 300) {
  const [v, setV] = useState(value);
  useEffect(() => { const t = setTimeout(() => setV(value), ms); return () => clearTimeout(t); }, [value, ms]);
  return v;
}

Rules of hooks: call at the top level only, only from components or other hooks.

q: How do you improve performance of a React app?
a: Measure with React DevTools Profiler first. Then: avoid unnecessary re-renders (state colocation, memo), virtualize long lists (TanStack Virtual), code-split routes (lazy + Suspense), useTransition/useDeferredValue for heavy updates, optimize images, reduce bundle size, cache server data (TanStack Query), SSR/RSC for faster first paint.

q: What are error boundaries?
a: Components that catch JavaScript errors in their child tree during rendering and show a fallback UI instead of a blank page. Must be class components (or use react-error-boundary). They don't catch errors in event handlers or async code — handle those with try/catch.

q: How do you connect a React SPA to a Laravel backend securely?
a: Same top-level domain SPA: Sanctum cookie auth — call /sanctum/csrf-cookie, then login; axios sends cookies with withCredentials/withXSRFToken. Configure SANCTUM_STATEFUL_DOMAINS, SESSION_DOMAIN, CORS supports_credentials. Mobile/third-party: Sanctum API tokens (Bearer). Or skip the API entirely with Inertia. Don't store tokens in localStorage if you can use httpOnly cookies (XSS risk).

q: What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
a: Passing props through many layers that don't use them. Fix with composition (pass components as children), Context for truly global values, or a state store. Don't reach for Context too early — composition often solves it.

q: var vs let vs const, and what is hoisting?
a: var is function-scoped and hoisted with value undefined. let/const are block-scoped and hoisted but in the temporal dead zone until declared (accessing throws). const can't be reassigned, but objects it holds can still change. Function declarations are hoisted fully.

q: What is a closure? Give a practical use.
a:
A function that remembers variables from the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.

function counter() { let n = 0; return () => ++n; }
const next = counter(); next(); next(); // 2

Uses: private state, debounce/throttle, factories, React hooks internally rely on closures (and "stale closure" bugs come from them).

q: Promises vs async/await; Promise.all vs allSettled vs race vs any?
a:
async/await is syntax on top of Promises — easier to read, use try/catch.

  • Promise.all: wait for all; rejects on the first failure.
  • Promise.allSettled: wait for all; gives each result/error.
  • Promise.race: first to settle (success or fail) — used for timeouts.
  • Promise.any: first to succeed.

Common trap

await inside a for loop runs requests one by one; use Promise.all(items.map(fetchItem)) for parallel.

q: How does 'this' work in JavaScript?
a: Depends on how a function is called: method call → the object; plain call → undefined in strict mode (window otherwise); new → the new object; call/apply/bind → what you pass. Arrow functions don't have their own this — they use the surrounding one (why they're handy in callbacks).

q: For a search box and a scroll handler, when should you use debounce versus throttle?
a:
Debounce: run only after the user stops for X ms (search box, resize end). Throttle: run at most once every X ms while events keep firing (scroll, mousemove).

const debounce = (fn, ms) => { let t; return (...a) => { clearTimeout(t); t = setTimeout(() => fn(...a), ms); }; };

q: In JavaScript, what happens to nested object references after a shallow copy, and when is structuredClone appropriate?
a: Spread {...obj} / Object.assign copy only the top level; nested objects are still shared. Deep copy: structuredClone(obj) (modern, handles Dates/Maps), not JSON.parse(JSON.stringify()) (loses Dates, undefined, functions).

q: Why TypeScript? interface vs type?
a:
TS catches bugs at compile time, documents shapes, and makes refactoring safe.

interface — object shapes, can be extended and merged (declaration merging). type — can also express unions, intersections, tuples, mapped/conditional types. Common rule: interface for public object contracts, type for everything else.

q: What are generics and utility types in TypeScript?
a: Generics make reusable typed code: function first<T>(arr: T[]): T | undefined. Utility types: Partial<T>, Required<T>, Pick<T,'a'|'b'>, Omit<T,'id'>, Record<K,V>, ReturnType<typeof fn>, Awaited<T>. unknown is the safe version of any — you must narrow it before use.

q: == vs ===, and null vs undefined in JS?
a: === compares without type coercion — always prefer it. undefined = declared but not assigned / missing property; null = intentionally empty. ?? (nullish coalescing) only falls back for null/undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0 and ''.

q: Vue 3 Composition API vs Options API?
a: Options API groups code by option type (data, methods, computed). Composition API (<script setup>, ref, reactive, computed, watch) groups by feature, reuses logic via composables, and has better TypeScript support. Vue 3 reactivity uses Proxies. Pinia is the official store.

q: Image vs container vs volume vs network?
a:
• Image: read-only template (app + dependencies), built from a Dockerfile.
  • Container: a running instance of an image.
  • Volume: persistent storage outside the container's lifecycle (DB data).
  • Network: lets containers talk by service name (mysql:3306 inside compose).

q: Write a production Dockerfile for Laravel. What best practices do you follow?
a:
FROM composer:2 AS vendor
WORKDIR /app
COPY composer.json composer.lock ./
RUN composer install --no-dev --no-scripts --prefer-dist --optimize-autoloader

FROM node:22-alpine AS assets
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci
COPY . .
RUN npm run build

FROM php:8.4-fpm-alpine
RUN docker-php-ext-install pdo_mysql opcache
WORKDIR /var/www
COPY --from=vendor /app/vendor ./vendor
COPY . .
COPY --from=assets /app/public/build ./public/build
RUN chown -R www-data:www-data storage bootstrap/cache
USER www-data

Practices: multi-stage builds, small base images (alpine/slim), copy lock files first for layer caching, .dockerignore (.git, node_modules, .env), no secrets in images, non-root user, one process per container (nginx, php-fpm, queue worker, scheduler as separate services), pinned versions, health checks.

q: What is Docker Compose? Describe a Laravel compose setup.
a: A YAML file that defines multi-container apps and starts them with docker compose up -d. Laravel stack: app (php-fpm), nginx, mysql/postgres (with a named volume), redis, queue (same image, command php artisan queue:work), scheduler, mailpit. Use depends_on with healthchecks, env files, and bind-mount source code in dev only. Laravel Sail is a ready-made compose setup.

q: CMD vs ENTRYPOINT; COPY vs ADD; RUN?
a: RUN executes at build time and creates a layer. CMD is the default command at run time (easily overridden). ENTRYPOINT fixes the executable; CMD then supplies default args. COPY copies local files; ADD also extracts tar files and fetches URLs — prefer COPY unless you need that.

q: How do you reduce Docker image size and build time?
a: Multi-stage builds, alpine/slim/distroless bases, combine RUN commands and clean package caches in the same layer, .dockerignore, order instructions from least to most frequently changed (dependencies before source), BuildKit cache mounts (--mount=type=cache), composer install --no-dev.

q: How do you debug a container that keeps restarting?
a: docker ps -a (exit code), docker logs <c> / docker compose logs -f app, docker inspect (env, mounts, health), run the image with a shell docker run -it --entrypoint sh image, check exit code 137 (OOM killed — raise memory), permissions on storage/, missing env vars, the DB not ready yet (healthcheck + retry).

q: What is Kubernetes and when do you need it over Docker Compose?
a:
Kubernetes orchestrates containers across many machines: scheduling, self-healing (restarts failed pods), rolling deployments, autoscaling (HPA), service discovery, config/secrets. Core objects: Pod, Deployment, Service, Ingress, ConfigMap, Secret, HPA.

Compose is enough for one server or dev. Choose K8s (or a managed option like ECS, Cloud Run, Laravel Cloud) when you need multi-node scaling and high availability — but it adds a lot of operational complexity.

q: Describe a CI/CD pipeline you'd set up for a Laravel project.
a:
On every PR (GitHub Actions): checkout → setup PHP with cache → composer install → Pint/PHPStan (Larastan) → Pest tests (with MySQL/Redis services) → npm ci && npm run build → security audit (composer audit).

On merge to main: build Docker image, tag with commit SHA, push to registry → deploy to staging → smoke tests → manual approval → production (zero-downtime) → run migrations → restart queues → notify Slack. Secrets in GitHub Secrets / OIDC to AWS, never in the repo.

q: Blue-green vs canary vs rolling deployment?
a:
• Rolling: replace servers/pods a few at a time.
  • Blue-green: run the new version (green) next to the old (blue), switch traffic at once; instant rollback by switching back.
  • Canary: send a small % of traffic to the new version, watch metrics, then increase.

Feature flags (Laravel Pennant) separate deploy from release.

q: Which AWS services would you use to host a Laravel app?
a: EC2 or ECS/Fargate (compute) or Lambda via Vapor; RDS (MySQL/Postgres); ElastiCache (Redis); S3 (files) + CloudFront (CDN); SQS (queues); SES (email); ALB (load balancer); Route 53 (DNS); ACM (SSL); CloudWatch (logs/metrics); Secrets Manager; IAM roles with least privilege; VPC with private subnets for DB/Redis.

q: Linux commands you use for debugging servers?
a: top/htop (CPU/mem), df -h / du -sh * (disk), free -m, tail -f storage/logs/laravel.log, journalctl -u php8.4-fpm, systemctl status nginx, ss -tulpn (ports), ps aux | grep queue, grep -R, chmod/chown for storage permissions, crontab -e, curl -I to test endpoints, supervisorctl status for queue workers.

q: What does Nginx do in a PHP stack? Key config points.
a: Reverse proxy and web server: serves static files, TLS, gzip/brotli, forwards PHP to PHP-FPM, load balances. Key Laravel config: root /var/www/public;, try_files $uri $uri/ /index.php?$query_string;, fastcgi_pass unix:/run/php/php-fpm.sock;, deny access to hidden files (location ~ /\.), long cache headers for /build/ assets, client_max_body_size for uploads.

q: How do you monitor a production application?
a: The three pillars: logs (structured JSON, central — CloudWatch, ELK, Loki), metrics (response time p95/p99, error rate, queue length, CPU/memory — Prometheus/Grafana, Pulse), traces (OpenTelemetry, APM). Error tracking (Sentry, Flare, Nightwatch). Uptime checks, alerts tied to SLOs, and on-call runbooks.

q: git merge vs rebase? What branching strategy do you use?
a: Merge keeps history as it happened (merge commit); rebase replays your commits on top of the target for a linear history. Never rebase a shared/public branch. Strategies: trunk-based (short-lived branches, feature flags, frequent merges — best for CI/CD) or GitFlow (release/hotfix branches — heavier). Use PRs with reviews, squash merges, conventional commit messages.

q: In a Shopify theme, how do Liquid objects, tags and filters work together to render product data?
a:
Liquid is Shopify's template language.

  • Objects output data: {{ product.title }}.
  • Tags add logic: {% if product.available %}, {% for item in cart.items %}, {% render 'price', product: product %}.
  • Filters transform output: {{ product.price | money }}, {{ image | image_url: width: 600 | image_tag }}.

Liquid is rendered on Shopify's servers — no database access, only the objects Shopify provides.

q: What is Online Store 2.0? Sections, blocks and JSON templates.
a: OS 2.0 made themes modular: templates are JSON files that list sections; merchants can add/reorder sections on every page (not just home) in the theme editor. Sections have a {% schema %} defining settings and blocks (repeatable sub-items). App blocks let apps inject UI without editing theme code. Dawn/Horizon are Shopify's reference themes.

q: Metafields vs metaobjects?
a: Metafields add custom fields to existing resources (product care instructions, size chart, variant extra info) — typed (text, number, file, reference, JSON). Metaobjects are your own custom content types (e.g. "Designer" with name, bio, photo) that can be referenced and even get their own pages. Both are editable in admin and usable in Liquid and the APIs.

q: Admin API vs Storefront API? REST vs GraphQL?
a:
Admin API: back-office — products, orders, customers, inventory, fulfillment; needs app authentication and scopes. Storefront API: public, customer-facing data for headless stores (products, cart, checkout URL) with a storefront access token.

Shopify is GraphQL-first: REST Admin API is legacy, and new public apps must use GraphQL. GraphQL uses cost-based rate limits (calculated query points, leaky bucket) — check extensions.cost and use bulk operations for large exports.

q: How do you build a Shopify app? Explain the architecture.
a: Scaffold with Shopify CLI (shopify app init) — official template uses React Router (formerly Remix) + Polaris UI + App Bridge, embedded in the admin. Flow: merchant installs → OAuth / token exchange gives an access token with requested scopes → store sessions → call Admin GraphQL API → register webhooks → add extensions (theme app extensions, checkout UI extensions, Functions, admin actions). Billing via the Billing API. Mandatory GDPR webhooks: customers/data_request, customers/redact, shop/redact. Laravel alternative: kyon147/laravel-shopify package.

q: How do you handle Shopify webhooks reliably?
a: Verify the HMAC (X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256) with your app secret over the raw body; respond 200 quickly (within ~5 s) and push processing to a queue; make handlers idempotent using X-Shopify-Webhook-Id (Shopify retries and can send duplicates, and order isn't guaranteed); run a periodic reconciliation job in case a webhook is missed. Shopify retries failed deliveries for up to 48 hours before removing the subscription.

q: Shopify Scripts vs Shopify Functions?
a: Scripts (Ruby, Plus-only) customised discounts, shipping and payments at checkout — they are being retired in 2026. Shopify Functions replace them: small programs (Rust or JavaScript compiled to WebAssembly) that Shopify runs on its infrastructure for discounts, delivery/payment customisations, cart transforms (bundles), validation and order routing. They're deployed inside an app, fast (strict time limits), and configurable by merchants in admin.

q: What is Checkout Extensibility? Why was checkout.liquid removed?
a: checkout.liquid let Plus stores edit checkout HTML — risky for security, upgrades and Shop Pay. It's deprecated (checkout pages in 2024, thank-you/order-status in 2025). Now you customise via Checkout UI extensions (React-like components in defined slots), Functions for logic, branding API for styling, pixels for tracking. Safer and upgrade-proof, but less free-form.

q: What is Hydrogen and when would you go headless?
a:
Hydrogen is Shopify's React framework (built on React Router/Remix) for custom headless storefronts using the Storefront API, hosted on Oxygen (Shopify's edge hosting).

Go headless for fully custom UX, complex content integration (CMS), multi-brand/multi-app, or very specific performance needs. Costs: you rebuild things themes give for free (theme editor, many apps' storefront features), more dev effort. Most stores are better served by a good OS 2.0 theme.

q: How do you optimise a Shopify store's speed?
a: Audit apps (each can inject JS) and remove unused ones; use image_url with width + srcset and lazy loading; defer/async scripts; avoid big JS libraries (jQuery sliders); limit Liquid loops over large collections and nested for loops; use {% render %} not {% include %}; preload key fonts; use the Theme Inspector for Chrome to find slow Liquid; check Core Web Vitals in the Web Performance dashboard.

q: How do you implement a custom AJAX cart in Shopify?
a: Use the Cart AJAX API: POST /cart/add.js, /cart/change.js, /cart/update.js, GET /cart.js. Then re-render the cart drawer with the Section Rendering API (?sections=cart-drawer) so HTML stays in Liquid. Use routes.cart_add_url for locale-aware URLs. Cart attributes and line-item properties carry custom data (gift note, engraving).

q: How do you develop and deploy Shopify themes professionally?
a: Shopify CLI: shopify theme dev (local preview with hot reload), theme push/pull, theme check (linting). Keep the theme in Git, use the GitHub integration to connect a branch to a theme, work on unpublished themes, use theme-check in CI, and never edit the live theme directly. Settings JSON conflicts are common — merchants' editor changes write to settings_data.json and templates.

q: Shopify vs Shopify Plus — what extra does Plus give developers?
a: Plus: checkout customisation (UI extensions on information/shipping/payment steps), custom Functions in custom apps, Shopify Flow automation advanced features, Launchpad, B2B features, higher API limits, expansion stores, organisation admin, dedicated support. Many Functions are now also available on regular plans through public apps.

q: How do you sync a large product catalog with an ERP?
a: Use bulk operations (bulkOperationRunQuery / bulkOperationRunMutation with JSONL files) instead of thousands of single calls; respect GraphQL cost limits with a throttled queue; store mapping IDs (ERP SKU ↔ Shopify GID); use webhooks for Shopify→ERP changes and scheduled jobs for ERP→Shopify; make each sync idempotent and log failures for retry.

q: What are Shopify Markets?
a: Markets manage selling to multiple countries/regions from one store: local currencies and pricing (fixed or converted), languages/translations, domains or subfolders (/en-ae), duties and taxes, and region-specific product availability. In Liquid: localization, request.locale, cart.currency.

q: Explain WordPress hooks: actions vs filters.
a:
Hooks let you change WordPress without editing core.

  • Actions run code at a point: add_action('init', 'register_my_cpt');, do_action('my_event').
  • Filters modify and return a value: add_filter('the_title', fn($t) => strtoupper($t));, apply_filters().

Priority (default 10) controls order; the last argument is how many parameters the callback receives. remove_action/remove_filter need the same priority.

q: How does the WordPress request / template hierarchy work?
a: index.php → wp-blog-header.php → load core, plugins, theme (functions.php) → WP::main() parses the URL into query vars → WP_Query runs the main query → template_redirect → the template hierarchy picks the most specific file: e.g. for a product post single-product.php → single.php → singular.php → index.php; for a category category-shoes.php → category-{id}.php → category.php → archive.php → index.php. Block themes use HTML templates in /templates instead.

q: What are Custom Post Types and taxonomies?
a: CPTs are your own content types (Projects, Events) registered with register_post_type() on init; taxonomies (like categories/tags) group them — register_taxonomy(). Set show_in_rest => true for the block editor and REST API. Custom fields via post meta (get_post_meta) or ACF. Flush rewrite rules after registering (visit Permalinks settings).

q: How do you write a secure WordPress plugin?
a:
