ur.hook: گروپ کا MAX، نام کے لیے RANK برابر ایک۔
ur.key: GROUP BY department with MAX gives the top salary; to also get the name I rank rows per department and keep rank one.

q: Find employees whose salary is higher than their manager's salary.
a:
SELECT e.name AS employee, e.salary, m.name AS manager, m.salary AS manager_salary
FROM employees e
JOIN employees m ON e.manager_id = m.id
WHERE e.salary > m.salary;
  • A self join: the same table used twice with aliases — e for the employee, m for the manager.
  • e.manager_id = m.id connects each employee to their manager's row.
  • Employees with no manager (manager_id IS NULL) drop out of an inner join — correct here.

ru.q: Woh employees jin ki salary apne manager se zyada hai.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** ek hi table ko do dafa use karo — ek dafa employee ki tarah, ek dafa manager ki tarah. Isay **self join** kehte hain.
- `employees e` aur `employees m` — dono same table, bas naam (alias) alag.
- `ON e.manager_id = m.id` — har employee ko uske manager wali row se jor do.
- `WHERE e.salary > m.salary` — ab dono salaries saath hain, seedha compare karo.

**Misaal:** ek hi register se student aur uske monitor ko saath rakh kar dekhna ke kis ke marks zyada hain.
ru.hook: Same table do dafa: e aur m, manager_id = id.
ru.key: I self-join employees to itself, match manager_id to the manager's id, and compare the two salaries.

ur.q: وہ ملازمین جن کی تنخواہ اپنے manager سے زیادہ ہے۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** ایک ہی table کو دو بار استعمال کریں — ایک بار ملازم کے طور پر، ایک بار manager کے طور پر۔ اسے **self join** کہتے ہیں۔
- `employees e` اور `employees m` — دونوں ایک ہی table، بس نام (alias) الگ۔
- `ON e.manager_id = m.id` — ہر ملازم کو اس کے manager والی row سے جوڑ دیں۔
- `WHERE e.salary > m.salary` — اب دونوں تنخواہیں ساتھ ہیں، سیدھا موازنہ کریں۔

**مثال:** ایک ہی رجسٹر سے طالب علم اور اس کے مانیٹر کو ساتھ رکھ کر دیکھنا کہ کس کے نمبر زیادہ ہیں۔
ur.hook: ایک ہی table دو بار: e اور m، manager_id برابر id۔
ur.key: I self-join employees to itself, match manager_id to the manager's id, and compare the two salaries.

q: Show each order with the customer's name.
a:
SELECT o.id AS order_id, c.name AS customer, o.order_date, o.total
FROM orders o
INNER JOIN customers c ON c.id = o.customer_id;
  • INNER JOIN keeps only rows that match in both tables.
  • The join condition links the foreign key (orders.customer_id) to the primary key (customers.id).
  • Aliases (o, c) keep the query short and remove ambiguity when both tables have an id column.

ru.q: Har order ke saath customer ka naam dikhayein.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** do tables ko common column se jor do — yehi **JOIN** hai.
- `orders.customer_id` (foreign key) ko `customers.id` (primary key) se match karo.
- `INNER JOIN` sirf woh rows rakhta hai jin ka match **dono** tables mein ho.
- `o` aur `c` aliases hain — query chhoti ho jati hai aur `id` jaise same naam walay columns mein confusion nahi hota.

**Misaal:** order slip par sirf customer number likha hai; customer register se naam dekh kar saath likh dena.
ru.hook: Foreign key ko primary key se jorna = JOIN.
ru.key: I inner-join orders to customers on customer_id equals customers.id, so each order gets its customer's name.

ur.q: ہر order کے ساتھ customer کا نام دکھائیں۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** دو tables کو مشترک column سے جوڑیں — یہی **JOIN** ہے۔
- `orders.customer_id` (foreign key) کو `customers.id` (primary key) سے ملائیں۔
- `INNER JOIN` صرف وہ rows رکھتا ہے جن کا میل **دونوں** tables میں ہو۔
- `o` اور `c` aliases ہیں — query مختصر ہو جاتی ہے اور `id` جیسے ایک جیسے نام والے columns میں الجھن نہیں ہوتی۔

**مثال:** order کی پرچی پر صرف گاہک نمبر لکھا ہے؛ گاہکوں کے رجسٹر سے نام دیکھ کر ساتھ لکھ دینا۔
ur.hook: foreign key کو primary key سے جوڑنا ہی JOIN ہے۔
ur.key: I inner-join orders to customers on customer_id equals customers.id, so each order gets its customer's name.

q: Write a SQL query to return customers who have never placed an order, and explain the anti-join.
a:
SELECT c.id, c.name
FROM customers c
LEFT JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.id IS NULL;
  • LEFT JOIN keeps every customer; order columns are NULL when there is no match.
  • WHERE o.id IS NULL keeps exactly those with no orders.
  • Also correct: WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM orders o WHERE o.customer_id = c.id).
  • Avoid NOT IN (SELECT customer_id ...) — one NULL in the list makes it return nothing.

ru.q: Woh customers jinhon ne kabhi order nahi kiya.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** `LEFT JOIN` har customer ko rakhta hai, chahe order ho ya na ho.
- Jin ka order nahi, un ke order walay columns mein `NULL` aata hai.
- `WHERE o.id IS NULL` — bas wohi customers bachte hain jin ka koi order nahi.
- Doosra tareeqa: `NOT EXISTS`. `NOT IN` se bachein — list mein ek bhi `NULL` ho to result khaali aa sakta hai.

**Misaal:** saare members ki list ko attendance se milao; jin ke saamne attendance khaali hai woh kabhi aaye hi nahi.
ru.hook: LEFT JOIN + IS NULL = jin ka match nahi.
ru.key: I left-join customers to orders and keep rows where the order side is NULL; NOT EXISTS works too.

ur.q: وہ customers جنہوں نے کبھی order نہیں کیا۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** `LEFT JOIN` ہر customer کو رکھتا ہے، چاہے order ہو یا نہ ہو۔
- جن کا order نہیں، ان کے order والے columns میں `NULL` آتا ہے۔
- `WHERE o.id IS NULL` — بس وہی customers بچتے ہیں جن کا کوئی order نہیں۔
- دوسرا طریقہ: `NOT EXISTS`۔ `NOT IN` سے بچیں — فہرست میں ایک بھی `NULL` ہو تو نتیجہ خالی آ سکتا ہے۔

**مثال:** تمام ممبرز کی فہرست کو حاضری سے ملائیں؛ جن کے سامنے حاضری خالی ہے وہ کبھی آئے ہی نہیں۔
ur.hook: LEFT JOIN اور IS NULL — جن کا میل نہیں۔
ur.key: I left-join customers to orders and keep rows where the order side is NULL; NOT EXISTS works too.

q: Find customers who placed more than one order.
a:
SELECT c.id, c.name, COUNT(o.id) AS orders_count
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 1;

Join, group per customer, count the orders, and filter the groups with HAVING.

ru.q: Woh customers jinhon ne ek se zyada orders kiye.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** JOIN, GROUP BY aur HAVING — teeno ka combo.
- Customers ko orders se jorein.
- `GROUP BY c.id, c.name` — har customer ka ek group.
- `COUNT(o.id)` — har customer ke orders ginein.
- `HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 1` — sirf woh jin ke ek se zyada orders hain.

**Misaal:** dukaan ke register mein har gaahak ki entries gino, jo baar baar aaya ho us ka naam likho.
ru.hook: JOIN, GROUP BY, phir HAVING COUNT > 1.
ru.key: I join customers with orders, group per customer, count orders, and keep groups with HAVING count greater than one.

ur.q: وہ customers جنہوں نے ایک سے زیادہ orders کیے۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** JOIN، GROUP BY اور HAVING — تینوں کا ملاپ۔
- customers کو orders سے جوڑیں۔
- `GROUP BY c.id, c.name` — ہر customer کا ایک گروپ۔
- `COUNT(o.id)` — ہر customer کے orders گنیں۔
- `HAVING COUNT(o.id) > 1` — صرف وہ جن کے ایک سے زیادہ orders ہیں۔

**مثال:** دکان کے رجسٹر میں ہر گاہک کی entries گنیں، جو بار بار آیا ہو اس کا نام لکھیں۔
ur.hook: JOIN، GROUP BY، پھر HAVING COUNT ایک سے زیادہ۔
ur.key: I join customers with orders, group per customer, count orders, and keep groups with HAVING count greater than one.

q: Find the highest-spending customer, counting only delivered orders.
a:
SELECT c.name, SUM(o.total) AS total_spent
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE o.status = 'Delivered'
GROUP BY c.id, c.name
ORDER BY total_spent DESC
LIMIT 1;
  • WHERE removes pending/cancelled orders before grouping.
  • SUM per customer, sort high → low, LIMIT 1 keeps the top row.
  • Ties: LIMIT 1 hides them — use RANK() if two customers can share first place.

ru.q: Sab se zyada kharch karne wala customer — sirf delivered orders gin kar.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** pehle ghalat orders hatao, phir jama karo, phir top lo.
- `WHERE o.status = 'Delivered'` — pending aur cancelled grouping se **pehle** nikal jate hain.
- `GROUP BY` customer aur `SUM(o.total)` — har customer ka total kharcha.
- `ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1` — sab se upar wala, yaani sab se zyada kharch.
- Barabari (tie) ho to `LIMIT 1` ek ko chhupa deta hai — us waqt `RANK()` behtar hai.

**Misaal:** mahine ke aakhir mein sirf wusool shuda bills jama kar ke sab se bara gaahak dhoondna.
ru.hook: Filter, SUM, DESC, LIMIT 1.
ru.key: I filter delivered orders, sum totals per customer, sort descending and take the first row; for ties I'd use RANK.

ur.q: سب سے زیادہ خرچ کرنے والا customer — صرف delivered orders گن کر۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** پہلے غلط orders ہٹائیں، پھر جمع کریں، پھر سب سے اوپر والا لیں۔
- `WHERE o.status = 'Delivered'` — pending اور cancelled گروپ بننے سے **پہلے** نکل جاتے ہیں۔
- `GROUP BY` customer اور `SUM(o.total)` — ہر customer کا کل خرچ۔
- `ORDER BY total_spent DESC LIMIT 1` — سب سے اوپر والا، یعنی سب سے زیادہ خرچ۔
- برابری ہو تو `LIMIT 1` ایک کو چھپا دیتا ہے — اس وقت `RANK()` بہتر ہے۔

**مثال:** مہینے کے آخر میں صرف وصول شدہ بل جمع کر کے سب سے بڑا گاہک ڈھونڈنا۔
ur.hook: filter، پھر SUM، پھر DESC اور LIMIT ایک۔
ur.key: I filter delivered orders, sum totals per customer, sort descending and take the first row; for ties I'd use RANK.

q: A table has 100 million rows. You must remove all rows as fast as possible but keep the table. Which command?
a:
TRUNCATE TABLE big_table;

  • TRUNCATE (DDL): removes all rows at once by deallocating the data; keeps the structure, columns, keys and indexes; resets auto-increment; very fast.
  • DELETE (DML): removes rows one by one (can use WHERE), fires triggers, fully logged — very slow for 100M rows.
  • DROP: removes the whole table, structure included.

Caveats: TRUNCATE can't target some rows, may fail when foreign keys point at the table, and in MySQL it commits immediately (no rollback).

ru.q: 100 million rows walay table ke saare rows jaldi se jaldi hatane hain, magar table rehna chahiye. Kaunsi command?
ru.a:
**Jawab:** `TRUNCATE TABLE`.
- **TRUNCATE** (DDL): ek hi dafa mein saara data saaf, lekin table ka structure — columns, primary key, indexes — waisa hi rehta hai. Bohat tez.
- **DELETE** (DML): row by row delete karta hai, `WHERE` laga sakte hain, har row log hoti hai — 100 million par bohat slow.
- **DROP**: poora table hi khatam, structure samet.

**Misaal:** TRUNCATE yaani almari khaali karna, DELETE yaani ek ek cheez nikaalna, DROP yaani almari hi phaink dena.
ru.hook: TRUNCATE khaali, DELETE ek ek, DROP sab khatam.
ru.key: TRUNCATE, because it removes all rows at once while keeping the table structure; DELETE is row by row and DROP removes the table.

ur.q: سو ملین rows والے table کی تمام rows جلدی سے ہٹانی ہیں مگر table رہنا چاہیے۔ کون سی command؟
ur.a:
**جواب:** `TRUNCATE TABLE`۔
- **TRUNCATE** (DDL): ایک ہی بار میں سارا data صاف، لیکن table کا ڈھانچہ — columns، primary key، indexes — ویسا ہی رہتا ہے۔ بہت تیز۔
- **DELETE** (DML): row by row delete کرتا ہے، `WHERE` لگا سکتے ہیں، ہر row log ہوتی ہے — سو ملین پر بہت سست۔
- **DROP**: پورا table ہی ختم، ڈھانچے سمیت۔

**مثال:** TRUNCATE یعنی الماری خالی کرنا، DELETE یعنی ایک ایک چیز نکالنا، DROP یعنی الماری ہی پھینک دینا۔
ur.hook: TRUNCATE خالی، DELETE ایک ایک، DROP سب ختم۔
ur.key: TRUNCATE, because it removes all rows at once while keeping the table structure; DELETE is row by row and DROP removes the table.

q: A new intern should only be able to view the employees table, not change it. How do you do that?
a:
GRANT SELECT ON employees TO intern_user;
-- take it back later
REVOKE SELECT ON employees FROM intern_user;
  • GRANT/REVOKE are DCL (Data Control Language).
  • Give only SELECT — no INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE — the principle of least privilege.
  • For many users, create a role (CREATE ROLE readonly; GRANT SELECT ... TO readonly;) and assign the role instead of granting user by user.

ru.q: Naye intern ko sirf employees table dekhne ki ijazat ho, badalne ki nahi. Kaise?
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** sirf utni ijazat do jitni zaroori hai — *least privilege*.
- `GRANT SELECT ON employees TO intern_user;` — sirf parhne ki ijazat. INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE nahi.
- `REVOKE` se ijazat wapas le sakte hain.
- GRANT aur REVOKE **DCL** commands hain.
- Zyada logon ke liye **role** banao (jaise `readonly`), ijazat role ko do, aur role users ko de do — waqt bachta hai.

**Misaal:** college mein "student" role ko library card milta hai; har naye student ko alag se ijazat nahi deni parti.
ru.hook: Intern ko sirf SELECT — least privilege.
ru.key: I grant only SELECT on that table to the intern, ideally through a read-only role, following least privilege.

ur.q: نئے intern کو صرف employees table دیکھنے کی اجازت ہو، بدلنے کی نہیں۔ کیسے؟
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** صرف اتنی اجازت دیں جتنی ضروری ہے — *least privilege*۔
- `GRANT SELECT ON employees TO intern_user;` — صرف پڑھنے کی اجازت۔ INSERT، UPDATE، DELETE نہیں۔
- `REVOKE` سے اجازت واپس لی جا سکتی ہے۔
- GRANT اور REVOKE **DCL** commands ہیں۔
- زیادہ لوگوں کے لیے **role** بنائیں (جیسے `readonly`)، اجازت role کو دیں اور role صارفین کو دے دیں — وقت بچتا ہے۔

**مثال:** کالج میں "طالب علم" کے عہدے کو لائبریری کارڈ ملتا ہے؛ ہر نئے طالب علم کو الگ سے اجازت نہیں دینی پڑتی۔
ur.hook: intern کو صرف SELECT — کم سے کم اجازت۔
ur.key: I grant only SELECT on that table to the intern, ideally through a read-only role, following least privilege.

q: Why can't you use a column alias from SELECT inside WHERE? Explain SQL's logical execution order.
a:
SQL is written as SELECT … FROM … WHERE … but evaluated in this logical order: FROM/JOIN → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT

WHERE runs before SELECT, so an alias defined in SELECT doesn't exist yet:

-- fails
SELECT salary * 12 AS yearly FROM employees WHERE yearly > 1000000;
-- works
SELECT salary * 12 AS yearly FROM employees WHERE salary * 12 > 1000000;
-- or wrap it
SELECT * FROM (SELECT name, salary * 12 AS yearly FROM employees) t WHERE yearly > 1000000;

ORDER BY runs after SELECT, so it can use the alias.

ru.q: SELECT mein banaya alias WHERE mein kyun nahi chalta? SQL ka execution order samjhaein.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** SQL likhi kisi aur tarteeb se jati hai, chalti kisi aur tarteeb se.
- Chalne ki tarteeb: `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`.
- `WHERE` pehle chalta hai aur `SELECT` baad mein — is liye `WHERE` ke waqt alias abhi bana hi nahi.
- Hal: `WHERE` mein poora expression dobara likho, ya query ko subquery mein lapet do.
- `ORDER BY` `SELECT` ke baad chalta hai, is liye wahan alias chal jata hai.

**Misaal:** naam ki takhti tab lagti hai jab cheez tayyar ho jaye; us se pehle us naam se pukaaro to koi jawab nahi dega.
ru.hook: FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT.
ru.key: Because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, the alias doesn't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT so it can use it.

ur.q: SELECT میں بنایا گیا alias، WHERE میں کیوں نہیں چلتا؟ SQL کی execution ترتیب سمجھائیں۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** SQL لکھی کسی اور ترتیب سے جاتی ہے اور چلتی کسی اور ترتیب سے۔
- چلنے کی ترتیب: `FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY → LIMIT`۔
- `WHERE` پہلے چلتا ہے اور `SELECT` بعد میں — اس لیے `WHERE` کے وقت alias ابھی بنا ہی نہیں۔
- حل: `WHERE` میں پورا expression دوبارہ لکھیں، یا query کو subquery میں لپیٹ دیں۔
- `ORDER BY` چونکہ `SELECT` کے بعد چلتا ہے، وہاں alias چل جاتا ہے۔

**مثال:** نام کی تختی تب لگتی ہے جب چیز تیار ہو جائے؛ اس سے پہلے اس نام سے پکاریں گے تو کوئی جواب نہیں دے گا۔
ur.hook: FROM، WHERE، GROUP BY، HAVING، SELECT، ORDER BY، LIMIT۔
ur.key: Because WHERE is evaluated before SELECT, the alias doesn't exist yet; ORDER BY runs after SELECT so it can use it.

q: With duplicate salaries, how do ROW_NUMBER, RANK and DENSE_RANK behave?
a:
Salaries 95, 92, 92, 80 ordered high → low:

  • ROW_NUMBER → 1, 2, 3, 4 — always unique; ties get different numbers.
  • RANK → 1, 2, 2, 4 — ties share a rank, then a gap.
  • DENSE_RANK → 1, 2, 2, 3 — ties share a rank, no gap.

Use DENSE_RANK for "Nth highest salary", ROW_NUMBER for de-duplication and "latest row per group".

ru.q: Duplicate salaries hon to ROW_NUMBER, RANK aur DENSE_RANK kaise kaam karte hain?
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** farq sirf barabar values (ties) par nazar aata hai.
- Salaries: 95, 92, 92, 80.
- `ROW_NUMBER`: 1, 2, 3, 4 — hamesha alag number, tie ho tab bhi.
- `RANK`: 1, 2, 2, **4** — barabar walon ko same rank, phir beech mein **gap**.
- `DENSE_RANK`: 1, 2, 2, **3** — same rank, lekin **koi gap nahi**.
- Nth highest ke liye `DENSE_RANK`, duplicates hatane ke liye `ROW_NUMBER`.

**Misaal:** do bachay barabar second aayein — RANK agle ko fourth kahega, DENSE_RANK third.
ru.hook: ROW_NUMBER alag, RANK gap, DENSE_RANK no gap.
ru.key: ROW_NUMBER is always unique, RANK gives ties the same rank and then skips, DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps.

ur.q: ایک جیسی تنخواہیں ہوں تو ROW_NUMBER، RANK اور DENSE_RANK کیسے کام کرتے ہیں؟
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** فرق صرف برابر قدروں (ties) پر نظر آتا ہے۔
- تنخواہیں: 95، 92، 92، 80۔
- `ROW_NUMBER`: 1، 2، 3، 4 — ہمیشہ الگ نمبر، برابری ہو تب بھی۔
- `RANK`: 1، 2، 2، **4** — برابر والوں کو ایک ہی rank، پھر درمیان میں **خلا**۔
- `DENSE_RANK`: 1، 2، 2، **3** — ایک ہی rank، لیکن **کوئی خلا نہیں**۔
- Nth highest کے لیے `DENSE_RANK`، duplicates ہٹانے کے لیے `ROW_NUMBER`۔

**مثال:** دو طالب علم برابر دوسرے نمبر پر آئیں — RANK اگلے کو چوتھا کہے گا، DENSE_RANK تیسرا۔
ur.hook: ROW_NUMBER الگ، RANK میں خلا، DENSE_RANK میں خلا نہیں۔
ur.key: ROW_NUMBER is always unique, RANK gives ties the same rank and then skips, DENSE_RANK gives ties the same rank without gaps.

q: A column has duplicates and NULLs. What do COUNT(*), COUNT(email) and COUNT(DISTINCT email) return?
a:
Emails: a@x, b@x, a@x, NULL, c@x

  • COUNT(*) → 5 — counts rows, NULL included.
  • COUNT(email) → 4 — skips NULLs.
  • COUNT(DISTINCT email) → 3 — unique non-NULL values (a, b, c).

All aggregates except COUNT(*) ignore NULLs (SUM, AVG, MAX too) — so AVG divides by the non-NULL count.

ru.q: Column mein duplicates aur NULL hon to COUNT(*), COUNT(email) aur COUNT(DISTINCT email) kya denge?
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** `*` rows ginta hai, column wala NULL chhor deta hai, DISTINCT duplicates bhi.
- Emails: a, b, a, NULL, c.
- `COUNT(*)` = **5** — saari rows, NULL samet.
- `COUNT(email)` = **4** — NULL ko nahi ginta.
- `COUNT(DISTINCT email)` = **3** — sirf unique: a, b, c.
- Yaad rahe: `SUM`, `AVG`, `MAX` bhi NULL ko ignore karte hain.

**Misaal:** class mein paanch kursiyan (rows), ek khaali (NULL), do par ek hi naam — 5, 4, 3.
ru.hook: Star 5, column 4, distinct 3.
ru.key: COUNT star counts all rows, COUNT of a column skips NULLs, and COUNT DISTINCT counts unique non-NULL values.

ur.q: column میں duplicates اور NULL ہوں تو COUNT(*)، COUNT(email) اور COUNT(DISTINCT email) کیا دیں گے؟
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** `*` rows گنتا ہے، column والا NULL چھوڑ دیتا ہے، اور DISTINCT دہرائی گئی قدریں بھی۔
- Emails: a، b، a، NULL، c۔
- `COUNT(*)` = **5** — تمام rows، NULL سمیت۔
- `COUNT(email)` = **4** — NULL کو نہیں گنتا۔
- `COUNT(DISTINCT email)` = **3** — صرف منفرد: a، b، c۔
- یاد رہے: `SUM`، `AVG` اور `MAX` بھی NULL کو نظرانداز کرتے ہیں۔

**مثال:** کلاس میں پانچ کرسیاں (rows)، ایک خالی (NULL)، دو پر ایک ہی نام — 5، 4، 3۔
ur.hook: ستارہ پانچ، column چار، distinct تین۔
ur.key: COUNT star counts all rows, COUNT of a column skips NULLs, and COUNT DISTINCT counts unique non-NULL values.

q: Show a contact number: primary phone, else alternate, else emergency, else 'Not available'.
a:
SELECT name,
       COALESCE(primary_phone, alt_phone, emergency_phone, 'Not available') AS contact
FROM contacts;

COALESCE returns the first non-NULL argument, left to right. It works in MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and SQLite (IFNULL/ISNULL take only two arguments).

ru.q: Contact number dikhayein: pehle primary, woh na ho to alternate, phir emergency, warna 'Not available'.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** `COALESCE` baayen se daayen dekhta hai aur **pehli non-NULL value** utha leta hai.
- `COALESCE(primary_phone, alt_phone, emergency_phone, 'Not available')`.
- Primary hai to wohi. Primary NULL aur alternate hai to alternate. Dono NULL to emergency. Teeno NULL to 'Not available'.
- `IFNULL` sirf do values leta hai; `COALESCE` jitni chaho.

**Misaal:** kisi ko call karna ho: pehle ghar ka number, na lage to office, phir padosi — jo pehle mile.
ru.hook: COALESCE = pehli non-NULL value.
ru.key: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, so I list the phones in priority order and end with a default text.

ur.q: رابطہ نمبر دکھائیں: پہلے primary، وہ نہ ہو تو alternate، پھر emergency، ورنہ 'Not available'۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** `COALESCE` بائیں سے دائیں دیکھتا ہے اور **پہلی non-NULL قدر** اٹھا لیتا ہے۔
- `COALESCE(primary_phone, alt_phone, emergency_phone, 'Not available')`۔
- primary موجود ہے تو وہی۔ primary خالی اور alternate موجود ہے تو alternate۔ دونوں خالی تو emergency۔ تینوں خالی تو 'Not available'۔
- `IFNULL` صرف دو قدریں لیتا ہے؛ `COALESCE` جتنی چاہیں۔

**مثال:** کسی کو فون کرنا ہو: پہلے گھر کا نمبر، نہ لگے تو دفتر کا، پھر پڑوسی کا — جو پہلے مل جائے۔
ur.hook: COALESCE یعنی پہلی non-NULL قدر۔
ur.key: COALESCE returns the first non-NULL value, so I list the phones in priority order and end with a default text.

q: Find each user's previous login date.
a:
SELECT user_id, login_date,
       LAG(login_date) OVER (PARTITION BY user_id ORDER BY login_date) AS previous_login
FROM logins;
  • LAG() reads a value from the previous row of the window; LEAD() reads the next one.
  • PARTITION BY user_id restarts the window per user; ORDER BY login_date defines "previous".
  • The first login of each user gets NULL. Gap in days (SQLite): julianday(login_date) - julianday(previous_login).

ru.q: Har user ki pichli login date nikaalein.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** `LAG` pichli row ki value utha kar mojooda row ke saath rakh deta hai.
- `PARTITION BY user_id` — har user ki logins alag window mein.
- `ORDER BY login_date` — tarteeb se "pichli" ka matlab tay hota hai.
- Har user ki pehli login ke saamne `NULL` aata hai, kyun ke us se pehle kuch nahi.
- `LEAD` iska ulta hai — agli row.

**Misaal:** diary mein har din ke saath likhna ke pichli dafa gym kab gaye thay.
ru.hook: LAG pichli row, LEAD agli row.
ru.key: I use LAG over a window partitioned by user and ordered by login date; the first login of each user gets NULL.

ur.q: ہر user کی پچھلی login تاریخ نکالیں۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** `LAG` پچھلی row کی قدر اٹھا کر موجودہ row کے ساتھ رکھ دیتا ہے۔
- `PARTITION BY user_id` — ہر user کے logins الگ window میں۔
- `ORDER BY login_date` — ترتیب سے "پچھلی" کا مطلب طے ہوتا ہے۔
- ہر user کے پہلے login کے سامنے `NULL` آتا ہے، کیونکہ اس سے پہلے کچھ نہیں۔
- `LEAD` اس کا الٹ ہے — اگلی row۔

**مثال:** ڈائری میں ہر دن کے ساتھ لکھنا کہ پچھلی بار جم کب گئے تھے۔
ur.hook: LAG پچھلی row، LEAD اگلی row۔
ur.key: I use LAG over a window partitioned by user and ordered by login date; the first login of each user gets NULL.

q: Achievement % = achieved / target. Some targets are 0. How do you avoid a divide-by-zero error?
a:
SELECT rep, achieved, target,
       ROUND(100.0 * achieved / NULLIF(target, 0), 1) AS pct
FROM sales_targets;
  • NULLIF(target, 0) returns NULL when target is 0, and anything divided by NULL is NULL — no error.
  • Show a label instead: COALESCE(...) or CASE WHEN target = 0 THEN ... END.
  • Use 100.0 (not 100) so integer division doesn't round the result down to 0.

ru.q: Achievement % = achieved / target. Kuch targets 0 hain — divide by zero error se kaise bachein?
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** `NULLIF(target, 0)` — agar target 0 ho to use `NULL` bana do.
- Kisi bhi cheez ko `NULL` se divide karo to jawab `NULL` aata hai — error nahi.
- Is tarah query chalti rehti hai aur zero target walon ke saamne khaali value aati hai.
- Label chahiye to `COALESCE` ya `CASE WHEN target = 0 THEN ...` laga lo.
- `100.0` likho, `100` nahi — warna integer division result ko 0 kar sakta hai.

**Misaal:** jis salesman ka target hi nahi diya gaya, us ka percentage "maloom nahi" likho, calculator crash na karo.
ru.hook: Zero ko NULL banao: NULLIF(target, 0).
ru.key: I divide by NULLIF(target, 0), which turns zero into NULL, so the result is NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error.

ur.q: کامیابی کا فیصد = achieved تقسیم target۔ کچھ targets صفر ہیں — divide by zero error سے کیسے بچیں؟
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** `NULLIF(target, 0)` — اگر target صفر ہو تو اسے `NULL` بنا دیں۔
- کسی بھی چیز کو `NULL` سے تقسیم کریں تو جواب `NULL` آتا ہے — error نہیں۔
- یوں query چلتی رہتی ہے اور صفر target والوں کے سامنے خالی قدر آتی ہے۔
- لیبل چاہیے تو `COALESCE` یا `CASE WHEN target = 0 THEN ...` لگا لیں۔
- `100.0` لکھیں، `100` نہیں — ورنہ integer division نتیجے کو صفر کر سکتی ہے۔

**مثال:** جس salesman کو target ہی نہیں دیا گیا، اس کے فیصد کی جگہ "معلوم نہیں" لکھیں، calculator کو crash نہ ہونے دیں۔
ur.hook: صفر کو NULL بناؤ: NULLIF۔
ur.key: I divide by NULLIF(target, 0), which turns zero into NULL, so the result is NULL instead of a divide-by-zero error.

q: Delete duplicate customer records, keeping only the latest one for each customer.
a:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT id,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC) AS rn
  FROM customer_record
)
DELETE FROM customer_record
WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1);
  • WITH ranked AS (...) is a CTE — a named temporary result.
  • ROW_NUMBER() numbers each customer's rows newest first, so rn = 1 is the latest.
  • Delete everything with rn > 1. Run the SELECT first to check, do it inside a transaction, then add a UNIQUE constraint so duplicates can't return.

ru.q: Duplicate customer records delete karein, har customer ka sirf latest record rakhein.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** har customer ki rows ko number do (naya pehle), phir 1 ke ilawa sab delete.
- `WITH ranked AS (...)` — **CTE**, yaani ek aarzi naam wala result.
- `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` — har customer ki rows alag, sab se nayi ko number 1.
- `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1)` — purani copies saaf.
- Pehle SELECT chala kar check karo, transaction mein karo, aur baad mein UNIQUE constraint lagao.

**Misaal:** phone mein ek hi dost ke teen contacts hon — sab se naya rakho, baaqi delete.
ru.hook: ROW_NUMBER naya pehle, rn > 1 delete.
ru.key: I number each customer's rows newest-first with ROW_NUMBER in a CTE and delete rows where the number is greater than one.

ur.q: duplicate customer records حذف کریں، ہر customer کا صرف تازہ ترین record رکھیں۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** ہر customer کی rows کو نمبر دیں (نیا پہلے)، پھر ایک کے سوا سب delete۔
- `WITH ranked AS (...)` — **CTE**، یعنی ایک عارضی نام والا نتیجہ۔
- `ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY customer_id ORDER BY updated_at DESC)` — ہر customer کی rows الگ، سب سے نئی کو نمبر ایک۔
- `DELETE ... WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM ranked WHERE rn > 1)` — پرانی نقلیں صاف۔
- پہلے SELECT چلا کر جانچ لیں، transaction میں کریں، اور بعد میں UNIQUE constraint لگائیں۔

**مثال:** فون میں ایک ہی دوست کے تین contacts ہوں — سب سے نیا رکھیں، باقی delete کر دیں۔
ur.hook: ROW_NUMBER نیا پہلے، ایک سے بڑے delete۔
ur.key: I number each customer's rows newest-first with ROW_NUMBER in a CTE and delete rows where the number is greater than one.

q: What are DDL, DML, DCL and TCL? Give examples.
a:
• DDL (Data Definition): defines structure — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE, RENAME.
  • DML (Data Manipulation): changes data — INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE (and SELECT, often grouped as DQL).
  • DCL (Data Control): permissions — GRANT, REVOKE.
  • TCL (Transaction Control): COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT, BEGIN.

In MySQL, DDL statements commit automatically — you can't roll them back.

ru.q: DDL, DML, DCL aur TCL kya hain? Misaalen dein.
ru.a:
**Asal baat:** SQL commands chaar khaanon mein bat'te hain.
- **DDL** — structure: `CREATE`, `ALTER`, `DROP`, `TRUNCATE`. Ghar ka naqsha.
- **DML** — data: `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, aur `SELECT`. Ghar ka samaan.
- **DCL** — ijazat: `GRANT`, `REVOKE`. Ghar ki chaabiyan.
- **TCL** — transaction: `COMMIT` (pakka karo), `ROLLBACK` (wapas lo), `SAVEPOINT`.
- MySQL mein DDL khud commit ho jata hai — rollback nahi hota.

**Misaal:** naqsha (DDL), samaan (DML), chaabi (DCL), aur save ya undo (TCL).
ru.hook: Naqsha DDL, samaan DML, chaabi DCL, save/undo TCL.
ru.key: DDL defines structure, DML changes data, DCL controls permissions, and TCL controls transactions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

ur.q: DDL، DML، DCL اور TCL کیا ہیں؟ مثالیں دیں۔
ur.a:
**اصل بات:** SQL کی commands چار خانوں میں تقسیم ہوتی ہیں۔
- **DDL** — ڈھانچہ: `CREATE`، `ALTER`، `DROP`، `TRUNCATE`۔ گھر کا نقشہ۔
- **DML** — data: `INSERT`، `UPDATE`، `DELETE`، اور `SELECT`۔ گھر کا سامان۔
- **DCL** — اجازت: `GRANT`، `REVOKE`۔ گھر کی چابیاں۔
- **TCL** — transaction: `COMMIT` (پکا کریں)، `ROLLBACK` (واپس لیں)، `SAVEPOINT`۔
- MySQL میں DDL خود بخود commit ہو جاتا ہے — rollback نہیں ہوتا۔

**مثال:** نقشہ (DDL)، سامان (DML)، چابی (DCL)، اور محفوظ کرنا یا واپس لینا (TCL)۔
ur.hook: نقشہ DDL، سامان DML، چابی DCL، محفوظ یا واپس TCL۔
ur.key: DDL defines structure, DML changes data, DCL controls permissions, and TCL controls transactions with COMMIT and ROLLBACK.

q: What are tokens and the context window, and why do they matter for cost and design?
a:
• A token is roughly ¾ of an English word; code and non-English text often use more tokens per word.
  • You pay per input + output tokens, and latency grows with output length.
  • The context window is the maximum tokens per request. Long chats, big documents and tool results all compete for it.
  • Design impact: send only relevant chunks (RAG), summarise old conversation turns, cap output length, and cache repeated prefixes (prompt caching) where the provider supports it.

q: What are embeddings and how does vector search work?
a:
An embedding is a vector (e.g. 1,024 numbers) that represents the meaning of a text. Similar meanings → vectors close together.

1. Split documents into chunks, embed each chunk, store vector + text + metadata. 2. Embed the user's question. 3. Find the nearest vectors by cosine similarity (or dot product). 4. For speed at scale, use an ANN index (e.g. HNSW, IVF) instead of comparing with every row.

Storage options: pgvector in PostgreSQL (simple, one database, supported by Laravel 13's vector search), or dedicated stores like Qdrant, Weaviate, Pinecone for very large or high-QPS workloads.

Common trap

Vector search finds *similar*, not *exact*. For IDs, SKUs and error codes combine it with keyword search (hybrid search).

q: Explain RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation) end to end.
a:
RAG = fetch relevant facts first, then let the LLM answer using them.

Indexing (offline): load docs → clean → chunk (e.g. 300–800 tokens with small overlap, split on headings) → embed → store with metadata (source, date, tenant, permissions).

Query (online): rewrite the question if needed → embed → retrieve top-k (vector + keyword hybrid) → filter by permissions/tenant → optional rerank → build a prompt: instructions + retrieved chunks + question → generate an answer with citations.

Quality levers: chunking strategy, metadata filters, reranking, "answer only from the context, say I don't know otherwise", and evaluation on a test set.

Cross-questionThe answers are wrong even though the document exists. Where do you look first?

Retrieval. Log which chunks were retrieved: usually the chunk was split badly, the query wording differs (add hybrid search/query rewriting), or a filter excluded it. Fix retrieval before touching the prompt.

q: RAG vs fine-tuning vs just using a long context — how do you choose?
a:
• RAG: knowledge that changes, is large, private or needs citations and permissions. Cheapest way to add facts.
  • Long context: small, fixed set of documents per request; simplest, but cost and latency grow with size.
  • Fine-tuning: teach behaviour or format (tone, a strict output style, a narrow classification task), or make a small model match a big one on one task. Poor at adding fresh facts and needs retraining when data changes.

Common answer: "Start with good prompting + RAG, measure, and fine-tune only if evals show a consistent style/format gap."

q: How do you reduce hallucinations in an LLM feature?
a:
• Ground it: RAG with the right chunks; instruct "answer only from the provided context; if missing, say you don't know".
  • Ask for citations (chunk IDs) and verify them in code.
  • Constrain output: structured JSON with a schema, enums instead of free text, validation + retry.
  • Lower temperature for factual tasks.
  • Let it think before answering on complex reasoning, but only show the final answer.
  • Check with code: numbers, dates, SQL results, prices come from your system, not the model.
  • Evaluate: a test set of real questions with expected answers, run on every prompt change.

q: What prompt engineering techniques do you actually use?
a:
• Clear role and goal in the system prompt; say who the output is for.
  • Specific instructions: format, length, what to do when unsure.
  • Examples (few-shot) of good input → output, including edge cases.
  • Separate data from instructions with delimiters or XML-style tags, e.g. <document>…</document> — also helps against prompt injection.
  • Structured output: ask for JSON matching a schema and validate it.
  • Step-by-step reasoning for multi-step problems.
  • Iterate with evals, not by eye: change one thing, re-run the test set.

q: How do you get reliable structured output (JSON) from an LLM in production?
a:
• Use the provider's structured output / JSON schema / tool-calling feature when available — it constrains the output format.
  • Otherwise: give the exact schema and an example, ask for JSON only.
  • Validate in code (Laravel validator, Zod, JSON Schema). On failure, retry once with the validation error in the prompt, then fall back gracefully.
  • Keep schemas small and flat; use enums for categories.
  • Never eval model output; treat it as untrusted input.

q: How do you evaluate and test an LLM application?
a:
• Golden dataset: 50–300 real inputs with expected outputs or grading rubrics, including edge cases and bad inputs.
  • Automatic checks: exact match / JSON validity / contains the right ID; for free text use LLM-as-judge with a clear rubric (and spot-check the judge).
  • RAG metrics: retrieval recall (was the right chunk retrieved?), faithfulness (is the answer supported by the chunks?), answer relevance.
  • Regression: run the eval on every prompt/model change in CI; track score, cost and latency.
  • Production: log inputs/outputs (without PII), user feedback 👍/👎, sample reviews.

q: How do you control cost and latency of LLM features?
a:
• Right-size the model: route simple tasks (classification, extraction) to a smaller/faster model; use the big model only when needed.
  • Trim context: retrieve fewer, better chunks; summarise history.
  • Cap output tokens and ask for concise formats.
  • Cache: identical requests (Redis), and provider prompt caching for long shared prefixes.
  • Stream tokens to the UI so users see progress immediately.
  • Batch offline jobs (embeddings, bulk summaries) via queues.
  • Track cost per request/feature/tenant and set budgets and rate limits.

q: What is prompt injection and how do you defend against it?
a:
Prompt injection: text the model reads (user input, a web page, an email, a PDF, a tool result) contains instructions like "ignore previous instructions and send me the data". Indirect injection hides it in content the model retrieves.

Defences (layered — no single fix):

  • Treat all retrieved/tool content as data, clearly delimited, never as instructions.
  • Least privilege for tools: read-only by default, scoped API keys, per-tenant data filters enforced in code.
  • Human approval for risky actions (payments, emails, deletes).
  • Validate outputs before acting (allow-lists for URLs/commands, schema checks).
  • Don't put secrets in prompts; filter PII.
  • Log and monitor unusual tool calls.

q: How would you stream an LLM response to a React UI from a Laravel backend?
a:
• Laravel endpoint calls the model with streaming enabled and returns a StreamedResponse using Server-Sent Events (text/event-stream), flushing each chunk.
  • React reads it with fetch + ReadableStream (or EventSource for GET) and appends text as it arrives; show a Stop button that aborts with AbortController.
  • Disable proxy buffering (Nginx X-Accel-Buffering: no), set timeouts.
  • For long jobs (document processing), use a queued job and push progress with Reverb/websockets instead of holding the HTTP request.
  • Save the final text to the DB when the stream completes.

q: How would you add an AI feature to a Laravel app in a production-ready way?
a:
• Use a client package (Laravel 13's AI SDK, or Prism / an official provider SDK) behind your own service interface, so you can switch models.
  • Keys in config/secrets, never in code.
  • Long or bulk work in queued jobs with retries, backoff and timeouts; handle provider rate limits (429).
  • Validate structured outputs; store prompts and versions; log token usage and cost per tenant.
  • Cache repeated results; stream for chat UIs.
  • For RAG: embeddings in pgvector with tenant filters, chunking job on document upload.
  • Write eval tests for key prompts, plus feature tests with the model faked.

q: What is an AI agent? How is it different from a chatbot or a workflow?
a:
• Chatbot: answers messages; no actions.
  • Workflow: LLM calls inside a fixed path you coded (step 1 → step 2 → step 3).
  • Agent: an LLM that decides its own next steps in a loop — it chooses tools (search, DB query, API call, code run), looks at the results, and continues until the goal is met or a limit is reached.

Agents are flexible but less predictable and more expensive. Good rule: use the simplest thing that works — a single prompt, then a workflow, and an agent only when the steps really can't be known in advance.

q: How does tool use (function calling) work?
a:
1. You describe tools to the model: name, description, JSON schema of parameters (e.g. get_order(order_id)). 2. The model replies with a tool call (tool name + JSON arguments) instead of plain text. 3. Your code validates the arguments, runs the function, and sends the result back as a tool-result message. 4. The model uses the result to answer or call another tool.

The model never executes anything itself — your code does, so your code enforces permissions, validation and limits.

Common trap

Vague tool descriptions. Clear names, descriptions, examples and small focused tools matter as much as the prompt.

q: Explain the agent loop. How do you stop an agent from running forever?
a:
Loop: think → act (call a tool) → observe (read the result) → repeat until done (often called ReAct).

Stopping and control:

  • Max steps / max tokens / max time / max cost per task.
  • A clear definition of done in the prompt, and a finish tool or final-answer format.
  • Detect loops (same tool + same args repeated).
  • Checkpoints: save state so a failed step can resume.
  • Escalate to a human when confidence is low or limits are hit.

q: What common workflow/agent patterns do you know?
a:
• Prompt chaining: output of step 1 feeds step 2 (outline → draft → polish), with checks between steps.
  • Routing: classify the input, send it to a specialised prompt/model (billing vs technical support).
  • Parallelization: run independent subtasks at once, or run the same task several times and vote.
  • Orchestrator–workers: a planner breaks a task into subtasks and delegates them to workers, then combines results.
  • Evaluator–optimizer: one call generates, another critiques against criteria, loop until good enough.
  • Autonomous agent: open-ended loop with tools, for tasks with unpredictable steps.

q: What is MCP (Model Context Protocol)?
a:
MCP is an open protocol for connecting AI applications to external tools and data in a standard way.

  • An MCP server exposes tools (actions), resources (data to read) and prompts (templates) — e.g. a GitHub, database or Slack server.
  • An MCP client inside the AI app (IDE assistant, chat app, your own agent) discovers those capabilities and lets the model use them.
  • Benefit: build an integration once and use it from any MCP-compatible client, instead of custom glue per app.
  • Security still matters: least-privilege credentials, trusted servers only, approval for write actions — tool descriptions and results can carry prompt injection.

q: How do agents handle memory?
a:
• Short-term: the current context window (conversation + recent tool results). Keep it lean: summarise or drop old tool outputs.
  • Long-term: store facts, preferences and past results in a DB or vector store and retrieve them when relevant.
  • Working state: a task record (plan, completed steps, files) saved outside the model so work can resume.
  • Rules: store only what's useful, respect privacy/retention, and let users see or delete memories.

q: When would you use multiple agents instead of one?
a:
Use multiple agents when the task splits into independent parts that benefit from separate context or specialised instructions — e.g. research several sources in parallel, then a lead agent combines findings.

Costs: many more tokens, harder debugging, coordination errors, results passed between agents can lose detail.

Default: one agent with good tools (or a simple workflow). Move to multi-agent only when evals show one context can't hold the task or parallelism gives a clear speed/quality win.

q: An agent can take real actions (refunds, emails, DB changes). How do you make it safe?
a:
• Least privilege: separate tools for read vs write, scoped per tenant/user, rate-limited.
  • Human-in-the-loop approval for irreversible or high-value actions (refund > X, bulk email, deletes).
  • Idempotent tools with idempotency keys, so retries don't double-charge.
  • Validation & policy checks in code before executing (amount limits, allowed recipients).
  • Dry-run / preview mode showing what will happen.
  • Audit log of every tool call with inputs, outputs and who approved.
  • Sandbox code execution; no raw shell/SQL from the model on production.

q: How do you monitor and evaluate an agent in production?
a:
• Tracing: every step — prompt, tool call, arguments, result, tokens, latency — linked by a trace ID.
  • Task-level metrics: success rate, steps per task, cost per task, time to complete, escalation rate.
  • Step-level checks: invalid tool arguments, repeated calls, tool errors.
  • Evals: a suite of realistic tasks run on every prompt/model/tool change, graded by code and rubric.
  • Feedback loop: failed traces become new eval cases.

q: What is context engineering, and how do you manage the context window in long agent tasks?
a:
Context engineering = deciding exactly what goes into the model's context at each step (instructions, tools, retrieved data, history), because quality drops when the context is bloated or noisy.

Techniques:

  • Keep system instructions and tool descriptions short and clear.
  • Retrieve just-in-time (search/read files when needed) instead of loading everything up front.
  • Summarise/compact old history and trim large tool outputs (keep IDs and key facts).
  • Save notes/plans to external memory and re-read them.
  • Split big tasks across sub-agents with focused contexts and return only summaries.

q: Design an AI customer-support agent for an e-commerce store (Shopify/WooCommerce).
a:
Scope: answer product/policy questions, track orders, start returns; hand off to a human when needed.

  • Channels → API gateway → conversation service (Laravel) storing messages.
  • Knowledge: RAG over policies, FAQs, product catalogue (pgvector + keyword search), refreshed by webhooks when products change.
  • Tools: get_order(order_id, email), track_shipment, create_return_request (needs confirmation), handoff_to_human. Tools call Shopify/WooCommerce APIs with scoped tokens; the customer's identity is verified before any order data is shown.
  • Guardrails: refunds above a limit require staff approval; PII masked in logs; prompt-injection defences on retrieved content.
  • Reliability: queue long actions, timeouts, fallbacks, idempotent tools.
  • Quality: eval set of real tickets, CSAT, resolution rate, human-handoff rate, cost per conversation.

q: Design a 'chat with your company documents' feature for a multi-tenant SaaS.
a:
• Upload → store file (S3) → queued pipeline: extract text (PDF/DOCX/OCR) → clean → chunk by headings → embed → save in pgvector with tenant_id, doc_id, permissions, version.
  • Query: authenticate → embed question → hybrid search filtered by tenant and user permissions → rerank → prompt with chunks → stream answer with citations linking to the source page.
  • Updates/deletes: re-index on change; delete vectors when a document is removed (data retention).
  • Cost: cache embeddings by content hash; small model for query rewriting; limits per plan.
  • Quality: per-tenant eval questions, thumbs up/down, show "I couldn't find this in your documents" instead of guessing.

q: How do you use AI tools in your own development work?
a:
A balanced answer interviewers like:

  • I use AI assistants to explore unfamiliar APIs, draft boilerplate, write tests, and review diffs — it speeds me up.
  • I treat output like a junior's pull request: I read every line, run the tests, check security (SQL injection, auth), and verify against the docs.
  • I don't paste secrets or customer data into tools that aren't approved.
  • For bigger changes I give clear context (files, constraints, examples) and work in small steps.
  • Example: "I used an AI assistant to generate Pest tests for our billing module; it found two edge cases, and I fixed one hallucinated method name before merging."

q: What are the main risks of putting an LLM feature into production, and how do you mitigate them?
a:
• Wrong answers (hallucination) → grounding, citations, evals, "I don't know" behaviour.
  • Prompt injection / data leaks → least privilege, tenant filters in code, output validation.
  • Privacy → mask PII, data-processing agreements, retention limits, no training on customer data unless agreed.
  • Cost spikes → per-tenant budgets, rate limits, caching, smaller models.
  • Latency → streaming, async jobs, timeouts.
  • Provider outages / model changes → fallbacks, pinned model versions, regression evals before upgrading.
  • Bias/tone → review prompts and samples, clear escalation to humans.

q: What is the difference between var, let and const?
a:
var is function-scoped and hoisted (initialised as undefined). let and const are block-scoped and sit in the "temporal dead zone" until their line runs.

  • const stops re-assignment, not mutation: const a=[]; a.push(1) is fine.
  • Use const by default, let when the value changes, avoid var.
  • Classic bug: for (var i...) setTimeout(()=>log(i)) prints the last value; let creates a new i per iteration.

q: In what order do synchronous code, Promise callbacks and setTimeout callbacks execute in the JavaScript event loop?
a:
JS runs on one call stack. Async work (timers, network, I/O) is handled by the browser/Node, and its callbacks wait in queues.

  • Microtasks (Promise .then, await, queueMicrotask) run right after the current task, all of them.
  • Macrotasks (setTimeout, events, I/O) run one per loop turn.
console.log(1); setTimeout(()=>console.log(2)); Promise.resolve().then(()=>console.log(3)); console.log(4)
// 1 4 3 2

A long synchronous loop blocks everything — split work or use a Web Worker.

q: How can a JavaScript closure preserve private state after the outer function has returned?
a:
A closure is a function that remembers the variables of the scope where it was created, even after that scope has finished.

function counter(){ let n=0; return ()=>++n }
const next=counter(); next(); next(); // 2

Uses: private state, factories, memoisation, debounce/throttle, event handlers that need context. Watch out for closures holding big objects (memory leaks).

q: How is `this` determined for method calls, plain calls, constructors, bound functions and arrow functions?
a:
this depends on how a function is called, not where it is written.

  • Method call obj.fn() → obj.
  • Plain call fn() → undefined in strict mode (window in sloppy mode).
  • new Fn() → the new object. fn.call/apply/bind(x) → x.
  • Arrow functions have no own this; they use the outer one — perfect for callbacks inside class methods.

q: Promises vs async/await — how do you handle errors and run things in parallel?
a:
async/await is syntax over Promises. Wrap awaits in try/catch; an un-awaited rejected promise becomes an unhandled rejection.

  • Parallel: await Promise.all([a(), b()]) (fails fast), Promise.allSettled (get every result), Promise.race/any for timeouts or first success.
  • Don't await inside a loop when calls are independent — it makes them sequential.
const [user, orders] = await Promise.all([getUser(id), getOrders(id)])

q: What is the difference between == and ===?
a: === compares value and type with no conversion. == converts types first, which causes surprises: '' == 0 is true, null == undefined is true, '0' == false is true. Rule: always use ===; the only common exception is x == null to check null *or* undefined.

q: What are debounce and throttle? When do you use each?
a:
Both limit how often a function runs.

  • Debounce: run once *after* the events stop for N ms — search-as-you-type, auto-save, resize end.
  • Throttle: run at most once every N ms *during* the events — scroll position, drag, analytics pings.
const debounce=(fn,ms)=>{let t;return(...a)=>{clearTimeout(t);t=setTimeout(()=>fn(...a),ms)}}

q: How does prototypal inheritance work? How do ES6 classes relate to it?
a: Every object has a hidden link ([[Prototype]]) to another object. Property lookups walk this chain until found or null. ES6 class is syntax over the same mechanism: methods live on Class.prototype, extends links the prototypes, super calls the parent. So dog.bark() looks on dog, then Dog.prototype, then Animal.prototype.

q: ES Modules vs CommonJS — what is the difference?
a: CommonJS (require, module.exports) is Node's original system: synchronous, loaded at runtime. ES Modules (import/export) are the standard: static (tools can tree-shake unused code), async-friendly, work in browsers, support top-level await. In Node, ESM is enabled by "type": "module" or .mjs. Mixing them needs care: ESM can import CJS, CJS must use dynamic import() for ESM.

q: Explain destructuring, spread and rest with examples.
a:
• Destructuring pulls values out: const {name, email='n/a'} = user; const [first] = list.
  • Spread expands: {...user, role:'admin'} (shallow copy + override), [...a, ...b].
  • Rest collects the remainder: function sum(...nums){} or const {password, ...safe} = user to drop a field.

Remember spread copies are shallow — nested objects are still shared.

q: What are optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??)?
a:
a?.b?.c stops and returns undefined if a link is null/undefined, instead of throwing. Works with calls too: cb?.(). x ?? 'default' uses the default only for null/undefined, unlike || which also replaces 0, '' and false.

const qty = order?.items?.[0]?.qty ?? 1

q: How do you deep copy an object in JavaScript?
a:
Use structuredClone(obj) — built in, handles Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references (not functions or DOM nodes).

  • JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) loses Dates, undefined, Map/Set and fails on cycles.
  • Spread/Object.assign are shallow only.
  • For immutable updates in React, copy just the path you change: {...s, user:{...s.user, name}}.

q: Map vs Object and Set vs Array — when to use which?
a: Map: any key type (objects too), keeps insertion order, has .size, fast frequent add/delete — good for caches and lookups. Object: fixed-shape records and JSON data. Set: unique values with fast has() — dedupe with [...new Set(arr)]. WeakMap/WeakSet: keys are held weakly, so metadata about objects doesn't cause memory leaks.

q: What causes memory leaks in JavaScript apps and how do you find them?
a: Common causes: event listeners never removed, setInterval never cleared, closures holding big data, global caches that only grow, detached DOM nodes still referenced, React effects without cleanup. Find them with Chrome DevTools › Memory: take heap snapshots before/after an action, compare, look for "Detached" nodes and growing retainers. Fix with cleanup functions, AbortController for listeners/fetch, WeakMap caches and size limits.

q: What is event delegation?
a: Instead of adding a listener to every child, add one listener on a parent and check event.target.closest(selector). Events bubble up, so the parent sees them. Benefits: fewer listeners, works for elements added later (lists, infinite scroll). Stop it with stopPropagation() only when you really need to.

q: fetch vs Axios — what are the differences?
a: fetch is built in; it does not reject on 4xx/5xx (check res.ok), you call res.json() yourself, and cancellation uses AbortController. Axios rejects on HTTP errors, parses JSON automatically, has interceptors (add auth token, refresh on 401), timeouts, upload progress and works the same in Node. Choose fetch for small apps/edge runtimes; Axios when you want interceptors and less boilerplate.

q: Why TypeScript? Explain interface vs type and generics.
a:
TypeScript catches bugs at compile time, documents shapes and makes refactoring safe.

  • interface describes object shapes and can be extended/merged; type can also express unions, intersections and mapped types. Both are fine for objects — be consistent.
  • Generics keep types flexible but checked: function first<T>(a:T[]):T|undefined.
  • Use unknown instead of any for untrusted data, then narrow it (for example with Zod).

q: How does Node.js handle thousands of connections on one thread?
a: Node uses a non-blocking event loop (libuv). Network I/O is handed to the OS; when data is ready, a callback is queued. One thread can juggle thousands of idle connections because it never waits. CPU-heavy work (image resize, big JSON, crypto) blocks the loop → use worker threads, a job queue, or another service. Scale across cores with multiple processes (PM2 cluster, containers).

q: Jest vs Vitest vs Playwright — what does each test?
a:
• Jest / Vitest: unit and component tests in Node (Vitest is Vite-native and faster in Vite projects; APIs are almost the same).
  • React Testing Library: test components the way users use them (by role/text).
  • Playwright / Cypress: end-to-end in real browsers — login, checkout, mobile viewports.

A healthy pyramid: many fast unit tests, some integration, few E2E on critical flows.

q: What are Web Workers and when would you use one?
a: A Web Worker runs JavaScript on a background thread, talking to the page with postMessage. It has no DOM access. Use it for CPU-heavy work that would freeze the UI: parsing big files, image processing, search indexing, encryption. Service Workers are different — they sit between the page and the network for caching/offline (PWA).

q: What makes an API RESTful?
a: REST treats data as resources with URLs (/orders/42) and uses HTTP methods for actions: GET read, POST create, PUT replace, PATCH partial update, DELETE remove. Key ideas: stateless requests (each carries its auth), standard status codes, cacheable GETs, consistent JSON shape. Use nouns, not verbs: POST /orders, not /createOrder.

q: Which HTTP status codes should an API use?
a:
• 200 OK, 201 Created (+ Location), 204 No Content.
  • 400 bad input, 401 not logged in, 403 logged in but not allowed, 404 not found, 409 conflict, 422 validation failed (Laravel default), 429 too many requests.
  • 500 server bug, 502/503/504 upstream/unavailable/timeout.

Always return a consistent error body so clients can show a message.

q: PUT vs PATCH — and what does idempotent mean?
a: Idempotent = sending the same request twice has the same effect as once. GET, PUT and DELETE are idempotent; POST is not. PUT replaces the whole resource; PATCH changes only the fields you send. For POST payments/orders, accept an Idempotency-Key header: store the key with the result and return the same result on retry, so a flaky network never charges twice.

q: How do you paginate an API? Offset vs cursor.
a: Offset (?page=3&per_page=20): simple, supports jumping to a page, but slow on big tables and items shift when rows are inserted. Cursor/keyset (?after=eyJpZCI6MTAwfQ): WHERE id > last_id ORDER BY id LIMIT 20 — fast on any size and stable; no page numbers. In Laravel: paginate(), simplePaginate(), cursorPaginate(). Return next/prev links or cursors in the response.

q: How do you version a REST API?
a: Most common: URL versioning /api/v1/... — obvious and easy to route/cache. Alternatives: a header (Accept: application/vnd.app.v2+json) or a query param. Rules: only bump for breaking changes; adding fields is not breaking. Keep old versions running with a deprecation date, Deprecation/Sunset headers and a changelog.

q: How do you secure a REST API?
a:
• HTTPS everywhere; auth with tokens (Sanctum, OAuth2/JWT) and short expiry.
  • Authorise every request (policies), not just authenticate — check the user owns the resource (avoid IDOR).
  • Validate input, return only needed fields (API Resources), rate-limit (throttle), CORS allow-list, no secrets in URLs, log and monitor 401/403 spikes.
  • Follow the OWASP API Top 10.

q: How do you add rate limiting to an API?
a: Limit requests per key (user ID, token or IP) in a time window and return 429 with Retry-After. Laravel: RateLimiter::for('api', fn($r)=>Limit::perMinute(60)->by($r->user()?->id ?: $r->ip())) and throttle:api middleware — counters live in Redis so all servers share them. Algorithms: fixed window (simple), sliding window, token bucket (allows short bursts).

q: How does browser CORS preflight work, and which server-side headers resolve a legitimate cross-origin request?
a: CORS is a browser rule: JavaScript on site A can only read responses from site B if B allows A with headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin. For non-simple requests (JSON body, custom headers) the browser first sends an OPTIONS preflight. Fix on the server: allow the exact frontend origins, methods and headers (Laravel config/cors.php). Never * together with cookies/credentials. Postman ignores CORS — that's why "it works in Postman".

q: How do ETags and caching headers help an API?
a:
• Cache-Control: max-age=60 lets clients/CDNs reuse a response.
  • ETag: a hash of the response. The client sends If-None-Match; if unchanged the server replies 304 Not Modified with no body — saves bandwidth.
  • ETags also enable safe updates: If-Match + 412 if someone else changed the resource (optimistic locking).

q: What is a consistent API error format? (RFC 9457 / Problem Details)
a:
Return the same JSON shape for every error so clients can handle it in one place:

{"type":"https://api.x.com/errors/validation","title":"Validation failed","status":422,"detail":"Email is invalid","errors":{"email":["The email must be valid."]}}

Include a machine-readable code, a human message and a request/trace ID. In Laravel customise the exception handler (withExceptions in bootstrap/app.php).

q: What are Laravel API Resources and why use them?
a:
JsonResource classes transform models into JSON: rename fields, hide columns, format dates, add links, include relations only when loaded (whenLoaded) — no accidental password leaks and a stable contract even if the table changes.

return OrderResource::collection(Order::with('items')->paginate());

Collections add pagination meta and links automatically.

q: What are OpenAPI (Swagger) and Postman used for?
a: OpenAPI is a YAML/JSON spec describing endpoints, params, schemas and auth. From it you get interactive docs (Swagger UI/Redoc), client SDKs, mock servers and contract tests. Laravel tools: Scribe, L5-Swagger, Scramble (auto-generates from code). Postman/Insomnia/Bruno: send requests, save collections, environments, automated tests and share with the team.

q: How would you design a public API used by thousands of third-party developers?
a:
• Clear resource design, versioning and a deprecation policy.
  • API keys/OAuth scopes per app, per-key rate limits and quotas.
  • Idempotency keys on writes, cursor pagination, webhooks for events.
  • OpenAPI docs, SDKs, sandbox environment, status page, changelog.
  • Observability: request IDs, per-client metrics, alerting; abuse detection.
  • Backward compatibility tests in CI.

q: REST vs GraphQL vs gRPC — when would you choose each?
a:
• REST: simple, cacheable, universal — default for public and CRUD APIs.
  • GraphQL: clients choose fields; one request for nested data — great for complex frontends/mobile with many screens.
  • gRPC: binary Protobuf over HTTP/2, fast, typed, streaming — internal service-to-service.

Many systems mix them: REST/GraphQL at the edge, gRPC or queues inside.

q: How should API authentication tokens be sent and stored?
a:
Send tokens in the Authorization: Bearer <token> header over HTTPS — never in the URL (logs, history).

  • SPA on the same domain: prefer HttpOnly, Secure, SameSite cookies (Sanctum SPA auth) — JavaScript can't steal them via XSS.
  • Mobile apps: secure storage (Keychain/Keystore).
  • Short-lived access token + refresh token rotation; revoke on logout.

q: How do you test a Laravel API?
a:
Feature tests with the HTTP helpers:

$this->actingAs($user, 'sanctum')->postJson('/api/orders', $data)
     ->assertCreated()->assertJsonPath('data.total', 150);

Use factories and RefreshDatabase, fake external services (Http::fake(), Queue::fake()), test validation (422), auth (401/403) and edge cases. Pest makes the syntax shorter.

q: How do GraphQL and REST differ in schema, request shape, caching and operational complexity?
a: GraphQL is a query language with one endpoint and a typed schema. The client asks for exactly the fields it needs, including nested relations, in one request. REST: many endpoints, fixed response shapes, can over-fetch or need several calls. GraphQL: flexible, self-documenting, but harder to cache at HTTP level and needs protection against expensive queries.

q: Explain schema, types, queries, mutations, subscriptions and resolvers.
a:
• Schema/types define the data: type Order { id: ID! total: Float! items: [Item!]! }.
  • Query reads, Mutation writes, Subscription pushes live updates (usually over WebSockets).
  • Resolvers are functions that fetch each field's data. The server walks the query and calls resolvers field by field.

q: How does GraphQL's N+1 resolver problem occur, and how does request-scoped DataLoader batching address it?
a: Resolving orders { customer { name } } naively runs one query for orders and one per order for its customer. DataLoader collects all customer IDs requested in the same tick and loads them in one batched query (WHERE id IN (...)), with a per-request cache. In Laravel Lighthouse, @belongsTo/@hasMany directives batch automatically.

q: How would you defend a GraphQL API against excessive query cost, unauthorized field access and data exposure?
a:
• Auth on every resolver/field, not only at the endpoint.
  • Limit query depth and complexity/cost; set max page sizes; timeouts.
  • Disable introspection in production if the API is private; use persisted queries (allow-list) for your own apps.
  • Rate-limit by cost, not just requests. Mask internal errors.

q: How do errors and HTTP status codes work in GraphQL?
a: GraphQL usually returns HTTP 200 even when something fails; errors come in an errors array next to partial data, with path and extensions.code. Good practice: typed error codes (UNAUTHENTICATED, BAD_USER_INPUT), or model expected failures in the schema itself (union CreateOrderResult = Order | ValidationError).

q: How do you build a GraphQL API in Laravel?
a:
The standard package is Lighthouse: write the schema in graphql/schema.graphql and use directives instead of boilerplate:

type Query { orders(status: String @eq): [Order!]! @paginate @guard }

@paginate, @find, @create, @can, @guard, relation directives with batching. Test with the GraphiQL playground and $this->graphQL(...) in tests.

q: Apollo Client vs urql vs React Query for GraphQL on the frontend?
a:
• Apollo Client: full-featured — normalised cache, pagination helpers, optimistic UI, devtools; bigger bundle.
  • urql: lighter, pluggable.
  • TanStack Query + graphql-request: simple request caching without a normalised cache — great when you already use React Query.

Pick based on how much shared cache you need across screens.

q: How does Shopify use GraphQL? What is query cost?
a: Shopify's Admin API and Storefront API are GraphQL-first (REST Admin is legacy). Every query has a calculated cost; you get a bucket of points that refills per second (extensions.cost.throttleStatus). Tips: request only needed fields, use first: limits, bulk operations for large exports, and retry with backoff when throttled.

q: How does pagination work in GraphQL (Relay connections)?
a: The Relay pattern uses cursors: products(first: 20, after: $cursor) { edges { cursor node { id title } } pageInfo { hasNextPage endCursor } }. Pass endCursor back as after to get the next page. It is stable when data changes, and Shopify, GitHub and Lighthouse use it.

q: How do you cache GraphQL responses?
a:
HTTP caching is harder because everything is POST to one URL. Options:

  • Client normalised cache (Apollo) by __typename:id.
  • Persisted queries sent as GET with a hash → CDN-cacheable.
  • Server response/field caching (Redis) with @cache directives, and DataLoader per request.
  • Cache-control hints per type/field.

q: What are GraphQL subscriptions and when would you use them?
a: Subscriptions keep a connection (usually WebSocket, sometimes SSE) and the server pushes results when an event happens: subscription { orderStatusChanged(id: 5) { status } }. Use for live dashboards, chat, notifications. For simple cases polling or plain WebSockets (Laravel Reverb/Echo) may be easier to run and scale.

q: What is JSON and what are its data types?
a: JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) is a text format for data: objects {}, arrays [], strings (double quotes only), numbers, true/false and null. No comments, no trailing commas, no dates (use ISO 8601 strings like 2026-09-25T10:00:00Z), no undefined. It's the default for REST APIs, config and storage.

q: JSON vs XML vs YAML vs Protobuf?
a:
• JSON: compact, native to JS, universal for APIs.
  • XML: verbose, supports attributes/namespaces/schemas — still in SOAP, feeds, legacy integrations.
  • YAML: human-friendly config (Docker Compose, Kubernetes, CI) — indentation-sensitive.
  • Protobuf/MessagePack: binary, smaller and faster, needs a schema — gRPC and high-volume internal traffic.

q: What is JSON Schema and why use it?
a:
JSON Schema describes the expected shape of JSON: required fields, types, formats, enums, min/max.

{"type":"object","required":["email"],"properties":{"email":{"type":"string","format":"email"}}}

Use it to validate API input/output, generate forms and docs (OpenAPI uses it), test contracts, and validate LLM structured outputs. In JS, Zod/Ajv; in PHP, opis/json-schema.

q: What are common pitfalls with json_encode / json_decode in PHP?
a:
• json_decode($s) returns objects; pass true for arrays.
  • Errors are silent by default → use JSON_THROW_ON_ERROR.
  • Unicode is escaped as \u0627; use JSON_UNESCAPED_UNICODE for Urdu/Hindi, and JSON_UNESCAPED_SLASHES.
  • Floats may lose precision; big IDs → send as strings.
  • Invalid UTF-8 makes encoding fail.

q: How do you store and query JSON columns in MySQL with Laravel?
a: MySQL has a native JSON type. In Laravel: $table->json('meta') and protected $casts = ['meta'=>'array']. Query: where('meta->color','red'), whereJsonContains('tags','php'). For frequent filters create a generated column with an index — JSON paths themselves are slow to search. Don't hide core relational data in JSON.

q: How do you parse JSON safely in JavaScript?
a: Wrap JSON.parse in try/catch — invalid input throws. Then validate the shape (Zod, JSON Schema) before trusting it; parsed data is still untrusted. Never use eval. Beware of __proto__ keys when merging parsed objects into others (prototype pollution). Large numbers above 2^53 lose precision — keep them as strings.

q: What is inside a JWT and is it encrypted?
a: A JWT has three Base64URL parts: header (algorithm), payload (claims like sub, exp, roles) and signature. It is signed, not encrypted — anyone can read the payload, so never put secrets in it. The server verifies the signature and exp. Pin the algorithm (reject none), keep tokens short-lived and use refresh tokens.

q: What are JSON:API and HAL?
a: Both are conventions for REST JSON shapes. JSON:API standardises data, attributes, relationships, included, sparse fields and pagination links — clients can be generic. HAL adds _links and _embedded for hypermedia. Using a convention stops endless team debates about response shapes; Laravel has JSON:API packages.

q: How do you handle very large JSON files or responses?
a:
Don't load everything into memory. Stream it:

  • PHP: halaxa/json-machine or cursor/lazy collections to stream rows; response()->streamJson().
  • Node: streaming parsers; NDJSON (one JSON object per line) for logs/exports.
  • APIs: paginate, gzip/brotli compression, field selection.

q: What does JSON.stringify skip, and what are the replacer and space arguments?
a: JSON.stringify drops functions, undefined and Symbols in objects (turns them into null in arrays), converts Dates to ISO strings, and throws on circular references and BigInt. JSON.stringify(obj, ['id','name']) keeps only those keys; a replacer function can transform values; JSON.stringify(obj, null, 2) pretty-prints. Objects can define toJSON().

q: What is a webhook and how is it different from polling?
a: A webhook is an HTTP POST another system sends to your URL when an event happens ("order paid", "product updated"). Polling asks "anything new?" every N seconds — wasteful and delayed. Webhooks are real-time and cheap, but you must expose a public HTTPS endpoint, verify senders, and handle retries/duplicates.

q: How do you verify that a webhook really came from the provider?
a:
Providers sign the raw request body with a shared secret (HMAC-SHA256) and send the signature in a header (Stripe Stripe-Signature, Shopify X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256, GitHub X-Hub-Signature-256).

$calc = base64_encode(hash_hmac('sha256', $request->getContent(), $secret, true));
abort_unless(hash_equals($calc, $request->header('X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256')), 401);

Use the raw body (not re-encoded JSON), hash_equals (timing-safe), and check the timestamp to stop replays.

q: How should a webhook endpoint process events reliably?
a:
1. Verify the signature. 2. Store the event (or push a job) and return 200 fast (within a few seconds). 3. Process in a queue job with retries.

Providers retry on timeouts/5xx, so slow inline processing causes duplicates and disabled webhooks. Log the event ID and payload for debugging and replay.

q: How do you handle duplicate or out-of-order webhook events?
a:
Assume at-least-once delivery.

  • Idempotency: store the provider's event ID with a unique index; skip if already processed.
  • Ordering: don't trust arrival order — compare updated_at/version, or re-fetch the current resource from the API before acting.
  • Make handlers safe to run twice (upserts, state checks).

q: How do Shopify webhooks work?
a: Subscribe to topics (orders/create, products/update, app/uninstalled, GDPR customers/redact...) via the app config/shopify.app.toml or the GraphQL Admin API. Shopify POSTs JSON with X-Shopify-Topic, X-Shopify-Shop-Domain and X-Shopify-Hmac-Sha256. Verify HMAC, respond 200 within 5 seconds, queue the work. Shopify retries and may remove subscriptions after repeated failures. Mandatory compliance webhooks are required for public apps.

q: How do Stripe webhooks fit into a payment flow?
a: Never trust the browser redirect alone. Stripe sends events like payment_intent.succeeded, invoice.paid, charge.refunded. Your webhook verifies the signature with the endpoint secret and updates the order/subscription. Laravel Cashier includes a webhook controller; the Stripe CLI (stripe listen --forward-to) forwards events to localhost for testing.

q: How do webhooks work in WooCommerce and WordPress?
a: WooCommerce › Settings › Advanced › Webhooks: choose a topic (order created/updated, product, customer), delivery URL and secret; it sends X-WC-Webhook-Signature (base64 HMAC-SHA256). Deliveries run through Action Scheduler. For custom events in WordPress, hook into an action (woocommerce_order_status_changed) and call wp_remote_post() — ideally from a scheduled action so the page isn't slowed.

q: How do you test webhooks on your local machine?
a: Expose localhost with a tunnel: ngrok, Cloudflare Tunnel, Expose (Laravel) or the provider's CLI (Stripe CLI, Shopify CLI). Inspect payloads with webhook.site or RequestBin. Save real sample payloads as fixtures and write feature tests that post them with a valid signature.

q: How would you build a webhook delivery system (sending webhooks to your customers)?
a:
• Customers register URLs + subscribed events; generate a secret per endpoint.
  • On an event, write it to an outbox table, then queue a delivery job per endpoint.
  • Sign payloads (HMAC + timestamp), include an event ID, short timeouts.
  • Retry with exponential backoff (e.g. up to 24h), then mark failed/disable and notify.
  • Delivery logs + manual "resend" in a dashboard; rate-limit per endpoint.

q: What security risks do webhook endpoints have?
a:
• Forged requests → verify signatures.
  • Replay attacks → timestamp tolerance + event ID store.
  • DoS → fast 200, queue, rate limits.
  • When *you* send webhooks to user-supplied URLs: SSRF — block private IP ranges and internal hostnames, no redirects to internal addresses.
  • Don't expose sensitive data in payloads; send IDs and let the receiver fetch details.

q: Webhooks vs WebSockets vs Server-Sent Events?
a:
• Webhooks: server-to-server HTTP callbacks for events (payment done).
  • WebSockets: two-way live connection, server ↔ browser (chat, live dashboards).
  • SSE: one-way server → browser stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect (notifications, AI token streaming).

Often combined: a webhook arrives → your backend broadcasts over WebSockets to the user's browser.

q: How do you receive webhooks cleanly in Laravel?
a: Use spatie/laravel-webhook-client: it validates signatures (configurable per provider), stores each call in a webhook_calls table and dispatches a job to process it — giving retries and a replay log for free. Exclude the route from CSRF, keep the controller thin, and alert on repeated processing failures.

q: What is Composer and what does composer.lock do?
a: Composer is PHP's dependency manager. composer.json lists allowed version ranges (^11.0); composer.lock records the exact versions installed. Commit the lock file for apps so every environment installs identical versions: composer install (uses lock) in CI/production, composer update only when you intend to upgrade. PSR-4 autoloading maps namespaces to folders.

q: Sanctum vs Passport — which one do you use?
a: Sanctum: simple API tokens (with abilities) for mobile/3rd-party clients and cookie-based auth for your own SPA. Best for most apps. Passport: a full OAuth2 server — when other companies' apps need "Log in with YourApp", authorization codes, client credentials. Neither is needed for a classic server-rendered app with sessions.

q: What are Laravel Horizon and Telescope?
a: Horizon: dashboard and supervisor for Redis queues — throughput, runtime, failed jobs, retries, auto-balancing workers, configured in code. Telescope: a debug assistant for local/staging — requests, queries (spot N+1), jobs, mails, exceptions, cache hits. Keep Telescope off or restricted in production; use Pulse or an APM there.

q: How do you add roles and permissions? (spatie/laravel-permission)
a:
spatie/laravel-permission stores roles and permissions in tables and integrates with Laravel's Gate:

$user->assignRole('editor'); $role->givePermissionTo('edit posts');
@can('edit posts') ... Route::middleware('permission:edit posts')

Supports guards, teams (multi-tenant) and caching. Combine with Policies for ownership checks ("can edit *this* post").

q: Name the Spatie packages you would use in a typical Laravel project.
a:
• laravel-permission — roles/permissions.
  • laravel-medialibrary — attach files/images to models, conversions, S3.
  • laravel-activitylog — audit trail of model changes.
  • laravel-backup — database + file backups to S3 with notifications.
  • laravel-query-builder — safe filtering/sorting from query strings.
  • laravel-data — typed DTOs; webhook-client/server; laravel-sluggable.

q: What are Laravel Scout, Socialite and Cashier?
a:
• Scout: full-text search on models with drivers for Meilisearch, Typesense, Algolia or the database.
  • Socialite: OAuth login with Google, GitHub, Facebook, etc.
  • Cashier: subscriptions and billing with Stripe (or Paddle) — trials, invoices, webhooks.

All are first-party, so they follow Laravel conventions and upgrades.

q: What is Laravel Octane and when is it worth using?
a: Octane keeps the app booted in memory on Swoole, RoadRunner or FrankenPHP and serves many requests per worker — big throughput gains because Laravel isn't bootstrapped every request. Watch for state leaking between requests: singletons holding request data, static properties, growing arrays. Worth it for high-traffic APIs; for many apps, caching/queries matter more.

q: Which tools keep PHP code quality high?
a:
• PHPUnit / Pest — tests. Larastan / PHPStan (levels 0–10) and Psalm — static analysis catching type bugs before runtime.
  • Laravel Pint / PHP-CS-Fixer — code style. Rector — automated refactors and upgrades.
  • Run them in CI on every pull request, plus composer audit for vulnerable packages.

q: What are Guzzle, Carbon and Monolog?
a:
• Guzzle: the standard PHP HTTP client (Laravel's Http facade wraps it) — retries, timeouts, middleware, async.
  • Carbon: date/time on top of DateTime — now()->addDays(3), timezones, diffForHumans(); use CarbonImmutable to avoid accidental changes.
  • Monolog: logging behind Laravel's Log — channels to files, Slack, stderr, Sentry.

q: What are Laravel Breeze, Jetstream, Filament and Nova?
a:
• Breeze: minimal auth scaffolding (Blade, Livewire or Inertia React/Vue).
  • Jetstream: bigger starter — teams, 2FA, API tokens. (Newer starter kits cover React/Vue/Livewire.)
  • Filament: free, Livewire-based admin panels, forms and tables — very popular.
  • Nova: Laravel's paid admin panel.

For a quick internal admin, Filament is often the fastest route.

q: What is a PSR and which PSRs matter most?
a:
PSRs are PHP-FIG standards so libraries work together:

  • PSR-4 autoloading, PSR-12/PER coding style,
  • PSR-3 logger interface, PSR-7/17/18 HTTP messages and clients,
  • PSR-11 container, PSR-15 middleware, PSR-6/16 caching.

Coding to these interfaces lets you swap implementations (Monolog, Guzzle) easily.

q: npm vs Yarn vs pnpm — and what is package-lock.json?
a: All install packages from the npm registry. pnpm uses a global content store with links — fast and saves disk; Yarn added workspaces and Plug'n'Play. The lock file (package-lock.json, yarn.lock, pnpm-lock.yaml) pins exact versions — commit it and use npm ci in CI. dependencies ship to production; devDependencies are build/test tools. npm audit checks vulnerabilities.

q: What is Vite and why did it replace webpack/Laravel Mix?
a: Vite serves source files as native ES modules in development, so the dev server starts instantly and HMR updates only what changed.
